speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In the first part, I will speak about the overarching thrust of the Budget.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: At last year's Budget, which was titled "Charting our way forward together", the Deputy Prime Minister outlined the Government's approach towards strengthening Singapore's social compact.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Wong reiterated a commitment to further improving social policies, saying that this would be a multi-year agenda to prepare Singapore for the future.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Workers' Party sees this year's Budget as another plank of that multi-year agenda.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This Budget also coincides with the Forward Singapore exercise launched last June.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Forward Singapore exercise is intended to build on the expression "social compact" that was employed at last year's Budget.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My view is that Singapore's social compact must be one where we move forward together as one Singapore to tackle an unpredictable and potentially disruptive future.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We must guard against a split in society, where the rich and the well-off high-earners are pitted against the rest of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To achieve that end, significant work needs to be done.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I say this because one theme that was carried by some outlets, both mainstream and online, was that this year's Budget was, I quote, a "Robin Hood" Budget.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Referring to it as such pits one group, high-earners and the rich, against the lower- and middle-classes.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Aljunied GRC Member of Parliament Leon Perera will speak more on this theme in his Budget speech.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: These are forces that have to be properly managed and it is critical for any Government to make the fight against inequality a central policy agenda and to decisively intervene to lift those at the bottom.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It would be remiss of me to say that the Government has not made moves in this regard.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In his Budget speech for example, Deputy Prime Minister Wong spent time highlighting how disadvantaged children need an early leg-up.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: One Singapore is connected to the world as a hub economy.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It is where high salaries and opportunities abound and where locals and crucially, many foreigners too, power diverse nodes of the economy.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This Singapore gives meaning to the promise and lure of Singapore and how we remain relevant to world.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It is a Singapore that always strives to be at the cutting edge of global developments.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The other Singapore is one where the majority of Singaporeans live.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It is one where there are perceptions of slowing social mobility, connected to the reality of high housing prices.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Today, the prospect of upgrading to a condominium or a landed property, unlike in decades past, is not as realistic for HDB home owners.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Buying a car is an out-of-reach luxury for most people, unlike in many other countries.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I have also heard it summarised this way.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In the past, you may not have done well in school, but if you were prepared to slog and save, you could become rich and successful.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Today, the view is that once you have not succeeded academically, even if you slog for years, success, let alone wealth, may not follow.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: These "two Singapores" could easily become a reality that causes frictions in society.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Singapore is a tiny red dot and both these Singapores would unavoidably rub up against each other.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There is no countryside to retreat to, where the pace is slower and prices of things are lower than in the city.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Human nature and the instincts of envy and chauvinism and a narrative of haves and have-nots can quickly poison society and accentuate cleavages.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: With people living cheek-by-jowl, such views can easily take root and manifest themselves in cruel ways.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As much as the Government endeavours to keep society open and bring new businesses and opportunities to Singapore and Singaporeans for the greater good, it is that second Singapore, where a very broad middle of Singapore lives and works and plays, which should never find itself unmoored and cynical about the future of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There are some Singaporeans within the bureaucracy and they include members of the Executive and other senior civil servants, who are fixated about keeping Singapore relevant to the world, thinking of how to enlarge the pie even as they keep the other eye on making sure the pie does not get smaller.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Their efforts cannot and should not be underestimated or ignored.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And I note also the policies that came through last year, such as hikes in personal income taxes.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In contrast, when some commentators characterise the Budget as a "Robin Hood" budget, they reinforce the perception of "two Singapores" being created.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To combat both the perception as well as the reality in some quarters of "two Singapores" inexorably emerging, redistribution must be at the core of Government policies.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To that extent, the Workers' Party supports the idea of a progressive society, where those who earn more pay proportionally more in taxes.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Equally, we honour the centrality of a strong work ethic even as we are not only empathetic but also sensitive towards the disadvantaged and those who need extra support.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The interventions of the Workers' Party for this debate would be in the spirit of this review of our social compact, envisioning how best society can position itself for an unpredictable and potentially far more disruptive future.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I will now go on to the second part of my speech that will address three specific announcements in the Budget.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In as much as the Budget is titled "Moving forward in a new era", a look back at the past is a useful guidepost for the new policies that are being introduced.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Onto the first point of jobs and specifically equipping and empowering workers through the Jobs-Skills Integrators, the Budget seeks to ensure that training translates into good employment outcomes.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Labour market intermediaries are being developed for two purposes: first, to ensure that training leads to real jobs; and second, to ensure job placement for those who have been properly trained.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: At first glance, the initiative holds much promise as many jobseekers may not have information on what opportunities there are out there, what they should train for or what organisations will need their new skills.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To get a sense of how this initiative might fair, we should look at past efforts in these sectors.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Specifically, the press release noted that the workforce could expect strong support from the Government and that a new skills framework for precision engineering would be launched under SkillsFuture Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In addition, employers and workers would be equipped with insights on career pathways for 13 occupations, job roles, and specifically training programmes.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Professional conversion programmes were also promised to support the reskilling of mid-careerists who were keen to embark on new careers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: When the Government was transiting to ITM 2.0, I asked in this House when the Government's report card on the first ITM would be ready.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Government replied that it was still early days and those details were not available.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We have yet to hear in this House a proper accounting of the success or otherwise of the first ITM.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I hope the Government can provide some details in this regard.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The then-Minister for Manpower Minister Lim Swee Say announced at Budget 2017 that the Ministry of Manpower (MOM), specifically Workforce Singapore (WSG), had roped in two foreign job matching firms, namely Ingeus and Maximus, to help unemployed professionals with their job hunt.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It was reported that Ingeus and Maximus would work on an outcome-based payment model.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In 2019, WSG reported that the two appointed firms had demonstrated an ability to deliver satisfactory placement outcomes, which were comparable to that of NTUC's Employment and Employability Institute (e2i) with more than six in 10 PMET jobseekers finding jobs within two months after tapping on Workforce Singapore and e2i's career matching services.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I note that the new Jobs-Skills Integrators have not been named.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Can the Minister tell us who they are and what KPIs will be used to determine the effectiveness of this latest pilot and which agencies will anchor this initiative?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Can the Government also flesh out the fiscal outlay set aside for the Jobs-Skills Integrators?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Separately, Sengkang GRC Member of Parliament Louis Chua and Hougang SMC Member of Parliament Dennis Tan will speak on the changes to the Working Mother Child Relief.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I wish to add some comments on the extension of paternity leave.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I understand some employers, particularly smaller SMEs, may find greater difficulty in accommodating two further weeks of paternity leave for their staff members because of manpower and operational challenges.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It is a legitimate concern but I hope employers can empathise with the importance of strong families and the lived reality of raising children in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The time dedicated to raising children is in addition to other filial responsibilities such as spending time with our seniors and parents.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is a fact of our Asian culture.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Many parents endeavour to strive hard and chase the pot at the end of that rainbow at the workplace for a better future for our children.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: More paternity leave is certainly welcomed and I hope SMEs make the adjustments necessary to accommodate male employees, just the same way as they do for their female employees with respect to maternity leave.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To better negotiate this transition, employers should review the important mindset shift that the Government has sought to cultivate for some years and that is the hiring of mature workers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: SMEs should adjust and constantly reconsider their HR policies and job scopes to hire seniors permanently, with a view to make up the temporary absences of younger staff not just due to either paternity or maternity leave, but also due to those unplanned days and events where young children fall ill and parents scramble to make alternative plans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, for workers between the ages of 55 to 64, this contribution from the Government pays only up to 3% of wages.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For example, a company that hires a worker who earns $3,000 and is between the ages of 60 and 64, the company would get about $90 for that senior hire.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I believe employers can be given more support to encourage them to hire senior workers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Studies should be carried out to see how the SEC can be increased to better motivate employers to hire seniors.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In view of our rapidly ageing population, has the Government undertaken any studies to consider the fiscal impact of raising the SEC?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There must be an upside for employers as we undertake this cultural shift towards making the workplace more family-friendly.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Notwithstanding the efforts thus far, greater support towards senior employability will open new vistas for our SMEs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Sengkang GRC Member of Parliament Jamus Lim will cover other Budget initiatives for businesses such as the Enterprise Innovation Scheme and advance other important Workers' Party alternatives, whose time we believe have come, such as the Redundancy Insurance.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: One additional point on paternity leave I wish to address is that some have commented that men be excused from their NS duties for the year they are child is born.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Speaking as an NSman, I would be very cautious about moving in this direction.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I would suggest leaving it to unit commanders to determine how best to accommodate the specific requests of their servicemen as they have been doing so for many years already.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If a unit is having a major exercise of conducting a critical operation, the needs of the Singapore Armed Forces (SAF) or the Home Team agencies cannot and should never be compromised.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: CPF rates and income ceilings have been used as a macroeconomic counter-cyclical tool in decades past to combat recession, help employers save jobs and the prospect of slower economic growth.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Finance Minister stated that the salary ceiling was last raised in 2016.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: While this is correct, it should be noted that the salary ceiling of $6,000 was first put in place in 1985.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In response to economic uncertainty, it was reduced to $5,500 in 2004 and further reduced to $4,500 in 2006 before re-establishing itself at the 1985 of $6,000 only some 30 years later in 2016.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There is much catching up to do with respect to retirement adequacy, particularly since so much of our CPF funds are dedicated to housing.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, I have a few questions for the Deputy Prime Minister.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: First, in view of the policy reason for this new salary ceiling which is to allow Singaporeans to save more for retirement, I am of the view that it would have been appropriate to simultaneously reconsider the percentage of CPF funds credited into the three CPF accounts with a higher proportion allocated to the Special Account.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For example, currently out of 37% of total wages for a member aged 35 and below, 23% of the CPF contributions is allocated to the Ordinary Account.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The contribution to a member's Ordinary Account drops to 21% when the member turns 36 years of age and is gradually reduced in five-year intervals to reach only 12% when a member returns 56.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In contrast, contributions to the Special Account increased from 6% to 7% when a member turns 36 years of age and peaks at 11.5% between the ages of 50 and 55.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The CPF system after all is designed primarily for our retirement needs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: On this point, Mr Speaker, numerous studies have been conducted on the income replacement rate, or IRRs of pension funds worldwide.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The IRR is the ratio of retirement income to pre-retirement income.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The World Bank recommends that countries should aim for an IRR of 53% of net final year wages or 78% of net average lifetime wages.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For many, their CPF LIFE payouts are unlikely to meet this threshold since much of our CPF funds are locked up in housing.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Deputy Prime Minister stated that the Government was considering what more can be done to enhance retirement adequacy in its Forward Singapore deliberations.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The decline in retirement adequacy in the past was mitigated by the appreciation of home values.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, the Government has also stated that housing is unlikely to see steep rises in value as in the past.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Government should begin a deep conversation to re-centre the CPF system towards its original purpose, especially as the cycles of job disruption, job redesign and job obsolescence become more pronounced and frequent in the face of rapid technological advancement.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There have been suggestions made most recently by former Nominated Member of Parliament Walter Theseira to reduce the usage of CPF funds for home purchases.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This call was met by consternation from the public because of the already high prices and the reduced affordability of housing.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, achieving better retirement adequacy would require a hard look at how much the CPF system dedicates towards home ownership.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: More affordable public housing will inevitably improve retirement adequacy.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This leads me to the next part of my speech – the announcement that CPF grants will be increased, which is for the ostensible purpose of making resale flats more affordable for first-timers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Some 10 days later, the Leader of the House was quoted in The Straits Times saying, "but I think in the longer term, we are looking to see how we can make housing more accessible and affordable".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Almost immediately, there were concerns about the impact of such measures on house prices by property watchers, especially for larger flats and those in popular areas.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: While these additional grants may appear on the surface to be a panacea, there is a real prospect of home prices rising to match the new grants for eligible first-timers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This could happen as a response to the increase in grants.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But more likely, price rises could happen because buyers will be tempted to bid more for a flat they want because they know they have the additional grant to enhance the price they can pay.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Aljunied Group Representation Constituency (GRC) Member of Parliament, Gerald Giam will further elaborate on the affordability of resale flats in his speech.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: More fundamentally in line with the renewal of the social compact through Forward Singapore, would the Deputy Prime Minister share more details on the differences between the valuation of land for public and private use?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I asked some questions about this recently in this House and asked if the establishment of a committee akin to the Land Working Group of the Economic Review Committee of 2002, but one that would include Ministry of National Development (MND) and Housing Development Board (HDB) to review the principles of how land is sold for public housing would be something the Government would consider.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Specifically, I also call for an understanding of the principles and rationale behind the market discount of up to 15% of land allocated for Government land sales and industrial Government land sales and the sale of some private land even below this market price threshold.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In addition, I enquired how such sales of private land below market valuation intersected with the Government's call that HDB land not sold at market valuation would amount to a raiding of the reserves.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Government should reply to these questions which are asked with a view to considering alternative approaches the valuing of land for 99-year leasehold public housing.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: These are questions that members of the public are interested in, particularly since the details and principles of this subject have not been significantly ventilated in public.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To illustrate the public interest in this matter, on 11 February, Gov.sg released a set of infographics on Telegram.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The lead slide was titled "Does disregarding land cost mean BTO flats will be cheaper?" The second last slide put across the Government's narrative as follows: "Selling land below fair market value = eroding reserves.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This diminishes resources available for you and your children." As of 21 February, 176 individuals gave the post the thumbs up while a far larger 553 individuals chose the emoji which I would describe as showing they were not being convinced.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In the spirit of refreshing our social compact, I renew my call for the Government to also release the price of land for specific public housing, projects and their associated subsidies on a BTO project basis, so that Singaporeans can more meaningfully engage the Government in the course of the Forward Singapore exercise.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Before I round up, I mentioned in the first part of my speech that the Budget titled "Moving Forward in a New Era", would find the past to be an important reference point.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The release of an occasional paper by the Ministry of Finance earlier this month on medium-term fiscal projections has been helpful to the extent that it responds to the calls by the Workers' Party at the last Budget for additional details on medium-term projections.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Singaporeans would recall that this was a call that had been made even earlier when the Goods and Services Tax hike was first mooted.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Sengkang GRC Member of Parliament Louis Chua will speak more about BEPS and share his analysis of the Budget in his speech.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The perception of two Singapores that we must guard against which I raised earlier in my speech reinforces the point that fiscal redistribution, better social protections and greater support for our most vulnerable Singaporeans must remain a mainstay of our future budgets.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It is imperative that policies should be continually refreshed and reviewed, including the applicability of the principles they were originally based on.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Singapore, a young country, where Singaporeans feel, live and experience the emotions of nationalism and citizenship must continue to thrive in a fair, broad and balanced way, so that we leave a better future for today's generation and those that come after.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I will first speak on the "give and take" part and thereafter, on Singapore's longer-term positioning in the new era.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The various support measures have been thoughtfully formulated with significant cash component and targeted assistances towards essential cost items like electricity, Service & Conservancy Charges (S&CC), medical and education.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: For the businesses, the Enterprise Financing Scheme and the Energy Efficiency Grant are extended to help companies weather the immediate challenges of tighter financial conditions and higher energy prices.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: This Budget also enhances various measures to support Singaporeans at various stages in life and in various circumstances.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I welcome the further measures to help first-time home buyers improved chances of owning Build-To-Order (BTO) flats with the additional ballots as well as the higher CPF Housing Grant to help first-time home buyers purchase resale flats as another option.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In my conversation with young parents, many told me that while they cherish the joy and fulfilment of being a parent, they are often worried about the costs of raising their children.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Understandably, we all want the best for our kids.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Currently, there are already a generous set of support package such as the Baby Bonus Scheme, preschool and education subsidies to support parenthood as well as the various tax benefits.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: But every bit of additional help the Government can give to our young parents would be most appreciated.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Middle-income group parents will see some cash impact with the WMCR no longer pegged to a percentage of income.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: On the seniors' front, we can expect the healthcare needs to increase in the years ahead.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I am already seeing these increases in my constituency at Bukit Panjang, where there are more requests to help pay for healthcare related and hospital expenses.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: These are the funds that we often tapped to help our senior residents meet their ageing related expenses.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The extension of Senior Employment Credit (SEC) and Part-time Re-employment Grant are helpful support to enhance seniors' employability, while the increased co-funding share for Progressive Wage Credit Scheme, Enabling Employment Credit and the Uplifting Employment Credit are meaningful additions to support the more vulnerable segments of our society.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: These moves, among others, are part of the overall effort to build a stronger social compact and a more compassionate society.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Budget 2023 outline some policy adjustments that would have some impact to Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The 15% increase in tobacco tax would add costs to smokers, of course, but I hope that it would help discourage the overall consumption in tobacco products.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: While they appreciate the good intention of Government to improve protection and retirement adequacy, they are also very concerned on how the changes to CPF contributions and other implementations would impact the viability of the delivery business and eventually their livelihoods.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, I would appeal to the Government, to not only provide transitional support to these workers but also dedicate resources to help with the reskilling and re-employment should their livelihoods be impacted.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We will await more details on the transitional support in the MOM COS debate.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: One other measure that I have also heard concerns is the phased increase of the CPF monthly ceiling to $8,000.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: While I can understand and support the rationale for the raise, I hope that the Government can review the implementation timing of this measure.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Beyond about how we slice the pie and who gets what, budgets must also be about how can we grow the pie bigger.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: And here we must not lose sight on the need to grow our economy.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: A growing and vibrant economy not only create good jobs; which is the best welfare for workers and best counter against inflation, but growing the economy also generate revenues to pay for our needs and wants.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The troubling external environment has made growing our economy an even more uphill task.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The US-China strategic competition continues to intensify and more countries are taking steps to shore up their economic security, through policies to safeguard strategically important technologies and data.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We have also seen countries attempting to decouple in areas of trade, technology, finance, investments and people flows.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The US has introduced the US Chips and Science Act while China has also implemented the China Export Control Law, just so that they reduce their vulnerabilities and dependence on other countries.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The original intent is meant to finance sustainable transition in America.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: However, it now appears more like a state-funded industrial policy plan.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The Act has trigger EU and other countries to call for their own policy response measures to rebalance the playing field.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: These developments will have profound implications how Economic Development Board (EDB) and our agencies attract direct investments into Singapore.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Against this increasingly complex and volatile operating environment, Singapore is also running up against serious resource constraints among others – our ageing resident workforce and rising wage aspirations, carbon constraints and longer-term fiscal constraints.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The growing pain question is: how can we continue to grow in a setting of an almost full-employment economy?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Economically, we are not only in full employment of our domestic economic inputs.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We are leveraging on significant pool of foreign labour to stretch our overall growth potential; which brings to my next point on economic competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: How do we stay competitive in this daunting external and domestic landscape?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Business costs have risen significantly in the last two years.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Though much of it are externally induced such as the rising prices of energy and materials imports, we do increasingly face domestically driven costs pressures.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Rising wages, escalating rentals, higher financing costs, impending higher carbon taxes, among others, would have the overall effect of diminishing our economic competitiveness vi-a-vis our competitors and negating the favourable economic attributes that we have.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Therefore, we need an even sharper prioritisation in the allocation of our resources going forward and to pace our policy initiatives roll-out so that it would not add further constraints and tightness in our resource utilisation.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In other words, we must pick the battles that play to our strength.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The Deputy Prime Minister and Finance Minister spoke about redoubling our efforts to attract high quality investments and to focus on growth sectors that we can be highly competitive, such as finance, transportation, logistics and advanced manufacturing.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: But, ultimately, to overcome our inherent resource constraint, we need to significantly beef up productivity as an economic system.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: While we continue to work on upskilling our workforce, the productivity of work is not solely dependent on workers.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: A company's overall productivity to a large extent depended on management, how resources and workflows are designed and organised, harnessing the use of data, technology, innovation and creativity to invigorate efficient solutions.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We need a more ecosystem approach to rev up productivity and I hope that the ITMs that we have set up can galvanise industry stakeholders to work productively towards this cause.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The Jobs-Skills Integrators is a refreshing approach to tackle stubborn jobs-workers mismatches.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: This is akin to having relationship managers bridging the information and connectivity gap between employers and jobseekers.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, I applaud the Government for getting down to the micro level to close the gap.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It shows the Government's resolve and commitment to improve employability of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I look forward to more positive outcomes in this endeavour.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The COVID-19 pandemic and the effects of the war in Ukraine further underscored the critical importance of being resilient against external shocks, catastrophic events, or a devastating crisis.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: During the pandemic, we experienced various supply disruptions, including sudden export restrictions on essential items by countries.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The economic blockade on Qatar by its neighbours in 2017 is another reference point.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: With land, air and sea lanes cut off by its neighbours, the population in Qatar were immediately hard hit by rising food prices and job insecurity.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It had to quickly find alternative sources of supplies and to also boost domestic food production.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Singapore has always taken the mindset that there will be a crisis around the corner waiting for us, whether it is the stockpile of food and various essential materials or our Four National Tap strategy for water or our Four National Switches strategy for energy, Singapore will always plan for various scenarios, invest in total defence and be operationally ready for any emergencies.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The war in Ukraine has triggered a major energy crisis in Europe with countries like Germany which heavily depended on Russia for piped gas for their electricity generation, among those most impacted.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: And this has led to a major scramble to build LNG terminals to import liquified natural gas to replace the lost supplies from Russia.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Fortunately, in Singapore, our LNG terminal was built more than a decade ago at Jurong Island.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It allows us to import natural gas from just about anywhere in the world and not having to depend solely on piped gas.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: This terminal has not only contributed to our energy security.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It has also enabled us to be a major player in the LNG market and help position Singapore as a LNG hub for the region.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, credit goes to Ministry of Trade and Industry (MTI) and Energy Market Authority (EMA) for the foresight and their will to press on with this massive project.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I believe Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong was the Chief Executive of EMA then and got the project off the ground.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: There are many more strategic projects that are needed to be built to strengthen resilience, to reduce our vulnerabilities – infrastructures, such as climate adaptation, energy diversification, food security and so on, which is why we need to continually strengthen our finances and not the other way round.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Healthcare, education, wage subsidies, security and other social spending are the expected key drivers.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Even in the non-operating expenditure areas, there are also a long list of infrastructural spending items, whether it is investment for capabilities building or for building a more resilient home.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We also need to keep the powder dry, so as to have the fiscal firepower to respond to external shocks or major disruptions which is likely to happen more often, in my view, going forward, and can be even more impactful than the pandemic that we have experienced.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, we cannot afford to decumulate or stop building our reserves.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Sound, prudent and fiscal management today will enhance our survivability, give us the safety cover when needed and importantly, position us strongly to seize the opportunities in the new era.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This is after three long years of restrictions, shielded by extraordinary Budget measures.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Even as Singaporeans return to their lives they were accustomed to, the effects of the pandemic coupled with the Ukraine war, has left the Government dealing with the significant inflationary pressures in a more fragmented world.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We are debating Budget 2023 one year after Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong was endorsed as the leader of Singapore's fourth generation (4G) political leadership.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: So, this Budget sets the tone for the years to come.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I am heartened by the Government's decisive moves to address Singaporeans' needs and aspirations.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: These include a slew of pro-family initiatives, coupled with generous support to cushion cost of living pressures and measures to bolster retirement adequacy.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Budget 2023 will give Singapore's social compact a significant boost.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: But amidst all this good news on continuing support for Singaporeans, Deputy Prime Minister Wong did not shy away from warning us about the sustainability of such Government support.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: In fact, some economists have cautioned that Government handouts, such as GST Vouchers and our cost of living support measures may increase demand and further stoke inflation pressures.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This is because redistribution is only possible if the economy continues to grow so that benefits of the growing pie from healthy tax revenues can be shared.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Singapore's continued growth in the new era of global development is not guaranteed.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: It is predicated on our ability to navigate the volatile and uncertain operating environment to steward industries, enterprises and our workers toward long-term, sustainable growth.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: To employers, especially our SMEs, these Budget measures, such as the raised CPF monthly salary ceiling and the doubling of paternity leave, are like adding fuel to the fire.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Even before they have had the chance to fully digest impact of earlier moves, such as cost increases associated with Progressive Wage Model and CPF contribution rate for older workers, employers feel overwhelmed by another flood of pro-worker initiatives.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The war on talent is increasingly a world-wide phenomenon.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We have seen moves made by other countries, such as UK's Global Talent Visa and Hong Kong's Top Talent Pass Scheme, designed to attract talent from around the world.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Even China, who has traditionally thrived on their pool of over 300 million migrant workers to maintain their reputation as the "Factory of the World", now struggles to attract workers back to their big factory hubs.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: So, employers must accept that the tight labour market is here to stay.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: They must embrace this new normal where the balance of power has shifted from employers to employees.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: They must up their game in offering compelling value proposition to attract and retain staff, rewarding them fairly, engaging them skillfully and investing vigorously in their capability development.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong announced the introduction of Jobs-Skills Integrators to further strengthen the SkillsFuture ecosystem.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We need to urgently shift to a higher gear in order to make training truly count.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The task of linking workers' training to securing good jobs is a huge challenge.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This requires fundamental changes in how the current lifelong learning ecosystem is set out and governed.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This is an area where strong Government intervention is needed, in the setting of standards, the rallying of stakeholders and the provision of resources beyond the simple training subsidies.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Evidently, Deputy Prime Minister has set his sights squarely on fixing this, and I look forward to understanding Government's plan to take SkillsFuture forward in the upcoming Ministry of Education (MOE) Committee of Supply (COS) debate.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We have historically leveraged tax incentives to encourage multi-national enterprises (MNEs) to place high value functions in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: BEPS 2.0 will impede Singapore's use of tax incentives to attract new investments, requiring us to compete on other capabilities to anchor quality investments.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The question is whether such moves will be sufficient to attract business investment into Singapore during this period of global change.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Other countries, such as US and China, are rolling out vast subsidies to build up their strategic industries.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Countries in the region are also strengthening their competitive positioning with respect to costs, manpower and energy.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The transition to a low-carbon future will also present significant challenges given Singapore's inherent limitations in energy resources.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: So, Sir, there is no shortage of support schemes to help companies based in Singapore build capabilities and invest in innovation.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: MNEs who operate across jurisdictions understand the attractiveness of our schemes and are well-positioned to take full advantage of the benefits the schemes offer.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We have also nurtured a vibrant start-up ecosystem in Singapore, including a cohort of Singapore-based unicorn startups with valuation exceeding US$1 billion.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: But more can be done to help our SMEs leverage public R&D and innovation capabilities to build new products and solutions.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This will require a closer nexus to be drawn between them and our public research institutes and Institutes of Higher Learning.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Catalysing high-impact research and translating them into enterprising innovations that benefit industry and society, should be a prioritised KPI when granting research funds.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Sector-based innovation roadmaps and solutions are the way to go, in nurturing an innovative SME ecosystem.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Our trust quotient has now been further strengthened by the way in which we navigated the pandemic.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Investors value our open economy, as well as the safety, reliability and transparency that the Singapore system accords them.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: With MNEs building resilience to secure their supply chains post COVID-19, we must leverage our trust premium to seize the re-shoring opportunities.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We should also fully leverage this window of opportunity to expand key sectors such as finance, services, logistics and transport and manufacturing to leap forward.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This is funded entirely from stronger than expected revenues.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Rather than record a surplus, the Government acted nimbly and tapped into its fiscal space to help people cope with inflation.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This I would like to ask the Deputy Prime Minister to share the reasons behind the top-ups and how this may impact Singapore fiscal space in the years to come.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The projections have not factored in future policy moves such as additional spending to further strengthen our social compact and economic competitiveness.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: It is clear that the Government will need to continue to review and adjust its fiscal strategies.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: On other areas worthy of review include a lift in gambling and alcohol taxes, as well as introducing tax on sugar.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Lastly, we need the fiscal buffer to give ourselves enough capacity to deal with future shocks, including black swan events like the COVID-19 pandemic, as mentioned by my hon Member, Mr Liang Eng Hwa.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, we are not sure whether more of the same short-term ad-hoc financial assistance will strengthen the resilience of Singaporeans and help them move forward in a new era.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The dozens of short-term handouts, like CDC vouchers, Assurance payouts, our Cost-of-Living Special Payment, Public Transport vouchers, and so on, are more likely to breed dependency – "what is in it for me?" – but unlikely to strengthen resilience.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We have said many times in this Parliament, that we need long-term programmes to give Singaporeans Comfort over their current and future financial positions.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Before they can concentrate on becoming Innovative workers and enterprising risk-takers to build Singapore into a competitive information economy.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We do not understand why the Government is reluctant to implement long-term programmes.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Although, according to our estimates, Singapore has sufficient fiscal resources to fund these programmes without drawing on the national reserves.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government likes to argue that alternative policy proposals will raid the reserves.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But Singaporeans should note that this is a baseless allegation.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singaporean should have guessed, from the COVID-19 experience, how large our reserves are and how strong our fiscal position is.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If we do not have that, the Government would not be able to commit to a $100 billion COVID-19 response package, which is equal to more than 20% of Singapore's GDP in 2019.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But the interesting part is how the Government has funded it.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This translates into an annualised amount of about $18.7 billion a year.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This amount is roughly equal to the Net Investment Return Contribution (NIRC) allocated to the Budget each year.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is proof that the NIRC has always been a slack in the Budget, which is normally not used to benefit Singaporeans in the year it was allocated.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government has argued that the NIRC is pooled with the rest of the budgetary resources and used for other purposes.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But by setting aside a sum of money almost equal to the NIRC in trust funds and endowment funds.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is equivalent to not spending the NIRC in the current year.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In fact, there may be more slack in the Budget because we cannot understand why the total expenditure has stubbornly stuck at the $100-billion level in 2023.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The total expenditure was only $75 billion in 2019, the year before the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It shot up to $100 billion from 2020, presumably for fighting COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Hence, we have expected the expenditure to drop significantly in 2023 as we wind down the exceptional COVID-19 expenditures.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We look forward to the Deputy Prime Minister explaining with specific figures why the total expenditure has not come down.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, even ignoring the potential spending cuts, it is quite safe to say that we have excess fiscal resources each year, mainly from the NIRC, which can be deployed more proactively for the benefit of low-income and middle-income Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Progress Singapore Party (PSP) has always been confident that we have excess fiscal resources from the NIRC and other potential spending cuts.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: That is the reason why we have argued during the Budget 2022 debate, that there was absolutely no necessity to increase the GST and other taxes to increase revenue.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This year, PSP will present an alternative Budget with long-term programmes to give Singaporeans an idea how our budget can be restructured to better strengthen their financial security.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: First, the alternative Budget will implement the Affordable Homes Scheme and Millennial Apartments Scheme to reset the public housing policy.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is a single most-important long-term structural programme that will boost the financial security of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In Budget 2023, the Government has increased the CPF Housing Grant to help young Singaporeans buy resale flats.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While we agree that young Singaporeans need help with affordable housing, the CPF grant may not be the best solution because it will further inflate the resale market.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This will necessitate higher CPF grants in the next round and the cycle will repeat itself.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In order to get out of this vicious cycle, we need a more fundamental solution and PSP has proposed the Affordable Homes Scheme and the Millennial Apartments Scheme as one policy option.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: With the schemes, every Singaporean in each generation will enjoy an affordable HDB flat to start a family, without sacrificing his retirement in the future.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, we do not understand why the Government said such schemes would negatively affect the future generation.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To counter other narratives that the Government is spreading, we would also like to reiterate that the schemes will not cause a sharp fall in resale prices because the demand and supply situation remains tight and the Affordable Homes sellers will need to sell above current resale prices in order to earn a profit.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On the other hand, Singaporeans who want to sell their flats after the Minimum Occupation Period need not worry about paying a big clawback because the breakeven price for a seller will be roughly the same whether under the current BTO scheme or the Affordable Homes Scheme.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Although land cost is waived for Singaporeans who live in HDB flats for their entire lives, most Singaporeans aspire to upgrade and about half to two thirds of the deferred land cost will be paid to the reserves eventually.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the alternative Budget, we have budgeted $2 billion a year from the excess fiscal resources to reflect the upfront investment cost.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Second, the alternative Budget will promote the financial security of middle-class Singaporeans as a priority.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is the decline of the middle class that has given rise to the "two Singapores" that the Leader of the Opposition has described just now.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While the middle class may not be a homogenous group, it stretches roughly from the 20th percentile to the 80th percentile income brackets and is the group targeted by the Government for spreading the tax burden over as wide a spectrum of the population as possible.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In contrast, the top 10% income bracket is doing well because Singapore's tax regime favours them and the bottom 20% do not pay taxes.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is not wrong as a fiscal principle to spread the tax burden as widely as possible.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, middle-class Singaporeans are already overtaxed relative to their income.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Personal income may be low but there is a whole range of indirect taxes they pay: the GST, high housing prices, stamp duties, MediShield and CareShield premiums, COE, ERP, ARF, foreign domestic worker levy and so on.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: During Budget 2022, besides the GST, we have spoken out against the property tax increase which affected middle-class Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This year, the stamp duty and ARF increases will affect them again.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The stamp duty increase will be limited to properties that are worth more than $3 billion and the ARF increase will be limited to cars with Open Market Value (OMV) of more than $60,000.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP believes if tax increases are really necessary, they should be targeted at wealthy individuals and corporates.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP would also budget $4 billion for the nationalisation of the MediShield and CareShield schemes, which we first recommended during Budget 2021.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This will relieve, especially middle-class and senior Singaporeans, of the anxiety over ever rising healthcare insurance premiums.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: After the HDB flat, healthcare expense is the largest drain on the CPF savings of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While we should maintain the MediSave Account for Singaporeans to share in their healthcare expenses to prevent over-consumption, the existence of multiple healthcare insurance schemes has added unnecessary costs and complications to the healthcare system.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: By taking over the whole healthcare insurance, we hope the Government will be in a better position to develop an optimal healthcare system together with the new Healthier SG initiative.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Third, PSP is very concerned about the job security and job prospects of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government should always be mindful that Singaporeans are disadvantaged when competing with Employment Pass (EP) holders who are exempted from CPF contributions.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While we welcome the move to increase the contribution cap to $8,000 to boost retirement adequacy, it will exacerbate the disadvantaged position of the Singaporean PMEs relate to the EP holders.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This EP levy is estimated to generate additional revenue of $2 billion to $3 billion, which will add to our excess fiscal resources.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In Budget 2023, there is one positive change in the Government's approach, which is the Jobs-Skills Integrator programme.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We have always been skeptical about the nearly $1 billion of annual spending on SkillsFuture and all the other spending on retraining and placements of Singaporeans who have lost their jobs, because it is unrealistic to expect all Singaporeans who have been displaced by foreign PMETs to acquire totally new skills and join new sectors.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should have focused our spending on training Singaporeans to acquire skills that help them to hold on to their existing jobs or find jobs in fields with similar required core competencies.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A good manpower policy is one that will not allow the displacement of Singaporeans from the job market.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Fourth, PSP will increase the amount of compassionate spending for low-skilled workers and disadvantaged segments of our society.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP proposes budgeting $3 billion for a living wage, which guarantees a minimum monthly take-home pay of $1,800 for all Singaporean workers.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The living wage will allow all Singaporean workers to attain the minimum standard of living.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Progressive Wage Model can remain but for helping workers to achieve a higher wage level than the living wage.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP has proposed an alternative Budget to demonstrate how the Budget can be restructured to deploy these resources.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I invite Singaporeans to be the judge of the merits of the proposals in the alternative Budget.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong delivered his Budget 2023 speech in this Chamber, one day after Singapore declared DORSCON Green.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I had goosebumps just thinking about how blessed we have been to have emerged from the COVID-19 pandemic and is in a reasonably good shape.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I am grateful to everyone – from President Halimah and the Presidential Advisory Council to Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong and his Cabinet Ministers, from the Multi-Ministry Task Force to the hon Members of this House, from our healthcare workers to our public transport workers, from our Police officers and Civil Defence Force to our SAF and diplomatic corps, from our locals to the migrants at the front lines – for leading us through the darkest nights of the COVID-19 pandemic to emerge on 13 February with a bright DORSCON Green and a future full of hope.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: A big thank you from all of us in the business community to all of you.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The Government is clearly moving away from giving handouts to survive COVID-19 to a Budget that invests to build for growth, sustainability and resilience.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time, it is apparent that the Government is mindful of the current business climate driven by high cost pressures, with inflation at a 14-year high level, fuelled by the Russia-Ukraine war, the US-China geopolitical tensions and the hangover of supply chain disruptions caused by COVID-19.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Budget 2023 has been hailed as a redistributive Budget.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Those who have more contribute more but everyone contributes what they can and together, we leave no Singaporean behind.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I am glad to see a Budget that appears to have taken an integral development approach that ensures that our people, our environment and our economy progress in tandem and in harmony.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Whether Budget 2023 delivers on its design now depends on how well Team Singapore executes together.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: For my speech today, let me start with the business lens on Budget 2023, with data points based on the latest National Business Survey 2022/2023.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Despite expecting inflationary pressures to persist, 80% of our businesses remain confident in the resiliency of their operations in the next 12 months.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: These measures will help businesses cope with the unusually high business costs.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Meanwhile, cash flow too is a major challenge for SMEs, and it will be of much help if the Government can take the lead to pay all invoices within 14 days, albeit electronically of course.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: This could perhaps even be the impetus needed for the nation-wide e-invoicing initiative to take off.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: As for manpower challenges, 96% of our businesses identified the following as key areas of concern: one, rising manpower cost; two, attracting and/or retaining younger workers; three, new foreign manpower policies that raises cost; four, limited pool of local high-skilled labour; and five, stricter policies that restrict the supply of foreign workers.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Finding sufficient and appropriate manpower to meet their business needs has been a key challenge for our businesses.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The new Jobs-Skills Integrators programme should help optimise training and job placements for Singapore businesses and help workers identify the right fit for training and ensure better earnings prospects.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The Government might want to consider the TACs and the IHLs in partnership with human capital experts to perform this role.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Employment support is another key feature of Budget 2023.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: This will help make inclusive workforce closer to reality.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Our older workers, vulnerable jobseekers like the physically disabled and the ex-offenders as well as current platform workers are resources who may be tapped and reskilled to work in sectors facing labour shortage.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: There is definitely a need to channel workers into jobs that are growing or into jobs that are being transformed.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Community initiatives like Yellow Ribbon and SBF Foundation’s Employability Fund and so on, complement what the Government is doing and should be encouraged.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: For example, SBF Foundation has set up a platform in partnership with social services agencies like New Hope, Daughters of Tomorrow, Singapore Association for Mental Health and SHINE Children and Youth Services to connect enlightened and compassionate companies with vulnerable jobseekers and journey with them from resume writing to onboarding to retention.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: To date, there are about 100 companies who are part of this network and we hope more will be inspired to come forward.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: This is the many helping hands approach in Singapore that will enhance employability and give vulnerable individuals dignity and hope through employment.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Lifting the wages of our low wage workers via the Progressive Wage Model is one of the most important policies that this House and collectively as a society we have made.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: It is good to see that our income inequality, as measured by the Gini coefficient, has been steadily declining.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Kudos to the Tripartite partners for doing what we all know is the right thing to do.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Of course, many opinions have been heard in this Chamber with regard to Singapore having too many foreign workers.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: And, yet we have our businesses screaming “workers not enough”.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Our businesses probably are experiencing “cold turkey” with the new foreign labour policies.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, from the many dialogues and engagements with businesses, it just might be that we simply do not have enough Singaporeans to do the jobs that need to be done.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: One, more perhaps need to be done to attract local Singaporeans into job roles at or higher than the S Pass and the EP qualifying salary levels.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: And if there are no takers, we need to understand why.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Two, perhaps the work environment and work conditions can be made more attractive to interest our local Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: For example, the jobs being enabled by productivity tools, a maximum number of work hours per day, flexible work arrangement, strong skills and career mentoring.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: If all done well, this could drive improved human capital productivity for the organisation and provide a more effective work-life health for our workers.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Three, tripartite partners will have to find the right balance between capital and local and foreign labour for their sector, and perhaps some re-balancing of foreign quota may need to be worked out.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Next, allow me to share the story of Singapore Polytechnic undergraduate, Ms Reis Lim who is taking the Industry Now Curriculum in Perfumery, a diploma with up to half of the polytechnic workload over three years made up of work-based training with industry partners, including internships.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Reis interned at Senses International, a Singapore-based fragrance manufacturer, acquiring deeper skills in fragrance evaluation.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Her outstanding performance led to her being offered a position even before graduation as a fragrance evaluator trainee, a position that is mostly filled by expats.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I am telling this story to encourage companies to tap on the polytechnic and ITE students as a valuable skilled pool of resources, right from even when they are still in the IHLs.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: There needs to be a re-think of the pathways to a career, one of the most important being the alignment of jobs to skills and pay for value.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: More than half of the businesses agree that transformation is very important.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: However, when it comes to R&D and innovation, more than half of the CEOs rated this as “unimportant or only somewhat important”.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: As for sustainability, 75% of our SMEs and 54% of our large companies are “not prepared at all or only somewhat prepared” for transitioning to low carbon.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: SMEs that are slow to adopt sound sustainable practices will eventually lose out on business opportunities.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: There is an urgent need to support the acceleration of SME participation in the green economy.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps the Government can consider a one-off top-up of the PSG specifically for the adoption of sustainability solutions and tools and do some risk-sharing to improve SMEs' access to sustainable financing.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Budget 2023’s highlight for me is the new Enterprise Innovation Scheme.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Forwarding thinking companies know that innovation is key to creating new value.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore companies, especially SMEs, should and must definitely leverage this scheme.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Next, SMEs need capital and talent, access and networks.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: What is the process of application and criteria for selection to be considered for such capital funding?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: To wrap up this section, let me share a quote from fellow SBF Council Member, Ms Kwee Wei-Lin, who is also President of Singapore Hotel Associations, and I quote: “Budget 2023 is a balanced and fair budget and we are glad to see the continued support from the Government in encouraging innovation and productivity, and the support for having a more inclusive workforce.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: However, the additional CPF contribution will further add to the escalating business costs”.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: One final feedback from the industry is that Budget 2023 is lacking on measures to support internationalisation.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: For my remaining time, I will share my reflections on Budget 2023 beyond the business lens.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I can also see that it is a budget that support families, encourage marriage and childbirth.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: It is also about tackling the related issues of inequality and social mobility, and providing better care for our rapidly ageing population.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: These expenditures need to be funded responsibly and Singapore’s approach of keeping our overall system of taxes and benefits fair and progressive is the right thing to do.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Our reserves have proven to be our greatest insurance.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: We have our generations of leaders to thank for their prudence and their stewardship in having shored up the reserves we have today.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore has been blessed in so many ways and if I have to name one, it would be the founding father of modern Singapore, Mr Lee Kuan Yew.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: There are probably many places which have similar geographic advantages like Singapore but it took a visionary, passionate and courageous leader like Mr Lee Kuan Yew, together with the Pioneer Generation of leaders, to make what many would see only as a large rock in treacherous waters, a mere fishing village and outpost for the British, into who we are today – a Singapore that is admired by many, a Singapore that you and I can be proud to call “Home”.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Had Mr Lee Kuan Yew been still alive, he would turn 100 on 16 September 2023.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I for one, look forward to paying tribute to his contributions to Singapore and celebrating the memories, legacy and wisdom of this great man.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Notwithstanding the good place that we are in today, there are a couple of challenges that we face in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: And I ask you to indulge me as I share my thoughts on three points.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The first point, I have said it during the recent Motion on housing and I thought it important to raise this here again.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: While we do want Singapore to be one of the top global financial hubs, how can we prevent and limit our risk of being in that same situation?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Tech can do a lot of good for society and has contributed much and its impact will be even more pervasive.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: But we have also seen the harms that tech can bring about, whether it is online scams, online bullying, unethical artificial intelligence – and the list goes on.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: We have debated in this House on this very issue, and bills have been passed to safeguard our people and our businesses from potential ills.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: But by the time the laws have to be called into play, it is already too far downstream.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I am encouraged and proud that Singapore was the first country who tabled at WEF, the Governance Framework for Ethical AI, a couple of years back.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: This is testimony of our values and our forward-thinking visionary approach.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: But we know that more needs to be done.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Developing Singapore to be a smart nation – that we must continue to pursue.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Our challenge is to remind ourselves ever so often that technology must be at the service of humanity and not humanity at the mercy of technology.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Thirdly, we have a good number of foreigners who become PRs and citizens over time.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: How well are we integrating our new PRs and citizens into the social fabric of Singapore?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Volunteering and engaging in purposeful and soul-ful activities can bring diverse people together, build bridges for each other to cross as they help and serve the vulnerable communities amongst us.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: And, of course, even guests who are here on S Pass, EP or work permits, should be encouraged to volunteer and to engage in service in the community.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Our sense of neighbourliness seems to be a challenge as I listen to the nightmares of litter bugs, the "neighbour from hell" and the story of an elderly dying alone in her HDB flat without anyone discovering her for days.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: It will have to take all of us – citizens, PRs, migrant residents, businesses, civil society, social services agencies and Government – collectively to be caring and purposeful in living out our social and civic responsibilities.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: On that note about being purposeful, I would like to share a quote by Mr Samir Singh, Chief Marketing Officer, Unilever Asia, during a panel discussion with Minister Edwin Tong at the Company of Good Summit in January 2023.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
