text: I quote: "Brands with purpose grow, people with purpose thrive, companies with purpose last." And to that beautiful quote, I add my line to close: "Communities with purpose serve." I stand in support of Budget 2023.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Prices of goods continue to escalate, access to supply has not returned to normalcy and the headwinds remain strong while we find a new balance and world order.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: In my conversations with residents the past week, some welcome the different measures in Budget 2023 to help address the cost of living, others are heartened by the support given to young families and some mentioned that the intent to strengthen our social compact is an area we need to put stronger focus as we progress as a nation.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: I am also supportive of the various measures to help those in need and how the Government is finding other sources of income to balance a tight fiscal position.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: In order for us to manage the challenges ahead and have financial wherewithal to provide for more diverse societal needs, I feel strongly that we must look at the topic of how to ensure Singapore's competitiveness can be sustained in the long run.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: This cannot simply be a quick fix or measures that allow Singaporeans to cope for the short term, but rather we need solutions that can enable us to navigate more complex environments and external threats which compete with Singapore for both investments and talent.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: As I have highlighted in my 2018 Budget debate speech, our competition today is no longer local.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: The real competition is dynamic and beyond our shores.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: I believe there are some important factors for our continued competitiveness.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: First, investing in our local workforce and the successful implementation of the Industry Transformation Maps (ITMs).

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: When the ITMs for 23 industries was first introduced in 2016, it was indeed a huge undertaking by the Ministry of Trade and Industry (MTI).

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: To develop roadmaps for each industry which is inherently different in nature, having wide ranging and some unique issues faced in each industry and the broad spectrum of stakeholders to be engaged made this task very challenging.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Yet, if we had not taken this first step, it would have been even more difficult today to keep pace with the rapid global market development and more workers would have been adversely impacted by the fiercer competition and the lack of skills to manage the changing nature of jobs.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: As we all recognise, skills or multi-skills of any worker cannot be developed overnight.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Keeping workers relevant on the long horizon takes more than just policies.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: SkillsFuture was introduced for this purpose and to send home the message about the need for continuous education training (CET) after formal schooling ends.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: From a talent pipeline perspective, how are we able to concretely identify the progress of this development and further complement the progress for future strategic investments that we wish to anchor in Singapore?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Second, leveraging overseas network as multipliers to develop our local talent.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: With a limited population and an ageing workforce, we must, first, acknowledge the need to retain our experienced workforce while we develop the next generation of workers.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: The pandemic has shown that work can take place virtually, productivity is not determined by the number of hours in an office and innovation can come about through collaboration of great minds.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Even with that, we must also allow our talents to explore and venture out as they become co-creators of work clusters globally that provide job opportunities for our workforce.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Attracting top talent to Singapore is one approach and over the years, we have been finding ways to have more global talents augment our ecosystem.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: It is true that on a broad level, these global talents will have a rub-on effect for our SMEs and make the local ecosystem more vibrant.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: On the other hand, we are still missing mechanisms that enable these global talents from directly benefiting SMEs through consulting services, being advisers to the local boards, providing expert sessions for the locals to learn alongside or acting as mentors to contribute deeply to the talent development.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: As we continue to monitor the efficacy of our measures and initiatives implemented for the dollar value invested, it is probably important, too, for us to understand if there are missed opportunity cost with the current approach.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Third, the Government as a catalyst, innovator or change-maker.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Often, when we talk about innovation, it is associated with having new technologies and doing things in a new way.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: But we sometimes forget that some innovations are not about radically new things, rather a new way of perceiving existing resources or chipping on ideas that were not rigorously pursued under past contexts.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: As we continue to attract investments to Singapore and create quality jobs for our workers, have we thought about what role the Government intends to play for future nation building?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Today, we maintain our competitive status with heavy investments in skills, knowledge, physical assets and upkeeping the Singapore brand.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: This is what we have going for us.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Indeed, it has given us the competitive advantage even with small acts of innovation.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: But what we may need to caution is that innovations responding to circumstances that are peculiar to our home context may result in impeding our international competitive success at some point.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: What if that role changes to be a co-producer with differentiated governance for critical resources that our country needs?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Will our pathway to achieving the climate target be accelerated and will this better secure our supplies with greater resiliency and reduce the overall cost of essential resources for our citizens?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: We need to know simply what works, why they work and how to apply them.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: In fact, it is fair to say that innovation usually requires pressure, necessity and even adversity to thrive.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: And I quote what Michael Porter said: "National prosperity is created, not inherited".

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Singapore, as a young nation, has much more to give and to constantly create for the benefit of our current and future generations.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: But the Government alone cannot fulfil this task.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: It takes our citizens, our industries, our talents, our global partners to collectively harness the strength, knowledge and our social responsibility towards one another to materialise our dreams.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Only we can define the social fabric and the signature of our society that we wish for.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Let us take the lead and not wait for the external environment to shape us, nor be limited by our imagination to achieve greater heights and greater things together.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Pain reminds us that something needs to be done.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: If we feel nothing, we do not react.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Therefore, we should not aim for analgesia to feel no pain but, instead, aim to ameliorate the pain.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I will take this occasion to speak further about how we should respond to pain.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: If pain is slight and fleeting, it can sometimes be dismissed.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: But when pain becomes more than a niggle here and a mild ache there, and is persistent, it is crucial that we acknowledge its existence and not dismiss it nonchalantly.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It is the same with the polity as it is with the human body.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The Government must recognise the pain that people are going through and, more importantly, act on them.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Today, there are a number of pain points that are evident.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: And here, I am not discomforted by high COE prices for big or luxury cars, but for smaller cars and motorcycles.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Many people need either a small car or a motorcycle for work.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Workers in the point-to-point transportation and platform delivery industries are good examples.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The PAP does not walk away from these pain points.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: We face them head on and we come up with viable and sustainable long-term solutions.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: But like a good doctor, we know that suggestions for instant pain relief, like instant gratification, is temporary and may cause us greater grief in the future.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: While we do not profess to have all the cures to all pains, we are prepared to take time to address the root causes of pain, while taking steps to ensure that the pain does not overwhelm us.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Loosely translated, this means that the path to wisdom is to know what you really know and to be aware of what you do not know.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The true danger then, lies in what some people call the "unknown of unknowns".

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Here, we need to gather information and listen to as many people and stakeholders as possible, to minimise the magnitude of "unknown of unknowns", so that we are not unnecessarily blindsided.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The next step is to come up with solutions.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: We can learn from what it takes to be a good doctor and the axiom which is taught to all medical students is, "To cure sometimes, to relieve often, to comfort always".

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: A good doctor knows that there is a limit to the illnesses he can cure.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Indeed, even with modern medicine, complete and permanent cures are rare.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: But he can often provide relief and, with empathy and compassion, he can always comfort his patients.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Likewise, there are few problems that politicians and governments can fix permanently with policies and programmes.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: There are few equivalents to smallpox in public policy-making, where an effective vaccination programme has eradicated smallpox from this planet.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: But policies and programmes do provide substantial relief.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: A listening ear, a gentle pat, a nod, all these are small things we can do to provide emotional comfort.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: And sometimes, I feel that we focus too much on finding solutions to the pain that we may well fall short on empathy.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Through our policies and programmes, we strive to improve the lives of the less fortunate.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The social mobility of Singaporeans over this period demonstrates this.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: But sometimes, we do come across as a bit lacking in empathy.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: And empathy goes a long way when it comes to providing comfort.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: But as I have said, we can improve.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It is like looking at whether a glass is half-full or half-empty.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: We need to also focus on the half-full glass and ask ourselves where do the possibilities lie, what is the potential to make the glass of water fuller than what it is now?

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Or do we believe that the glass will get emptier and emptier as time goes by?

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Is the best behind us or is yet to be?

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I might add, Sir, that it is also the aim of any Opposition who aspires to be the Government one day to convince the people that the glass is getting emptier and emptier and also to get them to focus on the pain points, to persuade the people that these pain points are unremitting, intractable and, in fact, getting worse and worse to the point of being life-threatening.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: But we have to ask ourselves: will this so-called new doctor have better solutions and cures or worse?

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Are they like the proverbial "koyok-seller" of yesteryear, trying to sell you miracle cures?

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: So, there are at least three broad responses to pain.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: One is to go for complete analgesia, which as I have said before, can be dangerous over a long period of time.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Another is to be overly focused on the pain and be paralysed by it.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: And then, there is the better way, which is to live with it and get on with life, but take pain relief when available and necessary, because life is seldom ever totally pain-free and miracle cures seldom, if ever, really work.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Now, as I turn 60, I believe that these fundamentals remain.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: How do we make sure that the glass of water gets fuller and not emptier?

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: If we can do that, we will continue to have the things that we want, such as good jobs for everyone and a safe environment and good schools to raise our children in, as well as affordable housing and reliable public transport.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I am optimistic for Singapore because I see these three important ingredients in the 4G leadership and the people.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: When the GST was first introduced at 3% in 1994, it had minimal impact on prices.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Our inflation rate rose marginally from 2% to 3% but fell below 2% after 1994 and stayed there.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And we were in a decade of robust economic growth.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, low inflation, high growth – when the GST was first introduced.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Then, in 2002, in then-Deputy Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong's first Budget as Finance Minister, he announced the increase in GST from 3% to 5%.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: At that time, our economy was at a different stage.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: It was facing a series of shocks and setbacks, and the growth outlook was troubled.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But inflation was projected to be zero or even negative.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And in this benign price environment, then-Deputy Prime Minister Lee said that, "I am confident that the 2-percentage point increase in GST will not significantly raise prices." Subsequently, when the GST went up from 5% to 7%, the economy was again back to a period of strong growth.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: GST is going up when our growth outlook is once again troubled, and concurrently, our inflation is high, and expected to be higher for longer.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: To be clear, GST is not the main factor driving prices up.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Indeed, as I said in my Budget Debate speech last year, we should "refrain from making GST a strawman, or a convenient scapegoat", for high prices.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: There are many other factors, external factors, driving prices up.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But when GST goes up in this environment, it adds to the overall pressures facing Singaporeans and it exacerbates Singaporeans' overall anxieties on cost-of-living.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Looking at the external factors driving prices up, take shipping, for example, thankfully, freight rates have come back down, quite significantly, from 2022 highs.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And we see this in the petrol stations.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The unit price is once again starting with the digit "2", rather than "3".

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And consequently, across the chain, price of chicken meat, for example, has stayed up.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Eggs have stayed up too, 25 cents at least per egg.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Overall, core inflation in Singapore is expected to ease off in the later half of this year, but only slightly.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, what can we do, what must we do, to help Singaporeans with cost-of-living pressures?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: First, our exchange rate policy has really helped.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Without a decisively stronger Singapore Dollar, we would be feeling the impact of imported inflation much more sharply.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Yet, the central bank would need to be very cautious with any further move, as a stronger Singapore Dollar makes our exports more expensive and the outlook for exports this year is already challenging.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Second, we need decisive fiscal measures to mitigate cost-of-living pressures.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And on this, I am cheered by the moves in this Budget.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And I wish to highlight, in particular, the permanent GST Voucher – Cash component.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: For eligible Singaporeans in larger flats, it is a similar story.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Based on last year's Budget, $200 in cash last year, and on plan, to go up to $250 this year.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But in this year's Budget, the payout for the year is raised from $250 to $350, and for next year, to $450.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: This will permanently deal with the effects of higher GST on overall cost-of-living pressures.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And his or her child, who may be an upper-middle-income working adult owning one property, will also receive $550 in cash alone.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And so, the Budget last year provided for $1.1 billion in such cost-of-living special payments and this year, another $1.3 billion has been set aside.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Taken together, these fiscal measures will go quite some way towards relieving cost-of-living pressures brought about by both higher GST and more saliently, larger inflationary drivers.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In fact, when speaking to residents about the Budget, some have turned around and asked me, is the Government giving too much?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: How is the Government going to sustain this, because we need to stay prudent?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I certainly agree, but I think the Government must also do what it can to address a clear and present concern of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And so, on this note, I strongly support the Government's fiscal measures in the GST Voucher Scheme and Assurance Package.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But third, beyond fiscal measures, I believe we can do more to keep in check the rental rates of Government-owned and managed commercial properties, especially for coffeeshops in our heartlands.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: To be fair, rental is not the largest cost component of cooked food and served meals in the heartlands, nor should we expect that lower or steady rental would bring down the overall prices of meals, as there are other cost drivers at play.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But I do believe that lower or steady rental would at least help to keep everyday meal prices steady and relieve the pressure on businesses to keep increasing prices to cover their costs.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Fourth and most importantly, to sustainably mitigate cost-of-living concerns, real wages and spending power of Singaporeans must go up.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Wages and spending power must grow faster than inflation.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Certainly, for the broad middle, but also, and especially for the lowest-wage workers amongst us, because consumption takes out a disproportionate part of income for low-wage workers, and so higher prices hit low-wage workers disproportionately hard.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: To help low-wage workers, the Government has announced decisive moves, especially in the Progressive Wage Model.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Many of these moves will start taking effect this year, to give wages at the bottom a sharp uplift over the next few years.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And paradoxically, these wage moves under the Progressive Wage Model would likely push prices up.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: We may all have to pay more for meals, for Town Council conservancy, and so on.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: One, the Progressive Wage Model should grow wages at the bottom faster than prices rise, so that our low-wage workers will get higher real wages eventually.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And as importantly, all of us will be sharing in the burden of these higher prices brought about by progressive wages.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: It is spread out across all of us, in order to support higher wages for a segment at the bottom.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, we can, and should all do our part, and pay a little bit more, in order to help those who are impacted the most, more than the rest of us, by higher costs of living.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: This must be a key part of our social compact.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And the Government is doing its part too.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: More than $5 billion in total over two years to share the heavier labour cost burden with employers in the next few years.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And on top of this, the Government is also giving directly to low-wage workers another $150 to $350 every month to further top up their wages through enhanced Workfare, announced last year and kicking in this year.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But ultimately, besides Government and consumers, employers of low-wage workers and buyers of their services – if these services are outsourced – must also play their part to uplift our low-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Because the Progressive Wage Model provides for a whole ladder of job grades and sets wage levels not only at the starting grade but at higher, more senior grades.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Employers, service providers and buyers of outsourced services must do all they can to keep to the spirit of Progressive Wages, preserve the ladder, keep the ladder intact and preserve an appropriate mix of junior and senior job grades in their workforce and keep alive for low-wage workers the hope and prospects of promotion and career advancement up the ladder.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Service providers and service buyers must do their part to prevent the collapse of the ladder and the regression of the mix of job grades in their workforce towards the starting rung, whereby the starting rung in the ladder effectively becomes the final rung.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And I would urge relevant regulatory agencies in the Progressive Wage Model to also regularly review if there is a need to possibly update their strategies from time to time to enhance alignment of the market with licensing frameworks.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: As for growing real wages and spending power in the broad middle, much has been said about productivity, upskilling and economic transformation to keep creating good jobs.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I wish to focus today on a sub-segment within the broad middle, a particular "sandwiched" group, comprising working adults in the 30s to 50s, with a school-going child or children between seven and 16 on one hand, and parents in their 60s and above on the other.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: This is not a big sub-segment, probably around 200,000 households or 20% of total households, but they face particular, "sandwiching" pressures in cost-of-living.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Now I believe as parents, all of them will want to do their best for their children and what is "best" can be very personal and varies from individual to individual.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But if we look at the Household Expenditure Survey in 2018, a household spends $112 per month on average, on private tuition and other educational courses.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But if we suppose that in fact, private tuition expenditure is concentrated within this sub-segment of "sandwiched" young parents, then the average amount that each of these households spends on tuition is probably closer to $600 per month.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And they spend on this because they want the best for their children.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: My point is this: we have been analysing household expenditure primarily by income bands, I think it would be useful to also study household expenditure by household archetypes and for an archetype such as this "sandwiched" sub-segment, we may uncover or confirm particular spending needs on tuition, for example.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And in turn, we can form a better, more nuanced understanding, of drivers of cost-of-living pressures for this particular sub-segment and work towards addressing these where possible.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Now I think this "sandwiched" group should get more support from the Government.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: First, beyond the Edusave account and Government top-ups thereto, I think parents should get a "Child Development Bonus", in cash, for each child seven to 16, each year.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Think of this as an extension of Government support, in the child's life, beyond the Baby Bonus Cash Gift which has been enhanced and beyond contributions to the Child Development Account for preschool years, which has also been enhanced.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Second, especially for the elderly parents of this "sandwiched" sub-segment and for seniors across the board, we should have more healthcare subsidies, especially in intermediate and long-term care such as nursing homes and in increasingly prevalent services in the hospitals such as MRI scans.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I started with a reference to the 2002 Budget, the first by then-Deputy Prime Minister Lee.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In other words, the Government has been spending more and more, and doing better and better for Singaporeans, year after year, and it has been doing so sustainably and responsibly.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: First, and most obviously, by ensuring our economy grows.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, between 2002 and 2023, our economy has grown by four times in nominal terms too, keeping pace with spending.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The Government has grown the pie, so that it can do more for Singaporeans, sustainably.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But second, in these years, the Government has also found new, important ways to maintain our fiscal sustainability.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: It transited from a Net Investment Income (NII) framework to a Net Investment Return (NIR) framework, to leverage more on the strength of our reserves to fund current needs.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: On the other hand, in 2002, taxes and fees amounted to 17% of GDP.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Today, it is 15%, lower than in 2002, although our spending needs have gone up – shot up dramatically.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And the Government has done this while keeping personal and corporate income tax regimes highly competitive.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: That is why we need GST, which taxes consumption rather than income, as another part of our fiscal base, and that is why GST has gone up.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Yet, with our unique system of permanent offsets, we make sure the bulk of higher GST is net-net raised from foreigners, tourists and higher-income Singaporeans, but channelled towards benefiting all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In our revenue base today, taxes and fees are already at 15% of GDP, how much lower do we want to go?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: NIR, on the other hand, is already at 4%, how much higher do we want to go?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: How much more do we want to leverage on our reserves?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: As a society, we will have to make our own judgement based on our shared values.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Higher GST, in a high-inflation era, creates anxieties for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But it is the right thing for all of us to do, for ourselves and for future generations.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: While raising GST, this Government has rolled out decisive moves to put cash in Singaporeans' hands, to uplift real wages, especially at the bottom and to provide immediate assurance.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: It shows a remarkable political will to do right by Singaporeans in the long-term and to take care of Singaporeans' needs in the short-term.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In management studies, there is a concept by Jim Collins about eschewing the "Tyranny of the Or" and exercising the "Genius of the And".

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In the context of governing a country, I would refrain from using the word "Genius", but "Gumption", perhaps, or "Steel".

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The Government has, over the decades, steadfastly eschewed false choices, avoided the "Tyranny of the Or", and held on to a "Gumption and Steel of the And", and it shows in how it has raised GST responsibly while taking care of cost-of-living concerns compassionately.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: There is something else to be gleaned from the 2002 Budget Statement.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Then-Deputy Prime Minister Lee introduced an offset package while announcing the increase in GST from 3% to 5% and he said this, in 2002, "the offset package will cover at least five years' worth of additional tax payable for all flat sizes.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In fact, those living in one- or two-room HDB flats will be covered for the next 10 years".

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In 2007, then-Minister Tharman rolled out an offset package along essentially, similar lines.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Twenty years on, today, the Government carries on the tradition and remains consistent in its commitment to take care of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Singapore was coming out of its worst recession at that time, since Independence.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Then-Deputy Prime Minister Lee said, "we are entering a very different world.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Conditions are uncertain and volatile, competition is intense, change is faster than ever… we cannot prevent the changes from happening.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Instead, we must act decisively…" Today, we are debating a Budget that is titled "Moving Forward in a New Era", indeed another different world and the words uttered in 2002 ring as true today.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But I am confident that if we stay open as a country and embrace the world, stay nimble as a tribe and seize opportunities to make hay when the sun shines, and stay united as a people and take care of each another, we will have another brilliant 20 years ahead of us, towards SG75 and towards SG100.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, while the acute phase of the COVID-19 pandemic is now over and we can all wave goodbye to the wearing of face masks, there remain many other challenges facing Singaporeans in the horizon.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The one thing that is top of mind for many of my residents during our house visits, is the mounting cost of living pressure they face.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Inflation, unfortunately, is not a phenomenon that Singaporeans can wave goodbye to in 2023.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While the Government still expects economic growth in 2023, amid recessionary concerns globally, I believe the risks to the economic outlook remain to the downside.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The MOM too has observed a recent uptick in retrenchments in Singapore and unemployment rates could trend higher.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Just over the last weekend, even Google is reported to have retrenched 6% of their Singapore workforce.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Against this backdrop of continuing household vulnerabilities, my speech today will cover three broad areas.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: First, my observations on the Government's fiscal position; second, suggestions on growing our recurrent revenue sources from those better able to contribute; and third, recommendations on truly strengthening our social compact.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Thankfully, it is not all doom and gloom when it comes to the Government's finances.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Over the past year, I shared in Parliament my observations on what appears to be the better-than-expected fiscal outturn in Financial Year 2021 (FY 2021) and FY 2022.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: It appears that against the spectre of COVID, operating revenues and the primary deficit in the last two years, have indeed, been much better than expected.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Despite higher expenditure and special transfers, the overall fiscal position is still expected to improve by $1 billion.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Had it not been for higher special transfers, the Budget would have similarly turned in a surplus instead of an estimated $3 billion deficit instead.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But, do not get me wrong, it is not that I am against the idea of these transfers in 2022, as I recognise that the top-up to the GST Voucher Fund following the enhancement of the Assurance Package announced in November 2022, was a key source of the increase in special transfers from $6.2 billion as initially estimated to $9.2 billion, thus contributing to the deficit for the year.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: After all, even without raising the GST rate to 8%, GST collections rose $1.8 billion in 2022.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Looking into FY 2023, I note that the Government expects a modest deficit of $0.4 billion.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Despite slowing growth, operating revenues are expected to see strong growth in the year, up S$6.4 billion compared to 2022.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Corporate income tax, personal income tax and GST are expected to reach new record highs for the third consecutive year.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Meanwhile, $185 billion is set to be transferred from the MAS to Government of Singapore Investment Corporation (GIC) in phases to reach the optimal reserves amount.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: With the deployment of these funds into a higher return seeking portfolio compared to that of the MAS, this would naturally mean higher potential returns to the Government and hence, higher NIRC contributions over time.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I thus hope that the Government will not hesitate to support the livelihoods of our fellow Singaporeans, should inflation pressures persist and not slow "more discernibly in the second half" as is expected by the Ministry of Trade and Industry (MTI) and if labour market conditions continue to deteriorate.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I do wonder though, what is the cumulative budget deficit from the start of the Government's term to FY 2023, and would the need to maintain a balanced budget constrain the ability of the Government to activate the "drawer plans" that Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong spoke about, should the need arise?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Moving into the second segment of my speech on suggestions on how best to grow our recurrent revenue sources and raise contributions from those segments that are better able to contribute.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I agree with what Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong shared about keeping “our overall system of taxes and benefits fair and progressive” and that “those who are better off contribute more”.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, I believe there is significant scope for us to do more to better achieve these stated objectives, such that the drive to have everyone contribute something does not risk morphing into common suffering for the man on the street.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In my Budget debate speech last year, I spoke extensively about BEPS 2.0.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Not only has corporate income taxes been consistently the largest contributor to the Government’s operating revenues, in FY2023, it is now the single largest contributor to the Budget, higher than that of the NIRC.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This is not surprising at all if we look at some of the largest companies here in Singapore, with DBS full-year net profit up 20% to a record $8.2 billion, while Sembcorp Industries’ net profit was up three times, supported by higher power prices and margins in Singapore and the UK.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I note that in the Ministry of Finance (MOF)’s Occasional Paper on medium-term fiscal projections, the impact to our single largest contributor to the Budget from BEPS 2.0 is not taken into account, which makes the published medium-term revenue and fiscal projections a lot less meaningful.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I recognise that there are uncertainties and the Government needs more time to study these issues thoroughly and will announce changes in the corporate tax system when ready.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, while BEPS 2.0 may have been delayed, the OECD has on 2 February released technical guidance to assist governments in implementing the global minimum tax.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While precise numbers may not be feasible, does the MOF have a range of blue sky and grey sky projections as to the impact of the implementation of a Domestic Top-up Tax?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Is the MOF sufficiently prepared to implement this landmark tax reform from 2025 as what Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong shared?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As I have shared in this House last year, I hope that the Government will view the global minimum tax reforms as an opportunity rather than a threat, given Singapore's strong non-tax advantages and attractiveness to MNEs.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: If a global MNE is already operating in Singapore, what incentive would it have to incur additional relocation costs when the minimum corporate tax rates of 15% would be normalised globally?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I hope it is not the case that over the past years, global MNEs’ decision to invest in Singapore boils down to mere tax incentives as the deal-breaker.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) has shared with the Pillar Two solution, all economies will benefit from extra tax revenues.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I hope the additional tax revenues from BEPS 2.0 will not simply be in substance returned to MNEs through other forms.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Next on wealth taxes, particularly, those relating to property which is the Government’s preferred way to tax wealth.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As I have shared last year, while the increase in headline marginal property tax rates appears high, the actual impact on the households involved are unlikely to be material.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I further shared about how, based on my analysis, high-end condos in Cairnhill and Nassim Road need only raise rents by 2% to 7% to offset the higher property taxes.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As it turns out, private residential rents rose by 30% in 2022.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: So, while I agree with Deputy Prime Minister that $380 million more per year in property tax revenues is not an insignificant sum of money, I still believe that it may not be that significant to those who are impacted.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But I do recognise that the Government is doing more on the property front, with the higher marginal Buyers’ Stamp Duty (BSD) rates for higher-value residential and non-residential properties.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In itself, again I do not believe the impact of the higher BSD rates to be that significant.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: To illustrate, for residential properties priced between $1.5 million and $5 million, the impact of the BSD rate increase only amounts to 0% to 1.1% of the purchase price of the property.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Again, in the context of the near 9% rise in private property prices in 2022, the higher BSD may simply be an afterthought.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I wonder though if more can be done for our property-related wealth taxes to be more targeted and progressive?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In Budget 2009, Senior Minister Tharman as then Finance Minister removed the tax on Net Annual Value with effect from YA2010, for those who own higher-value homes or secondary residences.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I hope the Government can consider re-introducing this tax, in which the AV threshold can be set at a high bar, for it to be effective as a wealth tax targeting on those who can afford the likes of our Good Class Bungalows (GCBs) and especially for those private residential properties that are not let out, given the situation we have today where private residential vacancies are near historical lows.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: To give credit where it is due, I welcome the Government’s recognition that there is scope to make our vehicle taxes more progressive.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Last year, I highlighted that the Government’s move to introduce a new Additional Registration Fee (ARF) tier for cars is not meaningful in the grand scheme of things.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: So, I do welcome the Government’s move to further adjust the ARF and cap the Preferential ARF (PARF) rebates at $60,000.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I hope the Government will continue to consider various options to tax wealth effectively and other forms of progressive taxes to raise revenues more equitably rather than via regressive taxes such as the GST.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Parenting is definitely a struggle, especially if one wants to be an involved parent.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But my wife and I have not and will not regret our decision to bring our two boys into this world, who are now about three-and-a-half and one-and-a-half years old today.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As Parliamentarians and leaders of this country, how then can we continuously strive to make it easier for Singaporeans to start a family?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: How can we make the sacrifices and trade-offs less stark and make parents and would-be-parents feel that balancing family, work and life is not a zero-sum game?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I will be elaborating further on Flexible Work Arrangements (FWAs) and parental leave during the subsequent Committee of Supply debates, topics which I have been speaking on for the last two years.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: On FWAs in particular, I am increasingly anxious that whatever gains we have made as a country when it comes to workplace flexibility during COVID-19 are now rapidly being eroded and my worst fears of a return to pre-COVID-19 workplace norms are starting to come true.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Residents, family members and friends are increasingly sharing that they are pretty much back to working from the office and working from home is now a distant memory.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: One friend quipped that his boss said, and I paraphrase, “If you are not in the office, how do I know that you are actually working?” Work from home is just one form of flexible work arrangement, but I fear that if we do not put in place legislation on this matter soon, the hard-earned gains from FWAs in the last few years will soon be permanently lost.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: On parental leave, I note that while unpaid infant care leave will be raised, there are no changes to maternity leave which was last changed 15 years ago in 2008.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: That said, the move to raise Government-Paid Paternity Leave from two weeks to four weeks is no doubt welcome, but I note that this is purely on a voluntary basis on the part of employers.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As it is, even though Paternity Leave is a mere two weeks, only more than half of our fathers take paternity leave.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Will would-be fathers be in a position to take their full entitlement of the expanded paternity leave and feel comfortable doing so?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: So, I do wonder if Deputy Prime Minister’s message that "we want paternal involvement to be the norm in our society” could in practice turn out as being construed as "paternal involvement is voluntary"?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: One of the most puzzling moves to me is the decision to worsen the Working Mother’s Child Relief (WMCR).

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While there could be a group of lower-income working mothers who would benefit from this change, the majority of would-be working mothers will be made worse off with the change in methodology.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In the context of "building a Singapore Made for Families", I find this move highly ironic and self-contradictory.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I did some calculations for WMCR for one child, assuming a working mother gets two months' worth of bonuses which is the average in Singapore, while benefiting from other standard reliefs such as earned income relief, CPF, NSMan (Wife) relief and shares the qualifying child relief with her husband.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I wonder if the WMCR truly seeks to reward families with children and encourage married women to remain in the workforce after having children, or does it have the unintended opposite effect?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: If the aim is to benefit lower- to middle-income working mothers, why not just give a motherhood tax rebate to working mothers earning below a certain income?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And I do not mean this as a motherhood statement as such a move can ensure that even a larger proportion of mothers will benefit as opposed to the design of the new WMCR.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: To further support lower-income working mothers, if the tax rebates granted exceed the tax payable, tax credits can be paid out in cash to ensure the reliefs are not lost.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, unwed single mothers are ineligible for this relief.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Single mothers already face significant challenges in singlehandedly raising their children and more often than not are working mothers.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Even if we cannot raise their children on their behalf, the least we can do is to ensure that our tax policies do not discriminate against them.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I strongly urge the Government to reconsider the changes to the WMCR.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: From those within this monthly income band, the lower monthly take-home salary could be a challenge given the pressures of being in a sandwiched class, with high monthly household expenses and relatively lower grants and support compared to the lower income.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, I do recognise that the benefits from a higher employers’ CPF contribution over time can contribute meaningfully to retirement savings.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Yet, where I think the move falls short is in keeping the annual salary ceiling intact at $102,000.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Can the Government raise the CPF annual salary ceiling in tandem with the monthly salary ceiling move to benefit this expanded group of workers?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I did some calculations for a worker who earns $7,000 a month with a three-month bonus.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In the case of a worker who earns $8,000 a month and has a four-month bonus, whether through his or her exceptional work performance or otherwise, the worker would not benefit from the raised monthly salary ceiling at all.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: When the Government says that it will review the annual salary ceiling periodically, what is the Government looking out for before deciding to make the move or rather what is stopping the Government from doing so immediately as it has done in the past?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: What is the coverage of the current CPF salary ceiling moves and what could it be if the annual salary ceiling was raised correspondingly today?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Already, the higher monthly salary ceiling will be increased in four steps all the way to 2026 to allow employers and employees to adjust to the changes.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I am sure everyone in this Chamber agrees that businesses value certainty and visibility on when exactly the annual salary ceiling move is going to take place, and this will be much appreciated by employers and employees alike.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Before I conclude, Mr Speaker, let me just say a few words in Mandarin.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Despite slowing growth, operating revenues are expected to see strong growth in the year, up S$6.4 billion compared to 2022.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Corporate income tax, personal income tax and GST are expected to reach new record highs for the third consecutive year.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I thus hope that the Government will not hesitate to support the livelihoods of our fellow Singaporeans if the need arises.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This is crucial, because inflation pressures will persist and are unlikely to slow down discernibly and labour market conditions might continue to deteriorate.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: One of the most puzzling moves to me is the change to the Working Mother’s Child Relief (WMCR).

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While there could be a group of lower income working mothers who would benefit from this change, the majority of would-be working mothers will be worse off with the change.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In the context of "Building a Singapore Made for Families", I find this move self-contradictory.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I wonder if the WMCR truly seeks to encourage married women to remain in the workforce after having children, or does it have the unintended opposite effect?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I hope the Government can reconsider the change to WMCR.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, to conclude, I would like to share some final thoughts on Budget 2023.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Recently, I read about the Cost-of-Thriving Index in America, which suggests that while many economists argue that America’s working families are more prosperous than ever before, families themselves feel that they have come under increasing economic pressure.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The report suggests that the families are right.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As the Government strategises on how to move forward in a new era, I hope the future Singapore will not be one where we worry about not being able to attract the rich and famous or the largest and most profitable corporations and hence, have the average Singaporean shoulder a higher tax burden.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I hope it will not be one where we have a shrinking middle class owing to income inequalities and I hope it will be one where every Singaporean family can thrive.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: The Budget Statement looks at the prospects for the country, taking into account both the current challenges as well as the opportunities.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: How did things look when the Minister for Finance presented Singapore's first Budget after gaining independence on 9 August 1965?

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: We can get a glimpse of how things look more than half a century ago from the 1970 Budget Statement presented by the then-Minister for Finance, Dr Goh Keng Swee, as he chose in that Budget Statement, to do a review of Singapore's economic performance during the preceding decade.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: He said: "On the morning of 9 August 1965, I was in Fullerton Building, brooding over the enormous problems facing the country and the Government.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: The problems of the future loom in awesome and intimidating proportions." Nevertheless, Dr Goh was able to say in his Budget Statement in December of 1967, that after two years of independent existence, the Republic of Singapore continued not only to survive, but also to flourish, to the surprise of many observers.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore's first Minister for Finance expressed hope when our country was still a newly emerging economy, while the present Minister for Finance expresses hope in presenting Budget 2023 when we are already a mature economy.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, in preparing the Government's Budget, I believe that there are enduring lessons from the past that are still applicable today which have to do with the role of economic growth in creating fiscal capacity, the necessity of integrating into the global economy for sustaining economic prosperity and the centrality of job holding in a dynamic economy.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: First, the role of economic growth in creating fiscal capacity.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: An analysis of the data shows the share of Singapore Government operating revenue as a share of GDP keeping pace with the Government spending as a share of GDP from 1965 onwards, except during the years of recessionary shocks, when we ran deficits.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: The more moderate growth rate is likely to be propelled by productivity growth.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: In the earlier years, the increase in investment rate, the increase in labour force participation, helped to boost growth.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: But in this stage of being a more mature economy, that moderate growth rate has to be propelled principally by productivity growth, which in turn will depend on technological diffusion from abroad as well as indigenous innovation.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Indigenous innovation is partly driven by spending on research and development by the private sector as well as the higher education sector and public research institutes.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: However, indigenous innovation is importantly undertaken also by economic actors at the grassroots, conceiving new products to launch and better processes to churn out existing products.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Established firms, the bigger firms, may be hesitant to launch new and higher quality products for fear that their existing product lines might be displaced as customers shift away their purchases.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Small firms and new startups therefore have greater incentive to find new niches because they do not have the same problem as these established firms.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: They dare to venture into the dark and try something new.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: However, they are limited by the availability of financing.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: As new business startups drive innovation in the new economy, a central relationship that comes into focus is that of financiers and entrepreneurs.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: As our education system invest in providing our students more and more, with the opportunity to venture into the unknown and increase the supply of entrepreneurs, the match between angel investors and people with good business ideas might improve.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: So, in this next stage of growth, as our students operate in a more innovative, exploratory, education system while learning all the basics, maybe we will see more of them daring to venture into the unknown, to try it out, being entrepreneurs.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: This will improve the expected returns to financiers and increase the number of startups that receive financing.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Second, the necessity of integrating into the global economy for sustaining economic prosperity.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: This is despite the fact that as the Budget Statement presented by the Minister has acknowledged the era of untrammelled globalisation is over and greater contestation and fragmentation of the global economy is likely.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Still then, integrating into the global economy remains very important.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Economic integration in the global flow of ideas, goods and services, capital and labour, I believe, remains necessary as this expands our GDP and provides the fiscal resources to strengthen economic inclusion.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Integrating into the global economy boosts our GDP through several channels.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: As the industry expands through selling into the external market, each firm, even though small, experiences the productivity boost that allows it to expand output.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: For example, industry level trade missions into the regional economies gather useful information that each firm can take advantage of to expand sales.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Another point, more productive firms also self-select into selling in export markets as they are better able to cover the fixed costs of establishing export platforms.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: You need to incur some fixed cost just to find out how the market looks like in an overseas economy.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Larger firms tend to devote more resources to screen workers and improve the quality of their work force.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Consequently, larger firms pay observationally equivalent workers more.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Empirical evidence suggests that neighbouring countries, after adjusting for country sizes, tend to trade more with each other.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: So, the regional market provides an opportunity for our domestic firms to gain experience of selling abroad and learn from exporting.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: The experience gained can later help this firm to achieve international competitiveness to sell beyond regional markets.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: The Budget Statement notes that our deep relationships with both the US and China as well as the ASEAN economies, make us an increasingly important place for global and regional businesses.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Demographic trends create headwinds for Singapore even as we move to develop indigenous innovation.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: As our wages increase from the 1960s, the opportunity cost of having another child has also increased.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: While higher incomes means that people can afford to have more children, it has been observed that the total fertility rate tends to decline as countries become richer.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: This suggests that the substitution effect dominates the income effect of higher wages.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: In other words, if my wages are higher, sure, I can afford to have more children.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: On the other hand, raising a child is a very time intensive activity and possibly having another child means having less time in the market workplace.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: That is the substitution effect and it is quite general across many countries of different cultures.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: As countries become richer, the total fertility rate steadily declines.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: So, people invest more in raising the human capital of their children, even as the family size shrinks.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: What poses a challenge for Singapore at this stage of our economic development is that an economy where older age structure appears to generate slower productivity growth.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: One reason for that, is that the lower labour force participation rate among older workers limits the extent of knowledge transfer from older and more experienced workers to younger workers.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: My final point, the centrality of job holding in a dynamic economy.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: A person's self-esteem tends to be very much tied up with the ability to tackle challenges that the workplace throws up.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: There is a sense of accomplishment that comes from being able to size up a problem at our workplace and to pull together the available resources to solve the problem.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: When one's contribution to solving a problem is acknowledged, even if only tacitly, it boosts our self-confidence and encourages greater initiative.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Many goals that we set are work related and these serve to give us a sense of purpose as we begin each new day.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: When we are absorbed in our work, time flies.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: On the other hand, there is a certain listlessness that accompanies prolonged joblessness.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Many meaningful relationships are also developed at our workplace.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: This is partly due to the fact that the production process in modern enterprises is a collaborative effort requiring teamwork.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: As we work along with colleagues to achieve common goals and contribute jointly to problem-solving, we develop a social bond and a sense of belonging that are important for our emotional health.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: When workers across the whole economy find their work meaningful and are ready to think constantly about how to do their work better in novel ways, the result can be higher job satisfaction and a boost to aggregate productivity growth.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: It is imperative that we should never either through extravagance or carelessness, fritter away all that we had so laboriously built up.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: We must build on the foundation of the accumulated experience of the decade and ensure that progress and prosperity will continue to higher levels of consolidation." I believe that Budget 2023 is consonant with this wise counsel.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong has said that we cannot simply do the same things as we have in the past and assume success.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It involves asking ourselves hard questions where solutions sometimes involve competing interests.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Instead of just raising questions on these topics, I would like to, humbly and sincerely, offer my own suggestions and solutions for this House to deliberate upon.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The first issue is something deeply concerning to me and many other Singaporeans – that is, the growing number of workplace injuries and fatalities.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Last year, on a Tuesday morning in December, Mr Ely Chow was struck and pinned down by a machine as it was being transferred by a forklift.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: He was taken unconscious to Ng Teng Fong Hospital and subsequently passed away from his injuries.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I was there at his wake in Ghim Moh and it affected me deeply.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Ely grew up in Ghim Moh, in Ulu Pandan, the constituency I serve, where his mother and father live.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: His sister, Ruth, and her husband also live in Ghim Moh.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Ely was just 31 years old and was, together with his fiancé, waiting to move into their Built-To-Order (BTO) home in Ghim Moh, a stone's throw away from where he grew up.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I felt the family's anguish at the wake.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I promised them that I would speak up for Ely in Parliament.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This year, there have already been five workplace fatalities in less than two months, most recently of which was the harbour pilot from PSA Marine.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is necessary and I am encouraged by it.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I also acknowledge that the Government has accepted the eight key recommendations by the International Advisory Panel on improving workplace safety and health.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Notwithstanding all that has been done by MOM and the relevant stakeholders, Mr Speaker, Sir, I believe there is far more we can do and we owe it to the workers to ensure their utmost safety.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I believe this is not only possible, but necessary as we continue to build and develop Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The men and women working in these high-risk sectors, both locals and migrant workers, help to build and maintain our buildings and keep the infrastructure of our nation running.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There are two things and two sub-issues I believe we can continue to strengthen our workplace safety.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This involves all stakeholders and goes beyond the physical workplace.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Many of the injuries and fatalities happen within the construction sector where there are high heights as well as the transportation and storage sector where vehicles are involved.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: A culture prioritising safety is a collective effort.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Designers and developers must take into consideration how something can be safely built and maintained.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Clear and simplified instructions of how to implement safety regulations can ensure that employees on the ground will be up to date.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We must have a framework of safety to ensure regular maintenance of all equipment and checks by MOM to see that standards are upheld by both large firms as well as SMEs.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Particularly for SMEs, where manpower constraints and the difficulty of implementing such safety regulations are more apparent, we need to consider how to make the adoption of industry safety standards as straightforward and sustainable as they can be.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This applies to employees as well as more senior management such that this safety culture is inculcated into each firm's core values.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Especially with new workers, proper training must be given so that each worker knows how to use the relevant equipment and knows what other safety measures to abide by.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Proper training imparts a culture of responsibility and watching out for other workers as well.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There is a crunch in manpower, delays in projects causing upward pressure to work faster and many workers and constructions resuming after a long time-off.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: A combination of all these, along with supply chain disruption, has increased the risk of hazards.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But this is a trade-off I am not willing to pay.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I am not willing to lose a life on the worksite.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I have provided some solutions in my speech already.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In relation to that, I believe we need better infrastructure of how we provide information and support for victims and their family members.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Losing someone is always painful and particularly so when it is sudden and unexpected, which is the case with all workplace fatalities.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There must be a more systematic way to inform family members if any incident has occurred so they can arrive as quickly as possible.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In addition, while of course investigations have to take place and run their due course, information can be provided to the victim's families to assist in at least some partial closure in a very painful episode.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The second topic I would like to speak on is education.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Singapore's education system is one that we can, and should, be proud of.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is world renowned for producing exceptional students across the board who are prepared to tackle the significant issues and challenges our world faces today and who consistently rank highly globally.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Some may then ask, why speak about, or fix something, that is not broken.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The answer is because we must focus on the true mission of education: to prepare our young for the world and give them equal opportunities to attain better lives.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Rankings do not tell the full picture of our education system.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Rankings have a purpose, but to an extent.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is especially so in uncertain times, where we must develop students holistically to achieve the best they can.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We must therefore continually evolve and adapt to ensure our system is prepared for the future.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Today, I would like to ask for a rethink of our education system and syllabus, and in relation to that, the PSLE and our heavy reliance on tuition.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In fact, the Ministry of Education has addressed concerns over the years and brought forth many changes in our curriculum to better equip our children, including removing the T-score for the PSLE.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Reducing a syllabus to an appropriate size cannot be done arbitrarily and the syllabus is crafted according to the changing needs of our nation.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, certainly, it would be hard to figure out what should be prioritised because every part of the syllabus is arguably important to prepare students for the future.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I also note that there have been many revamps of our curriculum including the introduction of the "Teach Less, Learn More" scheme.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Nevertheless, I take reference from the Finnish education system, an education system that has consistently ranked highly and is similarly well regarded around the world.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Not only does Finland perform well on PISA, students face less stress and after-school tutoring is rare.
