speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While a direct pari materia importation of Finland's model is certainly not possible because of cultural and structural differences, a page can definitely be taken from their book.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: When the Finnish education system was reformed in the 1980s, Finnish educators shifted their focus away from test scores and Math and Science comprehension to building a "happy, harmonious and healthy student and learning environment".

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This focus was to help "every single child" in a way to combat social inequality.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In Singapore, we already have, yes, the existing programmes to target inequality like the Uplifting Pupils in Life and Inspiring Families Taskforce (UPLIFT).

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But I believe, as the Finnish did, that we can consider a redefinition of success and the end goal of our education system.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Especially in an uncertain world, these transversal skills I have just mentioned – particularly critical thinking skills and learning to learn and research – are what we must focus on.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Having that in mind, we can tailor and reshape the syllabus around these core skills which hopefully would lighten the actual workload on students.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Finnish students have little homework and thus do not spend more than half an hour outside of school time to finish homework.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This lightened workload then allows for more sleep for students and less need to rely on tutors.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Creating such a culture in Singapore would reduce the need for tuition merely to do school homework but rather focus on tuition merely to boost a child in particular areas in which he or she struggles in, where needed.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, the syllabus needs to be less stressful so that there is small, or little, or no need for tuition.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There are already continuous assessments every year in primary school – and with a proper scheme of affiliation, students can focus on more holistic and long-term learning.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Currently, SBB does not apply to all schools and certain schools only accept express students and IB students.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is well known that the social environment of a school can positively influence a student's academic behaviour and performance.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is not a proposal I make lightly, nor is it something that can be simply implemented with the stroke of a pen or the wave of a wand.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We need only look to National Service – an education and training system in its own right – to see how it has helped Singaporeans learn to live and work together, unite and forge a common identity regardless of race, religion or background.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is something we have done before and I believe we can do it again – this time in our schools.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While it is certainly true that catering to specific segments of students, such as those with high academic ability or strengths in specific areas or those who prefer a more hands-on and technical training can have its advantages, these benefits are not necessarily negated if we start to mix streams within all schools.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Students would be geared towards education, not results.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Twenty-eight point eight kilobits per second was what we had.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Much later, the 56.8 modems were on after-burner.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: This was probably difficult to comprehend – why the hype over a computer lab?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Much earlier, I remember loading MS-DOS using floppy drives.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: I remember hardcoding my first html website in 1996 and uploading it onto Angelfire, a free hosting website.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Computers back then were the 486 Pentiums and the thought of having dual core and quad core chips were to me, space technology.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: February 2023 marks the dawn of generative artificial intelligence (AI).

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: This is becoming the new Internet in the pursuit of new experiences.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: But the pace of change has gained additional momentum with the arrival of tools such as ChatGPT.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: For a long time, the generic Google Search was much of everything we knew of the Internet.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: For a decade, we had Siri and Alexa, but the level of performance and adoption in Generative Pre-trained Transformer (GPT) is astounding.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: More recently, Microsoft invested $10 billion into ChatGPT.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: In response, Google has invested $300 million in its rival, Anthropic.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), an educational research institution with an endowment of $24.6 billion, committed $1.1 billion for AI research.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: A $2 billion investment from IBM, $4.6 billion from Volkswagen, and many more.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: From 1959 to 2012, computing power doubled every two years, tracking Moore's law.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: That is a rate seven times faster than before.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: If you think that this progress is rapid, this was limited because graphics processing units (GPUs) could only condense computational power over a few hundred cores.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: An AI chip maker, Cerebras, recently built the largest chip in the world – 22 inch on each side, 2.6 trillion transistors on a condensed computational power of 850,000 cores, with a 100 trillion parameters.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Compared to what I knew of 486 Pentium computers, this was not space technology.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: This progress will keep pace with machine learning and robotics.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: In 2022, Amazon invested $1 billion into robotics.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Amazon hires about 1.6 million workers at the end of 2021 and today, it adds about 1,000 robots a day.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The number of robots to workers today is about a third.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: By 2023, Amazon will have more robots than employees.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: With global investments reaching $232 billion by 2025, these capabilities will soon be quickly moved from supply chain to manufacturing.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Throughout history, there have been a handful of technologies that have truly transformed the world, unleashing new levels of productivity and prosperity.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Think of the steam engine, which took 100 years, 25 years for the telephone, 30 years for electricity, and the printing press, which was invented in 1439, only widely adopted 500 years later in the 19th century.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: These technologies changed the way we live and work.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: It took a few years for Kodak to slide into bankruptcy.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: But with AI, the time required for a Kodak moment by pressing the camera button on the latest iPhone, a single AI would have generated more than a billion bits of information – a quantum leap by any measure.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The UK plans to become a global AI superpower.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: From the codebreaker Alan Turing's early work to London-based powerhouse DeepMind, UK is ranked third in the world for investments to AI companies and a third of all Europe's AI companies – just behind the US and China.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: More recently, British Telecom quick-paced and established an AI developmental hub, launched an AI accelerator and registered more AIs than any UK entity.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: South Korea has similar ambitions and aims to become a powerhouse, with investments of $642 million into companies developing advanced AI chips.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: As part of the larger vision for South Korea, Seoul has set aside $795 million for AI semiconductors and another $235 million for next-generation platforms.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Looking deeper into the data, Singapore outperformed in government and infrastructure pillars and must strive to do better for the technology pillar – impressive for a small country of a population of 5.5 million.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We must continue to do this good work, to be courageous in investing and building our future capabilities.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We have a window of opportunity to become truly an intelligent nation to drive economic growth and improve the quality of life in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Quality of life is closely linked to our access to resources.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The world consumes about 92 billion tonnes of resources each year – approximately 1.7 times the amount consumed in 2000.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: In the last 15 years, the global consumption of commodities increased by 40%.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: At the same time, investments in new mining projects have fallen to 15-year lows.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The discovery of copper is on a gradual decline, with only one major discovery in the last five years.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We are just at the start of a long run of shortages and higher prices.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Even if supply was available, we cannot assume that it is accessible, not least until the producer country has stored ample supplies for domestic consumption.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Copper and critical materials are at the leading edge of this global shortage.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Who are competing with us for these resources?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: In the 1960s, most of the global population were living in poverty.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The uplift of the middle class, coupled with better access to healthcare and education, has increased the number of professionals and global talent.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: This will continue to increase by another 30% by 2050.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: This is the global competition for good jobs and quality investments and it will be increasingly difficult.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: This Budget will help us to build strong foundations for innovation and collaboration, setting the right tone and pace.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: It sets out the importance to work on the strategy collectively – every stakeholder and entity, every Singaporean, a role to play.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: It reflects our values to give every citizen opportunities to discover themselves and contribute meaningfully, each contribution appreciated and cherished.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: This Budget reflects our vision and ambition to build with courage the Singapore we want for tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Each year, natural disasters have shocked the world – earthquakes, tsunamis, pandemics.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: War conflict and failed government policies are disasters we strike upon ourselves.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Famine, economic collapse, inflation – we may be powerless in the face of a natural disaster, but we can prepare for them.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We may not have the influence over policies of others, but we can prepare for them.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: In the movie "World War Z", standing behind the impenetrable fortress and high walls, Mossad Chief, Jurgen Warmbrunn, explained the concept of the 10th person in the council of 10, the person charged with the responsibility, challenging every assumption, no matter how improbable it may seem to safeguard the "what-ifs" for the country.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: This gave them time to build up defences and face the threat.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: In the Six Thinking Hats of De Bono, white, red, blue, yellow, green and black, the black hat is to imagine everything possible that may go wrong and to build capabilities for it.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: In Finland, during the World War II, the Finns suffered greatly as a result of being cut off from imports.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Today, the Finns would study anything that would possibly go wrong and prepare for it, never again to repeat history.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Then, many say it was paranoid, excess, a waste of public funds.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: But for catastrophic event for once in 100 years, I say it is for survival.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We had the oil crisis of 1970s, the economic crisis, SARS and global economic crisis of 2008.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We also had our fair share of destructions throughout the years, some more dire consequences than others.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: But what's fresh in our minds was the COVID-19 pandemic and the conflict between Ukraine and Russia.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: It reviewed the vulnerabilities and independence of the global economy.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: First, medical supplies and equipment were in short supply.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Then, food shortages worldwide, with rising prices of fertiliser, oil and grain, amongst many others.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: This was a race for resources and for survival.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We must remember that, to survive, it is not just the 10th person or the black hat, but the contributions of all five other hats, doing their best to be innovative and creative with balance and poise, emotive and inclusive, building and fighting a strong team for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: In my maiden speech two years ago, I shared the importance of relevance and how Temasek's 700 years of history had its fair share of turmoil and success.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Last year, I spoke on the dramatic rise of China's AI development and holding more AI patterns than any other country.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Today, we observe the emergence of ChatGPT and other tools, reading articles on Google's Survivor and Meta Facebook existential struggles.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The pace of innovation, technological change and relevance is constantly shifting, more dramatic, the stakes much higher, opportunities and threats at every turn.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Singapore has been building his capability since our Independence, a strong banking and financial system, robust and progressive public housing.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Robust because HDB has enhanced our public housing for seismic events – earthquakes.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: For food, with several months of strategic reserves – rice, eggs, poultry, vegetables.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Reserves to rebuild our entire country in disastrous calamity.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: How do we retool our entire workforce when needed?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Do we shrug our shoulders and say, it is just bad luck, it is beyond our control?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: I say, let us continue to prepare for our survival.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We've heard those who suggested that we should prepare less, do less, take our time.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We can cut the little and assume disasters and its recovery is preordained.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We are not in the interest in building the country for a lifetime, but on a journey of building a country for many lifetimes – 100 years, 1,000 years, 10,000 years.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Yes, no civilisation has existed that long yet.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We may fail, but we will do our utmost.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: One of Mr Lee Kuan Yew's most memorable quotes, "Over 100 years, this was a mudflat.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Ten years from now, this will be a metropolis.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Today, we are here but we have not arrived.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We must never think that we have arrived.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We are on a journey, building a country and nation to thrive for 1,000 years and beyond.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Aged care is another area that is close to my heart.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Indeed, this topic is part of the everyday conversations I have with my senior residents when I talk to them in my house visits, or at the void decks, coffee shops, neighbourhood parks or the Active Ageing Centres (AACs) in Hougang.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Wong said that as part of the Forward Singapore exercise, the Government is studying how it can enhance the range of care and support options within the community and this includes the operating model of AACs and how it can strengthen and coordinate the providers in the aged care sector which is highly fragmented today.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I must admit having had similar experience when I tried to help some of my Hougang residents navigate their way through the system especially when it comes to different needs or problems.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I do agree with the need to review and sharpen how our AACs or eldercare centres can better serve the needs of our seniors in their cluster in a more holistic manner, all the more with Healthier SG coming on.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We should work towards centres which cater to different needs of seniors whether social or medical.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: And when it comes to so-called more specialist areas like mental health, disabled persons who are seniors, the centres should still be the referring centres even if other organisations or sub-units are involved.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In this way, seniors living in the cluster will be better served with less confusion and bureaucracy.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Centre staff will also have better knowledge of seniors under their care.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I would also like to repeat my call in my speech during the Healthier SG debate to the Ministry of Health (MOH) to study how outreach efforts can be made more effectively to seniors who are not active in the AACs, the eldercare centres or stay in touch with the centre staff or even with their neighbours, so that such seniors can better receive the intended care and support under Healthier SG as well as under the cluster support which can be provided by AACs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I understand that for purposes of mean-testing, the income of all family members living in the same household is taken into consideration.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Specifically, the monthly household income per person is used to determine the amount of subsidy allocated to eligible seniors.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: However, where households have no income, such as a retired couple or a retired single person, consideration for subsidies take into consideration the annual value of such retired seniors' residence.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: For retired seniors living alone and with no source of income, any increase in medical expenses adds burden and pressure.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Even if they can theoretically downgrade to a smaller or cheaper home, this may not always be an appropriate solution and it could be for a variety of reasons including mental health.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Some, if not many, may have bought into the notion that their house is an appreciating asset and it cannot be let go.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: There are seniors in my constituency who have continued to live in the same flats even when mobility issues and lack of lift access meant that they hardly left home or preferred to be physically carried to the next floor for lift access when they had to go out.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Telling people to downgrade and/or shift to different home is never as easy and definitely not an empathetic solution.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Wong also said that while nursing homes are suitable for the elderly with high care needs and little to no family support, we cannot rely on this as the mainstream solution.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: A few years ago, MOH began efforts to ramp up nursing homes.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In June last year, we were told that MOH planned to double the number of nursing home beds to more than 31,000 in the next 10 years.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I am reminded of this issue as I recalled being told by a resident last year how his father had to wait for some time to be allocated a nursing home.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This was under category 4 care, even though there were beds available for other categories of nursing home care.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This issue was also brought up by my colleague Sengkang Member of Parliament Mr Louis Chua not long ago.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Next, I would like to touch briefly on the proposed changes in this Budget to the Working Mother's Child Relief from 2024 onwards.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: At the onset, this relief is meant to encourage working mothers to stay on at work after having children by having a fairly significant tax relief.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Under the existing scheme, working mothers are entitled to a fixed percentage of income reliefs for every child.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The reliefs are capped at a maximum of 25%.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Essentially, such a change benefits the lower income earning working mother but for middle income earning working mothers from, say, $4,200 per month possibly onwards, they will experience relatively lower income reliefs from 2024 onwards as compared to what they are entitled to.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: If so, like what the hon member for Sengkang GRC Mr Louis Chua has said, why not just give a motherhood tax rebate to lower income working mothers and if the tax rebates exceed the tax payable, tax credits can be paid out in cash?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Regardless of the Government's intention, I think it sends a discouraging signal to affected working mothers and takes the shine off the originally intended symbolism of this scheme.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I am not sure this is the right signal to be sent to our working mothers.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Moreover, it is unfair to penalise only mothers who give birth or have children from 2024 onwards.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Also, there are many working women who may have married later and/or those who struggle with infertility and some of these already come with additional costs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The change may also inadvertently apply time pressure which is unfair to these women.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The Government has said that these for Singapore require catalysing business transformation, investing in low-carbon technologies, pursuing effective international cooperation and adopting low-carbon practices.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: These key thrusts are indeed necessary to achieve Singapore's net-zero ambition.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: However, we also need a check on demand.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: While we adopt low-carbon technologies, such as carbon capture, utilisation and storage and low-carbon hydrogen for industrial heating, we must not feel that this helps to decouple industrial growth from the carbon constraint and that it allows us to continue business-as-usual.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We live in an increasingly carbon-constrained world and we must downsize or allow carbon inefficient activities to leave our economy to decarbonise effectively.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In order to do this, we need a detailed roadmap for re-training workers in these sectors as Singapore intentionally decarbonises.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The management of transition of businesses and workers in carbon-intensive sectors contributes to a just-transition.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: SkillsFuture Singapore's Skills Demand for the Future Economy (SDFE) Report 2022 identified sustainability skills as one that has high demand and transferability.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Yet, between the need to reskill and retrain our workers, and them actually acquiring the skills and applying it to their existing job functions or in new roles, there is a time lag.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Understandably, businesses and workers need time to transition and pick up these new sustainability skills and transit to new jobs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I noted in my last Budget Debate speech that there were around 27,000 people employed in this sector in 2020, and I focused on the manpower transition and asked how the Government intends to manage the green transition, specifically in the petrochemicals industry.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: A year on, this is still a question mark and a concern of mine.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Do we have sufficient sustainability-related courses that businesses and workers can afford to attend, both in terms of time and money?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: How much more time will it take for the learning to be internalised and applied?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We must take deliberate steps to help workers transition and we have to do so mindfully, since jobs today still need to be done.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: But we can and must afford workers the time and resources needed to attend training, make it easier for course providers to provide subsidies, such as SkillsFuture Singapore funding to workers and to be patient as the learning-doing gap is bridged over time.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I hope to hear some update on the progress made last year for green transition in the petrochemicals industry, generally, as well as on the issues of manpower transition.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: If, indeed, the Government expects that emissions may peak earlier than 2030, it is even more critical to have an accelerated timeline for our manpower transition.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: While the vehicular road tax changes for EVs last year, coupled with the increase in petrol prices in Singapore in the last half a year, might have made EVs a little bit more attractive to would-be buyers, it would be helpful to have a detailed roadmap on EV roll-out, so that consumers can make informed choices earlier.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In addition to a strategic plan that defines a goal or desired outcome, a roadmap must also include the major steps or milestones needed to reach it.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Currently, the EV vision still lacks some more details on the steps and milestones.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Some key issues with EVs today include battery reliability, software problems and the lack of local infrastructures for charging EVs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It also remains unclear how fast certain logistics fleets, including but not limited to light goods vehicles, will be switching to EVs entirely and a number of prominent logistics companies have not yet made any plans, or have not announced any plans for EV conversion, or some have made only preliminary plans for limited initial conversion.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Yesterday's announcement of 2,000 EV charging points being slated to be installed in one-third of HDB carparks by the end of the year, is a welcome development.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I know Minister Iswaran explained at the EV Charging Bill debate that we are dealing with an evolving space, that the technology is evolving, the adoption rates and, therefore, the consequential demand are also changing and the usage patterns, both in terms of driving and charging habits, have yet to normalise.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I certainly hope this data will be out sooner, and meaningful and adequate adjustments will be made quickly, so that at least we can work towards ramping up on the EV conversion rate sooner.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: As we move towards active mobility, there may also be a case for allowing charging stations to be more flexible, to be able to charge other mobility devices, such as electric bikes to cover the last mile distance.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Since our national grid is still mostly powered by natural gas, I would also like to ask the Minister to elaborate on whether the Government is considering increasing the renewable energy choices for EV drivers.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Can the Ministry provide an update on whether the EV Common Charger Grant allows or encourages the building of chargers powered by solar or renewable energy?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: For example, given that some 40,000 chargers, of the 60,000 to be rolled out by 2030, will be in public carparks, is it possible to have some of these powered directly from some of the solar panels fitted on top of the multi-storey car parks and what are some of the challenges to doing this?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Presently, Sembcorp and Shell have faster-charging, solar powered stations but the reach is still limited as Sembcorp's solar powered EV charging hub only caters to their electric trucks and there are still too few stations offering renewable energy options.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: But may I also ask whether there are plans to roll out policies to incentivise more logistics companies to switch from ICE vehicles to EVs?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: So, may I ask whether the Government has staged plans on the conversion of these heavy vehicles, be they heavier vehicles or logistics vehicles or other types of heavy vehicles, and whether to electric, hydrogen or other fuel types, given the stated challenges?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: And what is the road map for this?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Will this affect our plans for 2030 and beyond?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Regardless of the classes of goods and different heavy vehicles, there is, of course, a need to look into the time taken to charge industrial vehicles as the owning companies will be concerned with efficiency.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Regular drivers may also be concerned with efficiency and securing a charger for when they most need one.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This is not to forget that, at least, certain categories of commercial, or even industrial vehicles, may be sharing charging points with passenger and other types of lighter vehicles.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: A detailed EV roadmap can also outline pricing, power rating and plug type to enable all EV drivers to plan their charging schedules, including real-time charging updates, which is currently not available on the MyTransport.SG app.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As the world is working to recover from the COVID-19 slump, the war in Ukraine, global supply chain disruptions and soaring global interest rates are just some unforeseen factors which has caused prices to go up in the past year.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The main focus of my speech today is very specific.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is on retirement adequacy for Singaporeans – how do we ensure that our people have enough to sustain their way of life after they stop working or as they grow older.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: To me, it is a slow boil concern or a clear long-term concern which needs to be raised now.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I decided to focus on retirement adequacy because Budget 2023 has brought the following three issues to the fore.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Second, as the Deputy Prime Minister has explained – while the Government will do its part to help, it is not sustainable to rely entirely on the Government to take care of our retirees.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: A significant part of the burden of care will fall on families and future generations, if we fail to plan adequately for our own retirement.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Third, the recent episodes of global uncertainty and inflation has shown us that unforeseen economic shocks can cause our money to be worth less in real terms.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, delaying in taking action on retirement adequacy has an impact on future Budgets, and that is why I am raising it now.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The main feature of Singapore's retirement planning system is the Central Provident fund (CPF), which Singaporeans are well-acquainted with and needs no introduction.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There are other schemes and Government programmes aimed at helping retirees, but these are designed around and in addition to the CPF system.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I will address our retirement planning system in three parts: first, the accumulation of retirement funds; second, the leakages of retirement funds; and third, retirement payouts – in that order.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The worker is made to save up to 20% of his wages.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The employer contributes an additional amount of 7.5% to 17% of the worker's wages, which is not subject to personal income tax.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Given the investment environment where stocks and bonds have been underperforming, I would like to take this opportunity to ask what is the net cost to the Government in delivering the higher-than-market interest rates on CPF funds in the past few years?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But first, I am heartened by the steps taken by the Government to bring more workers under the CPF umbrella more fully.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, this enforced long-term saving will naturally reduce the take-home pay of these platform workers, and I look forward to hearing the Minister for Manpower's plans to provide the CPF Transition Support to lower-income platform workers, who see an increase in their CPF contribution rates during the Committee of Supply.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But, one particular question that I have is whether such additional support will be available to platform workers aged 30 and above, who opt in to the full CPF contribution regime, or is it limited to platform workers below 30, who are mandated to contribute at the full employee contribution rate?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In the same vein, are there other groups which we are looking to bring under the CPF umbrella, or to enhance their participation in the CPF contribution regime?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For example, self-employed persons (SEPs) are presently only required to contribute a percentage of their net trade income to their MediSave Account, but not to their Special or Retirement Account.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But, has the Government done any studies on the proportion of SEPs who are able to meet the same amount, whether in voluntary CPF savings or their own private savings?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is important as it would mean future Budgets may need to address this.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As an advisor to the National Trades Union Congress (NTUC)-affiliated Education Services Union, or ESU, one of the first groups of SEPs that I think of, are the freelance adult educators who work across the early childhood, student care, universities, private education institutions and international schools.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: My understanding is that some of these adult educators work with their education institutions on the basis of longer-term contracts.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There is, thus, very little difference between these adult educators and platform workers.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Is there scope to also align the CPF contribution rates of these adult educators, such that they will benefit from additional contributions from the education institutions?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The announced CPF Transition Offset will help, but technically, there will still be a higher cost to employ someone who is between 55 and 70 years old.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The chilling effect would be a bad thing because active employment allows seniors to stay physically and mentally active, and to be engaged with a community.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: That is, in fact, part of our strategy of preventive care, as Deputy Prime Minister Wong had explained in his Budget Statement.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: My view is that we must pair these higher CPF contribution rates for older workers, with other incentives or measures, to encourage the employment of older workers, which I think the Government has done so.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But besides general training and reskilling efforts, what are we doing on that front beyond what we have already done?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can the Public Service, for example, take the lead in identifying roles that are suitable for older workers and perhaps "ring-fence" these opportunities for older candidates?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This appears to target workers earning more than $6,000 monthly.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Does the Government consider this group to be at-risk of retirement adequacy as well?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: One would expect this group to be capable of going out and investing in their own endowment insurance or other instruments for the longer term.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The aggressive rate hikes by the US Federal Reserve and other global central banks have led interest rates in the open Singapore market to cross the 4% mark earlier this year, up from an almost 0% interest rate from the large part of 2009 to 2021.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This has made the 2.5% interest rate for the CPF Ordinary Account and the 4% interest rate for the Special and Medisave Accounts relatively unattractive compared to the other investment options like fixed deposits.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I would love to hear Deputy Prime Minister’s reply to this.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: When I raised my Adjournment Motion on "Helping Singaporeans Navigate a High-Interest Rate Environment" in October 2022, I noted that HDB and CPF confirmed that rates will remain unchanged until the end of 2022 but did not receive any more advanced guidance on any potential rate changes over the medium term.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Fourth, and in my view most importantly, we must look to bridge the financial literacy gap and ensure that the majority of Singaporeans think about how they are going to grow their funds for retirement.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is important to get Singaporeans to "buy in" to planning for their own retirement adequacy.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Not only do individuals know their own needs and circumstances best, it is also critical for our governance and social trust for Singaporeans to appreciate that the CPF is designed for their long-term benefit and not some plan by an overreaching Government to keep people out of their hard-earned money.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While I am aware of the CPF’s efforts to raise awareness and literacy of retirement planning, such as through talks, webinars and roadshows, how effective has such outreach efforts been?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And what are the metrics that are applied to gauge the effectiveness of these educational efforts?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: From speaking to residents at my Toa Payoh East Financial Literacy Programme, a grassroots initiative led by volunteers and me, I have also found that some of our fellow Singaporeans are not aware of the various options and avenues that are available for them to plan and grow their retirement nest egg.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For example, some residents were not aware of the Supplementary Retirement Scheme (SRS) which complements the CPF by affording Singaporeans the opportunity to make tax-free investments for the purpose of retirement.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is also important to ensure top-ups for non-working women homemakers in our community who may lack enough CPF for their old age.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It needs to be decided at key turning points like at 55 years old.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, we besides encouraging more members to transfer their CPF savings above what they require for the Basic Retirement Sum to their spouses’ Special or Retirement Accounts, we should do more for this group.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This will allow both husband and wife to take full advantage of the extra interest on lower balances and enjoy a higher effective interest rate overall.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: On that note, perhaps we can mimic the successful LumiHealth app and design an interactive mode for Singaporeans to learn more about the mechanics of CPF and retirement planning.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Instead of walking and reading about healthy diets to chalk up milestone points and exchange for supermarket vouchers, Singaporeans can be incentivised to read or watch an informational video or even to practise using certain helpful tools like the CPF Planner for Retirement Income.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Unlike other publicly managed pension schemes elsewhere, the CPF does not include social risk pooling and redistributive elements.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Accordingly, the main challenge of our CPF policy is to ensure that not too much capital is withdrawn by the CPF member himself or herself during his or her working life and before retirement.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: One of the largest withdrawals that members make before retirement is for housing.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, if the concern today is more of retirement adequacy, is it time to look into adjusting the allocation ratios such that a greater percentage is allocated into the Special Account instead of the Ordinary and MediSave Accounts?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: One benefit of adjusting only the allocations of contributions rather than requiring more money to be contributed is that it will avoid increasing the financial burden on both employers and employees.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Among other suggestions in the report to improve the system further, it was proposed that Singapore should increase the age at which members can access their savings set aside for retirement as life expectancies rise.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is so that retirement funds are not drawn down too early.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: At this juncture, I am not in support of increasing the drawdown age purely on average life expectancy data.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There are a significant number of seniors in my constituency of Toa Payoh East and they have shared with me their real fears that they may pass on any time even as others are living longer lives.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Some of them have pre-existing medical conditions which only adds to their anxiety.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: To the contrary, would the Government consider permitting earlier drawdown of retirement funds for specified purposes, such as defraying medical bills for pre-existing medical conditions or obtaining more comprehensive medical or disability insurance coverage?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We obviously do not want Singaporeans to withdraw their retirement funds early only to blow it all at a casino, but the purposes which I have just described are in fact the costs and risks that we want to help our seniors manage.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Ultimately, as the CPF system was created specifically to fulfil multiple goals, including housing, healthcare and education, it has built-in leakages from retirement savings.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, we must still ensure that these allowed drawdowns from CPF money do not compromise an individual’s ability to save enough for retirement.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Where the BRS and FRS increases from cohort to cohort due to inflation, will we be expecting a sharp jump for the upcoming cohorts given the dramatic increase in prices and interest rates over the years?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If so, do we need to cater special assistance for more people who may not be able to meet their BRS or FRS?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This increase is targeted at seniors who are receiving the lowest payouts under the RSS.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Based on the CPF Board’s press release, about 112,000 members are expected to benefit from June 2023.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But what is that proportion of beneficiaries by percentage of the total number of seniors receiving CPF payouts?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And what is the range of monthly payouts that eligible Singaporeans now receive under the RSS or CPF LIFE?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With the rising prices today, is $350 per month enough to sustain a decent standard of living?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I appreciate that there are other benefit schemes that less well-to-do seniors can turn to in order to supplement their CPF payouts.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For example, through the payments under the Silver Support Scheme, ComCare and others.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Seniors can even monetise their housing through schemes such as the Lease Buyback Scheme and the Silver Housing Bonus, by reselling any excessively long remaining leases on their HDB flat to the Government or by right-sizing to a smaller flat type in retirement.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But do we presently have the ability to collate the data showing the support that each senior is receiving across the various schemes and programmes administered by different Ministries and agencies?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: That will give us a fuller picture of our seniors’ retirement adequacy and the gaps we should look to plug.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I am cognisant that the CPF Board already offers such an exercise when members approach 55 years old, but my suggestion is to go a bit further and provide such advice at earlier milestones or stages in one’s life.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This idea is not unlike the Jobs-Skills Integrators that has been announced to optimise training and job placement.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Instead of bridging the industry, training providers and employers, the "Retirement Planners" will bridge the gap between our lower to middle-income Singaporeans, financial advisors and the different government agencies administering the schemes that are applicable to them.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Before I end, Mr Speaker, I would like to declare that I was a part of the CPF advisory panel which came up with the recommendations for changes in 2015 and 2016.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Being on the panel opened my eyes on issues about CPF and the trade-offs to be made.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The panel was guided by three key considerations and the need to achieve a reasonable balance between them: (i) adequacy, (ii) flexibility and (iii) simplicity.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, I am mindful that as I talk about adequacy today, there needs to be reasonable balance across many other issues.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What I found was that the CPF system is fundamentally sound and has served Singaporeans well.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The recommendations then and in the past has helped improve the CPF further by providing greater certainty and assurance to CPF members while providing the flexibility of more payout and withdrawal options in retirement to meet the varied needs of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But we must ensure that the CPF system continues to remain relevant for Singaporeans today and in the years to come given the changes in the economic dynamics globally and domestically.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There are a few things I would like to suggest before I end.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Second, the panel then had recommended that for providing flexibility for an additional CPF LIFE plan with escalating payouts.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is meant to provide an option for members who prefer CPF payouts that are initially lower but rise with time to help with increases in the cost of living.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Hopefully all members in this Chamber know that there is an existing CPF LIFE plan that you can choose from.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The ability of Singaporeans to take care of their own retirement will also prevent the buck from being passed to our children and future generations of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is therefore central to our strategy in our future Budgets to renew ourselves as a country and to stay ahead of the world.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While providing the much-needed support to cushion the impact of inflation, I am glad that this year’s Budget continues to give emphasis to the importance of growth, attracting high-quality investments and investing in growth sectors where Singapore can continue to differentiate and be competitive.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: One of my residents said when I met him at a recent house visit, “Regardless of support given by the Government, high costs will continue for some time.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We need to also have a longer-term solution centred on growth.” Deputy Prime Minister Wong had said that, “Our best strategy to cope with inflation is to make ourselves more productive and competitive – so that our workers can earn more, and the increase in earnings can more than make up for the higher prices.” Growth does not automatically increase wages and Deputy Prime Minister Wong outlined the other key thrusts of this year’s Budget to equip our workers for good jobs and to strengthen our social compact to enable all Singaporeans regardless of their circumstances to move forward together in this new era.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: In my speech, I will cover the following areas: one, opportunities and preparing Singaporeans so that they are able to get good jobs and aligning skills training with jobs; two, structure of work and support for workers who have caregiving roles to enable them to stay in the workforce; and three, some of measures in the Budget and their impact on Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While there are opportunities, with the current economic conditions, disruptions as well as uncertainties, business will be required to adapt and to transform to stay relevant and competitive.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: New skills will be required and jobs will change.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This will impact young graduates entering the workforce as well as workers already in the workforce.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Better aligning skills training to jobs will benefit not only our workers but more importantly ensure the right skills and workers for businesses.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: In our Government Parliamentary Committee (GPC)’s engagement with business leaders, a key challenge they highlighted is the difficulty in finding the right skills for roles, and this is impacting their operations and ability to take on opportunities and grow.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I wish to seek clarifications regarding the Jobs-Skills Integrators as the devil is in the details.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: From what has been shared by Deputy Prime Minister Wong in his speech, the Jobs-Skills Integrators are required to identify skills gaps, scope appropriate training programmes and identify the profile of individuals for training and upskilling to fill the required roles.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: My questions are, how will the selection or appointment of the Jobs-Skills Integrators be done?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Who or which organisations can qualify to take on the role of the Jobs-Skills Integrators?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Apart from engaging enterprises and stakeholders to understand the manpower and skills gap in the sector, will there be support given to them?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: How will those who are seeking to enter the workforce, those who have been displaced or retrenched or those seeking a career transition engage with the Jobs-Skills Integrators?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Will the scope of the Job-Skills Integrators include working with businesses to align career planning and training to upskill their employees to stay relevant as the businesses transform?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I know there are a lot of questions!

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, let me now talk a little about senior employability.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With longer life expectancy and healthier longevity, a senior can continue to work productively and lead a meaningful life and seniors are a valuable pool of talent for businesses.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: In November last year, I raised an Adjournment Motion on Senior Employability.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I shared the feedback gathered from our PAP Senior Group (PAP.SG)'s efforts to reach out to hear the voices of seniors employed and unemployed, to understand their experience and the challenges they faced in finding employment.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Our engagements both online and through focus group discussions, allowed us to examine the matter from the perspectives of seniors and stakeholders, such as employers, HR professionals, younger workers who work with seniors and organisations such as NUHS who work on active ageing initiatives.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: All stakeholders agreed that it is not just the number of seniors being employed but the quality of the jobs and the work experience of seniors as well as seniors being able to fulfill the requirements of available jobs.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: What roles are seniors employed for in these organisations?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: As job-skills integration is implemented, we should take the insights to help with the understanding of what structural intervention is required to make learning as systemic for workers in the workplace as it is for the young in formal education.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: There should be multiple routes connecting the roles, opportunities and commitments of individuals throughout their adult lives.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We need to understand and support individuals to learn, work and age well throughout their lives, that fit their life stages and their abilities.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: If we are able to do this, it will grow a strong talent base and capabilities for businesses and provide fulfilling careers for workers.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Budget 2023 outlined the importance of the family as the foundation of our society and enabling a Singapore Made for Families.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The Budget sets out support for young Singaporeans to meet their housing aspirations and significantly increasing financial support for parents in the child’s early years as well as an increase in paternity leave.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With an ageing population and people living longer, families are multi-generational and caregiving needs will increase.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With smaller families, some families need to care for both the young and seniors.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While the Budget provides support for seniors, the enhancement to the care and support options for seniors in the community is still under study as part of the Forward Singapore exercise.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The "infrastructure" and services as well as resources and capabilities to support seniors to age well in the community need to be increased especially as our population is ageing rapidly.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Without such support, those providing caregiving will find it difficult to manage employment and caregiving responsibilities.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Just as working parents seek quality childcare for their children, families with seniors also require centres that provide not only care for our seniors but also keep them meaningfully engaged.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We are fortunate that in my constituency that we have service providers and centres that give quality care and have meaningful programmes to engage and help our seniors stay active.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The programmes are well attended and there is a waiting list for a place at the senior care centre.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Seniors and their families share with me the value that these programmes provide and the services contribute to the well-being of the seniors as well as their families.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: A point I wish to highlight and I hope that Deputy Prime Minister Wong would consider is the affordability of eldercare services for families that qualify for only a small amount of subsidies or do not qualify for any subsidies for eldercare services.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While we must provide lower-income families with more help, we need to also look at how we support Singaporean families to care for their seniors just as we support all Singaporean families to care for their young children as announced in this Budget without means testing.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The cost of eldercare services is not insignificant.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I took these numbers from the AIC portal.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: For families that have both young children and seniors to care for, these expenses can put a strain on finances.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: As we plan for funding and support to increase the capacity and capability for quality senior care and services in the community, I do hope that access and affordability of quality and appropriate care for seniors in the community is not focused only on the lower-income.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This is not only for the well-being of seniors but is important support for families and Singapore to enable our seniors to age well in the community.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: During my dialogue on the Budget last weekend with residents and feedback received when I visited residents, several highlighted the importance of work or organisational culture that understand and supports parenting and caregiving.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Having financial support, work arrangements and policies that support parenting and caregiving are important.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But this must be complemented with a work culture that empowers and fosters an environment of mutual trust amongst employers and workers, and between workers.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: CPF wage ceiling increase from $6,000 to $8,000.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This will help middle-income earners earning more than $6,000 per month as their employers will now contribute more to your CPF which will increase their retirement savings.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: However, my resident shared with me that this does affect his monthly take home pay as he will have to contribute to this as well.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: My residents did share that while the employees benefit in growing their retirement savings, in a time of pressing and increasing inflation, we must recognise that this results in less cash for their monthly spending.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I just wanted to share the feedback on the impact in a time of inflation now.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The other measure is the Working Mothers Child Relief (WMCR), which I think many have spoken on.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The intent of the change will enable lower- to middle-income working mothers to get more tax relief.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The WMCR tax relief is to encourage women to continue working after they are married and have given birth to or adopted children.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The feedback I have received is that, and this is not just with the change, but over the years, when this was in place, many working mothers share with me that this tax relief does mean quite a bit to them.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We are setting our ambition to continue to grow and to enable opportunity for all.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: In our new social compact, we are appealing for all to do their part, and for those who have more to give more, while we ensure that we give support to those who need help.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This will enable those who are doing well to continue to do well, and for all to have the opportunity to succeed and do better for themselves and their families.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I also declare, Sir, my speech today will be heavily informed by my experience as a trade association president.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I will be speaking on strengthening tripartism as a pillar of economic resilience in the new era.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: As a global city that built our fortune on trade, Singapore is particularly susceptible to global and regional developments.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The hon Deputy Prime Minister’s observations include that we have now entered into an era of zero-sum thinking with countries turning inward, looking at national gain and security rather than inter-dependence.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Importantly, the hon Deputy Prime Minister observed that this is a system that is less hospitable to small, and may I add outward-oriented, economies like Singapore and that we thus cannot assume that we will continue to be successful by simply doing the things we had in the past.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: We therefore need to build our national resilience on several fronts.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: But with regard to positioning our economy and businesses, this process had in fact started much earlier.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Industry Transformation Maps had been introduced in 2016 covering 23 industries to look at what these industries needed to do to promote growth, remain competitive and seize future opportunities.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Several years have passed since then and the ITMs are now going through a review, and the refreshed ITMs that take into consideration current realities are being launched.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In my view, the most important characteristic of the ITMs is something that has underpinned Singapore’s economic success and labour relations for decades.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This is our unique tripartism: Government, labour and business at the same table, trashing things out and coming to mutually-satisfactory policies and plans for the good of each industry and its workers.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: As a trade association president, I have been involved in the process.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: And the process works but it works best only insofar as parties come to the table understanding that this is an exercise in negotiation.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In the words of Mr Lim Swee Say, its objective is to achieve harmony, not just compromise.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Sometimes, interests align completely and it is easy to come to a landing point.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Most of the time there are protracted negotiations, seeking to reconcile polar positions.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: But it is precisely because each party has its own way of looking at things and its own considerations – all of course legitimate – that this tripartite process has its value.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: To me, our tripartism is a pillar of economic resilience and it is a force that will position us well in the new era.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: First, we should strengthen sectoral trade association involvement on tripartite platforms, even as we have the Singapore National Employer’s Federation (SNEF) as the overall key tripartite partner representing businesses.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Part of the ITM Refresh has been the move to cluster industries that are part of a broader industry sector and/or that have synergies with each other.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I think this is an excellent development with regard to the ITMs because it will encourage pollination across industries, that can result in higher productivity and new business opportunities.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The security industry comes under the Built Environment Cluster.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: A SNEF representative was appointed, instead, to represent our industry, together with a Government official.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In other words, our intended role was not to participate, but to merely to spectate.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: So, we wrote in a strongly-worded letter to try to understand why the composition of the committee was as such.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This, Sir, is not a matter of just being FOMO, or Fear of Missing Out.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: But of course, we would not want to miss out on the opportunity to get our industry involved in the larger transformation effort and to represent our industry because we are well-placed to do so.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: But why did we have to fight for this seat in the first place when we are the lead trade association in our sector?

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: SNEF, Sir, is the key tripartite partner at the national level, representing employers and businesses.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: But the sectoral trade associations have our ear on the ground and know the unique situations that our businesses face.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This is especially so when we look at clustering where we now have many industries at the table and some industries may have an adverse position, vis-à-vis other industries.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This is something that that has actually happened.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Can SNEF truly be an advocate for several industries on the same table?

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I confess that I do not know if SAS' experience is widespread or common or whether we are a unique case.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: But writ large, our tripartism will be strengthened if we include the sectoral trade associations as real partners with real participation at the table.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Separately, given how ubiquitous SNEF is, I think that SNEF has more engagement with the sectoral trade associations in order to be an effective tripartite partner.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This is something that I will take up with SNEF directly.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: On the Government's part, it should expect this of its tripartite partner and should query when SNEF makes representations on behalf of specific industries as to whether it had consulted with the relevant trade associations.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, SAS is a member of SNEF and SNEF plays a very important role.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: But I do have a question as to whether SBF could also play a great role in the tripartite process.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: But of course, to sit at the seat, to sit at the table, does not mean that one just becomes happy about it and twiddles their thumbs.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: So, I am happy to report, Sir, that as regards SAS' involvement, we are very active.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: And we are working very closely with the hon Senior Minister of State Tan Kiat How and with our sister trade associations in the facility management sector to achieve, amongst other things, the elusive integrated and aggregated facility management.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: We are developing an online outcome-based tender generator that can be used by all the industries in the sector.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: We are cognisant that our seat was granted on request, not ex-officio.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: So, we take it upon ourselves therefore to show why we deserve to sit at the table and we will earn our seat with our effort.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: A TAC, Sir, is only as good as its secretariat, simply because the executive committee members are all running their own businesses and their involvement in the TAC is essentially a co-curricular activity (CCA).

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Of course, this support should not be as of right – one way to administer such support would be to ask TACs to submit their plans for the coming year and how these would meet certain objectives and their funding plan, and then, it would be for the administering authority to decide based on these submissions the headcount it would support, if any.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Such a scheme could be dovetailed with other workforce priorities, for example, extending the headcount support grant to only mature workers.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: One such possible programme could be the Jobs-Skills Integrators initiative announced in this Budget.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, Sir, I have instructed my own secretariat to look into how we could possibly play that role regardless of Government funding because I do see much value in this function.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This, of course again, should be offered only to trusted TACs that the Government has confidence in, in terms of being able to deliver as programme partner.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: If we are able to support more secretariat-capability initiatives and funding, then we are more likely to see more TACs that will be able to step up to play this partnership role.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This having been said, I am also cognisant that we do not want TACs to be overly dependent on Government funding.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Amongst other things, this could call into question their independence as tripartite partners.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: As such, TACs should also look at how to diversify their sources of revenue so that they are able to independently build their secretariat's capabilities and stand on their own feet.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Government funding, if made available, should only be seen as a catalyst and not a crutch.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Third, Sir, I would like to suggest allowing TAC involvement in employment dispute resolution processes where appropriate.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This is in particular because of the changing nature of the employer-employee relationship and the fact that many businesses are in the process of transforming, and where the manner of transformation is unique to each industry.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
