text: Businesses are trying their best to deal with a challenging environment, but importantly, many businesses are also trying to transform.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This transformation invariably affects their workers: how they employ them, on what terms and how or whether to maintain their employment.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: A recent case in point was that of a security agency being called out by the NTUC for "egregious behaviour".

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The agency had sought to increase the working hours of its staff with a concomitant increase in salary.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: It had prior to this sought to demote some of its officers, based on the Security Officer PWM ranks, which, according to the agency, was in order to right-size its workforce.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This is also to be expected as we continue to push for industry transformation, greater productivity and job re-design.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Some industries will feel this more acutely, like the tech and manufacturing industries, but also the PWM sectors because wage increases are artificially created by Government policies – artificially but necessarily created by Government policies, let me add.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Businesses must be nimble and flexible to be able to deal with these changing externalities.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: So, when I looked at the incident involving the security agency, my first reaction was: okay, maybe forcing a change in employment terms may not have been the best approach, but at least the agency is trying to retain its workers.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This is surely preferable to simply firing all of them in a retrenchment exercise.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Further to that, the agency was also taking proactive steps to prepare for a very significant change to the security PWM coming up next year – a change that is precisely designed to allow more flexibility for employers and employees to negotiate working hours.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: So, my first impression, of course, was that it was the correct intention, the correct objectives, but perhaps not the best execution.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: But execution, of course, can be adjusted and can be changed to become kosher.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: On the other hand, it is trite that employment terms should be varied by mutual agreement and should not be forced on employees.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, I can understand NTUC's position – surely if there is an arising possibility of a forced demotion or increase in working hours of a large number of workers, the union must jump, as it did.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: And the NTUC was actually very kind in that it raised the issue but did not name the company.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: However, as quickly as this came out in public, it fizzled out in the news as quickly leaving many in the industry somewhat bedazzled and confused as to what actually happened.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Business owners in the sector are now worried that the very industry transformation we had encouraged them to embark on, the very flexibility that we had told them would arise from the changes in the PWM in 2024, which would necessitate new types of employment contracts and new types of employment relationships, could now get them in trouble.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This definitely is a good outcome, but we are still left with many questions.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: But the question still continues to be out there as to whether there were forced demotions, or whether there were not.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Whether there were increases in working hours; and again, were these allowed?

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: So, we have to find some ways, Sir, to harmonise the public messaging to businesses so that while they are engaged in the process of transformation, of changing how their business operates, they are not getting mixed messages and they can figure out how they can move forward.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This will ensure that a cookie-cutter approach is not adopted in adjudicating employment disputes in the first instance.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: These experts are not supposed to advocate on behalf of the company, but to give industry-specific insights to the adjudicator and to the party on the other side.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Courts frequently allow for expert evidence and there are many cases in which judges have expressed, in their written grounds, appreciation for the expert's insights into the particular matter.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: For the avoidance of doubt, my suggestion extends to conciliation, mediation and other forms of alternative dispute resolution, and only where deemed appropriate and useful by the adjudicator.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: My suggestion does not extend to the Employment Claims Tribunal.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This would be especially effective if the offending company is a member of that trade association.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Where there are errant practices, it is often easier for a peer to point it out and to encourage one to do the right thing.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This builds and leverages on the existing tripartite relationship and can help to defuse tensions before parties start taking adversarial positions.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Of course, if the offending company still does not take the necessary corrective actions to the union and the employee's satisfaction, then there are procedures and processes that the aggrieved party can avail of.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: As our industries transform, more of such cases will arise.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: It is the union's duty and I know that it is one that it takes very seriously, to protect workers and to champion their rights.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: And of course, this is very important, and upcoming legislation like the fair consideration law will ensure further protection for our workers.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: But at the same time, we do not want to stifle industry transformation or to give mixed messages that would be counterproductive to the efforts of the ITMs.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The Budget Statement has also set out a very realistic assessment of the rapidly changing external environment in the new era and the urgency with which we need to build our resilience to deal with it.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Tripartism is a key pillar of our economic and social resilience.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I have made some suggestions as to how we can strengthen our tripartism and how we can get trade associations involved in a bigger way.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: With businesses and unions working together, with the leadership of an actively involved Government and Government agencies, I am confident that we will be able to meet the headwinds coming our way with confidence, and that Singapore will thrive in the new era.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Last year, I rose to speak on three areas in my Budget Debate speech to urge stronger efforts by our Government to ensure: one, social mobility amidst COVID-19, economic restructuring and digitalisation; two, managing long-term healthcare needs; and three, fulfilling the housing aspirations of our younger generation.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I want to thank all Government officers and stakeholders for the contributions you have made, in making progress on all these fronts in the past year.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For this year's Budget, I would like to continue focusing my speech on considerations and support for our working adults, our seniors, our young couples and families.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In my Jalan Kayu constituency, the largest segment of residents is aged between 20 and 60 years.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This phase of life covers most of our productive work years, from getting our first job to staying gainfully employed over the decades and hopefully looking forward to retirement with confidence and comfort.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Yet, we know that the realities in this age range is far from easy going, especially in a world of high global competition, slowing social mobility and prolonged ageing population.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While I was delighted to read the recent Straits Times article on 21 February 2023 that more fresh university graduates in full-time permanent roles – comprising 87.5% of the cohort – have gotten higher pay, I wonder about the 6.3% who are in freelance or part-time or temporary employment and the 3.6% who remained unemployed and are still looking for a job.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For these unemployed or under-employed graduates, while the proportion is small, the question is if their progression would inevitably be pushed behind their peers.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What about the non-graduates who completed their highest education in polytechnic or ITE?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I do not have to belabour the well-known projection that we will have one in four Singaporeans over 65 years old by 2030.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Maximising the potential and progression of every cohort of our young Singaporeans graduating from universities, polytechnics or ITEs from now on, is ever more pressing to help them manage the burden that they will carry as our population continues to age.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We must constantly mitigate against the risks of Singapore's economic dynamism and competitiveness with a potentially shrinking pool of working adults.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: SMEs make up a significant portion of the total number of enterprises in Singapore, at about 99% of all enterprises and supporting 71% of total employment in 2021.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As working adults enter their mid-lives in their forties and fifties, I am assured that attention continues to be given to help them keep pace with changes and stay employed.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I look forward to the implementation of the new Jobs-Skills Integrators initiative, especially on the data on how the new effort is improving the job and skill matches of mature workers to help them remain employable.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The efforts for more vulnerable groups, including low-wage workers, seniors wishing to continue work, ex-offenders and persons with disabilities, are also important to ensure an inclusive workforce.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I will speak more about employment for persons with disabilities in my Committee of Supply cuts.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Now, let me move to the next group, to another important group of Singaporeans – our seniors.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In my Jalan Kayu constituency, they make up about 22% of our residents if we count above 60 years old but a lower 8% if we count above 70 years old.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This presents opportunities for us to promote preventive health and chronic disease awareness and management actively in my constituency, to help our residents take charge of their health from their early senior years.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Therefore, I keenly look forward to the rollout of the Healthier SG later this year, which I spoke in support of during the White Paper debate and will speak more about during my Committee of Supply cuts.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our grassroots leaders proactively piloted our first Jalan Kayu Community Health Club (JKCHC) in February to begin to connect the ecosystem of regional health partners, family doctors, social and sports agencies as well as community groups to complement the national Healthier SG rollout at our local level.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, even as we step up efforts to manage our own health better as we age, there will always be a segment of more vulnerable seniors who need more help.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With the current elevated inflation, we need to continue to assure a common seniors' concern of "money not enough" when they no longer have active recurring employment income.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The slew of support under the permanent GST voucher scheme and enhanced Assurance Package is most welcomed.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, there must continue to be considerations for also non-monetary support such as the expansion of Active Ageing Centres, Senior Day Care Centres and Dementia Day Care Centres across Singapore.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We must not stop at just estates with higher concentration of lower-income seniors but care for seniors living also in private estates who may be seemingly asset rich but are genuinely cash poor.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In the older landed private estates like Seletar Hills in my constituency, I often come across residents in their retirement who have purchased their houses decades ago when the prices were way below the current market prices.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many understandably stay on because of the familiarity of the environment.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They too need eldercare support funded by the Government.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I will speak more about this during my Committee of Supply cuts.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Lastly, supporting our young people, young couples and families.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I resonate with the aspirations of our young people, couples and families because I was also young once.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, I would like to go more upstream and suggest that the Government enable more resources to enable social interactions among our young people.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Of the other 50% who are not dating, 38% of those said that they have not dated before.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Fifty-eight percent of them expressed having a limited social circle and 57% of them said that they do not have many opportunities to meet potential partners.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Although there has been a growing acceptance for online dating methods, most individuals still prefer meeting potential partners through more organic and face-to-face meetings – 80% of them, through that survey.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A more local community approach may be a suitable alternative for the Government to consider to encourage more organic social mingling.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As this is a Budget that prepares Singaporeans for the future era, I hope that the Government will be open to investing money to help singles to expand their social circle and actively encourage our singles to mingle.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, Singapore faces a complex and challenging external environment now and in the next few years.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Hence, the "Moving forward in a new-era" Budget will help Singaporeans tide over the rising cost of living, look forward to and prepare for future economic opportunities.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The biggest impact on Singaporeans is the rising cost of living and the future outlook.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I will focus on how the Budget can help Singaporeans, including senior citizens, families and workers, and provide feedback and suggestions on the Budget.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: First, for the elderly, they want to spend their golden years with a healthy body and a positive mind.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To help seniors stay healthy, the Government has introduced the Healthier SG programme.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In addition, as we move into a new era, I hope the Government will also pay attention to palliative care and allow palliative care to go into the community to meet the needs of an ageing population.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Second, for families, the assistance proposed in the Budget such as increasing CPF Housing Grant, Baby Support Grant and topping up of Baby Bonus Cash Gift and the Child Development Account will help ease some of the worries that young couples have about starting a family and having children.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I also hope that the Government will strengthen the support for singles who wish to end singlehood, and increase their social networking opportunities, so that they can find suitable partners.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Third, for employees, job security is their biggest concern.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In recent months, several multinational companies (MNCs) that operate in Singapore such as Google and Twitter have begun to retrench workers.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Besides attracting MNCs, grooming local companies is important too.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Hence, I support the series of initiatives in this year's Budget that focuses on supporting local SMEs to invest in innovative projects and sectors to help them expand their businesses and venture abroad.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Through this, they can provide more attractive jobs to Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As we mark the 100th year of the birth of Mr Lee Kuan Yew, let us remember the values and foresights that our forefathers have in overcoming adversity and challenges to define and unite a nation.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: May we continue to carry on this strength and resilience as we move forward into a new era, shaping a brighter future for Singapore and Singaporeans together.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 5.20 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 5.00 pm until 5.20 pm.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In Pasir Ris, we have frequent dialogues and engagements with our residents both formal and informally.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: During these engagements, issues that weigh heavily on the minds of our residents which they shared are: firstly cost of living; secondly, challenges brought about by our ageing population; thirdly, housing affordability and availability, especially for our young first-time buyers, which we have debated on significantly in the last Sitting; and lastly, jobs, employability and work-life balance.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While individuals feel the pressure from these issues, in my conversations with associations and those in the industry, businesses both here and abroad, are worried about the rising costs of doing business in Singapore and if Singapore can continue to have and provide the competitive edge in the global market.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: But we are on this journey together, and we can draw confidence and strength from how we have overcome past challenges." "The road ahead is not easy" – and that is true.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our tight labour market and ageing population will have to contend with high inflationary global environment, the deeply concerning war in Ukraine, Sino-American relations, Protectionist practices and other grim macro-economic challenges.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, we have shown that for the past three years, regardless of how challenging the journey is, we are better off coming together, working together to come up with viable pragmatic solutions able to meet the immediate needs of our society while positioning ourselves favourably for our future.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Hence, I am glad that Budget 2023 has elements that attempts to address the challenges and issues that weigh heavily on everyone's minds, while working within the constraints of our limited resource, with tweaks to make our tax system fairer, more progressive and sustainable.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: If the Budget addresses the right issues, then it becomes a question of whether we have prioritised and apportioned enough within our limited resources to address the challenges that we have been identified both immediate and in the future and is the resource efficiently deployed through policies such that it achieves the collective social goal that we as a nation desires.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is through that lens that I will touch on four key themes: Firstly, the adequacy of the support for the current inflationary and cost of living pressures.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Thirdly, as we grow our economy, how do we ensure our workforce remains competitive to bridge the skills gap to alleviate structural unemployment and channel workers into jobs and industries that are growing and transforming?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And lastly, while we remain competitive in the global market, how do we realize our desire to have inclusive growth, in particular, providing meaningful employment for our seniors, part-time workers and persons with disability.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Allow me to begin with the adequacy of the support for the current inflationary and cost of living pressures.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We have weathered periods of high inflation before.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I am encouraged to see how support schemes are disbursed such that everyone – not just the less well-off – but everyone, receives something regardless of income, like the CDC vouchers.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While those without income and lower to middle-income receive more, like the GST vouchers, cash payouts, S&CC and U-save rebates.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: These one-off support measures are well suited to deal with these exceptional past three years.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The pandemic, inflation, tight labour market and geopolitical instability were amongst the many challenges we had to surmount.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, I worry that such levels of support if perceived as the norm in the future, may not be sustainable.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Given that the inflation levels are here to stay, how do we then beat the inflation without Government support?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The rising cost needs to be overcome by generating value and increasing productivity.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The costs of doing business in Singapore is continuously rising.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This is partly due to the rising costs of labour attributed to the tight labour market, aspirations of our workforce for annual pay increments and our collective desire to pay our lower-waged workers better.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our strong currency also means Singapore-based businesses are finding it harder to compete through cost in the global market.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Furthermore, additional headwinds such as the impending increase in carbon tax and the implementation of Base Erosion and Profit Sharing (BEPS 2.0) initiative will add even more costs to doing business in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While businesses in Singapore face these cost pressures, the US and other countries are rolling out aggressive tax breaks and subsidies to attract investments, such as the CHIPS and Science Act in US, to build up their industries and revitalise their domestic manufacturing, competing with Singapore in attracting more investments.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Tax equalisation in BEPS 2.0 also implies we have one less instrument to attract investments into Singapore.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In my earlier speech in November on the GST Amendment Bill, I challenged some of the members' perception that BEPS 2.0 alone can make up the "hole left behind by not raising GST".

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I mentioned that because of the headwinds on cost, we will have to do something and spend on non-tax incentives such as training, subsidies and grants to restore and enhance our business competitiveness to continue to attract foreign investment while we lose preferential tax rates as one of our competitive levers.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And this results in the nett income from implementing BEPS 2.0 to remain uncertain but likely it would not be a straight-through revenue as some may have previously assumed.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: What mix of industries will we be focusing on for investment promotion to create the optimal value and leverages on our current infrastructure and workforce that we already have?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How do we ensure that funds are effectively used to drive real productivity improvements that will help lower costs of doing business in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: What will be the measure of success for the National Productivity Fund?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As we bolster the National Productivity Fund to compete globally for more quality investments, we must also prepare our workforce for the needs of the future economy.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Addressing our skills mismatch to alleviate structural unemployment will be one of our key challenges and this is a concern in the industry.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While we unanimously agree that upskilling and retraining will be critical to our future success, the challenge is, how do we upskill?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In each of the industry, what are the skills and knowledge that is necessary to bridge the gap?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Where do workers go to gain these skills and knowledge?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The industry transformation map (ITM) provides a high-level overview of what are the skills that are required in the industry.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, when it comes to applying it on the ground, businesses and workers are simply overwhelmed.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Workers are overwhelmed by what skills to learn to find better jobs or be better at their jobs.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Employers are overwhelmed by the types of training and support packages that are available and the quality of training providers.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: A Straits Times article mentioned that there are more than 26,000 courses available on the MySkillsFuture portal and this does not include all the other platforms that provide both offline and online skills training, such as Udemy.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Finding the right source to train for the right skillset to bridge the skills gap to drive a real improvement to the business is an outright challenge.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In my earlier speech in January on the SkillsFuture (Amendment) Bill, I had mentioned that the training landscape is confusing.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: There is the SSG website, SkillsFuture website, MySkillsFuture portal, SSG-WSG portal, just to name a few.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I do hope these integrators, as its name implies, bring together all the schemes, courses and stakeholders to simplify and execute rather than creating more schemes and programmes to add to the already confusing landscape.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This is something that I will touch more in the subsequent Committee of Supply (COS) cuts.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How can we also increase the participation rate of eligible Singaporean utilising SkillsFuture to significantly more than 30%?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And as we provide support to transform and upskill our current workers, we need to stay committed towards inclusive growth.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We must provide opportunities and unlock potential through meaningful re-employment for our seniors, part-time workers and workers with disability especially in sectors and roles facing labour shortages.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Key to this is our societal approach, or adopting a societal approach towards flexible work arrangements which can take the form of flexi-time, flexi-place and flexi-load.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: What is the progress of the Tripartite Guideline on flexible work arrangements?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How can flexible work arrangements, together with job redesign, unlock employment opportunities for seniors, persons with disabilities, part-time workers and caregivers?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For example, call centre operators or helpdesk providers can be done remotely via flexible work arrangements and this can create opportunities for such individuals.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Or can our seniors be funded to be trained as trainers to impart their knowledge to the industry?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How do we ensure that these fundings translate to actual improvement in employment opportunities for our seniors, part-time workers and persons with disabilities?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In Malay):   Budget 2023 is a sensible budget that provides for current needs, prepares us for the future challenges and strengthens our social compact while maintaining financial prudence.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: What everyone is concerned about is the high cost of living that is felt not only in Singapore but all over the world.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Therefore, I am happy to see how support schemes are channelled so that everyone, not only the less well-off, but all families, will receive help regardless of income, such as the CDC vouchers.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Those who are not working or with low-to-moderate income will receive more support, in the form of GST vouchers, cash payments, and S&CC and U-Save rebates.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This is in line with our society’s values and reinforces those values through actions where we help each other collectively, with those who are less well-off receiving more help.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: These enhancements to the Assurance Package is justified in such a unique situation.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, we should continue to monitor the budget in future and fine-tune it as the situation improves.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This is necessary because spending of this magnitude is not sustainable in the long term.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With competition for investment and jobs intensifying around the world, I am also pleased to hear about the sustained commitment to helping businesses transform and grow in the global markets.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And at the COS Debates later, I would also like to understand more about how we can encourage more companies to take advantage of the Senior and Part-Time Worker Schemes to redesign jobs to provide more employment opportunities for older workers, part-time workers and persons with disabilities.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In English): In conclusion, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, Budget 2023 is a balanced Budget that addresses the key issues weighing heavily on everyone's minds while preparing us for the future challenges and it does so by working within the constraints of the limited resource that we have.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is important that the overall tax burden does not rest disproportionately on any category of taxpayers and it is equally important that we continue to have a balanced budget.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This is consistent with our values as a society and reinforces it with action where collectively, as a society, we support each other and the less well-off should receive more, while we move forward together towards a new era.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Notwithstanding the clarifications above, I stand in support of the Budget.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Most immediately, Singaporeans are worried about the high cost of living.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This impact is especially salient for middle- and lower income households, financially and psychologically.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, the enhancements to the GSTV scheme and Assurance Package are much welcomed.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Against a challenging macro environment and competing needs domestically, I am glad to note that the Government will continue to uphold the practice of fiscal prudence and principles underpinning the protection of our reserves.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In his Budget speech, Deputy Prime Minister Wong explained that the Singapore economy just recovered from the COVID-9 pandemic and with a tight fiscal position, the Government will not be putting back what we have drawn from the Past Reserves.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: However, I hope that we do not lose that discipline as years pass.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: And with external factors, such as continued geopolitical instabilities and higher than normal inflation amidst lower global growth, we may find it even more difficult to do so in future.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Should a major crisis hit again and sooner than expected, will we have the same financial muscle and confidence as we did during the COVID-19 pandemic?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I raised this during last year's Budget debate and I would like to raise it again today.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In case I get misunderstood, let me state that I believe it is necessary for us to draw on our reserves to help Singapore and Singaporeans get through difficult times and we need to spend enough to help Singaporeans with the immediate cost challenges.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But we must keep in mind that we cannot deplete our reserves and that we must guard it judiciously.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Our pioneers took more than 50 years to save up this pot of gold because they want to protect their children and future generations.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Similarly, we too have a duty to use this pot of gold wisely and make sure that we put back what we took once we can, so that our children and their children can continue to have this asset to fall back on when they face the crisis of their generation.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As a fairly young nation, we still have much to build.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As each new generation emerges and succeeds the preceding one, we can expect adjustments to be made, to match the broader trends around the world, and the changing values and expectations.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: On the whole, we aspire towards a fairer and more inclusive society, in which we respect diversity, maintain harmony and hopefully, will be kinder to each other.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, in strengthening our social compact, these aspirations and values need to be translated into tangible policies for Singaporeans and Singapore.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: On housing, this House saw a rigorous debate on public housing earlier this month.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I am glad that the Government reaffirmed its commitment to keeping public housing affordable and accessible, for this generation and the next.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Home ownership is one of the five most fundamental pillars of our social safety net.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I have met several young couples who feel highly stressed that they could not secure a flat in the ballots while their biological clocks are ticking away.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, it is heartening to note that the Government is responsive to citizens' needs.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: However, amongst these young couples I met, almost all of them have a strong desire to live near their parents, for mutual familial support.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Parents can help care for the couples' kids and the couples can in turn care for their parents as they age further.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But when they fail at the ballots or cannot afford a nearby resale flat, one can imagine the anxiety they feel.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Or give another additional ballot to first-timers repeatedly applying under the MCPS?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It is in the mature housing estates where we see more elderly parents, who are less likely to move out as they will have to unplug themselves from a familiar environment and existing social networks; and their adult children understandably want to live nearby for the reasons I articulated earlier.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Furthermore, first time buyers and these would include the young couples or families, who favour speed and affordability, would have already chosen non-mature estates.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: And so, those who continuously choose mature estates must therefore have good reasons to do so.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Next, on opportunities for children, I am heartened to note that the Government is spending more to narrow learning gaps for children and is reinforcing the important role of early childhood education in any child's development.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Scaling up the KidSTART nationwide is certainly noteworthy.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The move to increase 22,000 full-day childcare places and expanding the number of MOE Kindergartens are to be rejoiced as well.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As it is, the anchor operator partner childcare centres in MacPherson are already full and parents are anxiously on the waiting list.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hopefully, the announced increase will come to MacPherson's – and soon.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Children with special needs are already at a disadvantaged starting point and hence, ensuring their access to the right early childhood education is even more important.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In the first, there is a resident by the name KT, who first approached me to appeal for subsidies to enrol her daughter in a private kindergarten.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The child has been attending mainstream preschools until the schools found it too difficult to cope with caring for the child.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: KT managed to enrol her daughter in early intervention classes at AWWA, for which they are grateful to receive fairly generous subsidies which are helpful to the couple who do not have a fixed income.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: However, the intervention classes are on part-time basis only and the child would not be able to receive the full learning experience that her peers are receiving.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: After much heartache, KT managed to find a private preschool that her daughter could finally fit in and responded well to.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This preschool is not a high-end one but KT could not receive subsidies if her child is enrolled in it.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: My understanding was that this centre did not qualify a particular criterion and hence, the KiFAS subsidies could not be given.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Consequently, the family soon found it too challenging to continue.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: She really just wants to try her best to place her child at a centre where her daughter finally feels comfortable in, where the principal and teachers understand her daughter and where her daughter can finally learn and seem to thrive.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In another case, another resident XY approached me.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Her son was originally enrolled in a local anchor operator childcare centre.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: One day, her son was found to have special needs and the centre found it too difficult for them to manage.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I was told that the principal allegedly insisted that her son be taken out of the centre.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We appealed for the son to stay but the centre’s decision remained.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Understandably, XY was desperate and sought help again.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Thankfully, in this case, the Early Childhood Development Agency (ECDA) and my grassroots leader managed to find an alternative for XY’s child.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, preparing our nation to be senior-friendly is ever so important and urgent.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: So, what we do to care for our seniors today is also caring for our generation tomorrow when we have grown old.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, I support the efforts to ensure seniors live as much of their lives in good health as possible and to have ample options to age in the community.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I support the approach and measures set out in the Budget.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In addition, I would urge that we pay special attention to socialising our seniors in the community to ensure that they are plugged into social networks and have a diverse range of activities to choose from.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We must strive to help our seniors avoid a sense of loneliness and avoid social isolation as these can lead to rapid mental and physical deterioration.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Even the fittest elderly can also be vulnerable to loneliness and social isolation.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Apart from preventive healthcare and Immediate and Long-Term Care (ILTC), community hardware and programmes need to be carefully designed with today and tomorrow's elderly in mind.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I believe we have been doing well in providing for seniors of today.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But building infrastructure and developing programmes need lead time, and we must hasten our efforts as we project into the future.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Recently, I received email requests from residents of the “young-old” profile who asked for Gym Tonic, which is less intensive than normal gyms but more sophisticated than the usual neighbourhood fitness equipment and programmes.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This, to me, is an early signal of a generational shift in "taste" and preference for what constitutes active ageing.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In the past, I often heard seniors lament about “waiting to die”, which seemed to reflect a certain grief over losing mental and physical capacities.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We must work to deliver a different, better future for our seniors.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Aging need not be a countdown to life.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, looking at the present and the future, the challenges we face cannot be underestimated.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: How to avoid obstacles and press on requires wise leadership and a united people.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Therefore, with the rise of a new generation of Singaporeans, our social compact needs to be adjusted to keep up with times.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This year's Budget dealt directly with our future needs and immediate concerns.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: While it is heartening, I still have some suggestions to the Government.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Second, increasing the number of preschool places will ensure that children will have a better start and that parents can work worry-free.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: However, there are still not enough preschool centres for children with special needs.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Children with special needs already have learning difficulties.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Third, growing old is inevitable but this does not mean that we should be counting down to our last days.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: (In English): Sir, Singapore's social compact have evolved over time.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: From focusing on survival as a nation in the 1960s to 1980s, to the "Many Helping Hands" approach that encouraged a greater sense of collective responsibility from the 1990s to the mid-2000s, to recognising that Government and the community need to play a bigger role to complement individual and family efforts.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As we look ahead, there are many complex challenges that we have to grapple with.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We face macroeconomic uncertainties, geopolitical instability, rapid social change and game-changing technological innovations.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: These can change the world as we know it.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Since then, it has been used in almost every Budget debate in recent years, and certainly the last few speakers.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: A social compact is essentially an exchange of promises – each of us give up our freedoms to pursue selfish interests in an unfettered way in exchange for a stable, ordered, fair society in which we all have an equal chance to flourish.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In the founding days of Singapore, these ideas were front and centre in all that Mr Lee Kuan Yew and his colleagues did.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: An examination of records around Singapore’s Independence would show that Mr Lee and his colleagues were very clear in their purpose. “My business is the people’s happiness”; this is what Mr Lee Kuan Yew said on 27 May 1965 in the Malaysian Parliament. “My business is the people’s happiness”.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: And “happiness of the people” appears in the Proclamation of Independence on 9 August 1969.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: And the word “happiness” is enshrined in our National Pledge.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: All these formed part of the social compact that he and his team forged with the people of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Over the years, our social compact was not lost on successive Prime Ministers and their teams, from Mr Goh Chok Tong, Mr Lee Hsien Loong and their teams.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: So, I am very glad that Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong called this out in his Budget Statement last year and that this year’s Budget had many good measures which will certainly help strengthen our common identity and social compact.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The Budget is the most binding version of our social compact because it allocates resources that put these big ideas to work for the future of Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In many ways, it is a decisive break from the past.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: To show how and why, let me contrast this with the political language and financial principles outlined in 1996 by the person who first used the words “social compact” – and this was by Nominated Member of Parliament and economics Prof Lee Tsao Yuan.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In her speech that year which argued for increased subsidies for transport, she said, “Education, health and housing have, from the very beginning of the PAP Government, been treated differently.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: To me, subsidy is not a dirty word.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Making basic health, education and housing affordable is and always has been, the social compact between this Government and the people.” She then outlined her own ideas of four financing principles used in the provision of public services by the Government.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: First, she argues, and I quote her again, “There is no such thing as a free lunch.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: A price tag is put on almost everything in Singapore by the Government.” In the 1990s where there was a wave of experiments on privatisation, this could be true.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The second principle is: "You get what you pay for".

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Her example was on hospitals, and she said, “If you want the comfort and privacy of an "A" Class ward, well, you pay hotel prices.” This principle certainly holds for the upper end of the market, but increasingly, not for the lower, especially in this Budget.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The Assurance Package, the increases in CPF housing grants and subsidies for the elderly, they all show that we are not slaves to the market and in fact, we are going quite far in the opposite direction.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I shall say more about these two principles in my cuts during the Committee of Supply on Ministry of Social and Family Development (MSF).

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The third principle, Prof Lee Tsao Yuan says, applies to the provision of three public goods – health, education and housing – and is that of progressive subsidisation.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In this, I would like to say that this Budget shows clearly that the progressive element, both in our tax and subsidy, remains core to our financing philosophy.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: It is a political, not mere fiscal, commitment – one which goes to the provision of all Government spending, not just social spending.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: And this is because of political origins of the PAP Government, born of our socialist beginnings, that those who have the most should carry the heaviest tax burdens in order to benefit those who have the least.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: And in this, I would like to make a point about tax on cars and how we can improve our current COE system to make it even more progressive.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: There are cars which cost upwards of a $1 million – the Ferraris, the Lamborghinis, and the McLarens; and even more exotic ones that could cost up to $6 million.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The tax that they attract is certainly higher than those cars which cost say $100,000.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But the price of the COE they pay, in the "open category", is the same.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This will have little impact on the majority of Singaporeans, who own only one, and relatively moderately priced, car.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In general, however, this year's Budget shows that the socialist heart of policy-making is still beating strong, from housing, to workers' welfare, to specific social groups.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This is possible only because of the judicious and careful husbandry of public funds and wise investments over the last 57 years.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In these years, we have resisted over-spending, maintained a strong sense of self-reliance and continued giving all workers opportunities for training and progress.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: These were all ingredients of the current strong financial position that we are in today.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: How do we ensure that, with greater welfare provision, that the self-reliance and ambition of our pioneering years remain strong?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: First, it is important to keep our debates both vigorous and honest so that we know when and where subsidies are truly needed.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Second, to keep opportunities open and plentiful for us all is by growing our Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) which collectively provide the most number of jobs to Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Yes, SMEs occupy a special place in my heart, which is why in the last Budget Debate, I also spoke about them, and today, I want to say a few things about them.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Many of our SMEs are dealing with a myriad of challenges.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: There is added pressure all round as SMEs face higher operating costs, be it rental, energy, manpower, financing and so on.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Vendors may also artificially increase prices, which can in turn negate the costs offsets by existing grants that SMEs have applied for.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: More specifically, it is the lack of manpower and challenges in hiring local workers that is worrying for many of them.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: SMEs with labour shortages are occupied with day-to-day operations, and constrained in planning for longer-term business transformation and digitalisation.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Hiring local workers with relevant skillsets is made more difficult if the sector is unattractive to locals, for example, retail, F&B, manufacturing.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: As a result, SMEs in these sectors have called for an increase in foreign worker quotas or to relax the criteria to qualify for foreign worker quotas to ease their labour shortages.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We also ask for the Government to support SMEs in hiring local workers and their training efforts.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Can we also increase avenues for companies to obtain local accreditation for specific skillsets and improve funding support?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: With a vibrant and strong SME sector, we will be able to ensure opportunities for all.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We see more fully why this Budget is such a big step forward.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: These are three big ideas that form the bones of our new social compact, a greater distribution of welfare and duties among all of us who live on this tiny island, so as to ensure new and continued opportunities for us all, that we may achieve happiness, prosperity and progress as a nation.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: With this, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, I support the Budget.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Last year, amidst the challenge of COVID-19 and unprecedented economic conditions, my Budget Debate speech focused on maintaining fiscal discipline so that we can continue to build up our reserves for future generations.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This year’s Budget seeks to strengthen our social compact including the needs of our Singaporean families and at the same time, ensure that our businesses and economy have the best springboard to progress, after COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: To quote Benjamin Franklin, "Beware of the little expenses.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: A little leak will sink a great ship".

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We must ensure that the help given out in Budget 2023 will be used and disbursed and efficiently to those who need help.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For instance, I had recently filed a Parliamentary Question (PQ) on the process of appeals for CDC vouchers.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As a grassroots advisor, I receive many appeals from Keat Hong residents on their entitlement to CDC vouchers.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The reasons for appeal differ – for example, the vouchers had been redeemed by someone who is no longer residing in that household or by a tenant.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: While we want to help as many people as possible, I hope the Ministry of Finance (MOF) can work with the relevant ministries handling the implementation of the various measures such as the CDC vouchers or other schemes set out in this Budget to ensure the efficient use of our resources.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In this regard, I had also previously asked a PQ on the findings of the AGO and the Public Accounts Committee on COVID-19 related procurement and expenditure.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We must continue to steward public funds and guard our resources jealously.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Next, on expanding our tax base by exploring alternative tax revenue streams and investments.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In this regard, I have three humble suggestions.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is to ensure that the public property market does not spiral out of control.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is not to say that there can never be a profit but if the profit is so excessive and disproportionate to the current fair valuation or initial purchase price, then perhaps a portion of that profit can be considered a windfall.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In the future, when more HDB BTOs are built in mature estates including prime or central areas, there is a high likelihood of such windfall profits.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Some Keat Hong residents gave me feedback that a lucky applicant should not be enriched solely because of fortuitous BTO balloting.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Second, perhaps the Government can also consider and study the feasibility of a windfall tax on companies that have benefited enormously from a particular situation.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Recently, oil and gas companies in the UK posted record profits due to the energy prices hike fueled by the Russia-Ukraine conflict.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Shell reported profits of $39 billion in 2022, the highest in its 115-year history.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: BP made profits of $27 billion in the same year.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Nevertheless, I do admit that such windfall tax is not a foolproof solution because companies are nimble and will relocate and restructure their profits and revenue streams accordingly to avoid such tax.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For example, BP said that its UK businesses account for less than 10% of its global profits, while Shell makes about 5% of its revenue in the UK.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Both firms argue they have also lost a lot of money as a result of stopping investments in Russian oil firms.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: My third suggestion is to explore alternative investment spaces to build up our reserves again.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We cannot continue to tap on our reserves in the long term as this is not sustainable.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: With increasing spending, we will face bigger deficits in the future.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Deputy Prime Minister said that it is unlikely that we will be able to put back what we drew from the reserves in the near future.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In this regard, there is a great opportunity and synergy in the Islamic finance sector, in particular the Green Sukuk and ESG space.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: At this juncture, I declare that I am a legal practitioner in the Islamic finance space.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: While the global issuance of Sukuk marginally dropped in 2022, ESG Sukuk grew 35% year-on-year.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Green and sustainability Sukuk have reached a new high, with demand driven by ESG-centric investors.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In the Philippines, recently the Department of Justice (DOJ) said the Department of Finance (DOF) is legally empowered to issue Shariah-compliant financing instruments like Sukuk to make the country appealing to Islamic investments.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We should seriously look at all opportunities and how Singapore can be positioned in this unique space.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In Malay):   On the issue of housing, I welcome the announcement in this Budget for more support in the form of grants and more balloting chances for young couples for BTO flats.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The definition of "first-time" applicants for BTO flats may be broader now and comprises not only young couples who wish to purchase HDB flats, but many other groups.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Therefore, we need to further tweak our BTO and HDB flat application process, to give young couples who wish to get married, the best opportunity to meet their housing needs.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Based on feedback from Keat Hong residents, many young couples with children welcome the higher balloting chances for BTO flats and enhanced HDB housing grants.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For instance, there can be a phased or staged approach similar to Primary One school registration.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Each phase can have a fixed quota for different groups, for instance, young couples, elderly and families with children.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The final phase can be opened to everyone.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This will ensure that there will be a diverse mix of residents in an estate and give young couples a equal and fair opportunity.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In this regard, the Minister for National Development’s reply to my previous Parliamentary Question that, following the ForwardSG conversation, respondents mostly agree that we should prioritise first-timers who are looking to purchase their first home, especially for those with more urgent housing needs, such as first-timer couples who already have children but are without their own home, as well as lower-income families, who have fewer options in the open market.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In addition, I welcome the pro baby initiatives such as the Enhanced Baby Bonus and the extension of the Baby Support Grant.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This will likely help alleviate the costs and expenses related to raising a child.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The CDA account promotes co-saving for a child’s future.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This will help lighten the financial burden of families.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Baby Bonus and BSG, which are given in cash, may not be sustainable for the long run.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: With the successful rollout of CDC Vouchers in digital format which are easy to use on mobile phones without the need to download an app, there is potential to extend targeted help to families with young children and based on the number of children in the household.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This special voucher should only be used for expenses for their baby or for educational expenses.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In English): Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, not everyone will be fully satisfied with the measures proposed and changes announced in this Budget.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For example, the change in the Working Mother's Child Relief from a percentage to fixed dollar relief.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Those with higher income will thus have a lower claim compared to a lower-income mother who can now claim a higher amount.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Another change is the increase in tax rates in the form of buyer stamp duties for residential properties in excess of $1.5 million.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In this market, many condominiums of a certain size which can accommodate a family of five can fetch higher than $1.5 million and so such buyers and families would be impacted.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Personally, I do not think this is a "Robin Hood" Budget.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is one in which everyone shares and gives a little for the other.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Instead of focusing on what goodies we did not receive from this Budget, we should focus on what we have given instead, what we have given up for the sake of Singaporeans who are more in need in our society.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The working mother who earns less should be helped more as this will impact her disposable income to spend on her children.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The family who wants to live in a condominium and can afford it should pay a bit more in taxes, which would help subsidise the grants of public housing or rental flats for those who otherwise cannot even afford a roof over their heads.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is our social compact, where everyone pitches in to help raise the other.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Our policies and ideals are always a work in progress, fine-tuned to adapt to our changing societal needs and global challenges.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Pro-family measures will hopefully spur our young couples to settle down and build their own families.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This time last year, I welcomed my fourth child.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I understand that next year is the Chinese zodiac year of the dragon, which typically records the highest number of births.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: So, we have to wait for all the appeals for Primary 1 registration.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But I hope with these measures, the years ahead will not only be productive for Singapore but also be reproductive for our fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is heartening to learn from this year's Budget that one emphasis is on building a Singapore Made for Families.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: At this juncture, I should first declare that I also fall under the category of a parent with young children.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Such COV amounts, unfortunately, cannot be covered by housing loans or CPF and must be paid for in cash, which young couples with limited savings are unable to afford.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In this regard, would HDB be introducing any measures to curb the COV situation or could the relevant regulations be amended to allow housing loans or CPF monies to pay off the COV component?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: My second point is on the issue of affordability of raising children.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In past school reunion gatherings, I often took the opportunity while catching up with my peers to find out why several of them are putting off the idea of having a child or having more than one child.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Several whom I have spoken with shared that while they and their spouse aspire to have children, they are worried about the rising costs of raising a child in Singapore and thus have put off having children until they have achieved stability in their careers.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The issue of financial safety is therefore constantly on the minds of would-be parents and the recent increases in the cost of living has also done little to ease these worries.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Besides increased day-to-day expenses, the policy changes that affect household finances can also influence a family's decision to have children.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As an example, the incoming changes to the Working Mother's Child Relief (WMCR) from a percentage-based calculation to a fixed sum has brought mixed feelings on the ground.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I am therefore concerned as to how this change will affect those who are under the sandwiched middle-income group.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Considering the purpose of the WMCR, what were the considerations behind this change and to what extent was the impact on mothers from the middle-income brackets being taken into account?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Although the increase in the Baby Bonus Cash Gift and the increased Government contribution to the CDA do promise to offer some financial assistance to defray child-raising costs, the impact of the decrease in the WMCR will impact working mothers on an annual recurring basis until either when her income decreases or when she is no longer eligible for such relief.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I therefore hope that the Government can consider making a slight tweak to this policy, retaining the percentage and the fixed quantum, whichever is higher shall apply.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Such an amendment will create a win-win situation by allowing lower-income working mothers to receive adequate tax deductions and motivate them to continue to remain in the workforce after having children and continue to pursue their future career aspirations.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Under the current rules, new working mothers are allowed to share up to four out of 16 weeks of their allocated Maternity Leave with their spouses, which has allowed new families greater flexibility in infant care arrangements, with family bonding time.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: With the latest Budget announcement, fathers who are currently employed will have their paid Paternity Leave increased from two to four weeks.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This is surely a welcome change as fathers are increasingly becoming more involved in the day-to-day upkeep and care of their newborn children.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: With that being said, are there plans to allow the sharing of Parental Leave to become even more flexible such as allowing couples more freedom to transfer their respective allotted leave days among themselves, be it Maternity or Paternity Leave?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As each family situation is different, I believe that allowing this freedom will grant a net positive benefit for those expecting new members in their family.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Over the years, Singapore's infrastructure has been consistently upgraded, with consideration towards greater convenience and accessibility requirements.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Our public housing is one such example through HDB's various initiatives such as the Home Improvement Programme (HIP).

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: During HIP, apart from improvements such as replacing the clothes drying rack, families with seniors can take the opportunity to opt in for Enhancement for Active Seniors (EASE) improvements, furnishing these older flats with safety features such as a slip-resistant treatment to floor tiles and grab bars in the bathrooms.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: On the same purpose that HIP is intended to update older flats with new features that make life easier for its inhabitants, some of these features to be introduced therein should therefore also look into how to benefit families with young children.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This is so especially when we are now encouraging young couples to consider purchasing older resale flats in the open market.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The COVID-19 pandemic has taught us that in times of weariness and difficulties, our homes remain as a haven as we work towards overcoming obstacles in life.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: For parents with young children, this means ensuring that their homes are well equipped to cope with the pressures of parenting along with the usual demands of work and household upkeep.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As families begin to spend more time outdoors following the relaxation of COVID-19 protocols, there will be more demand for family-friendly features that allow for a more comfortable bonding experience.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: While I applaud the introduction of these facilities, it should be noted that most of them focus on meeting the minimal requirements, causing them to not meet the satisfaction of the users' overall experience.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I spoke to Mr Phua Wee Seng of Rare Disorders Society Singapore on this issue recently.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Wee Seng's teenage son suffers from a rare and life-threatening genetic disorder, which requires him to manoeuvre around on a special wheelchair.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Wee Seng shared that many of the lifts and handicap toilets in the malls in Singapore are in fact too small and cramped, which has caused tasks such as the changing of diapers for his son to be of a great challenge.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Our amenities and infrastructures will therefore need to be designed with the end users in mind.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Say, a stay-at-home mother who has to take care of two young children and needs to bring them to the polyclinic for their occasional vaccinations, for example.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Are there any family-friendly parking lots within close proximity to the polyclinic for someone like her?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: When it rains, is the route from the carpark to the polyclinic entirely sheltered and with barrier-free access?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Besides providing more family-friendly amenities, we can also look into creating an express lane system for more locations catered towards senior citizens, people with mobility issues and families with young children.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This is a good start and we should continue to explore introducing more efficient queue systems to places, including banks, community clubs and polyclinics, just like countries such as Japan have implemented.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Workplaces also plays an important role in encouraging a more family-friendly culture.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
