text: Many companies have since mandated a return to the office to increase productivity back to pre-COVID-19 levels, but this decision may not necessarily be welcomed by many of its employees, especially parents with infants, who have become used to the flexibility of remote working over the past couple of years.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is important that employers and employees continue to have candid discussions amongst themselves to better understand each other's needs and concerns, with a view towards maximising productivity, while ensuring that the workers have sufficient work-life balance.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: A Singapore Made for Families will need a concerted effort from the whole-of-society in order to make it a reality, namely those from the 3Ps: People, Private and Public sectors.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Only when everyone is aligned towards this common goal, with more empathy and understanding raised in this regard, will we be able to achieve it.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: A successful transformation to a Singapore Made for Families will be complete when we can answer the following questions in great confidence: When the childcare calls the working parent to inform that the child is sick, would the working parent be able to take urgent leave to pick up the child?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Would the employer be understanding to allow the employee to continue to work from home for the next few days in order to take care of the child at the same time?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Is the home deemed conducive, equipped with features ensuring that the working parent is able to cope with working from home and caring for the child?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And when the parent sends the child, who has been running a high fever in the night, to the hospital's A&E or its Children's Urgent Care Clinic, would the premises have already looked into how to reduce the waiting time, and at the same time, trained their staff to provide adequate interim support to reduce the helpless parents' anxiety on the child's conditions?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Over the last decade, we have seen the development of growing anxiety and erosion of trust between people and governments around the world.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The combination of factors that lead to this varies across nations, but they can be grouped broadly into three different categories: First, factors that contribute to the middle-class squeeze, for example, wage stagnation, increased costs of goods and services, an over reliance of debt and tax bands that place a heavy weight on the middle-class.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Second, disparity of access to resources and opportunities across different groups including overwhelming student debt burdens, hard choices between furthering education and earning to support the family, career opportunities being afforded via a network effect with little consideration for capability.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And third, the increasing use of ideological differences in fanning the flames of identity politics, where competing ideologies turn into competing identities, which makes it increasingly difficult to achieve majority consensus for what is good for society.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As a young nation which grew up fast, Singapore is not immune to the factors above.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We are an open society with immigrant roots, reliant on trade and investment.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Government has historically managed the risk factors in these categories and continues to place an emphasis in tackling most of these issues in Budget 2023.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: One of the factors that has helped wage growth continue to rise in Singapore is the Government's focus on upskilling and attracting investment.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I applaud the top-up of the National Productivity Fund and expansion to include investment promotion as a supportable activity.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And this will include supporting companies in their efforts of building new capabilities, adding greater value to domestic ecosystems and opportunities for better jobs for our workers as long as we remain hungry.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Also, social mobility continues to be a cornerstone of society.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While education systems are often touted as a great leveller, we must pay careful attention to how we create access, so as to also meet the needs of children from more disadvantaged households.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A featured story by the World Bank in November 2021, cites research from India and Indonesia that is shedding new light on low intergenerational educational mobility, highlighting that education systems can entrench inequality, rather than combat it if designed poorly.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am heartened to hear that KidSTART will be expanded nationwide, coupled with efforts like ComLink and Project DIAN@M3, I hope that we can truly make a difference for the next generation.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This Budget, the Government has laid out its commitment towards tackling cost of living and affordability issues, which are a part of every maturing economy.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And the difficulty of this task is exacerbated by extenuating market conditions: a hawkish federal reserve combating inflation, disrupted supply chains, geopolitical uncertainties – all of which contribute towards price instability on goods and services.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A wise friend once told me, we cannot attribute what we know from our unique experience to what we expect people to know.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Seeking our people's understanding of the difficult decisions and trade-offs will not change the everyday reality that our morning kopi peng with eggs and kaya toast set has become more expensive, which is why I applaud the Government's efforts in the tangible development of the Assurance Package, and other schemes that seek to help a majority of citizens address these cost-of-living issues.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We must continue to communicate these assurances concisely and clearly.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Having said the above, even with the assistance provided, uncertain conditions create fertile ground for hopelessness and anxiety to take root.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While we attempt to shield Singaporeans from economic headwinds, we must also invest in schemes and programmes that help our citizens achieve better resilience and mental well-being outcomes.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Without effective support, mental disorders and other conditions can affect a person's confidence, identity, capacity to work productively and the ease with which to gain and retain work.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Mental health conditions also impact families, carers, colleagues, communities and society at large.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, one possibility is the pilot of a mental well-being credit scheme that could incentivise companies to truly invest in the mental health of their workers.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The framework for this credit scheme could be developed in partnership with tripartite partners, healthcare practitioners and the inter-agency task force on mental health and well-being.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Such a scheme should focus on scoring a workplace's mental wellness protocols, instead of scoring employees, just to be clear.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And this could provide us a base to develop better frameworks to facilitate the acceptance and integration of mental health as a part of our working culture.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Investments that focus on emotional well-being, stability and diversity are also critical in tackling the issues that arise from competing ideologies.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Achieving consensus in society is a Sisyphean task.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some people like the otters and roosters, others want them removed or do not care.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some are willing to bring their own bags to grocery shopping while others want more plastic bags to dispose of the waste.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some champion low-income workers and would pay more for services and goods, while others want to keep their cups of teh tarik to 90 cents.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some modern ideologies clash with beliefs which are rooted in tradition.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Every decision requires careful deliberation, consultation, trade-offs and tough choices.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Efforts like Forward Singapore help to bring dialogue to our people, encourage diverse voices to raise their views and allows people to have that tactile experience of conversing with someone who may not see the world the same way that they do.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We are moving away from quiet tolerance and building the muscle of discourse.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In this process, there will be growing pains.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Stewarding a peaceful and fruitful exchange of ideas is a difficult, but necessary task to undertake before we can build bridges, in the spirit of our shared social compact.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I look forward to hearing more from our 4G leadership on their takeaways from this exercise in due course.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I recently had the chance to participate in a dialogue, in my capacity on the REACH Panel.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It was a weekday after work and around 40 youths, between 20 and 32 had shown up to make friends in their neighbourhood, and to discuss what Vision 2050 Singapore might look like.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As I listened to their thoughts, topics such as tech layoffs, support for healthcare workers, trading off some order for a little more "rough around the edges", upskilling and housing were all topics which came to the fore.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But one of the most common thoughts were that, firstly, we were so very lucky to be where we are today and to have this foundation and we must not take it for granted.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Singapore must continue to be that place where people see value in staying and are willing to protect each other and what we have.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Budget lays out and suggests what kind of future we want to see for Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I have grown to know and love many elderly in my constituency.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There is something about the way they take my hand and tell me to look after my health that never fails to fill my heart right up.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: During my house visits, I recently met one aunty in her 60s, who looked like she was in her 40s.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I asked her to tell me her secret, and she told me: "哈哈大笑。有钱就吃多一点，没钱就吃少一点", or "Laugh and smile.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If I have more, I eat more; if I have less, I eat less".

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many of them continue to hold jobs too.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Beyond the economic factors, I also hope we can improve the quality of life for our seniors, strengthening the family nucleus and caregiving.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For those who may not be as close to their children, that we can expand community care apartments and encourage society to step up as eyes and ears on the ground, so that our elderly feel supported, valued and that they matter.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: On our middle class, we allocate more resources to those who need it more.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But more and more, on the ground, we hear from people who may be just priced out of housing grants and schemes, but can ill afford a private home; older retirees who may be "asset rich" but cash poor; and those who care for their parents as well as their children amidst rising costs.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As highlighted in the earlier part of my speech, wage growth continues on an upward trend and that is the best lever.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Having said the above, there some young professionals who say half in jest: "Work hard so you have more money to actually buy a flat, but don't work so hard that you earn so much and you might bust the HDB income ceiling." Narratives like these may not apply to the majority of the population, but they can lead to a disheartened and disgruntled sandwiched middle class.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope that the Government continues to engage this segment of Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Earlier on I spoke about some the youths I met about their vision of Singapore in 2050.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: One other point resonated consistently throughout the evening – is there more than one version of the Singapore dream?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Are we too deep in hustle culture, primary one registration, being the first in the queue, growing reliant on incentives in order to do what is for the broader good, aiming for that elusive Built-to-Order (BTO) ballot number, to slow down?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In our garden city State, can farming, working with wildlife, the social sector, heritage and the arts have space in this Singapore?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Can a gap year while we figure out things be forgiven?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Can there be second chances and a life beyond grades?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How can this be a part of every child's upbringing, just as important as algebra?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How can we live out what it truly takes to reach Net-zero so that there continues to be a green, blue and brown world for our next generation?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A few words in Malay before I end.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In Malay):   Prior to this Budget, some Cheng San-Seletar residents spoke to me about their concerns on the rising cost of living.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They were also concerned whether they will be able to have adequate savings for retirement.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With the announcement of Budget 2023 by Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong, I hope that this will in some way ease their concerns.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am very happy to see the Government's commitment to support the aspirations of young families.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Considering that the gig economy will be permanent, I look forward to hearing more details during the Committee of Supply (COS) debate.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In English): In closing Sir, I am looking forward to participating in this year's Committee of Supply debate.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As Members of Parliament, we all feel the sentiments on the ground keenly, and know intimately the worries as we emerge from COVID-19 into an uncertain environment.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am glad that Budget 2023 focuses on moving forward together in a new era and appreciate many of the decisive measures we are making with our people.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In my speech last year, I gave an analogy that we were taking a roller coaster ride in the dark.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: We do not know where and when the twists and turns are, but we stayed united and trusted each another, and now, we are out of the tunnel and can anticipate the turns and the twists.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: And that is what this Budget is about.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It is about knowing there is much global uncertainty, cost of living issues, an ageing population and the need to sustain social mobility.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This Budget anticipates these issues and aims to navigate Singapore onwards in solidarity and unity in an ever-dynamic landscape.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: We must continue to support them by providing a better work-life balance.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: For teachers, a suggestion from the Singapore Teachers' Union (STU) is the introduction of a whitespace for marking, lesson planning, student guidance and counselling.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This will allow the teacher some focused time to get some work done rather than doing it after school hours.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: A second suggestion by STU is the enhancement of effective communication channels between teachers and management.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: For example, how do we empower teachers and cultivate teacher agency, so that teachers can negotiate deployment such that win-win outcomes are achieved for the teacher and the school?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Third, I am also aware of the abuse healthcare workers and teachers may encounter.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I ask that we explore and provide practical ways to support and protect them.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: We must do more to say that if you harass or abuse our officers, there will be consequences.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I will touch on these two broad areas: education and health.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I welcome the announcement that that we will invest more in our children – to scale up the KidSTART programme nationwide to support more children in disadvantaged families.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I note, however, that for children aged three to four years old residing in public rental flats, the preschool enrolment rate is lower than the national average.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Residents have shared their challenges and I empathise.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: But I do believe that the mindset of preschool education must change.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In early childhood education, children are provided with opportunities for deliberate play and exploration, allowing for social interaction and problem-solving skills beyond what books can offer.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This will underline a strong commitment to tackle inequality at the earliest juncture possible and ensure that every child can discover the joy of learning, exploration and play.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Thus, I am heartened that we will continue to invest in our people and the Jobs-Skills Integrator is an excellent initiative.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This will plug the gap and ensure that training improves employment and earnings prospects.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Additionally, if successful, it could be the building block as to how we address the issue of increasing income wage gap between non-graduates and graduates.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I hope the pilot programme will succeed and we can extend this further to other industries.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Going upstream, I hope such integrators can be embedded in our Institutions of Higher Learning (IHLs).

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Apart from the main programme where our students may specialise in, flexibility could allow them to take up other modules of interest.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: These integrator-like modules could stack on top of their specialised course and this increases their employment opportunities and allows them to remain agile in a dynamic job space.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: For example, the enhancements to the GSTV scheme and Assurance Package will cushion the pressure of the cost of living.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It covers not only the lower-income families but also the middle-income families and families that are much larger.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This includes those with the elderly and children.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: For the lower-income individuals and seniors who face difficulties with their medical bills, the MediFund would go a long way in ensuring a safety net for them.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: But Sir, to me, the greatest positive impact is on families.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: A family, the bedrock of society, is our source of love, support and strength.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I am heartened that in this Budget, the anxieties and concerns held by young families are addressed.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: First, supporting housing aspirations through the additional ballot for their BTO flat applications and the enhanced CPF housing grant.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I know many of the young families welcome this.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: However, I also know that not all families are identical for various reasons and circumstances.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: For instance, more could be done to support single-parent households, who often face greater financial strain.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I received feedback from a single mother who shared her concerns about raising three school-going children and aspired to own her own flat.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: She shared that she had no CPF as she was not working previously but currently holds a good job and wants to be self-reliant.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Additionally, the Government could consider increasing support for families with children with disabilities or special needs.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: These families also face additional financial burdens due to the higher care and education costs.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Collectively providing additional financial assistance and support services for these families would help ease their financial burden and improve their quality of life.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The second concern is the cost of raising children.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I know many of my younger married colleagues welcome the many related announcements.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: But beyond the monetary support, the support for parents to manage their work and family commitment is, in my opinion, the most impactful.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Numerous studies have shown that the time spent with children is the best investment.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: While many factors contribute to a child's development and well-being, spending time with children has shown to have numerous positive outcomes.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: At the same time, I urge employers to review their mental wellness programmes and consider providing workers with a time-out where they can unwind, recharge and be free from work emails, texts, or calls.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Recently, there has been an alarming number of workplace accidents.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: MOM and the National Trades Union Congress (NTUC) have made efforts to foster a workplace safety and health culture.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: These representatives know the ground well and they are familiar with the safety processes.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The Government can incentivise companies to form these committees with union representatives through grants to foster work-safety culture and processes.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: (In Malay):   This year's Budget is a thoughtful and inclusive one.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I support the Deputy Prime Minister's call to strengthen our social compact.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In my English speech earlier, I touched on three issues: Comprehensive support for workers, Education and Health.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: First, I urged that we provide more comprehensive support for workers, especially for healthcare sector workers and teachers.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I called on the Government and employers to review workload and job scope to ensure quality work-life balance.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: These include setting clear guidelines on working hours and introducing WHITESPACE or time that is set aside specifically for workers to perform additional work or projects.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This move demonstrates a strong commitment to combat inequality as early as possible and ensures that every child is given the opportunity to fulfil their potential.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Although this year's Budget did not directly mention mental health, it is clear that this Budget will have a positive impact on mental health.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: For example, improvements to the GSTV Scheme and Assurance Package will reduce cost of living pressures.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It covers not only low-income families but also middle-income families and large households.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: For low-income individuals and senior citizens facing financial difficulties with their medical bills, MediFund will help and ensure that there is a safety net for them.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: For me, the biggest positive impact is on families.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I am heartened that in this Budget, the concerns of young families can be addressed.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Second, help for parents towards the cost of raising children, and support to manage work and family commitments.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I hope that young families will take advantage of the support and grants provided.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I believe that, through this Budget, Singapore will emerge stronger in our effort to move forward in the new era.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: (In English): Mr Deputy Speaker, in conclusion, the Budget is well-balanced and a well-conceived plan that addresses the country's immediate needs while investing in the future.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The focus on enhancing social safety nets, promoting economic growth and investing in the future will benefit Singaporeans from all walks of life.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The support for vulnerable groups, particularly in the areas of education, young families and the elderly, is a testament to the Government's commitment in creating a more equitable and caring society.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: These measures will go a long way in reducing income inequality, improving access to healthcareand providing a more supportive environment for families.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Overall, the Budget is a positive step forward in the new era.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Leader of the Opposition, you have a clarification for a Member?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Just a small technical clarification in my speech which I would like to clarify.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But it still does not change my fundamental point which was to re-allocate early on in a member's working life.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: So, it is a clarification in relation to your own speech.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There were there with me when my first child Ella was born, celebrating with us as we welcomed Ella into our lives.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There were there with me when I said goodbye to my dad.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I remember the nurse crying together with us as they processed the terminal discharge so we could fulfill my dad's wish of passing on at home.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Part of me was surprised that the nurse was crying.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I thought they would be used to seeing patients come and go.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: He could not have been better cared for and I am very grateful for the nurses at SGH who made his final days more comfortable.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: And nurses were there with me when we welcomed my twins Katie and Poppy into the world almost exactly six years ago.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It was both a happy and extremely worrying time as Katie and Poppy were born premature and spent 10 weeks at the Neonatal ICU (NICU) and High Dependency Ward at SGH.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As I shared in my Adjournment Motion in 2017, "it was surreal sitting at the NICU, doing kangaroo care with my baby, singing to her while watching the mayhem in NICU.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Watching the staff handle a never-ending arrival of pre-term babies and a never-ending chorus of alarm bells as babies stop breathing.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The staff members handle each situation so professionally, so meticulously and with so much tender loving care." I do not think we can thank nurses enough for the work they do for all of us.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I sincerely thank all of our healthcare workers – our nurses, doctors, therapists, pharmacists, TCM physicians, allied healthcare professionals and many, many more.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Today, I will focus my speech on nurses who form the largest proportion of our healthcare workforce.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The reality is that, as most Singaporeans are celebrating the move to DORSCON Green, nurses would not have the chance to celebrate.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Emily, a nurse, told me, "There is not enough trained people to handle the cases.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Everyone is exhausted from the lack of staff, resignation rates.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have recently been attached to a few different hospitals and I see the same issue everywhere.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Patient's safety is compromised and nurses are just burnt out.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We are thankful that the Government has been increasing our pay and giving us special payments.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But what I really, really want is more quality time with my family.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Better shifts, better working hours." I spoke with nurses across multiple dialogues last year and this year and collected their ideas in a public survey of 173 nurses.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Based on these consultations, I will raise three recommendations today: first, protect rest time for nurses between shifts; second, protect rest time for nurses during shifts; and third, provide more ancillary support staff for nurses.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first recommendation is that we ensure that nurses have protected rest time between shifts.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The first problem is that nurses often stay on average one to two hours after every shift to ensure that their work is complete.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But for nurses on shift work with irregular hours, working overtime means that they lose precious hours of rest between shifts.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The second problem is that nurses often do a morning shift (AM) which starts at 8 am immediately after doing an afternoon shift (PM) the day before which ended at about 10 pm.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Some do this on consecutive days, so PM, AM, PM, AM and they call this the PAPA shift.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They often get home at midnight, sleep for a short while before they wake up to prepare for the AM shift, which again starts at 8 am.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Some nurses have shared with me that they work such punishing shifts almost every week or every other week.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: One nurse shared with me, "As I am typing this message now, I am in the train, on my way back home.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will be doing morning shift tomorrow and that would mean about five hours of rest for me before my day starts again." Constantly working overtime and four, five hours of sleep – how can that be enough sleep?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: That is why we have regulations in other industries setting basic requirements to manage fatigue.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For example, we require flight crew members to get an equivalent amount of rest when they work 10 to 16 hours.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If they work any longer, they must get at least 24 hours of rest.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can our nurses get the same level of protection as our air stewardess and stewards?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Many studies have been done on the importance of fatigue management in healthcare.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A 2019 meta-study on fatigue in healthcare found that it increases error rates, slows reaction times, increases likelihood of accidents and injuries, and reduces motivation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is not just about nurse well-being but also about patient-safety.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Our nurses have to make life and death decisions on every shift.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Government cannot just leave this to the hospitals to manage and decide on their own.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Fatigue affects the well-being of nurses and the health outcomes of patients.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will the Government look into regulations to address nurses' fatigue instead of leaving again these matters to hospitals to decide on their own?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This will also not be new for the Government.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Government has introduced regulations for the airline industry.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Ministry of Manpower (MOM)'s Workplace Safety and Health Council also has guidelines on fatigue management.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second point is on protected rest time for nurses during their shifts.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While they usually have a one-hour rest of rest time, many nurses have shared with me that they simply do not have enough manpower to rest for a full hour.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: So, they do not enough rest between shifts and even during shifts.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They shared that they have to do so because of patient needs and administrative work.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Emily, the nurse, shared with me a day of work for nurses in her ward, "one junior takes care of and showers 16 patients.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: At the same time, we have to make sure they get their breakfast and lunch, while checking their vital signs twice per shift or according to their doctors' orders.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We have to make sure every intake or output – drains, urine, motions – of every single patient is charted and diapers are changed." She continues, "The nurse in charge will have to serve the medication.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is very common for patients to have more than 10 medications, be it IV, oral, pre-meals and post-meals.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We have to follow doctors' rounds, carry out orders, and make sure that the physiotherapist, occupational therapist, speech therapist and medical social worker have seen our patients.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We have to do dressings and help the junior out." At the end she said, "we hope we get to finish our report before the next shift comes so that we get to go home on time." I was exhausted just from reading that.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: MOH has shared that it is working closely with public healthcare institutions to shore up recruitment, for both local and foreign staff.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, time is needed to recruit and train nurses.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Meanwhile, our nurses are on the brink of burn-out.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Concurrent with recruitment efforts for nurses, will the Ministry work with hospitals to ensure that the rest time of nurses during their shifts are protected?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I understand that current realities of nursing means that there has to be some flexibility around rest times.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But we must mandate some level of protection of rest.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: MOH is already looking into recruiting healthcare ancillary staff for non-clinical duties.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But beyond non-clinical administrative duties, patients and next-of-kin also demand customer service from nurses.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: One nurse commented that patients and families "want us to clean their surroundings for them, want us to heat up their food and water and even collect their food delivery orders." Another nurse said, "Sometimes patients and relatives will tend to request for nurses to do unreasonable things like washing their underwear, buying food for them, fixing their spoiled charger/handphone.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Even as simple as changing the channel of the TV, they will ask nurses to do it for them.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Sometimes, patients and relatives treat nurses as their personal helper." I understand that patients who are unwell and next-of-kin who are stressed understandably look to nurses for support.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But the kind of customer service demanded by some patients and next-of-kin is a misuse of invaluable time and expertise of nurses who are already overworked.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Yes, we can do a public education campaign on this, but nurses need us to do much more to help them.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Nurses shared with me that they appreciated the 900 Singapore Airlines cabin crew who were redeployed as Care Ambassadors during the height of COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These Care Ambassadors worked with nurses and doctors on non-clinical nursing tasks.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A nurse said, "The Care Ambassador helped to offload some of the non-nursing work and allowed nurses to be more focused on caring for sick patients who need more attention.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Care Ambassador was able to spend time talking to patients, allay their anxiety and make them feel supported." MOH has recognised that Care Ambassadors' service and communication instincts helped to alleviate the manpower tightness in healthcare institutions during the pandemic, allowing again nurses to focus on more complex clinical and care-related work.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Khoo Teck Puat Hospital (KTPH) has been working with SIA to train KTPH's new Patient Care Officers, a new role inspired by the Care Ambassadors.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I hope MOH will consider studying and expanding KTPH's Patient Care Officers programme to other public hospitals.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This will relieve the workload of nurses, enable them to deliver better patient care and ultimately reduce the attrition rate.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Many nurses were upset when we shared in this House that "The typical nurse-to-bed ratio for general wards in public acute hospitals is one nurse for every four or five beds." The reality on the ground is far, far from this typical ratio that MOH shared.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Nurses stressed to me that we should also ensure that the hiring of more ancillary healthcare workers or even Patient Care Officers should not affect the nurse-to-patient ratios.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is good news that MOH has acknowledged the manpower needs in the nursing industry and is working on recruitment.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, concurrent with shoring up recruitment, let us retain those already in the profession.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: To retain nurses, we of course have to ensure that salaries are competitive.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But we must also go beyond the monetary.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The need for more rest is the recurring cry for help that I hear from nurses.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Nurses care for us and those who are dear to us.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But the burden of that care is now too heavy for them.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As one shared, "Our health and our relationship with our families are compromised.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We are taking care of people when we can’t even take good care of ourselves and our family." I have been struck by how many nurses I talked to spoke of their love for the profession and their desire to serve, even as they talked about how exhausted they are.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We end up feeling burnt out and essentially hating the very job that we started loving.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There are there for us in good times and bad times and we need to be there for them now, to protect them and help them when they need us the most.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Inflation in food and services have also increased steadily, hitting 7.5% and 3.7% respectively in December 2022.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This has clearly had an impact on many Singaporeans and their families.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Interestingly, during the same period, we saw more super-rich families setting up family offices in Singapore to manage their wealth.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The number of ultra-high net worth individuals, defined as individuals with at least US$30 million in investible assets, grew 8.6%, reaching 4,206 individuals in 2021, amongst which 28 are billionaires.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The number of ultra-high net worth individuals in Singapore is projected to increase to about 6,000 by 2026.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But taken together, one cannot help but express concern if our society will eventually become more stratified with the existence of two perceived "Singapores" – a Singapore that caters to the lifestyle and consumption demands of the wealthy and ultra-high net worth individuals; and another "Singapore" for everyone else.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Such perceptions are potentially divisive and might fracture the social compact that the Government has painstakingly built with Singaporeans over generations.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Much of this perception perhaps comes from the ostentatious display of wealth by these ultra-high net worth individuals.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While I believe that one should not hold anyone's wealth against them and each individual should be free to spend their money as they wish, I can also understand why conspicuous displays of wealth would not be well-received by many and could even lead to unhappiness and frustration and resentment amongst others.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I believe this is a risk that the present Government is aware of and this year's Budget sends a signal on how the wealthy can, and should, contribute more to our nation building.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The increase in consumption-based taxes such as higher Buyer’s Stamp and Additional Conveyance Duties for Buyers of higher-value properties and higher marginal Additional Registration Fee for higher-end luxury cars will potentially increase the tax base from which the Government can affect social transfers from those who can afford it to those who need more help and support.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This approach is a balanced and fair one since a consumption-based tax that targets luxury consumption does not significantly alter Singapore's competitive corporate and personal income tax because these taxes kick in only when one purchases high-end luxury properties and cars.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Ultimately, the increase in consumption tax of these high-end luxury properties is unlikely to dampen the demands for them since they can be considered as Veblen goods, that is, the increase in tax might actually drive up the demand for such products as they are now regarded to be even more exclusive.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This further increases the amount of tax that the Government can draw when the wealthy and ultra-high net worth individuals purchase them.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: From those who have more to those who need more.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am personally heartened to know that the Singapore Government, has through this Budget, further strengthened its commitment to support the majority of Singaporeans, especially those who need an additional leg up.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Enhanced GST Vouchers and the various support payouts under the Assurance Package will help to cushion some of the impact of the rising cost of living.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While we can never fully mitigate the impact of the rising cost of living, especially when many of the factors that drive costs up are external to our shores, what we can do is to minimise or assuage the impact of the increased costs by providing targeted assistance.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope that the Government will continue to support the more vulnerable communities through direct assistance such as CDC vouchers and GSTVs, and also strengthen short term assistance such as ComCare vouchers and financial assistance through the Social Services Offices.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I would now like to speak about enhancing the roles of fathers and men in families.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While the extension is presently still voluntary, this is nonetheless a step in the right direction.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At present, pro-family measures are mostly targeted at women, specifically, with tax incentives and support schemes for working mothers.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In comparison, there are fewer schemes in place to encourage men and fathers to play a more active role in their families and in parenting.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I would thus hope to see if more measures could be rolled out to support and enhance the role that men and fathers could play in their families over the course of their children's lives.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I would also like to ask if the Government can consider restructuring the present childcare leave structure so that parents are entitled to tiered childcare leave until their children turn 18.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At present, parents are entitled to six days of paid childcare leave until their youngest child turns seven years old.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The first three days of leave are paid by employers, with the remaining three days paid by the Government, subjected to a cap of $500 per day including CPF contributions.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I feel that we need to revisit this assumption.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Any parent would tell you that a child above the age of seven requires differentiated, but no less attention, as children below the age of seven.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As parents, we want to be there for our children, and with our children when they celebrate major life events and milestones, or simply just to spend time with them as they journey through life.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Speaking as a parent of a 15- and 12-year-old, I can tell you, Mr Deputy Speaker, and you might agree with me, that the journey only gets more challenging and intense after the age of seven.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I have also spoken before about the platforms to support the mental health and well-being of men in one of my previous speeches.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Making the same point, I hope that the Government can also better support men in their fatherhood journey and to enhance their roles as caregivers to complement the roles played by mothers.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Women are still naturally associated with being maternal and nurturing – terms that are still not naturally associated with men.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These perceptions are quite gender stereotypical and frankly, might actually be unfairly burdening women and mothers with more societal responsibilities and expectations.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Can we not do more to encourage fathers to play a larger role in nurturing their children, being there for their families?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Can MOE and MSF consider partnering NGOs like Dads for Life to conduct more workshops for fathers on parenting?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Similarly, can MOM consider how it could work with corporations and companies to support fathers?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At present, more support could be given to fathers at work.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many companies have initiatives that celebrate motherhood and have HR schemes such as flexible work scheme or part time work arrangements for working mothers.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Can we not do the same for fathers?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For instance, can fathers take on part time work arrangements without having to fear that such arrangements would be held against them, thus allowing fathers to play a more effective familial role without sacrificing their careers?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While a significant portion of this Budget is focused on providing near term support, other measures such as parenting and pro-family measures are longer term focused.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: One of the most crucial lynchpins to promoting parenting and pro-family measures is of course, public housing.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Public housing matters have been hotly debated in this House at the recent parliamentary sessions, mostly debating on the affordability of HDB flats for young Singaporeans who wish to own their first flat.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Let us not also forget that there is another group of Singaporeans who also deserve housing support – mid-age Singaporeans with children.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope that the Government does not forget this group and would like the Government to consider enhancing housing support for them, especially if they would like to purchase a resale flat in a mature estate to live close to their parents so they can form that extended, larger, familial support network.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Of course, caveats must be put in place to ensure that this system is not abused by those who choose mature estates for their own personal preferences albeit no familial ties in the estates.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, we must recognise that there also those whose elderly parents are living in mature estates where the prices of resale flats are high – what can we do to better support these buyers of resale flats in their desire to build and develop an extended family nucleus?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The full force of the crisis had been mitigated by decades of careful savings and implementation of sound measures.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Thus, we all have to do our best to save where we can.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is necessary to prepare for potential future crises, whether they are triggered by geopolitical tensions, extreme weather conditions or any other causes.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Most importantly, we must stay united as a people.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is our unity which has enabled us to overcome the crisis together.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: On the ground, many individuals and groups had come together to help those most badly hit by the pandemic.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: One of the first COVID-19 clusters was in my constituency in Henderson-Dawson.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: More specifically, it was at Bukit Merah View.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Quite a few residents had to be quarantined, leaving young children and the elderly at home.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: My community centre coordinated home care, delivery of food and necessities to these households.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I was heartened by organisations, volunteers, residents and grassroots leaders who stepped forward to help.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: There were also residents who donated money to their favourite hawkers whose livelihoods were hit hard by the COVID-19 restrictions.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Youth and children pitched in, drawing cards to comfort those in hospitals who could not receive visitors.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How can we keep these relationships and networks warm so that we can tap on them should another crisis strike?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Or rather, without the sensational nature of a crisis, how can we encourage more of us in the community to offer just that little bit of additional help and support to each other and lessen the burden together?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As expected, during a Budget debate, there will be many ideas put forth on how we can provide more support to Singaporeans and inevitably, that would mean we have to spend more.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, as fellow Singaporeans, we can all play our part to make this country a better place – and every little bit of effort counts.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If everyone can chip in just a bit more in their own way, be it to look out for each other or to lend a helping hand and with some creativity, I am very sure we can bring about a better Singapore for all.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In addition to asking each other how much you are getting from this year's Budget, can we also ask ourselves how we can do more to look after our families, our friends, our neighbours and our fellow Singaporeans?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The COVID-19 cluster incident in my constituency proves that indeed, we have many willing helping hands in our community.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What is needed is for all the stakeholders in an estate, in a community to be familiar with what to do in emergencies.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How can we set up and maintain crisis activation centres and keep the relationships among stakeholders, including residents, grassroots leaders, community organisations, places of worship and more, warm through regular bonding and training programmes?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We need more than Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) for emergencies like fires, floods, power failures and such.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: When the representatives on the ground know one another, can put a face to a name, the effectiveness of crisis management will be higher, and in some emergencies, every minute counts.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In countries like Japan, where they are constantly threatened by earthquakes, regular drills with high participation rates are the norm.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Beyond emergency preparedness exercises, our residents should know what to do when there is a fire, power or communications failure, flooding or more dramatic scenarios such as bomb threats or someone with a weapon on the loose.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We must co-create solutions in preparation for such threats.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In Mandarin):   I urge the Government to enhance the funding, support and resource allocation for crisis preparation amongst its agencies and on the ground.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is time for SGSecure to go beyond the threat of terrorism, and to mean more than "Run, Hide, Tell" to our people.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I hope that we can gather at least half of all Singaporeans to step forward to be trained in things like First Aid, CPR, basic firefighting and other critical life-saving skills, and to start training our younger generation in all these skills as well.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It takes time and effort to understand and nurture bonds among people with different backgrounds, gradually building mutual trust and solidarity.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Unity is only possible with these bonds and a willingness to place the interests of community above self, with the stronger helping the weaker.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is assuring that quite a few pressing issues have been addressed by this Budget.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Today, I would like to speak on two topics.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The first, is how to provide greater support for our small- and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and the second, is on assistance for special needs Institute of Technical Education (ITE) students from disadvantaged families.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Our SMEs contribute to almost half of our Gross Domestic Product (GDP) and employ at least two-thirds of our Singaporean workforce, playing a crucial role in our economy.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: They need supportive measures to ensure their growth and sustainability in an increasingly competitive business environment.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Presently, businesses face logistics problems as supply chains remain disrupted amidst increasing geopolitical tensions.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: They also must deal with rising wage bills as there is a shortage of skilled manpower.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The rising cost of business operations puts an enormous strain on their cashflows.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I am grateful for the various policies and schemes which the Government has implemented to assist them.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Government is also investing in the creation of innovation hubs, such as the Jurong Innovation District, to promote collaboration among companies, technology and education providers as well as research centres.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Is it to produce a certain number of unicorns by a certain timeline?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How soon do these SMEs receive the grants or reimbursement from the time they submit their applications?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Sometimes, the application process takes too long and they may not receive the subsidies in time to meet their operation cashflows.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Some commerce and trade associations assist SMEs with their applications for Government schemes and support measures too.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Ministry of Trade and Industry (MTI) may consider boosting financial support for chambers of commerce and business associations to better assist SMEs in this respect.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I understand that business consultants promote these Government schemes to their SMEs and their earnings are predicated on the loan amount approved or the amount of grant received.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Therefore, if the application cycle is too long for a particular scheme, it is less likely that a business consultant would promote this scheme to his or her clients.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I also urge our Government agencies and Government-linked companies to support our SMEs by providing more business to them so as to benefit almost 70% of the Singaporean workforce indirectly.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For example, the Government can divide big projects into smaller contracts, allowing SMEs to compete with one another to undertake such projects.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The winners will be able to establish reliable business channels and prove their performance abilities and competence to Government agencies, going on to achieve growth, expand their scale and develop to a size big enough to compete with foreign companies and compete for larger Government projects.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In Mandarin):   In terms of funding and resource support, the Government may wish to consider providing more support to SMEs that are already established and connected to our local networks, before considering whether it should support their overseas ventures.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Our local companies should develop an ecosystem comprising SMEs and local large companies (LLCs) to market their products and services as a team to multinational companies or when expanding to overseas markets.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Within this local network, our companies can share information on customers, other companies, industries and the economy, as well as services such as legal and translation services.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: There is also room for further collaboration between our businesses and our Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs) and research centres.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This type of team strategy had been used effectively by companies from countries such as Japan and Israel.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We can start from the 23 Industry Transformation Maps (ITMs).

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In English): As for the problem with manpower constraints, would the Government consider reviewing the foreign worker work permit quota?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Some SMEs argue that the quota is too low and does not reflect their actual labour needs.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As a result, they are unable to hire enough workers to meet their operation needs and are struggling to remain competitive.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: All these quotas are being taken up despite the high price of foreign workers levies.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Does that mean that the quota system is not working as desired?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: One of the major expenses for businesses is the Certificate of Entitlement (COE) for vehicles.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The cost of obtaining a COE can be significant, especially for larger vehicles like vans that are used for commercial purposes.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In addition, businesses must also pay for vehicle registration fees, road taxes and maintenance costs.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How about establishing an Alliance-for-Action involving Ministry of Manpower (MOM), Enterprise Singapore (ESG), Land Transport Authority (LTA) and companies like supermarket chains so as to explore the possibility of operating a fleet of commercial vehicles like vans and trucks 24 hours a day?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is to minimise lull time and mitigate the shortage of heavy vehicles carpark.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Can MOM issue more work passes to businesses like confectionaries, supermarket chain, essential services providers whose operations can function overnight?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: By doing so, our businesses can employ more foreign workers to overcome manpower shortages for roles which Singaporeans will not take up and as a result, the businesses' productivity will improve.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I spoke with a few SMEs owners who own diesel-fuelled buses and trucks.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Besides the high upfront cost, they also need to upgrade their substation which requires another sum of capital expenditure.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Next, I would like to advocate for special needs students from disadvantaged families while studying in ITEs.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: With more teaching staff, the lecturers will be able to provide more individual attention to students and customise their teaching to the specific needs of each student.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Significant progress in providing support and services for students with special education needs (SEN) has been made.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, may I suggest the following for further improvement?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Would the Government consider targeted public education campaigns, community outreach and increase the visibility of special needs students in mainstream settings to raise public awareness and understanding of special education needs to reduce stigma and gain acceptance?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I was informed that the current waiting time to be seen by Institute of Mental Health (IMH) or other restructured hospital can be long.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Proper assistance can only be rendered towards the special education needs students who have been diagnosed formally.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: There is also a need to expand support services, such as therapy, counselling and mental health services to meet the diverse needs of these students.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This could include increasing funding for services, expanding the pool of qualified professionals and increasing the availability of assistive technologies.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: These programmes can be tailored to meet the individual needs of students and provide them with the necessary skills to join the workforce.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This could include providing ongoing professional development opportunities and creating specialised training programmes.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: More inclusive classroom environments, providing more support services within mainstream schools and increasing the number of specialised schools and programmes would be a big step forward.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Parents of children with special education needs need more support and information on available support services, parent support groups and how they can be involved in decision-making processes related to their child's education.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: ITEs can support and improve accessibility for students with disabilities by making its facilities and campus more accessible.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This includes providing ramps, elevators and other assistive technology.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Last but not least, may I request support for ITEs to collaborate with community organisations and businesses and create internship and work opportunities for these students?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Internships will help students to gain practical experience and improve their chances of finding employment after graduation.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The crux of this Budget focuses on keeping our economy competitive and innovative, equipping our workers and providing a fuller range of opportunities for everyone to reach their potential.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Like all parents, they hope to secure the children's future.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: They want to ensure that their parents can have an adequate and dignified retirement.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: They are concerned on whether they can keep up with the cost of living.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These are on-going concerns of Zhenghua families which forms the central motivation of my speech.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As a nation, we need to ensure that we have the fiscal capabilities and revenue to sustain our social and healthcare needs.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To ensure continued real income growth for Singaporeans and adequate retirement savings, we must support local employers to compete and stay relevant on higher value products and services.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: First, by remaining competitive and relevant in an increasingly hostile world.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And second, by continuing to build a resilient nation.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I will first touch on remaining competitive and relevant in the global market.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As Singapore's workforce ages and the cost of doing business increases, we run the risks of pricing ourselves out of the region and becoming irrelevant.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is clear we are dealing with an ageing population and a higher average age of our workforce.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, other countries with a larger, younger and increasingly educated labour force are catching up.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The external environment is also becoming more hostile due to geopolitical tensions and rivalries.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This has led to greater onshoring of key manufacturing processes which threatens our livelihoods.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To safeguard our livelihoods and provide real wage growth for Singaporeans, we need to stay relevant in this new environment.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I would lay out three key areas of focus in my speech.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: First, we need to support employers to compete and stay relevant by providing higher value products and better service experience.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Second, we need to ensure employers can compete for, grow and retain talent.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Third, we need to support employers to compete on environmental sustainability credentials as more multinational enterprises (MNEs) and regional economic blocs are actualising emission cut targets and factoring this in their purchasing evaluations.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: First, our nation needs to stay relevant on providing the best customer experience value.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We are no longer competing based on costs, but rather on perceived value.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To ensure continued real income growth for Singaporeans, we must support local employers to compete and stay relevant on higher value products and services.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The importance of building strong relationships between organisations and their customers has taken on added significance.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As economies around the world develop in sophistication, consumers are offered greater choice and form higher expectations.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Higher expectations specifically on the overall customer experience.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Singapore can do more to improve our service culture.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The honesty in accepting that service levels can be improved marks the first step towards building a strong service culture.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: With it, comes the commitment to improve and it is believed that it is not an impossible task.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Soft skills such as tone, general demeanour and body language need to be further developed.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Indeed, these "soft skills" are important horizontal skill sets that apply across industries and engender greater self-awareness.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Our national airlines, Singapore Airlines, is a stellar example of what excellent customer experience is around the world.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: How can we achieve this in other sectors?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These soft skills are a part of SkillsFuture Singapore (SSG)'s Critical Core Skills and that it is a good start.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Under the "Interacting with Others" cluster, identifying internal and external needs of customers to deliver an effective customer experience is mentioned as a key competency.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: How can we encourage more employers to send their employees for training in these areas, to support businesses and workers' growth?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Importantly, how do we evaluate the effectiveness of this training?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: One way to evaluate is to scale up national benchmarks yearly when measuring service delivery and customer service standards.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We currently have the Institute of Service Excellence at Singapore Management University (SMU) doing a robust yearly review of the Customer Satisfaction Index in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It measures a gamut of customer satisfaction including customer expectations, the perceived overall quality of the product and service as well as its value.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Can this review be expanded to do a horizon-scanning against other comparable and emerging economies?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Our enterprises will also need to compete for, grow and retain talent.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To do so, our enterprises will need to benchmark human capital standards vis-à-vis industry and regional peers.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: At present, the Institute of Human Resource Professionals has a free Human Capital Diagnostic Tool (HCDT).

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The self-diagnostic HCDT Navigator covers 11 areas of human capital measurements and provides a diagnostic report within 30 minutes.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: A more comprehensive diagnostic is led by a qualified assessor, the result is an organisation report detailing the calculated human capital maturity level for processes and practices.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Employers will then be able to assess key areas to improve and benchmark against industry peers.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is a good tool that needs greater awareness amongst employers and be scaled up as every organisation's basic tool kit.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Through more tools like this, we can encourage higher adoption of human capital diagnostic and benchmarking.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Any form of transformation needs to begin with human capital improvements.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
