text: Human capital practices form a foundation for any ability to attract and retain talent.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This foundation would also maximise the value of the new Job-Skills Integrator scheme announced in this Budget.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Conversely, if an employer has a weak human capital quotient, the resource to integrate jobs and skills would be wasted, as there will be eventual churn than integration.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Certainly, we need to support employers to execute more progressive HR policies and I will share more recommendations during MOM's Committee of Supply debates.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Two key areas of benchmarking, customer experience and human capital quotient, these provides a constant health check for employers on competitiveness based on perceived value to customers and manpower talents.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To stay competitive in the global markets, aspects such as the cost issue may be difficult to compete on.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But we can be a strong contender in the realms of service culture, overall value and experience underpinned by strong human capital management.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We need to support employers to compete on environment sustainability credentials as more MNEs and regional economic blocs are actualising emission cuts' targets and factoring this in their purchasing evaluations.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Therefore, there is an increasing emphasis on carbon accounting in global supply chains.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Carbon accounting is a way of measuring how much greenhouse gas an organisation emits.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Like financial accounting, carbon accounting quantifies the impact of an organisation's business activities.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There is now a focus on "Scope 3" of accounting, referring to indirect emissions that occur in the value chain of a company and are not already included in Scope 1 and 2.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Tackling Scope 3 presents an additional layer of complexities, including opaque carbon accounting and tracking practices, the need to work collaboratively with customers, supply networks and industry groups; and the difficulty of keeping stakeholders engaged in a complex change effort.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As such, Scope 3 measurements and management can be daunting for many companies in Singapore because the data coverage is comprehensive while the data sources fall out of the companies' direct control.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Collecting this data requires collaboration with companies' value chain partners and is an important effort.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This will be seen as an effort to future-proof our industries and dovetails with the Singapore Green Plan.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I have heard of cases where MNEs prefer one hotel over another to conduct their yearly corporate conferences and Dinner and Dance (D&D) because it is more sustainable.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Therefore, by equipping our local enterprises with the abilities and tools to account for carbon, we future-proof their relevance in a world increasingly being traded by green measurements.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We can build this new capability on our competitive advantage, on our reputation as a trusted, transparent financial hub.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I will now move on to the importance of building a resilient nation.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: A very important aspect of "resilience" is climate resilience and adaptation, something which cannot be ignored.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Singapore is not insulated from the impact of climate change.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Last year, I spoke on climate resilience and adaptation.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I am heartened that this year, it is mentioned in the Deputy Prime Minister's Budget.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: No matter what we do to advance the green economy and reduce the rate of temperature increases, we are already experiencing the effects of climate change.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Climate adaptation should not just be seen as a defensive mechanism.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We should regard this as an offensive strategy by turning this into a new exportable technology and service to societies around the world.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As Singapore is not endowed with renewable energy resources such as land for solar energy production or large river dams for hydropower production, our ability to create value in this area is limited.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, Singapore has built up deep expertise in engineering and design over the past few decades.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Indeed, there are manpower constraints as businesses continue to face issues.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: If businesses do not have the available manpower, they will be hard pressed to deliver the best service experience in a timely manner.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: With our ageing workforce and low birth rates, in comparison to the younger workforce in the region, in the longer run, other concerns emerge.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Hence, I call on the Government to continue to ensure Singaporeans have access to the best jobs.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But growing jobs for Singaporeans is a non-zero-sum game.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Employers need complimentary manpower to stay competitive and relevant.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While I do not believe that this is the case as supporting society and businesses goes hand-in-hand, I hope that the Deputy Prime Minister can allay such concerns.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We need SMEs to feel that they are being supported in their growth journey, so that we have more large local enterprises (LLEs).

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: LLEs and SMEs are rooted to Singapore and can provide longer-term jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Overall, this Budget will continue to strengthen our common resilience agenda and reinforce Singapore's strong social compact.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is exactly the price spiral I spoke about during the debate on public housing two weeks ago.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: More tax revenue would also be needed to fund the additional grants.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As land costs is determined based on resale transactions, the increase in resale prices would result in higher land cost.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The amount that HDB pays to Singapore Land Authority (SLA) for land would increase, thereby, increasing the cost of new flats.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This would mean that either new flat buyers have to pay more, or subsidies and grants for new flats must be increased to make the new flats affordable.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: More tax revenue would be needed to fund any increase in subsidies and grants.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Such a cycle of more and more tax revenue being needed to be paid into reserves in the form of land price is unsustainable and places an unnecessary tax burden on taxpayers.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Deputy Prime Minister and Finance Minister has said that we continue to be in a financially tight situation and the reserves drawn out to fund the COVID-19 packages were unlikely to be paid back.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: An occasional paper from the Ministry of Finance (MOF) on medium-term fiscal projections has also warned of the need to raise further taxes to fund the expected increase in expenditures.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Under such an environment, any increase in subsidies and grants for housing would necessitate an increase in taxes.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This situation is caused by the way we treat land sales proceeds.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Under current practice, the proceeds from the sale of land are put into reserves.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government argues that to do otherwise would reduce the value of the reserves.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Back in the days when land was sold on a freehold basis, this practice made financial sense and was the prudent thing to do.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, when land is sold on a freehold basis, this practice should have been reviewed.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Since land reverts to the state at the end of the leasehold period, there is no reduction in the value of the reserves at that point.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On what basis do we claim that our future generations have been deprived?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The same piece of land the Government now owns will still belong to the Government 99 years later, or 20 years later or at the end of any other lease period.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The land sale proceeds is payment for the use of the land over the lease period.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is similar to rental payments which is also payment for the use of land over a fixed period, albeit a shorter one.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Whether the use of the land is given on a three-year basis, 20-year basis or 99-year basis, the same principle applies.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At the previous Budget, I have argued that land sales proceeds should be treated as revenue divided over the period of the lease.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I have also illustrated via a table how this can grow into a significant revenue stream in a steady state.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: MOF's response to my proposal then was that this is a different concept.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They do not deny the soundness and financial prudence of the proposal.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Today, I venture further to point out that the situation we are facing with home affordability issues highlights how the current practice of putting land sales proceeds into reserves is not sustainable and places unnecessary tax burden on taxpayers.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The increasing land cost that necessitated higher subsidies and grants in order to keep houses affordable makes higher taxes necessary.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, if the land sale proceeds were taken as revenue, higher land costs mean higher revenue which can fund the higher subsidies and grants without needing higher taxes.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is inherent stability in this approach and the concept is sound.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Against the backdrop of the tight fiscal position shown in MOF's paper, if we continue with the current accounting practice, the tax burden of HDB subsidies and grants will get increasingly painful in the years ahead.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Proceeds on the sale of leasehold land is income generated from land reserves, similar to the investment returns from our Sovereign Wealth Funds.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Treating the proceeds from sale of leasehold land as revenue is thus similar to Net Investment Returns Contribution (NIRC).

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Whereas in the case of financial assets, we may need to retain part of the investment returns to ensure the value of the assets keep up with inflation, the value of the land that reverts to the state at the end of the lease period is inflation-proof.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP therefore urges the Government again to review its accounting treatment of land sales proceeds.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Coming after the announcement of the 2% GST hike, MOF's paper warning of tax increases raises worries of further tax burdens on the people who are already straining under the rapid increase in cost of living.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The additional taxes in this year's Budget have fallen primarily on individuals rather than companies.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, higher GST, higher taxes on tobacco and higher-end properties and vehicles.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Companies, on the other hand, have either new tax incentives or existing ones extended.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP is of the view that the more profitable companies should pay more taxes.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Those with higher profits paid a lower percentage.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Companies with the highest profits actually pay the lowest percentage of their profits as tax!

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In their reply, MOF stated that effective tax rate should be calculated based on percentage of chargeable income, not profits before tax.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Profits before tax is calculated based on internationally accepted accounting standards but chargeable income is affected by things like which expenses are tax deductible and which are not, what income is taxable and what is not, which capital expenditure can be expensed over one year and which over longer and so on.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In other words, chargeable income has already incorporated part of our tax policies and treatments.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Therefore, to see the full effect of our tax policies on companies in a holistic manner, not just of the corporate tax rate but also tax incentives, exemptions and other treatments, we should be comparing the amount of tax paid with profits before tax.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should review the tax incentives and treatments given to companies earning profits beyond $10 million so that they pay more taxes.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is time for companies to pay a fairer share of their profits as taxes.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Even in the absence of any global agreement, this is something we should do, not because we are forced to and it need not be tied to any global timetable.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We have traditionally used low corporate tax as a means to attract investments.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When the global minimum corporate tax is implemented, this strategy will lose effectiveness.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: With the loss of this tool, it has become even more urgent for us to find ways to address the high cost in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP therefore urges a thorough review of our policies on property and transport to bring down costs.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The Labour Movement welcomes Government's support for workers in this year's Budget Statement to grow our economy, improve training and job placement, enhance employment support for those who may need more help and to tackle the rising cost of living.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The COVID-19 pandemic has taught us that trust between people, institutions, businesses and Government is critical.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: When businesses in some sectors were badly hit and jobs were uncertain, it is this trust that enables National Trades Union Congress (NTUC) and our tripartite partners to work closely to save jobs, support our businesses and workers.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: We cannot assume that the trust we have built with our workers will continue to be strong over time.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: We have to engage with each generation of workers to listen to their needs, anxieties, their aspirations and to provide assurance that we will walk the journey with them.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: With these in mind, NTUC launched the #EveryWorkerMatters Conversations or EWMC in short, last year.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Since its launch, NTUC has been listening to a wide range of workers from youths to mature workers, Professionals, Managers and Executives (PMEs), the self-employed, essential service workers, caregivers and to ex-offenders.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: We are excited to share our recommendations when they are ready, sometime later this year.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: We aim to put forth valuable feedback and useful recommendations that can shape policies with our workers' interests at its core.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: After all, workers are at the heart of our nation's progress." Through the #EWMC engagements, key themes and preliminary ideas are emerging and taking shape, which my fellow Labour Members of Parliament (MPs) will cover in their respective speeches.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: This includes retirement adequacy, un-employment support, supporting younger workers and workers in the lower-wage sectors, workplace health and safety, caregiving, training, among others.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: And in the next part on my speech, I will provide an update on NTUC initiatives to support training and upskilling of our workers.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: I believe that to empower our workers with opportunities and abilities, we need to build a culture of lifelong learning.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: In Randstad's recent 2022 Workmonitor study, 91% of employees surveyed in Singapore have indicated an interest in career learning and development opportunities.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Despite this, only 22% said that they have received training and upskilling opportunities from their employers in the past 12 months.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: That said, since 2015, around 30% of eligible Singaporeans have utilised their SkillsFuture credit.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The first reason is a practical one regarding time, money and manpower.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: At the focus group discussions, participants shared that manpower-lean firms may not allow workers to go for training and might call workers back even if they were scheduled for training due to operational needs.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Many find training course fees rather high despite subsidies from SkillsFuture Credit and other funds.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Companies also do not provide protected time and employees often have to take time outside of work to upgrade themselves.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: And this often has to be balanced with other priorities like caregiving.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The second reason is the lack of confidence in the returns on training.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Employees had expressed their doubts if training could bring about any real positive impact for their careers, in terms of job or wage growth.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Employees also questioned how useful or relevant training could be, if there are no real opportunities for application within the company.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Similarly, employers expressed concerns that employees might change jobs or change companies after receiving training.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The third reason is the lack of awareness towards training needs and opportunities.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Workers may not have sufficient knowledge to diagnose their own skills gap and the skillsets required for their next intended career move.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Similarly, employers find it challenging to identify the required skill sets or knowledge that employees might need for certain job roles.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: These findings do suggest that employees are more prepared to go for training if they were initiated by the employers, when training is for purpose of meeting specific job demands within the company and with better assurance of time support and wage outcomes.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: One example of a CTC company is the Royal Plaza on Scotts (RPS).

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The company formed a CTC and had two rounds of Operations Technology Roadmap to transform its business and to redesign its jobs.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: One direct beneficiary of CTC is Mr Hamid bin Selamat, who was an engineering supervisor.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Positive and open-minded towards upgrading, he took up security modules and became a certified Security Officer at the age of 65.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Now, he can perform two roles in the company – engineering and security – with benefits such as better wages and better work prospects.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: We hope more companies will follow suit and will work with NTUC in forming CTCs, because we are committed to support you in the journey of enterprise and workforce transformation.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Last year, brother Chee Hong Tat spoke about the challenge of jobs-skills mismatch, where employers, on the one hand, are short-handed and could not find enough workers to fill vacancies, and workers, on the other hand, find the skills they acquired are not a good fit to what employers are looking for.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: With the involvement of industry, training and employment facilitation partners, we envisage that the Jobs-Skills Integrators will help to bridge the information gap for workers and employers, who may find it difficult to identify high-quality training which industries will find relevant.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Our Government has always been supportive of continuous learning and skills upgrading.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Many initiatives have been introduced to support workers’ upskilling, whether at work or during job transition.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: I hope SkillsFuture Singapore will progressively expand the SCTP to more sectors so that more workers can benefit from this scheme.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: I also call on the Government to consider protected training leave for employees and review training fund and allowances, to support our workers in alleviating their concern for the lack of time and finances and for opportunity cost when they had to attend training.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: For example, the Government can consider introducing training allowances that are tied to the trainees under the SCTP.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Supply chain disruptions caused by the war in Ukraine and the COVID-19 pandemic have impacted our economic and labour landscape significantly.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: In many countries, this heightens the risk of conflict and instability.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: As risk intelligence company Verisk Maplecroft’s chief analyst said, and I quote, “We are talking about numerous powder kegs around the world simply waiting for that spark to be ignited.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: We just don’t know where that spark will come first”.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Recently, we have seen these “sparks” flying through bitter strikes in countries such as the UK, France and South Korea, which threaten the delivery of essential service in healthcare as well as in public transportation.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: In the UK, strike actions were carried out by workers such as nurses, rail workers, postal workers, ambulance workers and airport staff.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Workers there demand for higher wages due to higher inflation.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Because of the strike by ambulance workers, residents with serious but non-life-threatening conditions might not be immediately attended to by an ambulance.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Closer to home in Asia, the truckers in South Korea initiated strike actions against their government.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: They were calling their government to make permanent a policy on minimum freight rates for container and cement truck drivers.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: To end the strike, the government had to issue “back-to-work” orders, by which the strikes had already lasted for two weeks and cost US$2.7 billion to the economy, according to their government’s estimates.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: These strike actions had caused disruption to public lives, demoralised workers, discouraged investments and destabilised the economy.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: In Singapore, we have managed to avoid such stand-offs through tripartite arrangement and with each tripartite partner doing its part and working hand in hand.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: One example is the Progressive Wage Model (PWM).

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: PWM was first implemented in 2014 for the cleaning sector.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Since then, we have progressively rolled out PWM in seven sectors and two occupations.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: With PWM, workers can be assured that they will not only receive a minimum wage corresponding to their sector and occupation, but also defined career pathways that would ensure that their wages increase as their skills and responsibilities increase as well.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Together with the expanded Local Qualifying Salary (LQS), this would benefit more than 90%, in fact, 94% of lower-wage workers.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: At this juncture, I would like to make a comment on the proposal by Mr Leong Mun Wai on "Living Wage", which is a guaranteed take-home of $1,800 for all Singaporean workers.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: It is noteworthy that Mr Leong agrees with the PWM, as he also said that the PWM can remain to help workers achieve a higher level of wage than the "Living Wage".

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The PWM mandates fair and sustainable wages according to skill level.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: It is tailored to each sector and agreed upon by the tripartite partners – the Government, the employers and unions.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: As mentioned, we have steadily expanded the PWM into seven sectors and two occupations, and together with the LQS which is set at $1,400, our low-wage workers can also receive a Workfare Income Supplement (WIS) of up to $350 per month.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: PWM and LQS combined already cover a wide base of 94% of all low-wage workers within this year.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The remaining 6% are small family-owned businesses which would usually not be covered by minimum wage in other countries as well.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: We need a sustainable and systematic mechanism to set and review the floor.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: My colleague Fahmi Aliman will suggest a way to review our LQS in his speech later.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: I recognise that we all want wages to be high.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: In NTUC it is our raison d'être to have better wages, welfare and work prospects.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: But we must also do this sustainably, without causing unintended consequences like disemployment.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: We want higher wages but we also want higher employment rates and there had been studies that showed clear downsides on minimum wage, including disemployment and the perverse outcome that the minimum wage becomes the maximum wage.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: And this is of concern especially in a small economy in Singapore where SMEs form the bulk of our workers.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: So, in NTUC, we support a PWM that is customised to sector or occupation, ensure productivity improvements with clear career pathways.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: In this way, we can move confidently with our tripartite partners and our workers get their assurance of a basic wage and a ladder for increase over the years as their skills upgrade.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, the challenges posed by the pandemic over the past three years have highlighted the need for Singapore to build a more flexible and adaptable workforce to respond to the rapidly changing labour market and industry needs.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: NTUC must also constantly transform to better serve workers in all sectors regardless of job position, industry, full-time or part-time, platform worker or self-employed.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: NTUC is committed to safeguarding your interest and providing you with better wages, welfare and work prospects.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: For employers, we hope that they will continue to drive business transformation.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Although this year is the Year of the Rabbit, we should not adopt a wait-and-see attitude.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Instead, we should be as nimble as a rabbit and use the keen sense of business acumen to drive business transformation and bring about business growth by leaps and bounds.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: (In English): Charting our paths forward, the NTUC affirms the importance of tripartism.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Since the NTUC Modernisation Seminar in 1969, generations of Government, businesses and union leaders have worked hard to build and sustain Singapore’s brand of tripartism.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: I quote Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong’s speech during NTUC National Delegates Conference in 2011.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: He said this about tripartism, and I quote, “We have to preserve this ability, this trust at all costs.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: It’s an intangible national treasure; we built it up through our young history.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: It’s one of the most valuable things we can pass on to our future generations.” Tripartism is Singapore’s national treasure.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: And we must never be complacent or take it for granted because one misstep can break this trust.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: It works when all parties represent our constituents' interests well.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Regarding the case he mentioned of how NTUC raised an issue with the security agency, I want to assure him and his industry colleagues that in NTUC, our unions believe that companies must be given the flexibility to transform and right-size.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: But the company must also do so fairly and adhere to the established principles and guidances, such as in this case the Tripartite Guidelines for Fair Employment Practices both in substance and in spirit.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The Labour Movement will continue to work with our tripartite partners to resolve any differences that may arise every now and then amicably and through established processes.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Ultimately, we want our companies to do well and to create good jobs for our workers.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Through the #EWMC, the NTUC will renew our social compact with our workers and bring to the table of tripartite partners the collective sentiments of our workers.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: And in so doing, strengthening tripartism, preserving industrial peace and building a more resilient nation as we move into the new era together.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: To every worker in Singapore, on behalf of the Labour Movement, we want to thank you for your hard work and sacrifices throughout the pandemic.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The NTUC will continue to champion for your interest to achieve better wages, welfare and work prospects because every worker matters.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: It is a thoughtful and forward-looking Budget which supports the diverse needs of society while ensuring judicious spending as we build our resilience to embrace future challenges and opportunities.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The nature of our economy as we know, is shifting and changing due to digital disruption and the green transition.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We cannot shy away from these, and in fact, we must be at the forefront to ensure that Singapore remains a competitive and attractive investment location.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In the longer term, this will lead to better jobs, better wages and better opportunities for our local workforce.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: However, because of this rapid restructuring, the nature of work is transforming and the half-life of skills is shortening.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Understandably, this has caused greater uncertainty and anxiety for our local workforce.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This is further exacerbated by demand softening in various parts of the world, resulting in cyclical headwinds in sectors such as manufacturing in the electronics and semi-conductor space.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: On top of this, there is also the challenge of soaring energy prices which is eroding profits of companies.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I do hope the Government will also consider helping other critical sectors to cope, such as through energy rebates for export-focused electronics firms, to keep these high-value industries afloat and ensure workers’ livelihoods.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In my past speeches, I have highlighted a segment of our workforce which has been impacted immensely.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: They are the Professionals, Managers and Executives – PMEs for short – especially those 40 to 60 years of age.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: They are in a particularly precarious position when they lose their jobs as they generally have more dependents.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: They also take a longer time to find a new job in view of their age and may lack relevant skills to take on the new and growing areas and jobs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Upon re-entry to employment, there is also an increasing propensity for them to suffer from a drop in wages.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: As we move forward, we need to keep a look out for every worker and bring everyone along together on this journey of progress because every worker matters.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Some of these, such as the short-term financial support, are part of the recommendations presented by the joint NTUC-SNEF PME Taskforce which I co-chaired with the Singapore National Employers Federation (SNEF).

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I also spoke about them in my last Budget speech.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I am heartened that the Government has taken these recommendations to help our local PMEs into serious consideration, but there is also still more that we can do to support our workers facing anxieties about unemployment.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Today, PMEs are generally less likely to receive support from the Government in view of their earlier higher income.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: However, as I shared earlier, PMEs are an increasingly vulnerable group because of rapid economic changes and cycles.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: When complemented with active labour market interventions, unemployment support – or using another term, re-employment support – can help displaced PMEs in their job search journey.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The support provides displaced workers the space to upgrade their skills and look out for suitable employment, with the knowledge that they would be able to continue supporting their family’s basic needs during this difficult period.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This increases the likelihood of PMEs looking for jobs that are a good match to their skillsets or which offer progression opportunities.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: With a better job match, their employment duration at their next job could be longer and any under-employment mitigated.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This finding echoed the calls I made consistently since 2014 when I first started lobbying for some form of unemployment support for our PMEs and workers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We still hear the same today, as we carry out our #EveryWorkerMatters Conversation.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Indeed, we have seen how unemployment support can serve as a lifeline while facilitating workers to upgrade their skills and actively search for jobs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: To be eligible, unemployed workers must prove that they have actively participated in job search or training or attempted to improve their business revenue, if self-employed.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: NTUC’s e2i will contact individuals who are receiving their third tranche of CRG to refer them to resources that can support their job search efforts.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I am grateful that the CRG has been extended till the end of 2023, as many workers are still recovering from the pandemic’s economic impact.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: However, I would like to reiterate the call for the Government to go a step further and introduce a permanent scheme that would provide short-term unemployment support for all workers who are involuntarily displaced, including PMEs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Beneficiaries could similarly be required to prove that they are actively trying to re-enter the job market.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In this way, it provides targeted support, coupled with upskilling and job matching which NTUC is well-placed to support, to help workers rebound and re-enter employment.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I acknowledge that a scheme of such scale will be challenging to introduce, but I implore the Government to seriously consider this proposal.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This scheme would reassure our workers that we will work hand-in-hand with them to navigate through the exacting changes and challenges in the global economy.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The second important element is facilitated employment and training.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Job-seeking can be a very daunting experience, especially when the individual is forced to seek new employment involuntarily.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Our employment facilitation landscape must optimise the job-seeker experience by funnelling them seamlessly to the support they need at various stages.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This could be in the form of customised career counselling and advisory or training that would equip them to take on jobs in growth areas or redesigned job roles.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Thereafter, we need to enable a good career match via schemes such as the Career Conversion Programmes, which allow workers to be placed in new roles, and then undergo structured on-the-job training to transit into the new role.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: NTUC’s e2i is committed to working closely with the Government to support jobseekers, particularly the more vulnerable, mature tech mid-careerists as well as those most likely to be affected by the green transition, such as workers in the oil and gas industries. e2i’s Lift-and-Place model can be leveraged to facilitate the movement of workers from sectors that are declining to adjacent sectors that require similar skills, or sectors that need to quickly ramp up operations.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Our unions and union leaders will also work together to improve career matching and transition assistance to workers at the grassroots.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: While we embark on these efforts, I hope employers will also do their part by recognising vocational certifications of mid-careerists who have upskilled or reskilled themselves and want to enter different sectors, such as the tech sector.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In the long run, this will help the local talent pipeline and strengthen our Singaporean Core.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Beyond supporting displaced workers, we must also facilitate upskilling and reskilling amongst those who are still in employment.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I urge the Government to consider incentivising more employers to send their employees for training, by providing higher funding support for Absentee Payroll and providing maximum funding for courses relevant to sectors where there is a shortage of local PMEs and workers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This enhanced funding of both training and absentee payroll can also be extended to sectors and companies facing difficult cyclical challenges such as in the electronics sector, even as most of our industries recover post pandemic.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We should also facilitate access to career coaching to empower workers to chart their career paths.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The last element, or should I say the last "F" is fair access to PME roles for our locals.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We must ensure a level playing field for our local PMEs and the foreign talent that we bring in to complement our local workforce.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: NTUC as the Labour Movement have been lobbying for and watching this space, whether it is discrimination with respect to age, gender, nationality, or even disability, whether physical or mental, as well as all other forms of discriminatory practices.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We now have the tripartite guidelines for fair employment practices, as well as the Tripartite Alliance for Fair and Progressive Employment Practices (TAFEP).

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Employers should establish and implement policies and practices to foster a fair and inclusive workplace and provide a safe environment for workers to report concerns.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: To do so effectively, it is crucial for companies to have certified Human Resource (HR) professionals, either by the Institute of Human Resource Professionals (IHRP) or other internationally recognised organisations.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: SMEs with lean manpower should also be equipped with such HR professionals, perhaps through the introduction of shared HR services.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Where retrenchments are inevitable, the Government must ensure fair and responsible retrenchment practices are adopted.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Our local workers, especially mature PMEs, will continue to face volatility and uncertainty.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: What matters is that we remain resilient, seek out opportunities amidst these disruptions and adapt to ride the waves of change.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I believe we have the means, the resources, the capabilities and the right people to make this happen in Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Nevertheless, I believe it falls short in a number of areas.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: My speech will begin by offering some direct responses to the Budget before moving on to offer suggestions on how we may inspire growth via three of its key drivers: labour, capital and productivity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: My first observation is that the fiscal policy stance will be contractionary.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But Members will undoubtedly be aware that this fiscally conservative approach tends to reduce the amount of available revenue, which in turn is more likely to throw up a deficit.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I will not quibble over whether this methodology is justified.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It has been litigated and relitigated already in this House.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But I simply point out the fact, evident to all economists, that the Budget is, by conventional international standards, in surplus.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We may argue that this position is well justified; after all, we are not currently in a recession and we do need to build up a fiscal buffer should one visit us next year, and the Government is also constitutionally bound to run a balanced Budget during its full term.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But let us just recognise that just two years after the worst recession in our country since Independence and notwithstanding the many giveaways in this year’s Budget, our fiscal impulse has decisively turned negative.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In my speech on the Income Tax (Amendment) Bill last year, I had suggested that one option available to the Government for rebating some of the unexpectedly higher revenue receipts to the people was to beef up of the GST Voucher (GSTV) scheme.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In particular, I had suggested that the Government’s claim that GSTV would offset 20 years of GST payable had been eroded by inflation, by between one month and a year, depending on one’s flat size.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It therefore offers much-needed support for coping with higher costs of living.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Of course, the increase in cash quanta of between $100 and $150 has been somewhat diluted by higher sticker prices.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Still, even taking inflation into account, the Budget still offers real increases of between $94 and $104measured in last year’s dollars, or $90 and $135 in 2021 dollars.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In my speech on last year’s Budget Statement, I had also outlined a number of alternative revenue levers that the Workers’ Party believes are viable ways to raise revenue.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: These included an externalities lever, which would increase sin taxes as well as a wealth tax lever, which requires greater contributions from those who can afford to pay more.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As I explained then, it would be even possible to mix and match between the levers to derive a revenue mix that we can all accept.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I note that this Budget, by introducing additional taxes on high-end properties, luxury cars and tobacco, pulls some of the levers that we had previously suggested.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To paraphrase Groucho Marx – a few hundred million here, a few hundred million there, and soon, you are talking about real money.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Minister Wong explained that this was about "keeping pace with inflation".

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I understand that this will not affect lower-income earners who earn below the ceiling and that, while it will reduce take-home pay for those earning more than $8,000 by about $400, the increased employer contributions mean that certain workers would enjoy a modest pay bump of around $340 as their employers' contributions rise.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Pay increases to cope with inflation are certainly a good thing as is making sure that our savings are adequate for retirement.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: However, for the typical middle-class family in Sengkang, the smaller take-home will stretch already tight budgets.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The $400 could mean cutting back on tuition fees or that extra visit to the dentist for the family.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: One wonders why the Government did not choose the route of returning the employer contribution to the full 20% instead.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: After all, this was the status quo in the 1990s until the Asian Financial Crisis.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The employer share has since been cut and raised a number of times since but the equal share that was the case in the past has never been restored.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While I understand the need to provide employers with relief in the wage bill during a recession, we are not in one now.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While restoring the employer contribution alone will not fully make up for the additional CPF savings that would result from an increased ceiling, one is still left to wonder why this approach was not part of the consideration for addressing the effects of inflation on CPF.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I now move on to discuss three ways I think we can do even more.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: During 2021's Committee of Supply debate, I sketched out the case for heightened total R&D expenditures, noting that its share – of a little shy of 2% of GDP – fell behind not only the global average of 2.3% but also those of leading knowledge-oriented nations such as the United States, Japan, Korea and Israel.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The latest data reveal that spending by these other nations have all ticked up, as has world R&D spending, which is now up 0.3 percentage-points to 2.6% of GDP.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In contrast, our national R&D rose only to 2.2% as a result of a collapse in output that year.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As a share of GDP in the prior year, it remained mostly stagnant at 2%.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: At the time, the Government stressed that our public expenditures do not significantly lag that of a number of advanced economies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But where is the discrepancy between the public and the private?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It starts with an acknowledgement, which I believe that the Government will agree with, that public R&D cannot be expected to carry the load on its own.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Rather, it needs to be a catalyst for our otherwise woeful private-sector spending on R&D.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Recognising this is key since there is evidence that the two are indeed complements and raising public R&D directly will contribute to greater business R&D.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, such spillovers may be even greater for open economies such as our own.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But what is necessary to elevate our lagging national productivity is both of these working in tandem.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This will take advantage of exemptions for R&D credit in the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)'s Base Erosion and Profit Shifting (BEPS) framework.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Specifically, countries are indeed allowed to continue awarding R&D contracts to reduce the tax bills of multinational corporations (MNCs).

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Generous tax credits create incentives for firms to locate their R&D activities in a subsidiary in Singapore, which in turn books R&D fees off revenue from the firm's entities in other jurisdictions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Singapore is a signatory to the agreement and so adhering to the stipulations to BEPS eventually will be a given.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: R&D credits offer an opportunity for us to stimulate our domestic research activity in a perfectly legitimate fashion.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But aspiration aside, up till now, the absolute number of firms assisted remains small – to the tune of about 520 companies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The question is how the Government plans to scale up this assistance, especially among SMEs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This echoes a point made by my hon friend, Leon Perera, in a speech that highlighted our missing mid-sized firms, way back in 2016.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: What has been the main inhibitor to more enthusiastic take-up?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Could these constraints be relaxed especially if we were to ease up on the need for recipients to demonstrate short-term results?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is welcome, especially if it is directed towards investment and innovation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Our public expenditure on R&D remains inadequate, especially, in my view, in the "D" part of R&D.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In 2020, applied research expenditures actually declined by 4.3% even as spending in a number of other classes rose.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is especially worrisome since it is translational research of this form – basically, adapting basic research into commercially viable products, which often experiences a higher failure rate – where the Government can play a critical role in risk sharing, with a potentially high payoff for the economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Such vehicles already exist, such as A*STAR, EDBI or EDB New Ventures.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But in my conversations with those in the sector, the need for officers in such agencies to meet short-term key performance indicators (KPIs) has been cited as a constraint.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Adopting the "venture" mindset requires tolerance of higher loss ratios.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Would the Government consider setting up specific funding buckets that will allow the funding of moonshots with more flexible targets and fill more of the gap between seed and Series A funding?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Another approach is to undertake the exercise hand-in-hand via a more involved public-private partnership (PPP) model.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: There is evidence that public credits directed towards PPPs can spur private sector innovation as can a better matching of universities with startups.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Such an approach would be especially fruitful in areas such as biotech and pharmaceuticals where we have world-class upstream research produced by our universities along with excellent specialised downstream production capacity but, up till now, insufficient midstream capabilities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Speaking of BEPS, it is worthwhile thinking carefully about the practical rollout of the treaty.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The terms require that the global minimum corporate tax rate be set at 15%.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: My hon friend, Louis Chua, had previously made the point that the effective tax rate faced by MNCs and SMEs differ.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: According to the Government, the effective corporate tax rate averages between 8% and 10% for MNCs and around 3% for SMEs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Notwithstanding the ongoing uncertainty about the implementation of BEPS, the Workers' Party continues to urge the Government to maintain this differential treatment of MNCs and SMEs, insofar as the effective corporate tax rate is concerned and to treat all MNCs regardless of size equally.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: By our calculations, even with a reasonable loss of corporate and personal income taxes arising from the agreement, this approach to BEPS will still be a net positive for Government revenue.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Placing the burden of higher corporate taxation on the shoulders of MNCs that are more able to afford it – a point that the hon Member Hazel Poa has mentioned earlier on – and who are the primary targets of the agreement in any case will provide a better business climate for our SMEs to eventually grow and become international companies in their own right and help rebalance our economy away from our historical reliance on multinationals.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: At the time, I had also suggested a natural end-to-end complementarity between redundancy insurance at the point of separation, to re-training, to eventual reintegration into the workforce.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In his speech, Minister Wong spoke about introducing Jobs-Skills Integrators as a means of better empowering our workers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: He also spoke about strengthening our safety nets but glaringly misses out how our net still provides inadequate support at the point of unemployment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The Stanford economist, Paul Romer, once quipped that "a crisis is a terrible thing to waste".

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is a pithy way to emphasise how competing interests may be willing to question their long-held assumptions and come together to confront a common problem.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: COVID-19 was our crisis du jour and the generous support we offered then to displaced workers offered us a tantalising glimpse of how valuable redundancy insurance can actually be.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This Government likes to reiterate that "a job is the best welfare." But what happens when our workers lose their jobs for reasons little related to their performance or ability?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It seems to me that as a society, we need to help these workers get back on their feet.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In other words, we need a backup support system for redundant workers to access their first-best welfare system – which is a job.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: One of the common reasons cited for not deploying an unemployment insurance scheme is the potential corrosive effects that having such insurance could have on workers' incentives to search for a job, at least until the payout period ends.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In the worst-case scenario, detractors fear that having unemployment insurance will encourage quits because workers are confident that they will have a fallback source of income.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is the crux of the objection by the then-Second Minister for Manpower, Mrs Josephine Teo, in her response to then-Workers' Party Non-Constituency Member of Parliament Daniel Goh's speech on redundancy insurance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Notwithstanding how our proposal is for involuntary redundancy and not all forms of unemployment, these so-called "moral hazard" concerns are well recognised.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: However, the theoretical fear does not find much support in the empirical data.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Studies of advanced economies that have rolled out such insurance schemes tend to find little adverse effects for employment outcomes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, we should not simply focus on the negatives and conclude that the scheme is a bad one.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The flip side of a greater willingness to quit is the reduction of insecurity and worry associated with a lost job or an end to the helplessness and frustration felt when stuck in a job that is making one unhappy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The converse of a possible free rider who is soaking up welfare payouts and therefore voluntarily remaining unemployed is a parent who does not need to worry about being able to afford sending their child for tuition or to the doctor just because they lost their job.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, economists understand full well this trade-off and suggest that the optimal design of unemployment insurance schemes is to properly calibrate the tenure requirement – that is, how long an unemployed worker can benefit from the scheme – with a monetary requirement, which determines how much payout a worker can receive.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Interestingly, optimal schemes tend to pair a larger monetary requirement with a low tenure requirement.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Other tweaks may entail a diminution of benefits over the course of one's unemployment spell or to deploy a wage tax after re-employment that increases the longer an individual has remained unemployed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: However, we leave open the door for increases based on consultation and social consensus.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Workers made redundant may choose to front-load their benefits if they have urgent bills to pay but may opt to rely on savings initially and only receive payouts later in the event that their unemployment turns out to be longer than anticipated.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In the spirit of encouraging risk-taking and entrepreneurship, we can also consider including the self-employed in the scheme, perhaps with different contribution shares, as we did during COVID-19.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Another major thrust of Mrs Teo’s critique of our proposal at the time was that it was better for the Government to bear the burden of unemployment support, rather than to layer another cost onto our businesses.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As this House is aware, the incidence of a tax differs from those who are asked to pay it.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In our view, part of the contributions toward redundancy insurance will be passed on to the workers.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: This would certainly make training more meaningful for both workers and employers.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: The enhancements to the existing schemes reflect the Government's continuous commitment to support Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: This is over and above what we have received recently.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: As the sole breadwinner of my family with three children over the age of 20, I have always been receiving various forms of support, ranging from subsidised school fees for my children, U-Save rebates and many more.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Nonetheless, the Budget is not a "one-size-fits-all" and there will always be voices of unhappiness and complaints that the amount of support is not enough.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Regardless, I have picked up this catchy phrase from my fellow technical officer – "life goes on!" Sir, the focus areas in my last two Budget debates were about strengthening our Singaporean workforce and providing support for the middle-income group.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Today, I will reiterate on the former with a focus on desired outcomes for workers.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: But before that, I would like to give special mention to a group of fellow Singaporeans who sacrifice their personal time and commitments to be the heart of the Labour Movement by serving working people at workplaces.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: I will share more about their selfless contributions shortly.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: As cliché as it sounds, all changed in 2004 when I had an exchange with my colleague on income tax matters.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: I was unaware that I could offset my income tax payment with the Parenthood Tax rebates.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: After writing to the Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore (IRAS) to seek clarification and further advice, I was shocked and beyond overjoyed to see that previous payments for my income tax were credited back to my bank account within a month.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Since then, I started to acknowledge and appreciate more, as the Government does support fellow Singaporeans in a fair and responsible manner.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Curiosity got the better of me and the rest is history as I stepped into the shoes of a union leader, to be an advocate and voice for all workers, representing their interests in the areas of wages, welfare and work prospects.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Since then, it has been an enriching and fulfilling journey, and I have not looked back.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: The group of people that I would like to give special mention to is none other than my fellow unionists.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Many take this group for granted and often overlook their contributions.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Unions are one part of what we call tripartism.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: This model is unique only to Singapore due to the strong collaboration between all three parties – unions, Government and employers – to achieve a common outcome of harmonious labour management relations resulting in better wages, welfare and work prospects for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: I have had the privilege to get to know and work alongside many senior leaders in my short span of 16 years as a unionist to ensure that our members in the represented group of companies are rewarded fairly and well taken care of.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Like myself, this group of people are not chosen by the management.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Rather, we made the conscious choice to volunteer, or are volunteered by fellow workers, to be their voices at the workplace.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Unionists are ever ready to represent their members in any instances of workplace grievances or issues relating to unfair practices.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Cases are primarily settled amicably with management partners at the earliest possible moment.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: However, when the situation warrants, cases will then be escalated to either MOM or the Industrial Arbitration Court (IAC).

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: With the presence of union leaders, I can attest and assure that such cases are few and far between.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: At this juncture, I would like to call on MPs who are advisors to our unions to consistently engage with them so as to hear, understand and feel first-hand the challenges faced by my fellow union leaders, especially when dealing with unsupportive and stubborn management partners.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: I strongly believe that you can value-add to the respective unions.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: I say this with the benefit of hindsight when I presented the case to our advisor and he exerted his influence over the management partners, hence ensuring that our workers were treated with dignity.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: This particular MP has since retired, but I will never forget his commitment to be by the side of the union leaders when we needed him most.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: This is just one of the few incidents that I have personally experienced.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: I also believe many other union leaders have had similar experiences like me.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: I call upon on workers to reach out to your union leaders, join the union, be part of this family of the Labour Movement as we will always be alongside you because for us, "Members First, Workers Always".

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: It is also about ensuring that the livelihoods and dignity of our fellow Singaporeans are protected and being ready to step forward quickly to help workers when they face any issues or unfair practices at the workplace.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Our leaders from the Union of Security Employees (USE) played a very active role to step in whenever they hear of such cases and ensure the perpetrators are dealt with by the respective authorities.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Many of us remember recent cases such as the one where a luxury car driver had injured a security officer stationed at a primary school, or another, where a security officer was assaulted in a lift at a condominium located in Bukit Batok.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: For these two cases, USE made their presence felt and extended support for the affected officers even by helping to lodge Police reports.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: We are grateful that the perpetrators for these cases have since been charged in Court.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: This are just few examples of our unions in action.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Many of the NTUC-Affiliated Unions and Associations (NTUC-ARU) staff and industrial relations officers were activated and mobilised to man the centres at Devan Nair Institute, One Marina Boulevard and Downtown East to assist our SEP in their claim submissions while in need.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Also, let us not forget our social enterprise NTUC Club which supported our nation through the COVID-19 crisis practically and housed our affected COVID-19 patients.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: It took years of painful lessons to achieve what we have today.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: On this note, I want to record my appreciation for all my fellow union leaders for all your hard work at the workplace.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Concurrently, I encourage all management partners to increase your appreciation for our union leaders in your company and industry.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: The peaceful and harmonious industrial relations that we experience today did not happen by chance, but only through the efforts, and sacrifices of our union leaders.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Not forgetting also, I would like to thank the NTUC staff for their tireless support and efforts in going the extra mile to support the administration for the SIRS scheme and other schemes that NTUC rolls out for members and workers.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: While there is no doubt that NTUC and our unions have been the voice of workers, we will not and never rest on our laurels.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: We recognise the need for continuous training and upskilling of our workers, so that they will be skilled, efficient and productive contributors to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: This model targets the training needs of every worker based on three broad areas, namely, adaptability, technology and training.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
