text: With our workers attending the relevant training lessons and applying their new skillsets, we hope to achieve the wins for our workers; and also strive for better wages, welfare and work prospects.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: This training is not just business as usual, but new skills to transform the workforce to meet the new business demands.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: It requires an intermediary body like NTUC to ensure that training benefits both workers and employers.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: After our workers attend the training, we hope and strive that workers will progressively achieve the "three Ws", while employers get better skilled workers.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: This would also make training more meaningful and not just clocking the hours and collecting allowances.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, I remind myself and call on fellow workers to learn, unlearn and relearn the skills to broaden your knowledge that will increase your value at current workplace.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Do not miss out to seize any opportunities for growth and self-improvement that come with better pay and work prospects.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: (In Malay):   This year's Budget signifies the Government's promise to help Singaporeans cope with the cost of living, raise families, empower Singaporean workers, and most importantly, to take all Singaporeans towards a new direction.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: This year's support is rather unique because the Government is focusing on efforts to expand the available support by increasing its amount appropriately.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, the Government also promised to continue monitoring both the economy and our people and is willing to render more support if the situation requires it.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: This can be seen last year when additional assistance was given to the people in their Assurance Package.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: But we must acknowledge the challenges faced by Singaporeans working in the platform industry who need to make CPF contributions.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: This is a responsible measure to ensure that such workers possess enough savings to own a home and secure their retirement later.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Let us not see this step as an obstruction to one’s livelihood.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Instead, it displays responsibility on the part of the Government.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Many within our community, I believe, have the qualifications and capabilities that enable them to secure permanent employment.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: If it this is not the case, we should redouble our efforts in upskilling to secure permanent employment opportunities that are available.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: There are many Government support schemes that enable you to undergo training and acquire the necessary skills so that you can seize the available job opportunities.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: For Singaporeans who are newly married and intend to start a family, there are many support schemes available and the amount has been increased in this latest Budget.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: On a personal note, I have friends who work as postmen and technical officers but manage to start a family with six to 12 children, still with the same one wife and residing in an HDB flat.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: This is because there is adequate Government support to ensure that every child gets the necessary assistance from childhood until they finish school at the tertiary level.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Have faith that every child is a blessing.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: The more the merrier, and Singapore will not have to go through the trouble of finding outside talent in the future.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: (In English): Sir, before I conclude my speech, I would like to put forward four requests based on the conversations I had with a group of young union leaders.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Speaker Sir, I am thankful and support the Budget.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Indeed, the three long years of COVID-19 winter has brought about significant shifts in our community and workforce.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As we adjust and settle into new equilibrium, we need to pay particular attention to social, economic and livelihood inequalities that may have bubbled to the surface during the pandemic.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Two tectonic shifts have impacted our workforce norms and they are: one, the rise of the gig and self-employed workers and the need for level playing fields; two, the prolific adoption of flexible work arrangements, its impact on women returning to work and balancing caregiving with work responsibilities.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And I would argue that the self-employed gig workforce will continue to grow as more Singaporeans embrace the flexibility freelancing work allows for.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, this flexibility does come with its trade-offs and these trade-offs are numerous.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Unlike the self-employed of yesteryears, where our self-employed persons (SEPs) have total control over their terms of work – when they work, where they work, how much they charge – many self-employed of today no longer have full control over their terms of service as they: one, depend on platform partners to hook them up for gigs; two, are less skilled or have no core technical skills; and three, are price takers impacted by controls from the platforms, doubled down by the lack of control on mitigating the changes in the greater geo-economic environment.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Thus, as the fortunes of our gig workers ebb and flow with the gig platforms and with the general flow of life, many of our self-employed workers find themselves caught in a bind where they hope to transit out of a vulnerable situation.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: They are unable to do so easily as upskilling and training can be costly.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: But it comes at a greater cost as it impacts the gig workers' daily takings and hence, their livelihoods.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Indeed, our self-employed workers, like Alexander the Great, face a Gordian knot when it comes to their financial future.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And as the legend goes, a headless knot cannot be undone, unless one takes extreme measures to cut it apart.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I believe as a society we need to support and arm our vulnerable, self-employed workers better when they decide to face their Gordian knots.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: A headless Gordian knot to a typical freelance driver looks like this: Gabriel is one of our leaders at the National Private Hire Vehicles Association (NPHVA) and he is about to turn 50.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: He is a provider to his very young family.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: He has had several recent conversations with me on his plans for retirement and is making serious decisions on his CPF contributions.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: To improve his income, he hopes to upskill, but to upskill, he must take time off for training.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Yet, training will take time up and eat into his daily income, coupled with fluctuating fuel prices in an unstable geopolitical landscape, inconsistent trip prices with his platform and daily rentals he needs to make, Gabriel literally has miles to go before his dream of a comfortable retirement can come true.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We must assist our SEPs and improving their productivity through upskilling and providing level playing fields to mitigating their business costs.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This is especially so for SEPs working in sectors where there have been technological disruptions, such as the media and transport industries.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Thirdly, for Government procurement to take the lead in recognising SEPs who trained under the abovementioned craft and trade skills frameworks when awarding Government contracts.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The COVID-19 situation has allowed us to celebrate the contributions of our freelance community.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: At the height of the pandemic, our drivers ferried COVID-19 patients to isolation facilities while we stayed in the safety of our homes.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our riders brought warm food to our tables while we settled in our comfortable work from home pattern.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While we celebrate and thank our gig workers for making the pandemic safer and more comfortable for everyone, the last three years has also allowed Singaporeans a glimpse into the lives of our SEP workers and a deeper appreciation of the challenges they face.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The SEPs in Singapore are capable of generating incredible value for our economy and society if only we would hand them the tools they need to loosen their Gordian knots.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: By supporting them to upskill, providing skill frameworks for their professions and alleviating their cost of businesses, I have confidence that the investment they receive will leverage disproportionate returns for our economy.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The call echoes the Labour Movement's own advocacy of enhancing support for workers with caregiving responsibilities, of which women constitute a large proportion of those who managed to double shift in the workplace and at home.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And yes, I can completely relate to this.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: During COVID-19, many women came up to me wanting to look for work.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Some wanted to supplement their diminished household incomes, others wanted to do their part to bolster the Singapore economy during our times of need.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, even as we match jobs to them through job fairs and job mentorship programmes, the same caregiving concerns that keep our women out of the workforce are still barriers that do not go away.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The seniors are still seniors, the young are still young and unfortunately, the infirm are still infirm.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is with this in mind that I underscore the urgency of enhancing the inclusivity of our jobs and reimagining the way we work by adopting family-friendly FWAs.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: First, encourage employers to implement flexible work hours and allow employees more autonomy in calibrating their schedules.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Flexi-time arrangements help workers better meet their personal responsibilities such as those tasked with taking care of young children and their loved elderly family members.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Third, implement telecommuting arrangements so that employees can carry out their work in a location away from the conventional office.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Flexible work options facilitate work-life balance and can accommodate workers with diverse and varied responsibilities and needs.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Fourth, while embracing these changes, it is imperative that companies fairly assess their employees on FWA for their work performance and opportunities for promotion.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: A worker who works on FWA must never be unfairly compared to a worker who works full-time in the office.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I believe that this would be key to the long-term norming of FWA in workplaces.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Fifth, while the dust settles on FWA norms, we must ensure that there are sufficient safeguards in place to protect them from workplace discrimination and to the extreme, harassment.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Owing to the power of symmetries that workers faced, a fear of repercussions such as losing one's job while being marginalised at work and the lack of anonymity may discourage our employees from reporting incidents of discrimination.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Employers therefore need to be engaged and educated on strategies to manage these cases while creating safe independent avenues for workers to seek recourse without fear of backlash.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Silver linings and silver bullets notwithstanding, it is paramount for us to recognise that some companies and industry face greater hurdles in adopting FWAs in a sustainable way due to the current nature of work and the sector they are in.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: These includes SMEs and sectors with front-facing, customer-facing workers and those which include workers using specialised equipment.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is also of note that these are also the very same industries and sectors that face manpower shortages.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And while the task of job redesigning can seem to be daunting or impossible, I believe that with some innovation, some thinking out of the box and support from the Government, the impossible can be made possible.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I have seen this being done in several sectors to very good outcomes.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The health and wellness sector is often one where FWA seem to be out of the question, given the high touch nature of frontline job roles.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, innovative companies such as the Singapore Spa Institute have started to pilot out a ninja workforce.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This is a float of part-timers or gig workers, who would take up short stints when the regular full-timers are on FWAs.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Job redesigning can also be a clear and transparent part of HR practices.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: When we introduced the Progressive Wage Mark at Uniqlo, I was very impressed by how transparent the company was in terms of what employees need to achieve in order to be promoted to the next level.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This includes clear indications of internal exams that needed to be taken, scores to be achieved, daily tasks to be completed and these were all available for all employees to see on their staff notice boards.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And one of the most innovative job redesigns that I saw was also one of the simplest.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I am sure we all love the fluffy and light dough fritters for breakfast, what we call "you char kway", but the process of making these dough fritters sure is not light.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Flour sacks can weigh up to 50 kilogrammes, and the boss of Xi De Li, a 100-year-old you char kway company here in Singapore, was finding it hard to get employees.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In a eureka moment, she asked the supplier to repackage the flour sacks to 25 kilogrammes and below.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And then, she started to get more females and seniors to join her company.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: These are wonderful and effective examples of how thinking out-of-the-box can allow companies to job redesign.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And I believe that with more targeted support from the Government and focused action from businesses, more SMEs can reap the benefits of FWAs, while allowing caregivers to stay or return to the workforce.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: During the job redesign process, companies may face manpower crunches and need help through redesign consultancy or facilitation.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While FWAs and job redesign processes bode well for our back-to-work women, it is worth noting that facilitating the transition back to work is equally as important.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The NTUC's Women and Family unit has, over the past 24 months, introduced a Women Supporting Women Mentorship Programme, and this has been introduced in over 10 locations all over the island.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This growing programme is targeted at supporting women returning to the workplace and addresses the issues that women face when they are looking for a smooth transition back.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Together with the larger NTUC family of social enterprises and our partners in the Labour Movement, we have put into place: (a) A mentorship network, consisting of community leaders and unionists to support women returners who report challenges in adjusting to the culture and pace of the workplace, and thereby, a lack of confidence in their new job roles.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (b) A suite of training programmes conducted by NTUC Learning Hub to uplift skillsets which are outdated or irrelevant, especially if our women returners have been out of the workplace for a longer period of time.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (c) A network of connections to career opportunities and job vacancies through NTUC's e2i (Employment and Employability Institute) and our trade association partners.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is exciting times ahead for Singapore, and with a keen focus on balancing inequalities, opening up new livelihood opportunities and building safety nets for our vulnerable, I look forward to creating a new social compact.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The world is opened for business after COVID-19 has eased globally, but it is a world marked by geopolitical tensions and high inflation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Government's Cost of Living support packages will help Singaporeans to cope better with inflation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Critical to coping with inflation is to ensure wages keep pace with rising prices.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Inflation is likely to stay for quite some time.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The measures announced in this Budget to improve productivity structurally, are especially important.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Many of these improvements will require many years of effort, and central to long-term productivity gains resides with our younger people and our younger workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I will first speak on helping our in-school younger Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Second, on younger Singaporeans already in the workforce, who are currently in their first and second careers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Our younger Singaporeans in the Institutes of Technical Education (ITEs) who are soon to join the workforce face a daunting challenge.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The starting salary gap between university and non-university graduates continues to widen.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The wage premium given to degree holders is understandable.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The degree holder has spent more years preparing for the workforce compared to the Nitec or diploma holder.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: An ITE graduate enters the workforce in three years, while a university graduate takes another three to four years.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: However, in the longer term, the same phenomenon occurs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Studies have also shown that a large proportion of non-university degree holders took up roles as associate professionals and technicians (APTs).

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In comparison, university degree holders largely took up roles in professional occupations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The value APTs bring to our economy might not be valued fairly by the market currently.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Without APTs, those in professional occupations possibly cannot complete their work with quality, or at all.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We need to move towards a better balance in valuing both technical and academic routes of career advancement.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: First, we need to strengthen vocational training and apprenticeship programmes for ITE students, or even graduates.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Recently, National Trades Union Congress (NTUC) engaged ITE students who took up the ITE Work-Study Diploma to understand how their experiences have helped them in their careers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: One participant, upon completing his higher Nitec, took up a Work-Study Diploma in Automation Engineering.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Through his diploma, he was given the opportunity to undertake full-time employment in the host company he was attached to during his studies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The company has set out a good career pathway for him.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There are structured avenues for deepening industry knowledge and skillsets.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This includes a company-sponsored overseas study programme with a bond to work in the company's overseas branch for at least three years, which he is considering taking up.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: While early days yet, the future for him is bright.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The issue for us is: can we scale this up further?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We can incentivise more companies to develop structured work-study diplomas, and even overseas training stints.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This improves not only productivity but also Singapore's pool of talent.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Next, we need to have better quality internships to strengthen the nexus between school and work.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This can reduce the number of younger Singaporeans not going into jobs that they are trained for.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Through the NTUC Youth Taskforce surveys and engagements, we found that internships rank highly in easing the transition from school to the workforce.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Our engagement findings also suggest that students who had internships gained valuable work experience, better understanding of the industry and career prospects within their sectors.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They were also able to appreciate prospective job roles better.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The reticence of employers to offer internships is not unfounded.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Resources must be dedicated to guide interns; this can be difficult when manpower is tight.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: But, at the same time, this is what our social compact is about; companies in Singapore offering younger Singaporeans opportunities to build a stronger Singapore.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It requires thinking beyond just a company's immediate needs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Therefore, unions and schools can work with companies to put in place good internship programmes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Structured mentorship programmes can be a vital tool in easing career navigation and improving studies to work nexus.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We often associate mentorships for older working people, but there is equal value to extending this to ITEs and polytechnics.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: By connecting students with mentors from their interested industries, their ideas on potential careers and aspirations are potentially broadened.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They receive targeted career advice and counselling particular to their field.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: An example is the SIT-Young NTUC's Industry Mentorship Programme (IMP), which is in its sixth iteration this year.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Young NTUC plays a bridging role in IMP, providing linkages to career mentors for SIT students and also hosts various networking opportunities.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This is also another way for us to strengthen our social compact.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Our compact is strengthened when more successful Singaporeans provide career mentorship to those who might not have easy access.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There is scope for the tripartite partners to extend and scale structured mentorship programmes across the different Institutions of Higher Learning (IHLs), especially, in part, ITEs and polytechnics.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The labour movement is committed to build such a compact and would share more information soon on its mentorship centre.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Next, on our youths who are in the workforce in their first or second careers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: These younger Singaporeans, as I shared in Budget 2022, comprise of Generation COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Generation COVID-19 is now coming out of the previously uncertain job market.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: As our economy recovers, we are also faced with structural labour issues.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Certain job pathways are still undervalued and the demands of employers are rapidly evolving alongside job opportunities, in sunset and sunrise industries.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This affects not only non-degree holders, but our degree holders too.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: To help Generation COVID-19 emerge stronger from the battle, I would like to focus on two areas.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: First, enabling Generation COVID-19 to tap on overseas work opportunities; second, allowing for smoother career conversions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Singapore's strong performance during COVID-19 has buttressed its reputation as a regional hotspot for business opportunities.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The question then becomes: how can we enable our people to capitalise on this, and go out in the world to explore and build greater networks to bring opportunities to other Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Supporting our young people, including Generation COVID-19, would be a good way to start.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Earlier this year in January, Young NTUC conducted a focus group discussion with 38 working younger Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They believed that this would be beneficial to their longer-term career prospects, gaining essential transferable skillsets and building professional networks.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Support measures cited include remuneration support, relocation incentives and of course, mentorship with others who have been in their position.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We could consider changing the current IHL overseas exchange programme for our students into something a more work-based or company-centric.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This can give our students an early taste of working overseas while sharpening the studies to work nexus.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: As I mentioned in Budget 2022, the pandemic has hastened the emergence and decline of multiple industries, professions and skillsets.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It is not inconceivable for youths to now find themselves on the opposite end of the growth trajectory, unable to seize opportunities in bright-spot industries due to skills mismatch.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Even if our younger Singaporeans choose to specialise in a bright-spot industry now, no one is to say how bright the said industry would be in a few years' time.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I believe this has partly contributed to anxieties amongst our younger people.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They do stress over having to choose the "right" first degree.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This could partly be due to the fact that only the first degree is being subsidised by the Government, or too much emphasis is on getting it right the first time.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: An anecdotal example of this is one of our ex-colleagues with over 10 years of experience.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Recently, at age 35, she decided to switch from the public sector to merchandising and commercial space, which was her lifelong interest.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Her biggest challenge in making the switch was the lack of experience or training for the new role.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Although she possessed transferable skills, her employers were looking for the latest skills and experience, even for an entry-level position.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Thus, she took up an entry-level position, took a pay cut and juggled working full-time and night classes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This anecdotal experience shows that the pains of career conversion can similarly affect those who are relatively younger.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The current support for career conversion is weighted towards older workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This is rightly so, as older workers do find it even more difficult to switch careers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: However, the ever more dynamic economy will require Singaporeans to make more career switches even earlier in life.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This can help in making career pivots easier and earlier.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Labour Movement will work closely with the Government and employers to do right by our workers and ensure that no worker gets left behind.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We need to ensure that the successes enjoyed by Singapore today will continue to be shared with future generations by enabling our young workers to be well-equipped and form our new future-proof workforce.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: But it is not all back to normal as we face many challenges on the global and national front.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The Budget unveiled by Deputy Prime Minister Mr Lawrence Wong is one which acknowledges that Singaporeans are going through hard times.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The financial help and various relief schemes announced are much welcomed and recognised as a means to help Singaporeans cushion what might be a hard landing to come.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: I believe that resilient families are the pillar of our society.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Many people in Singapore feel that property prices are high.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Back in 2011, I recall relating this to our former Prime Minister Lee Kuan Yew.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: I told him that young people were very concerned that property prices are very high in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Mr Lee said that if Singapore continued to be successful, property prices will remain high or continue to rise.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: If we think deeply about it, land has no value unless there is a future for it.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The more successful Singapore is, the more expensive the property prices will be given the limited land supply.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: I share this anecdote also to remember Mr Lee, for whom we are celebrating the 100th anniversary of his birth later this year.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: If we followed the paths of many successful cities like Hong Kong, Tokyo, London, New York, it is likely that many young Singaporeans will never be able to own their own homes in their lifetime.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: It is thus important that HDB flats are made accessible to young Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: In May last year, National Development Minister Mr Desmond Lee said that median waiting times for new BTO projects should come down slightly to four to 4.5 years, compared to the previous waiting time of four to five years.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: In 2017, HDB also introduced a scheme where construction on selected BTO projects in Sembawang, Sengkang and Yishun started about one year ahead of their launches and buyers can expect to get their flats in less than three years from the time they selected their flats.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: I urge HDB to continue to increase the supply of SWT flats to comprise up to 50% of all BTO flats and possibly shorten the waiting time to below two years.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: This is important especially since home-buying has accelerated in the wake of the pandemic and many young Singaporeans who are working from home more than ever want to create their own work-from-home (WFH) havens.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The significant increase in SWT flats would still be relatively safe in terms of the Government's commitment and capital expenditure.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Having 50% of the SWT flats would most likely not lead to many empty and unwanted flats as demand for HDB flats is unlikely to drop by 50% overnight.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Having 50% SWT flats would still allow HDB sufficient leeway to adjust its pace of building BTO flats according to changing demands and this would go a long way to help young families to get their flats earlier.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The perennial issue of how to raise Singapore’s birth rate is a challenging one.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: I am also happy that it would start immediately which is very important as this relates to my personal experience.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: When the Baby Bonus scheme was first introduced by then-Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong during his National Day Rally speech in August 2000, it was a big thing.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: It was a sharp reversal of the two-child policy.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: At about that time, my wife was also pregnant with twins and that was the third pregnancy.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: We thought we would be able to receive the baby bonus.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: However, the bonus was only meant for babies born after 1 April 2001.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: While my wife was due to deliver in mid-April 2001, our twins were born earlier in March.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: We did not get our baby bonus, which is why I am delighted that the Government today is dispensing the enhanced baby bonus with immediate effect after Deputy Prime Minister Wong’s announcement on Valentine’s Day.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: I also applaud the decision to double the paternity leave to four weeks from 1 January 2024.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: However, what I have heard from the ground is that more childcare leave is required.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Currently, an employee is entitled to a maximum of two days of childcare leave per year if the youngest child is between seven and 12 years old, regardless the number of children they have.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: One teacher related to me recently that parents were reluctant to fetch their children home even when they were sick in school.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The parents often request the school to hold their children at the sick bay until the parents finish work.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Childcare is a marathon, not a one-off effort after birth.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Hence, I hope Deputy Prime Minister Wong could consider increasing the childcare leave to two days per child when the child is in primary school, up to a cap of say four days a year.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: This represents a 41% increase over just 10 years and the proportion is growing.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The above suggestions to improve the Silver Housing Bonus scheme would not only provide elderly Singaporeans with more options to increase their retirement nest but would also increase the pool of resale flats to better meet the housing needs of families with young children.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: However, Singapore and the world entered 2023 facing a confluence of continued geopolitical tensions and slower economic growth alongside persistent inflation and higher interest rates.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: We therefore cannot take our past successes for granted.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: To me, this signals the balance of fiscal prudence along with continued support to Singaporeans to overcome near-term challenges and secure long-term prospects.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Last year, during the GST debate, I expressed my concerns from my Yishun residents about the impact of a GST increase to the cost of living, so I am heartened by Budget 2023, given the improvements to the Assurance Package and further enhancements to the Permanent GST Voucher scheme.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Evidently, the Government has followed through on its commitment to make a regressive GST increase even more progressive, when taken as a whole.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: The pandemic has changed the way we live significantly.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: As such, it is critical for the Budget to continue focusing on how we can move Singapore forward to increase our standard of living and strengthen our social fabric.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: There are three areas I would like to highlight: one, strengthening our economy and workers by better supporting and transforming our SMEs; two, enhancing the safety and security of Singapore by boosting efforts to tackle worrying crime trends, particularly scams and youth crimes; thirdly, fostering greater social harmony by improving the way we manage community disputes.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Our SMEs continue to navigate a challenging environment with many forces beyond their control.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Higher business costs are being driven by higher energy prices, wages and a tight labour market where vacancies are hard to fill.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: The interest cost businesses will shoulder will easily be twice given that rates are expected to be higher for longer, while revenue growth are less certain despite some bright spots, like China’s early reopening.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Given the above, some local businesses have given feedback that Budget 2023 seems to be pro-distribution and seemingly a shift away from pro-business growth.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: They wonder if this means that they should fend more for themselves and expect less help going forward.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: If indeed Budget 2023 is being rated by many as an A-grade for families and individuals, I suppose SMEs would score this Budget as a B or even a C!

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: While I look forward to more details, I hope this can benefit SMEs, particularly smaller ones lacking a full HR function, through more relevant training with a targeted outcome to improve productivity.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Crucially, better training and job-matching will give residents who are unemployed opportunities to learn by doing and gain confidence to re-enter the workforce.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Hopefully, more incentives can be considered for SMEs to take a chance to hire them to fill the vacancies and help improve the mismatch between labour supply and demand.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I also hope that the administrative journey for grants and support schemes can be made more seamless.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: This will improve accessibility for more SMEs to benefit swiftly and minimise the need for intermediaries and documentation.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: This view is echoed by the industry such as the Association of Trade and Commerce, from which I had earlier received feedback.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Beyond the tactical aspects of the above schemes and from a strategic perspective, I wonder if these business initiatives, including the innovation grants, are enough to help our local businesses and SMEs capture new opportunities in the longer term.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: For Singapore, we progressed with our Singapore Green Plan 2030 and committed to net-zero by 2050 alongside many countries.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Our SMEs must hence: one, boost efforts to reduce carbon footprint and two, be ready to capture new business opportunities.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: However, I am uncertain if these are enough to help push our SMEs to step up their game sufficiently and in time as changes in the ESG space are rapid and exponential.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Notably, MNEs are focusing on ESG to meet demands from regulators, investors, lenders and consumers.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: They in turn expect their SME suppliers to be ESG-compliant.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Our SMEs must therefore adopt greener practices in their delivery of services and products.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: They too must apply the mind-boggling methods to measure, track and report their own carbon footprint.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Otherwise, they could risk being disregarded as a preferred supplier or worse, being entirely left out of tomorrow's greener supply chain.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Beyond internal transformation, SMEs who are more advanced in their green transition should venture out and capitalise on regional prospects such as helping businesses in the region to accelerate their sustainability efforts.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Businesses should also be encouraged to co-create and contribute to the establishment of a sound classification and regulatory framework for voluntary carbon credits in Singapore to develop a transparent, liquid and scalable market.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: These efforts will help establish Singapore as a growing and leading green hub, leveraging on and furthering our status as a trusted international centre for finance, consulting and legal services.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: In a nascent and growing market, it is not size but trust, credibility and speed that are fundamental, which we should capitalise as our competitive advantage.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Like ESG, not much was discussed specific to digitalisation in the 85-page Budget speech, so I hope that the Government can re-emphasise the continued measures to encourage SMEs on their digitalisation journey, which is difficult but also very rewarding.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: To SMEs who may give Budget 2023 a B or C grade, I would encourage them to adopt a holistic view and factor the generous support measures provided by the Government over the last few years.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Nonetheless, I hope the Deputy Prime Minister can clarify the Government's commitment to local businesses in this Budget debate so that we can achieve a vibrant and growing SME and startup landscape, which can offer good jobs and opportunities for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I welcome Budget 2023's estimates for the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA)'s expenditure to increase by 4% compared to a 1.8% increase last year, which I previously said seemed low.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I hope this represents the re-doubling of efforts to tackle some worrying trends such as scams as well as youth crimes.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Despite commendable efforts by MHA and its partners, scams remain unabated and continue to evolve.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I look forward to hearing more details of MHA's plans in terms of resources and capabilities to fight scams with a concerted all-hands-on-deck strategy, through deeper partnerships with entities in the digital value chain.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Singapore has often been lauded as one of the safest cities in the world and we should extend this standing into the digital sphere.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Our youths, our perpetuating crimes are also under the spotlight.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: The Singapore Police Force (SPF) reported that the majority of those arrested for e-commerce scams were youths and the Central Narcotics Bureau (CNB) also highlighted a worrying trend of more youths abusing cannabis.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Some abusers were even as young as 14 years old.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I hope that MHA can continue to engage with all in the ecosystem – schools, parents, youth groups, media and so on – for swifter intervention so that their lives will not be marred by crime.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: We therefore need to keep investing and working on improving our social harmony as attitudes and norms evolve.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: One significant way our lifestyles have changed is with hybrid working.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Many continue to work and learn from home, which inadvertently results in more friction in our high-density heartlands, particularly regarding noise.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I raised this point at last year's debate and want to again highlight the need for a better framework to manage and resolve community disputes.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Residents have also provided feedback that the current framework remains cumbersome and hence ineffective.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I look forward to the Government's consideration of the Panel's proposals as well as other measures for more proactive engagement by agencies, for quicker and more effective dispute resolution.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I support the Budget and am confident that it can move Singapore and Singaporeans forward in a new era.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: My speech will touch on how we need to strengthen our social compact for a post-COVID-19 world, specifically, how consumers will need to adapt to a new era of higher for longer inflation to better protect themselves and the need to urgently refresh our social compact to engender a safer workplace for every worker.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Budget 2023 comes on the back of significant global inflationary pressures and at a time where central banks globally have significantly hiked up interest rates to tamper inflation.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I am therefore heartened that the Government has recognised inflation concerns and will provide significant cash assistance under the Assurance Package to provide comprehensive help to the majority of Singaporean households.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: During my house visits over the weekend, many residents told me that they appreciated the various help packages, in particular, the CDC vouchers, which come in very handy as they purchase their daily necessities in the neighbourhood.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: At CASE, we believe more can be done to help consumers make informed purchasing decisions.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: That is why we launched the Price Kaki mobile application – to allow consumers to compare prices of household essentials, groceries and cooked food and help to stretch their dollar.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I am glad that Price Kaki has been well received by consumers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: With our sizeable community of price transparency advocates, CASE will expand Price Kaki this year by introducing community and gamification features to benefit more consumers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Through these features, we hope to encourage our advocates to share deals with other like-minded users and help them compare prices across a wider range of products and promotions.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We will also integrate Fuel Kaki, a fuel price comparison website, into Price Kaki.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This is but a first step in Price Kaki's evolution into a one-stop platform for all consumers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: To combat and mitigate the issue of shrinkflation, I announced last year that CASE would display unit price for items listed on Price Kaki.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Consumers have told us that this is an effective way to compare prices and found this feature useful.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: But the efforts of CASE alone cannot stop shrinkflation.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I call on the Government to mandate the display of unit pricing.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: With digital price tag displays, I do not see a reason why companies, particularly our supermarkets, cannot do this.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In my Budget debate speech last year, I called on major supermarket chains to do their part to cushion the impact of rising prices and support everyday consumers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I am heartened that these major supermarket chains have leaned in to do just that.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: FairPrice will extend these schemes for 2023, which is expected to cost the social enterprise an additional $10 million more.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: FairPrice is also absorbing the additional 1% increase in GST for 500 essential items for the first half of 2023.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Elsewhere, Sheng Siong provided a 4% discount for senior citizens while Giant is absorbing the GST increase for 700 essential items.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Beyond supermarkets, DBS has also launched an initiative to subsidise five million hawker meals for Singaporeans and residents for a year.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I encourage all companies with economies of scale to do the same in the coming months.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Lastly, we need to pay special attention to vulnerable consumers who might be struggling to adapt to a new era of high interest rates.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Our sandwiched class, in particular, often face a financial squeeze due to the need to care for their elderly parents and younger children.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: According to a report on the auctions market by real estate consultancy Knight Frank, more homes in Singapore could be put up for auction this year as the number of bankruptcy petitions rise.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We also need to address the vulnerabilities of consumers in markets where high prepayment sums are involved but the sector does not provide any prepayment protection.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I will speak more about mandatory prepayment protection during the Ministry of Trade and Industry's (MTI) Committee of Supply (COS) debate.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This is a significant increase from 37 workplace fatalities recorded in 2021.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Even more appalling was the news that many of the lives lost were due to a fundamental lack or inadequate workplace safety arrangements that could have and should have been in place.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In September 2022, the Ministry of Manpower (MOM) introduced the Heightened Safety Period (HSP).

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In the initial three months of its implementation, we saw a promising decrease in the number of workplace fatalities.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The Labour Movement had hoped that the HSP would prove decisive in preventing workplace accidents, injuries and fatalities.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Unfortunately, this has proven to be a false dawn, with the number of cases rising once again in the later months.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We are barely two months into 2023 and we have already recorded five fatalities at the workplace.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Could it be that companies had become complacent with the HSP’s end within sight?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: While I am heartened that the HSP has been extended for another three months, I would like to urge the Government to seriously consider making permanent some of the HSP requirements, such as higher penalties for WSH breaches, so that we send a strong message that every worker deserves to return home safely at the end of each workday.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: One example is the sectoral tripartite committee on rail safety comprising the National Transport Workers’ Union (NTWU), the Land Transport Authority (LTA) and our two rail operators.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I would also like to reiterate my call on the Government to provide greater support to our SMEs to adopt new safety technologies at the workplace.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I will speak more about this at MOM’s Committee of Supply debate.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Man and machine simply do not mix and should not be placed together, especially at the rear deck of lorries.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I will further elaborate this point during the Ministry of Transport (MOT)’s Committee of Supply debate.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: A more comprehensive social compact on providing a safe workplace needs to also incorporate mental health.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I first spoke about the need to give employees a right to disconnect from work in July 2020.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Almost a year later, in September 2021, the Alliance for Action on Work-life Harmony issued a policy template to help companies set clearer boundaries for after-hours work communication.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: But how many companies have actually adopted these recommendations?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Are company leaders simply paying lip service to disconnecting after work, but continue to expect their employees to respond anytime and anywhere?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I will speak more about this during MOM’s Committee of Supply debate.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: As the Government does its utmost best to help Singapore and Singaporeans navigate an increasingly complex global environment, I hope that more emphasis can be placed on strengthening our social compact to better protect consumers and workers, because every consumer matters and every worker matters.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Wong mentioned that as part of the Forward Singapore exercise, we would rethink about how we want to augment the range of care and support options within the communities.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: This will, of course, enable our seniors to age in place.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: And therefore, I would like to contribute to this discussion today.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Many seniors wish to stay in their familiar surroundings, near family, friends, neighbours or even their beloved pets.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: As they age, however, their lives become more restricted and they require more assistance near or within their homes.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: More resources are needed to care for them.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Caring for seniors is not an easy task for any society; yet, Singapore faces unique challenges as one of the fastest ageing societies in the world.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: There will be fewer young Singaporeans to support each senior, as many of our youth are needed for our economy and our society.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: We must not over depend on foreign manpower to care for our seniors because even our neighbouring countries are ageing fast.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Furthermore, as a small city-state, our seniors cannot just move to rural areas with cheaper cost of living and there is not enough land for purpose-built retirement villages for everybody.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Therefore, we must retrofit our existing towns and estates to meet their needs.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: To achieve this ageing-in-place vision, we need bold and creative ideas.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: First, we need to ramp up care and supporting services in the estates.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: AACs can be largely staffed by part-time and full-time seniors and be homely rather than clinical.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Residents can work with the community to make it feel more like a group home and conversions can therefore be done relatively cheaply.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Furthermore, in both HDB and private estates, we need assisted living service centres staffed by a combination of foreign and local part-time workers.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Not all seniors can afford a live-in domestic helper so we need such centres to provide affordable and basic services to a number of our seniors.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: HDB can consider allowing AACs and service providers to potentially use golf carts and other small service vehicles to transport frail travellers.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Town Councils today have small service vehicles where we shuttle things around.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: It is conceivable that we can introduce a small number of these in the estate to support our seniors, as long as we start with proper trials and enforce speed limits.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: For private estates, I feel that autonomous vehicles can provide that last-mile connection to MRT stations, bus stops, healthcare facilities, and AACs.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: This will help seniors who no longer drive or cannot afford private hire cars.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Therefore, we should focus their use to seniors, the disabled, and parents travelling with infants.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Kebun Baru's Teachers Estate, with many seniors, could perhaps host a pilot programme if the Government is interested.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I hope that the Government can adopt IT aggressively to take care of our seniors.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: We must get as many of our doctors, nurses, and therapists to adopt tele-consulting for suitable seniors.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: We should allow as many services as possible for seniors to be coordinated digitally and deploy AI-powered services to interact with and care for our seniors.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Over the last few months, AI developments have skyrocketed.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I am now far more optimistic about leveraging AI to support senior care.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: ChatGPT, for example, can understand, communicate, break down tasks and complete them.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: In the future, imagine, seniors could use AI-powered services over the phone or use home-speakers to ask the AI to coordinate appointments, seek general help and even get basic counselling.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Although it seems impossible now, the technology already exists.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Just last week, I tried an AI service that played the role of a psychologist.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I am not saying that it replaced one, but it is just supplementing whatever care that our service providers are providing.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: AI will also radically reduce the cost and time to develop software.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Today, AI can already write low-level code automatically if you can articulate clearly what needs to be done.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Therefore, seasoned programmers can achieve much more with less.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: It will also significantly lower the barrier for non-IT professionals, including our healthcare professionals to learn computing.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: With some training, they can quickly come up with good proof-of-concepts and pass them on to IT professionals to scale up.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: In short, AI will help turbocharge IT, which can be used to improve the lives of our seniors.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: My final point is, we should empower our seniors to tap into their own assets to pay for services related to ageing-in-place.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: HDB owners today already can do Lease Buybacks, but more solutions are needed, including for those in private estates.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: This will allow the next-of-kin or the Government to use maybe just a portion of their wealth, depending on the net worth, to provide the necessary care.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: To conclude, Singapore has taken many steps in the past decade to prepare for ageing.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: We have increased healthcare capacity, fine-tuned financing frameworks and enhanced befriending services.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Through Healthier SG, we can also help our seniors stay happy and healthier for longer.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Even as we prioritise the roll-out of Healthier SG, we must also act swiftly to create the infrastructure and the care services and a whole ecosystem to allow our seniors to age-in-place with dignity.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: To do so, we must pilot and scale ideas, while also supporting, but not supplanting, caregivers.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: As we continue to find ways to deal with the ever-evolving nature of the pandemic, we must also set our eyes on how we can prepare Singaporeans for a post-pandemic future riddled with uncertainty.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: My esteemed colleagues and I in the Labour Movement strongly support and welcome the slew of measures introduced to strengthen our social compact, thereby helping Singaporeans cope with the rising cost of living amidst global uncertainties.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Strengthening our social compact means uplifting marginal groups as we progress in society.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: During the Budget Statement this year, I was heartened to learn that the Government will be allocating more resources to help all Singaporeans, especially our brothers and sisters in the vulnerable facets of society.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: As we chart our way forward, we ought to remain sensitive to the challenges and concerns of our vulnerable workers, especially our lower-wage and middle-income workers.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: The best way to address our workers' concerns over inflation and cost of living is through better wages and better jobs.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: There is more we can do for vulnerable groups in society.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: The reality is that rising prices would continue to exert pressure on all income groups, especially our middle-income workers.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Our middle-income workers are vulnerable to inflation because as prices for goods and services rise, their purchasing power decreases and it becomes more difficult for them to afford their daily necessities.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Overall, based on public data published by the Ministry of Manpower (MOM) and the Department of Statistics, we note that when adjusted for inflation, median wage growth between 2014 and 2019, which was pre-COVID-19, stands at 21.5%.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: However, the median wage growth of certain worker groups lags behind the overall median wage growth.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: This is particularly so for our Associate Professionals and Technicians (APTs) and Professionals who have experienced real median wage growth of between 5% and 8% during this same period.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: As Deputy Prime Minister Wong also shared in his Budget speech, Singapore's headline inflation is likely to remain high, at least for the first half of this year.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: As such, some of our middle-income workers will continue to feel its effects.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: As such, inflation affects different income groups differently, and middle-income workers are often hit the hardest as they are unable to receive Government subsidies and support as their salaries tend to be higher than the qualifying threshold.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Those who need to take care of dependents may also feel the pinch more.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: As a result, inflation can have a significant impact on their standard of living and ability to save for the future.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: My fellow labour MPs as well as myself have lobbied for such reviews to WIS over the years, and this is heartening to note and is certainly a step in the right direction to assist the sandwiched class amidst rising costs.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: There is room to better address the needs of our middle-income workers.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: That way, more middle-income would be covered, providing them with more support to cope with rising prices.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: (In Malay):   Our lower-wage workers play a critical role in maintaining essential services and keeping the nation running during times of crisis or disruption.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: This includes workers in sectors such as cleaning, security and waste management.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: In my Budget speech last year, I spoke about the ongoing efforts to support lower-wage workers as we transitioned to a post-pandemic future.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: In recent years, the collective support from various stakeholder groups to uplift the incomes of our lower-wage workers have been encouraging.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: NTUC, alongside our partners, will remain committed to help workers improve their income security, give them confidence to progress in their careers and help improve their quality of life overall.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: As mentioned in my Budget speech last year, NTUC and our tripartite partners have worked hard to enhance and expand the Progressive Wage Model (PWM).

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: With the PWM, workers can be assured that they will not only receive a minimum wage corresponding to their sector and occupation, but also defined career pathways that would ensure that their wages increase as their skills and responsibilities increase as well.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: The four ladders of the PWM – skills, wages, productivity and career – work hand in hand to ensure that our lower-wage workers can seize the opportunity not just to earn an honest day’s work, but with the dignity they place in their jobs, to progress upwards and better secure the future for themselves and their loved ones.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Subsequently, the PWM was implemented in 2014 for the cleaning sector, followed by the security and landscape sectors in 2016 and the lift and escalator sector in 2019.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Since 2014, we have progressively rolled out PWMs every two to three years.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: As we strive to narrow the wage gap between P20 and P50, PWMs have also been recently introduced in Retail, Food Services, Waste Management, and just recently, this week, for the occupations of Administrators and Drivers.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: An important facet of the PWM is how wages are linked to skills upgrading and productivity gains – workers are equipped with the required skills to be better and more efficient in their jobs and empowering them to scale up the career ladder, like in the case of Senior Escalator Specialist Jeremy Yap.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: He has worked in the industry for over 20 years, and he harbours hopes of advancing to become a foreman and has recently taken one step closer to achieving his goal by taking a course to become a lift and escalator inspector.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: As he continues his path towards becoming a foreman, his wages may also be even higher.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Jeremy’s aspirations show how our workers can benefit from the clear progression pathways set out via the various PWMs, with some like Jeremy, setting their sights to achieve even more.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: (In English): The Progressive Wage Model (PWM) has proven and will continue to benefit our lower-wage workers and assure them of wages and work prospects on a sustainable basis – and this is especially crucial in an era of rising cost of living.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: The success of PWM so far lies in our not-so-secret ingredient of tripartism, where unions, employers and Government come together to reach win-win-win outcomes for all parties.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: This is why PWM is a sustainable model to uplift wages, welfare and work prospects for our workers.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: This secret ingredient of tripartism is not new – and it is built upon another important ingredient that unions and management have worked hard to establish and strengthen – harmonious labour-management relations (LMR).

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: We do not take either LMR or tripartism for granted.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: NTUC will continue to work with our tripartite partners to further bolster efforts to uplift our lower-wage workers, and where necessary, resolve any differences through established processes.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Another area that I would like to talk about is the Local Qualifying Salary (LQS).

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: LQS refers to the minimum salary that employers must pay to local employees to qualify for various work pass types, for example, E Pass, S Pass and Work Permit.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Previously, employers hiring foreigners were only required to pay the LQS to local workers whom they need to count towards their foreign worker quota.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: This expanded requirement has had an impact of uplifting more than 100,000 full-time resident employees, who were previously earning below $1,400.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: While the implementation of LQS is necessary to protect local workers and prevent the displacement of low-wage jobs by foreign workers, it can also potentially be problematic for lower-wage workers, because the current amount of $1,400 is much lower than the P20 wage levels of about $2,800 in 2022.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Further, most of the Progressive Wages are also pegged at higher amounts, ranging from $1,500 for a data entry clerk to $3,330 for a principal lift and escalator specialist.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: PWMs are also designed such that their wages are increased at an agreed-upon rate annually.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: This can be done through a mechanism like the National Wages Council, which already provides annual guidance on the range of progressive wage growth for lower-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Despite the challenges, many Singaporeans have stepped up to support our vulnerable groups.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: The truth of the matter is that uncertainties will continue to persist in the year ahead.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: However, I am confident that we will overcome any challenges that come our way.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: As we tread uncertain waters, the Government and NTUC are committed to helping workers in every step of the way, help them achieve better wages, welfare and work prospects.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Rest assured – NTUC will continue to champion all workers because every worker matters.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I speak as a Labour MP and my focus will be on advancing the interests of senior workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The top concerns of our senior workers, aside from the cost of living, will be that of retirement adequacy and healthcare cost.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: At the same time, NTUC has embarked on a series of dialogues with workers from different segments under the banner of Every Worker Matters Conversations, what we call EWMCs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This is part of our efforts to refresh our Compact with Workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The ones that engaged senior workers received the same feedback.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: We have highlighted this clear feedback to our Government partner as part of our Social Partnership and are keen to work with Government and tripartite partners to proactively and systematically strengthen existing arrangements to make further progress – to reassure senior workers as they prepare for retirement.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The feedback from senior workers validates the strong emphasis that Government, NTUC and Singapore National Employers Federation (SNEF) have put on improving senior employment and employability.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Wong announced in this year's Budget of increments in CPF contributions for senior workers in January 2024, again according to a tiered structure, with provisions of transition offsets to help employers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: These moves are the fruit of tripartite negotiations and agreements struck under the auspices of the Tripartite Workgroup on Strengthening Support for Older Workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
