text: These are concrete steps taken in the national interest and that reflect correct understanding of the realities that Singapore faces.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: At the same time, I want Singaporeans to know and to appreciate that our ability to do this, the whole of Singapore's ability to do this – to come together, to negotiate strongly from each side and then to reach a fair and feasible balance of interests and to then implement it effectively and in good faith in a timely manner – reflects the deep trust and value that tripartism has yielded for Singapore and Singaporeans over many years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: In many other countries, they try to do similar things but they meet with protests and they meet with paralysis because of the lack of trust.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The recent protests in European countries such as France serve as a good example.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: You just get gridlock and everybody, all parties suffer – degradation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: So, the fact that we are actually able to make progress for a segment of our workforce, namely our senior workers to be able to provide better for them, better assurance for them in terms of their employment, giving them a chance and a choice, to prolong it where they can and when they want and, at the same time, in the course of that to provide better for their retirement adequacy – this is no small achievement, and we must never take this competitive and social advantage for granted as we go on and tackle more and, indeed, endless challenges.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I started the speech by sharing that cost of living, retirement adequacy and healthcare cost are top concerns for senior workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Enabling senior workers to earn more, save more and earn for longer are, therefore, clearly among the best ways to help generate resources and engender confidence in these areas.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Hence, Mr Speaker, Sir, as we complete the implementation of the agreed first tranche of moves, namely, the increase in the statutory retirement age and re-employment age ceiling by one year, we should consider a suitable juncture to commence tripartite deliberation to formulate the second tranche of moves to progress the Workgroup’s recommendations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This process will take time because there is a need to consider economic and business realities and the experience of the first tranche implementation and what would constitute a viable balance and pace.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Hence, while we need not rush, should not rush, we should make sure that there is sufficient traction along this journey and that such tripartite discussions be convened in due course, in good time.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: SEC improves the wage competitiveness of senior workers and strengthens their employment and re-employment prospects.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: These are the figures as reported by the Ministry of Manpower (MOM).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: These we achieved despite the challenges of COVID-19.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: We must make every effort to anchor these gains as the Singapore economy emerges from COVID-19 to meet new challenges.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The past three years of COVID-19 have demonstrated many more possibilities of flexible work arrangements (FWA) that can be leveraged for win-win outcomes, when used wisely and not mechanically.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I certainly agree with the elegant elaboration earlier by my parliamentary colleague Ms Yeo Wan Ling on this aspect and I shall not belabour the point.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: It has proven to be something that we have all learned – companies, workers – that under given circumstances, it can really be win-win and we should leverage that the best we can.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I urge Government to strengthen its support for companies to acquire the practical know-how on the smart use of FWA to strengthen their manpower models and sources.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Next, onto the raising of the CPF contribution ceiling from $6,000 to $8,000.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: There is every reason to encourage saving more and earlier to strengthen retirement adequacy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Raising the ceiling has the advantages of upkeeping the real value of CPF savings and enables workers to also benefit from longer periods of compound interest.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This move benefits both current cohorts of Senior Workers as well as future cohorts of Senior Workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Because then you can already begin to earn and save more into your CPF at the wage range of between $6,000 and $8,000 as the rates are raised.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I had called for such a review in last year’s Budget debate and I am, indeed, happy to see the Government had taken this move this year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I urge that such reviews be carried out periodically for the reasons that I have discussed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: A volatile economic environment heightens the risks of intermittent unemployment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Rapidly changing business models and technology force an equally rapid need to reskill and raise the risks of premature exit from the workforce.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: These are just some of the challenges that can complicate and undermine retirement adequacy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The future may yet bring even more and even harder tests.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This is also why retirement adequacy features as a significant concern among the senior workers as revealed in NTUC’s survey.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I therefore agree that this is a critical area to pay attention to because it concerns a basic sense of security and confidence of Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The NTUC wants to work closely with Government in this area to see what additional innovations can be arrived at that can yield practical and sustainable improvements, and then to help Government and to help all of society rally our workers’ support for those.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I look forward to the final report of the Tripartite Committee and the implementation of its recommendations to further strengthen workplace fairness for all.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Beyond individual cases and claims of age discrimination, I hope that the tripartite partners can work closely to leverage on in-company mechanisms to proactively ensure that senior workers are given due consideration and opportunity for training and skills-building.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Relevance of skills is a factor that all parties agree will materially impact the employability of a worker.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Hence, all efforts aimed at boosting employment and earnings of senior workers will be seriously hampered if they are rendered skills-obsolete through not being given fair consideration and opportunity compared to younger workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The NTUC-initiated Company Training Committee (CTC) is an in-company mechanism that can serve this purpose of ensuring fair and productive conduct of training for all workers, including senior workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I hope that we can fully leverage on such relevant mechanisms and regulations to accelerate fair and productive outcomes for companies and workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: At the same time, we also learnt in tackling and overcoming these that unity, rationality, ability to build and mobilise trust and always wanting to build a better future Singapore are priceless traits that will set us apart as a country and as a people.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: So, we, today’s generation and the generations to come, must learn this and must always remember this and come back to this basic tenet which is that we will be stronger together.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I agree that the sense of post-COVID-19 normality is more than welcomed, but we must slow down and give pause.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We must ask ourselves about the important lessons from the last three years and ask if we as a society have really "returned to business as usual".

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Recovery from COVID-19 has not been equal for all of us.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Some close to us may still be suffering the debilitating effects of long COVID.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I would be surprised if anyone in this House can say that they do not have residents still seeking assistance because of lingering economic or other adverse effects of the pandemic.  "Resilience" has been a key word used to describe the ambition of this Budget – and the ambition that we as a nation need to trek down to ensure we are ready to navigate future challenges that might come our way.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Yet we can take lessons from psychology on what "resilience" really looks like and apply that to how we build resiliency as a nation.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In psychology, resilience is not just about harnessing our own individual inner strength.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is also about strengthening our ability to deal with challenges.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is done through building a connected network, learning from our experiences and taking care of our own mental and holistic well-being.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Applied to the context of a country, this means that we must not find resilience by simply looking inward or becoming more insular, but by continuing to stay connected within the communities around us in Singapore and also with the world at large.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We must be open to constructive criticism and be enlightened enough to translate mistakes into lessons learned.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We need to walk together, bringing every corner of Singapore along equally on the journey forward.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: That is why it is critical that we have policies that holistically ensure the well-being of our economy, our society and our planet.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Focusing on our economy, we know that our most vulnerable may find themselves between Scylla and Charybdis, moving from the pressure that movement controls had on incomes, to the inflation that accompanies the loosening of restrictions and economic recovery.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In particular, there is concern that poorer segments of the population are facing greater food insecurity in the wake of the pandemic, something exacerbated by recent increases in food and hawker prices.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We should strive to understand shifts in nutritional consumption that occur in response to fluctuating macroeconomic circumstances.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is imperative that we ensure that lower-income households do not end up drastically cutting back on nutrition given ever-increasing costs.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In this, I am reminded of a retiree who came to my Meet-the-People Session who told me that he was sometimes reduced to filling his stomach with white bread because anything else was a luxury.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The impact of this falls disproportionately on children and the elderly, with many adverse health effects taking root from poor nutrition.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: If left untackled, it has the potential to further entrench generational poverty.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Poor nutrition also has an effect on outcomes for various chronic illnesses like diabetes and cancer.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In the wake of Healthier SG's launch and the pivot to preventative healthcare, we must pay more attention to this.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Aside from the support packages announced this year, there may be many initiatives and support schemes available to help these residents, but a lack of awareness and the scarcity effect means that vulnerable residents do not always get the help that they need when it is most needed.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Next, I move on to the well-being of our society and people.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This year's Budget emphasises the family and its well-being.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Enhancements to the tax and financial incentives for young couples to have children, along with the introduction of tripartite guidelines to allow parents to request for flexible working arrangements are undoubtedly welcome.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: However, economic incentives and tinkering around with the way our workforce is structured are only part of the greater picture when it comes to building a Singapore for families not only to survive, but also to thrive.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Additionally, headline announcements in Budget 2023 appear to leave out groups of our population, namely, those of us who are unmarried or childless.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: They are Singaporeans too and are and will continue to be part of our families.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is concerning in an age where we trumpet greater inclusivity and claim to celebrate diversity, especially as the number of single Singaporeans has increased across all age groups, according to the 2020 census.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Children of unmarried mothers do not have a choice.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Most single, unmarried mothers, given a choice, would also hope to be part of a stable, fulfilled marriage.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Yet, in our haste to ward off the hex of "encouraging single parenthood", we appear to either be punishing innocent children born to unmarried mothers or encouraging hasty, possibly unsuitable marriages.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This may lead to further difficulties down the line, ending in strife within the home or even divorce.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: My Sengkang colleague, Mr Louis Chua, spoke about the limited impact of the housing shortage on married couples seeking homes since statistics show that singles tend to apply for smaller flats.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: COVID-19 and its aftermath seems to have left behind epidemics of loneliness and mental health struggles.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: These are threats to the progress that we hope to make in strengthening our country's resilience.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Recent studies indicate that larger numbers of Singaporeans are feeling isolated in a post-COVID world – from working adults speaking through Zoom, to students missing out on the crucial years of social life that tertiary education usually brings to the 30% to 40% of senior citizens who still feel isolated even while living with family.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: A recent Duke-NUS Medical School study also quantified what psychologists have known for a while; that loneliness has real, measurable consequences on physical health, negatively affecting life expectancy and healthy life expectancy.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While loneliness is something we may associate with retirees, studies found that younger people were in fact more likely to report loneliness across cultures, genders and geographies.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is compared against the one in seven estimated to suffer from a mental health condition in the general population.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: These are sobering facts, and while our Ministries and various agencies are aware of the magnitude and severity of the issue and are working on it, it is no secret that even if individuals or their families are willing and can afford to seek help now, wait lists for professional help are long.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Untreated mental health issues in children and adolescents can leave lasting damage into adulthood.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: These also correlate strongly with poverty, reduced life expectancy and reduced potential and achievements in all aspects of life.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Compared with adolescents, mental health struggles may be even harder to spot in children under 11.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Young children can struggle to describe their emotions and often the only way they can express themselves is to "act out".

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: These signs can be so subtle and easily characterised as "bad behaviour", which means that adults often try to punish or discipline these children to make them "behave".

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: These children consequently miss out on getting the support and treatment needed.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In fact, the problem may be exacerbated by well-meaning but ultimately erroneous interventions to treat the behaviour rather than the cause.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, many educators and mental health professionals that I speak to have shared anecdotal observations that our youngest members of society do seem to be struggling recently and are unable to communicate to us how bewildering they have found the last few years.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We owe a debt to those who work with children as psychologists, counsellors and therapists in our schools, our medical institutions and private practices.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: They often go over and beyond in trying to secure the well-being of our children.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Yet many of them speak of concerns stemming from a lack of central regulation and of burning out due to a lack of resources and manpower.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: More awareness and sensitivity, both at the individual and systemic levels, is required to spot issues early and to get our children and people the help they need.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Compounding the problem are knock-on effects that having a family member struggling with mental health has on the rest of the household.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: As the saying goes, a parent is only as happy as their unhappiest child.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is so easy to forget that in order to care for kids – especially kids that are struggling, whether because they are differently-abled, or living with mental health conditions – we also need to care for our parents.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Yet, there is often little discussion on and even less support for this aspect of the parenting journey.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Parents and carers can themselves be overloaded and overlooked as they strive to do everything, sometimes inhumanly possible to support their struggling child.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is despite research showing the important role that the home environment plays in helping children learn to regulate themselves.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And we know that a dysregulated family often causes challenging situations to spiral.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Even as we continue to ensure that our existing networks and services provide the necessary support for our parents to lean on, an overwhelmed parent is going to find it challenging to navigate the myriad schemes and agencies that provide the help needed.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We need to help our parents along, to offer them support, compassion and non-judgement.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We need to let our parents know that it is alright to struggle along with our children.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We need to let our parents know that sometimes it is okay to not enjoy being a parent – especially when the going gets tough – and that non-judgmental help and a listening ear is available to offer suggestions and strategies to make the tough hours and days a little easier.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I fear that sometimes in our haste to encourage more young Singaporeans to have children, we focus so much on how fulfilling the journey is and neglect to address and normalise how we as parents do not have all the answers and can find it really difficult too.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This may have an inadvertent consequence of adding to the stress that parents feel, especially when faced with glossy social media feeds of how everyone else seems to "have it together" when reality leaves them feeling exhausted and terrified.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Psychological and medical research indicate that stress and clinical burnout can be equally damaging to physical health.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Stress is not just in the mind, but can affect people physiologically too, especially chronic stress, which leads to high levels of cortisol, which in turn affect the body's ability to regulate blood sugar, reduce inflammation, regulate metabolism and formulate memories.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: For parents, there appear to be fewer studies on the severity of this phenomenon in Singapore.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While platforms such as Parentwise have highlighted the real presence of and danger posed by parental burnout, more accessible and effective measures must be in place, particularly as COVID-19 changes from pandemic to endemic.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Among lower-income groups, research in the last decade shows links between stress, deprivation and how this can sometimes lead to bad choices, including counterproductive economic behaviours.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: One of the forms of chronic stress facing Singaporeans is the lack of sleep.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Sleep deprivation, like chronic stress, has adverse effects on an individual's ability to function.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And sleep deprivation also extends to our children.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Many of us have children who cry when woken up before the crack of dawn for school, because they are just not getting the required sleep that their growing bodies and minds need.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We must pay more attention to this issue and mitigate some of these ill effects while recognising that they are not a panacea.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: One possibility is to implement later school start times to align with the natural body clocks of our children and adolescents.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Our policies and systems need to be flexible and compassionate enough to keep up with the rapidly changing and challenging environment that our children, parents and families find themselves in.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While we have policies with good intentions, our systems have to be mindful of the amount of mental effort and resources needed from individuals to battle challenging situations.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Our systems also need to work together with the people whom they serve to reduce the stress that our people and families are facing in this uncertain world.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is only when we and our systems are optimised to extend help and support without judgement that we can lay that crucial feeling of security that is essential for us to build resilience.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Moving to the macro, the topic of climate resilience was briefly mentioned in the Budget.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Yet, climate resilience goes beyond energy security and adapting to rising sea levels.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It encompasses building the resilience of our people and businesses to navigate the climate crisis and ensuring a smoother transition to a more equitable and sustainable future.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Blue-collar workers, migrant workers and gig workers will bear the brunt of rising temperatures more than others.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: With Singapore's temperatures rising twice as fast as the rest of the world, more measures will be needed to enable them to adapt to the effects of extreme heat.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Extreme heat and weather events also affect our families.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Households in rental flats report that the temperatures in their homes during the day can be quite unbearable, particularly during the dry and hot seasons.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: More needs to be done to sustainably cool down our buildings, and we need investment in better cooling infrastructure when building flats.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: So, it is that even as we support this year's Budget, I hope that we will make true and meaningful progress that our people will feel supports them to better navigate the challenges facing us as individuals, as families, as a society and as citizens of the blue planet that we call home.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Speaker, Sir, the outlook for the global economy is uncertain.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Achieving economic growth in the current environment will be challenging, due to the decoupling of the US and China, the Ukraine war, supply chain disruptions and rising interest rates, among other reasons.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With the slowing global economy, one after another, tech companies are retrenching worldwide.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And there may be ramifications across other sectors.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We need to stay prudent and exercise great care in how we manage our expenditures.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I would first like to speak on the property market.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Despite the dark horizons around us, Singapore remains attractive as a hub for many investors.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Robust demand from investors who have the confidence to invest in Singapore also helps to drive the demand for rental private properties.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would the Government review and consider boosting the supply of public and private housing even more?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Similarly, will the Ministry of National Development (MND) consider implementing measures to support and facilitate the development of more private housing, especially on some lower density land plots in the central region?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some are occupied by ageing, even decrepit or neglected buildings, which require high maintenance and repairs.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many are in good locations with excellent amenities.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Redeveloping these plots and intensifying the use of these mature centrally located estates will make better planning and financial sense.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There is a need to check on the HDB resale market too.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The increase in grants to first-timers for the purchase of resale flats is certainly welcome.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, the sudden and rapid increase in the prices of resale flats without the support of economic fundamentals would affect some more, such as non-first-timers, including divorcees and hard-pressed families with unfortunate circumstances who can only buy resale flats.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This also has a serious impact on those whose incomes are unable to progress to match the rapid increase in resale prices.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There are suggestions to apply the same income ceiling for Build-To-Order (BTO) applicants to the buyers of resale flats and to disqualify those who can afford to pay exceptionally high Cash Over Valuation (COV) from buying resale flats.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: On the other hand, there are others who want the income ceiling caps to be removed to help the sandwiched classes who can neither afford private housing nor are eligible to buy public housing.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I urge the Government to review these feedback and suggestions and consider a balanced solution.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The limited supply, rise in EC prices as well as the rise in prices in private property in areas other than the central core area are other contributing factors to be dealt with.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am in full support of ensuring stable public housing prices, which is important for providing a social safety net for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The people trust the Government to safeguard Singaporeans' interests and be the buyer of last resort for public housing.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: On the one hand, this may have led to the perception that property prices will only go north, not south, thus driving up their demand and prices.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: HDB flats are perceived to be risk-free and underwritten.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: On the other hand, this has consequently led investors into thinking that the same would apply to private property.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It can be applied to both buyers and sellers.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This may help cool down the market, especially the HDB resale prices and tax more equitably high cash over valuation (COV) above the average and the norm.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For young families, in addition to the extra chance for balloting as first-timers with a child, the Government may consider another extra chance for those with two children and so on.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Likewise, those who have registered at the Registry of Marriages (ROM) should also be prioritised ahead of those who have not.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Next, I would like to appeal for the Progressive Wage Model (PWM) to be extended to skilled tradesmen.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am heartened that the PWM covers workers in the cleaning, security, landscape, lift and escalator, retail, food services and waste management sectors.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The PWM will ensure sustainable wage increases for these workers that commensurate with their skills, productivity and career progression.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Together with the Occupational Progressive Wage and Progressive Wage Mark, these are concrete measures to show that we value their work and compensate them adequately.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many of our local skilled tradesmen are graduates from our Institutes of Technical Education (ITE) or polytechnics.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We should recognise and value their expertise and experience and ensure a sustainable supply of locals into these trades to meet our national needs.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The seafaring career has always been tough but it presents many opportunities to Singaporeans when they achieve a certain level of competency as their skillsets are highly sought after in Singapore's vibrant and diverse maritime industry.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They are essential to our country as we aim to develop Singapore into a premier global hub port.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We need locals to provide high service levels for maritime-related activities in port.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This will also decrease our dependency on foreign labour in this sector.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: We have transitioned to DORSCON green after three years of battling COVID-19 and it seems that we are finally returning to normalcy.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: However, there are still many worries that Singaporeans are grappling with.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Geopolitical tensions from the year-long Russian-Ukrainian war and US-China rivalries still remain.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: There have been massive tech layoffs from big tech companies like Gojek, Amazon and Google throughout the last few months.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Resale housing prices rose for the 11th straight quarter.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: It becomes almost imperative for the Budget to protect and support Singaporeans, particularly those who are more vulnerable.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: A Budget reflects the priorities of the Government.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, I am heartened that this year's Budget reflects a kinder approach – one that is listening to its people amidst many uncertainties.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: These are good measures with positive socioeconomic objectives and I am very happy that we have this in the Budget.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: I recognise that there is already a strong focus on the people.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Nevertheless, I wish to speak about a certain vulnerable group that I believe we can do more for.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: I am speaking of the unwed single mothers – the mothers who are trying to make a living while raising their kids, who are doing their best to provide for their kid so that he is not left behind.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: It is already hard raising a child alone.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: It is even harder when our policies become inadvertent structural roadblocks that result in unequal access.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: I recognise this Government's pro-family policies and myself agree that parenthood within marriage increases the likelihood of a stable family.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: However, we should consider the knock-on effects of certain policies on the children of these single mothers, namely the Working Mother's Child Relief, Parenthood Tax Rebates as well as certain housing policies.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: It is imperative to remember that measures that penalise single mothers or leave them out of society-wide benefits ultimately do not just penalise these women but also penalises their children.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: It affects how these children live and grow and their experiences during this time.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: It affects the possibility of social mobility and it affects their future.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Let us not forget that in the end, these children will form the next generation of Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: The Parenthood Tax Rebates and Working Mother's Child Relief require the single unwed mother to marry the biological father of their child.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: An ancillary consequence of some of these measures is that a single mother may feel they are penalised so drastically as a single parent in the Singapore system that it is impossible to walk away from a bad or abusive relationship to avail themselves to the Budget incentives.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: If that does happen, the likelihood that the family unit breaks down is higher.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: From unwed single mothers, I would like to now speak about working mothers.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: The Working Mother's Child Relief was converted from a percentage-based calculation to a fixed sum.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: I appreciate its intent to redirect more support to lower- and middle-income working mothers.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Nevertheless, I question if doing so may also unwittingly deter, especially the higher-end middle-income mothers from having more children.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Notably, Singapore is trying to raise the total fertility rate (TFR) and having this change might discourage higher-end middle-income mothers from having more children.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: In this way, it will strengthen the Government's position to encourage families to have more children as well as encourage mothers to return to the workforce after having their children.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Thirdly, I applaud the increase in paternity leave from two weeks to four weeks.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Having had my first child last year, I realised how I really needed my husband for support those first two weeks and wished that he could have returned to work later.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Postpartum recovery is difficult and the additional two weeks of support is invaluable.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: As such, could I request that this increase in paternity leave start a bit earlier to benefit more couples?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: I understand that companies may need time to adjust to this change in manpower, so can I suggest increasing in tranches, starting with three weeks in the second half of the year and to the full four weeks in January next year?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: The increase in paternity leave as well as unpaid infant care leave is a welcome move but one that may be taxing on the workplace.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Even with these positive changes, I find that a supportive workplace and colleagues are just as important.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: One common example is when children fall sick and children fall sick a lot.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Working parents may need to take urgent leave.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: I have heard many stories of workplaces giving parents a hard time when this happens.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: It may be mandated by the Government but it may be frowned upon by the company – unofficially, I must add.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, I would like to implore to employers to instil a strong pro-family work culture where flexible work arrangements are the new norm and where work-life balance is respected.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: As a working individual as well, be kind enough and willing to pick up the slack during these moments when a parent has to take some leave as it will ease the parent's mind greatly.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: I hope this kindness extends to other working individuals with other needs as well, like adult children who are caregivers to their elderly parents or the new mother who just returned from maternity leave and needs time and a place to express her milk.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Let us not wait for incentives and legislation from the Government.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Only then can we move the needle for supporting families in Singapore.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Along with the many other policies introduced in preceding Budgets, we have a comprehensive coverage for Singaporeans and Singapore that is the envy of many.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Today, I wish to dive a little deeper into the topic of strengthening our social compact and building a Singapore Made for Families.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Whilst the Budget provides generous support in the form of Baby Support Grant, Paternity Leave, Baby Bonus Cash Gift and Child Development Account (CDA) to name just a few, I believe that there are many reasons why young couples still find it challenging to want and have children.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: In speaking with many young residents and many others who reach out to me, I often ask about these reasons and I will share some of them today.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: The Government has provided much housing support for young couples to stay near their parents so that childcaring duties can be shared.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: However, this may not be a suitable arrangement for some.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: There seems to be an increasing number of young parents who want to raise their children themselves, they want to be very much more hands-on and involved.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Anecdotal evidence suggests that the children may sometimes bond more with their grandparents or domestic helpers.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Grandparents also tend to dote on grandchildren and even "spoil" them, inadvertently undermining the relationship between the child and his or her parents.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: The parents would also need to step in to impose discipline and dial back on the indulgence.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: In order to support parents who want to be present and active in raising their children, it is essential that we provide them with sufficient infant care and childcare facilities near their home or workplace.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I visit my new BTO estate Green Verge mainly on weekends.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: This is the result of the lack of ready infant care and childcare facilities when they moved in.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Therefore, some young couples continue to live with their parents on weekdays when they cannot get childcare places in their new estates and stay over in their new homes only on weekends.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: For example, Green Verge residents had to register for childcare in Green Meadows, Green Ridges and Sunshine estate’s childcare around them.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: As their children assimilate to the childcare centres, they usually would not move their kids back to Green Verge's new childcare centres that are now up and running.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: As a result, we end up with a tight situation in terms of childcare spaces in Green Meadows, Ridges and Sunshine, and the parents there have to in turn register their children in Green Verge’s new estate.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: The savvier ones in the upcoming estate, Green Court, have also put their children on the wait list there.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: So, at dismissal time, you will see parents, grandparents and helpers crossing roads to each other’s estate to pick up the children.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: This messy arrangement creates a lot of unnecessary anxiety on everyone.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: A recurrent observation, and no surprises here, is that the cost of raising children is prohibitive.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Many are appreciative of the generous support provided by the Government and this year’s measures are most welcome, it is still however only a small part of the total investment in a child over the course of their first 18 years.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Modern couples want quality time, more hands-on parenting.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: If our society can evolve to allow both parents to take turns to be around, it will motivate more couples to have children and it will serve our next generation well too.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: During the COVID-19 outbreak, the Government encouraged the work-from-home model.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Many that I have spoken to said it was a good thing for the family and enabled parents to spend more meaningful time at home.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Perhaps this is a hint at what we can do to encourage more young couples to build and expand their families.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I wonder if there has been an uptick in babies birthed nine months after the periods of work-from-home.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: This is a very important group of people that will help improve our total fertility rate (TFR) because they are determined to have children.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: And no, I am not asking for more money in co-funding – yet.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I believe there are practical things that we can do to help them.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Many couples told me that they give up because of the process.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: It was not just about the physical strain but it is incredibly, emotionally draining.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: They are often in a confused state as doctors rush them through the consultation as the queues are long in public hospitals.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: In one hospital, they had to keep repeating their responses to the same questions at every appointment, since each time, it is a different doctor.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: They feel bad holding up the queue and wondered why the records were not updated.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: What I know is the National University Hospital (NUH) used the same doctor from consultation to stimulation and birth, which some feedback that it felt more personable.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Last week, I did a support group Zoom session with a small group of ladies who underwent ART in different public hospitals.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: It was to understand their experiences in the respective hospitals.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: After the session, a few ladies texted me to say the session was quite informative.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: It will help to prepare couples to prepare for what to expect in reality as they listen to the different experiences.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: They said that they want to listen to more such sessions in case they want to try again in future.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: One added that she had not thought of asking the doctor those questions and the support group had prepared her better.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I realised that each and every hospital had their unique way of managing their client.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Hence, I am going to make some suggestions on possible areas of improvement.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Hospitals should hold more online dialogues to prepare couples better.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Doctors and couples sharing would help them to have more insights and help allay their concerns as they embark on this journey.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Some commented that they leave the doctors’ consultation feeling confused and discouraged and if they are lucky, an experienced nurse might notice and help them with their queries.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: It is cost effective and also efficient to have experienced nurses counsel couples.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: A few joked about how they went into the counselling room and were shocked that it was about financial counselling and felt that it was so transactional at a time when they were struggling with their emotions.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Some centres are too swamped and felt chaotic and rushed in consultations.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Another joked that it was so crowded that they stood around waiting for appointment and it was like musical chairs, because when someone stood up, another would quickly take the seat.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: The good thing, of course, is the medical chit was always issued at the beginning of the appointment as the consultation and scan would usually take half a day.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: She said her experience in Hospital B was not as good as in Hospital A.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: She presented her set of known problems to Hospital B’s doctor, but the doctor did not really follow up on her medication unlike the doctor in Hospital A.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: But the doctor in Hospital A had gone into private practice and due to co-funding being only for use in public hospitals, she did not follow.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: She added that she did not get to see the doctor in Hospital B throughout the stimulation process or scans, and the nurses would just relay the messages.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: While the waiting time was shorter, she felt that the experience was less personable and felt like a wasted cycle.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: She is now on her fourth try, this time in a private clinic.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: An embryologist was there to explain things she felt she should have learnt in her first cycle such as the grading of embryos of 5AB, 4BB, 3BCs.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: And this is why online talks might be useful.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: She has decided this would be her last cycle as the psychological pain was too trying.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: She wanted to discard her last frozen embryo and the embryologist spoke to her for nearly half an hour and persuaded her to keep it first.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: The Ministry of Health (MOH) together with NUH had the pilot project on PGS some years ago.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Do we have more information to improve the couples’ chances with PGS?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I also ask for attention on some of the more nuanced aspects of addressing our TFR, including facility support for families in new estates and work-from-home support.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: For the women undergoing ART, we need more community support and information and simpler, easier and supported response from the hospitals.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Even though we are recovering well from COVID-19, there are still many geopolitical headwinds to contend with.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The ongoing war in Europe and the tensions between the US and China have caused much uncertainty on a global scale.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A small country like Singapore is certainly not spared.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In this Budget, I am pleased that we are taking a bolder approach to increasing revenue.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is by getting those who can afford it to contribute more, thus lessening the burden on the less privileged.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In my Budget response, I will focus on seniors.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This topic is close to my heart for several reasons.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Next, we should view the silver sector as an opportunity, not as a burden.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Foremost, I will share my perspective on the need for a holistic review and consolidation of senior-related initiatives.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I will then share my thoughts on areas where we can do more for seniors, which were not touched on in this Budget.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: To start, we should systematically review all the senior-related initiatives and consolidate them as far as possible.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is with the goal of making them more easily understandable and accessible for our seniors.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: There are also existing schemes for seniors today.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This includes the Pioneer and Merdeka Generation packages.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While all these initiatives are appreciated, it is important to consider whether there is a holistic view of all these schemes.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And seniors do find it difficult to navigate through all the help that is available to them.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We should consolidate and communicate these schemes to seniors better.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Such schemes have to be translated into tangible support.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I often hear from seniors during my house visits or at the market that they do not fully comprehend or know how to access many of the schemes.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Our grassroots team is always glad to do our best to address these queries.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But the fact remains that many of them are unable to understand the schemes without external help.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Some do not even know that they are beneficiaries of these schemes.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Effective schemes should be implemented and communicated in ways that make them readily accessible to beneficiaries.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Beneficiaries should not have to go through multiple agencies or move mountains to get the support they need.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: That can be discouraging, considering that our older generations have always had a fiercely independent spirit that helped build the Singapore we have today.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I will now move on to speak on areas where we can do more for seniors.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First, we need a greater push to help seniors benefit from the digitalisation of services.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Digitalisation is the way forward for our Public Service.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is worth noting that during the pandemic, we have seen seniors embrace digital technologies.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I have seen seniors using Zoom to connect with their loved ones overseas, when borders were closed.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Seniors also use WhatsApp video calls to communicate with us during our Meet-the-People Sessions.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: When physical activities were stopped, many went online and took part in Zoom cooking classes and other activities.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I will cover this topic in greater detail in my Committee of Supply cut for the Prime Minister's Office (PMO).

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: One area where we can go big on is in telehealth.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Seniors will be the biggest beneficiaries of this technology.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I have met many seniors who found it a hassle to go to the clinics and hospitals for their follow-ups because of mobility issues and the long wait times.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Telehealth can be a game changer in this regard.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: By adopting telehealth, we can provide seniors with access to medical care and support from the comfort of their own homes, or at convenient nodes in the community.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Next, we can also do more for the sandwiched families.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: When we think of seniors who need help, seniors who live alone or with their spouse comes to mind, but this is not always the case.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Seniors exist within the context of families, and many families are struggling to balance caring for both their children and their parents.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Although financial relief is always appreciated, there are other ways that we can support these families.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For instance, we could provide resources and materials to help them navigate the complexities of caring for aged parents.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We can also provide more assistance for end-of-life care, which can be an especially difficult time for families.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I will touch on these issues in greater detail in my upcoming Ministry of Health (MOH) cut.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must recognise the importance of caregivers and the critical role they play in our families and communities.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Caregivers are often the unsung heroes, quietly providing for their loved ones, without much recognition or backing.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We need greater social health integration on this front.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must not neglect emotional and psychological assistance for caregivers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Navigating a fragmented landscape of caregiver assistance and services can be frustrating and intimidating for an average Singaporean, let alone one who is already acutely stressed from custodial duties or limited in their English language proficiency.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Much as the Agency for Integrated Care (AIC) currently helps in this area, we also do not want to go to the extreme of providing case management for every single case.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This will be resource intensive for a care sector already dealing with a manpower crunch.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Having a dedicated care coordinator for a family makes sense for a few reasons.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They can guide caregivers to assess practical help.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They can also help to look out for caregivers' psychological well-being.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A coordinator can spot early signs of caregiver mental stress and provide timely intervention.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If I can work, I would certainly like to continue contributing to the workforce.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If I am retired, I would like to rediscover myself through new passion projects or pick up interests where, previously, I did not have time for.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Former US President George Bush Senior used to mark every fifth birthday after his retirement in a very special way – by putting on a parachute and jumping from a plane.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: His last skydive took place on his 90th birthday in 2014, despite him being confined to a wheelchair.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I do not think I am as adventurous as President Bush, but I would certainly like to pick up a musical instrument, enhance my skills in photography, travel around the world, and take in the new experiences and sights.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And if I have the blessings of having grandchildren, I would love to spend time and share my life experiences with them.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How would you like to spend your silver years?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How can we, as a society, enable our seniors to pursue their passions, stay energised and continue to be enthusiastic about life?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must view them beyond just a group that we support with schemes and social assistance.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is a phase where they get to live a fulfilling life at a more relaxed pace.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We should empower them to stay independent and confident.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This includes, as I have said above, empowering them to leverage technology in their daily life.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It also includes enhancing their understanding on how to make the best use of Government schemes that are available to them.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is so that they can have access to a good quality of life and live out their aspirations.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: So, how would you like to spend your silver years?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Let us work together as a society to create a Singapore that values our seniors and enables them to live out their aspirations.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Let us support their caregivers and the sandwiched families.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is so that they may continue to find pride and value in giving their loved ones the best kind of care possible.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Only then, can we truly establish a Singapore Made for Families.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Only then, can we make Singapore a great place to live and age in.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 4.40 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 4.21 pm until 4.40 pm. ﻿Sitting resumed at 4.40 pm.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In my response to the Budget Statement, I would like to discuss challenges faced by three stakeholders in our society – businesses, workers and families.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Singapore is generally a price taker on raw materials and energy.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Higher manpower cost, while challenging to businesses, can improve the welfare of our workers by increasing their income.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: As long as the wage increases do not set off a sustained wage price spiral.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: High rental costs, however, benefit a smaller segment of society, namely landlords and property owners, and come at the expense of tenants, especially SMEs who may struggle to afford the rent.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: They can also affect the competitiveness of these businesses which have to allocate more resources to rental expenses and less to other productive aspects of their operations.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Government needs to look for ways to moderate industrial and commercial rental costs for SMEs.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This will benefit a broader base of businesses which plays a critical part in growing our economy and providing good jobs for our people.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Next, I would like to discuss the challenges faced by workers in Singapore, particularly those in industries that rely heavily on foreign workers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In recent years, the Government has implemented various work pass restrictions to manage the inflow of foreign workers and professionals.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Additionally, the Government has allocated funding to help local companies become more productive and manpower lean.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, there needs to be more emphasis on attracting Singaporeans to work in industries that are currently overdependent on foreign workers, such as the marine, manufacturing and construction industries.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Government has introduced several programmes such as career conversion and professional conversion schemes to equip those who have decided to switch to these industries.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, there has been less success in urging our local workers to switch to these industries in the first place.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: While the Government has been working to raise awareness of the job opportunities and career prospects in these sectors, more needs to be done to address the perception that these industries are less prestigious than other sectors like finance, technology and law.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It is commonly believed that Singaporeans are not interested in these industries due to the long hours, shift work, low pay and difficult working conditions.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, the popularity of platform food delivery jobs indicates that many Singaporeans are willing to work in physically demanding jobs.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Food delivery riders work long hours, with many cycling around town for over 12 hours a day.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The IPS paper also found that our platform delivery workers who intended to leave the food delivery industry for other industries were looking for higher salaries, longer-term career pathways and opportunities to learn new skills in their next jobs.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: A significant number was seeking flexible work hours, although less than a third were looking for jobs in air-conditioned offices.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: If the industries that are currently lacking in local workers can provide these benefits, they will be able to attract more locals to join them.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Some progress has been made in attracting more locals to work as nurses and early childhood educators.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The same effort could be undertaken to upgrade other industries which are facing local worker shortages.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, even if these human resource matters are resolved, these industries may still face difficulties attracting job applicants from Singaporeans due to a lack of awareness of jobs in these industries.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: To address this, there is a need to increase awareness of these industries amongst students early on their school life.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Schools can work with industry representatives to introduce these career opportunities to students even as early as lower secondary school.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: By doing so, students and their parents will be more aware of the career prospects in these industries and be better equipped to select suitable subject combinations in Secondary 3 and eventually make informed career choices when they are graduating from school.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Our success in reducing dependence on foreign workers and professionals relies heavily on being able to raise local talent in these occupations by providing better pay, training and career pathways and better work-life balance.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: By increasing awareness of these industries among young people, we can attract more locals to work in these industries and reduce our dependence on foreign workers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The hon Member Hazel Poa also raised this concern in her speech earlier.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This could potentially offset any progress made towards enhancing the affordability of resale flats.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Has the Government projected any resale flat price increases as a result of the CPF Housing Grant increase by modelling the huge amount of housing transaction data available to HDB?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Additionally, since only first-timers will benefit from the increase in the CPF Housing Grant, non-first-timers may end up having to pay even more for their resale flats.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I hope the Government can provide more information on its projections to help Members assess the net effect of the CPF Housing Grant increase.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Has the Government considered the alternative proposals which I shared during the debate on the housing Motions earlier this month to moderate resale flat prices?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This include: one, providing more help to empty nesters who are prepared to sell their larger flats to obtain 2-room Flexi flats and community care apartments; two, requiring future buyers of private properties to sell their HDB flats; and three, incentivising those who currently own both a private property and a HDB flat to sell their flat by rebating the additional buyer's stamp duty they paid on their private property.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These proposals may provide longer-term solutions to moderating the prices of HDB resale flats.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The soaring property prices have made it increasingly challenging for families to purchase a new home.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Deputy Prime Minister has cautioned that we may continue to confront a period of high inflation, which is highly to persist throughout the first half of this year.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In these trying times, it is imperative for us to keep our minds open to workable solutions, regardless of where they may emerge from, so that we can help our fellow Singaporeans in need and progress and prosper together as a nation.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Global disruptions and macroeconomic headwinds show little signs of slowing.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It all makes for unprecedented complexity and uncertainty in the economic and competitive environment for companies and for countries.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Given our size, lack of natural resources and reliance on trade, it is an environment that makes us more vulnerable than many.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But it is an environment that Singapore is prepared to handle – if we leverage on our solid financial foundations to buffer ourselves against disruptions and seek out opportunities amidst uncertainly, if we can build resiliency.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Before I elaborate on building resiliency, I would like to thank the Ministry of Finance (MOF) for its work on the Occasional Paper on Medium-Term Financial Projections.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: In debating fiscal policy, it is always helpful to take a medium-term view and understand the drivers of Government finances.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The Occasional Paper outlines the external and internal challenges that will shrink our fiscal space.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The term "resilience" was introduced into the English language in the early 17th century from the Latin verb "resilire", meaning "to rebound".

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: In recent years, as we moved from one crisis to another, the word has become more commonly used and taken on a broader meaning.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Resilience is not only about bouncing back but about being prepared for bigger shocks and about seizing opportunities that arise out of uncertainty.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It is not only about grit and determination in the face of adversity but about being able to anticipate adversity, cushion its impact, adapt and even shape the future.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: There is personal resilience, organisational resilience and national resilience.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Personal resilience and organisational resilience are mutually reinforcing.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Resilient individuals can contribute their skills to making their organisations more resilient and resilient organisations can develop and invest in their staff to build their resilience.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Similarly, for Singapore to be resilient, Singaporeans and Singapore businesses must be resilient – with one important caveat – that care must be taken to ensure that resilience is built in an inclusive way so that we do not end up with widening inequalities where some people and some businesses are better able to bounce back and exploit uncertainty than others.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Second, building resilience means different things to different people and organisations.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: How best to build resiliency depends on one's starting position.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: For example, a company with a strong financial position operating in a volatile market might best act by diversifying its business model, expanding its supply chain and looking to get a leg-up on its competition.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: A company with a weak financial position in a more stable market has to focus first on changing its business model in ways that will shore up its financial position and consolidate its supply chain.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Similarly, while a rich man could build financial buffers with insurance, a poor man may turn more to belt tightening and community support.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Budget 2023 contains several initiatives and programmes designed to help companies build resilience, such as the extension of productivity grants, energy efficiency grants, support for nurturing and sustaining innovation and developing local enterprises, including the Singapore Global Enterprises.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I will discuss some of these in my Committee of Supply cuts but I will focus today on helping individual Singaporeans to be more resilient.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Beyond financial support, the Government has made huge investments in lifelong learning, from early childhood education to new education pathways, to upskilling and reskilling.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The Government has also encouraged Singaporeans to seize new opportunities and embrace change, risk-taking, failure and learning, though admittedly, this shift is a work in progress.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Budget 2023 goes further in this direction and I welcome the move to strengthen the link between training and job placement with Jobs-Skills Integrators to enhance employment support and to strengthen retirement adequacy despite the pain that some will feel in the short term.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The Government has built up many schemes to help Singaporeans who lose their jobs, from short-term relief through ComCare to extensive subsidies on skilling programmes like Career Support Programmes, Professional Conversion Programmes and so on.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: During the pandemic, the Government turbocharged this with the COVID-19 support grant and SGUnited training programmes and helped many Singaporeans, including middle-income Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But these moves are sometimes not enough for middle-income Singaporeans who have larger financial commitments – commitments that payouts from ComCare cannot support.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: He had a high paying job in an MNC but was retrenched in his 40s after a merger.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: He struggled for more than two years to find suitable employment.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: He tried his hand at his own business but it did not work out and cost him a chunk of his savings and put him in debt.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: He could not pay off his renovation loan and his business loans, ended up under a debt repayment scheme (DRS) and becoming a platform worker.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: One day, he shared with me a picture of his bank balance.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I asked him what he spent his income on: his DRS payments, household expenses, car, the money he gives to his parents and health and life insurance.
