speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I could not with a clear conscience tell him to let his health and life insurance policies lapse.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The Government has cited concerns on the moral hazards and the cost of such insurance.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We also know that people have other formal and informal forms of insurance such as retrenchment benefits, savings, the ability to cut discretionary spending and, for dual income couples, the income of their spouse.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: While we cannot be certain what the takeup would be, in a straw poll that I conducted of middle-income earners, very few said they were likely to take up a voluntary scheme and even fewer would support a mandatory scheme, say, one that deducts premiums from CPF.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: So, how would we create the market needed for the premiums to be super affordable?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Arguably, this is where we are in Singapore – with very low unemployment.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But perhaps existing schemes could be tweaked to make it easier for people who have lost their jobs to bounce back.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I know there may be concerns over equity of having higher tiers of assistance for some.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But on balance, I believe there is merit in considering ways to moderate the impact of a job loss on middle-income Singaporeans, helping them to meet their commitments and focus on recovery and growth.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We know how challenging it can be for ex-offenders to integrate back into society and pick their lives back up.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But I think we can be more holistic in our support.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: One area that ex-offenders I see could use more help in is housing.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Many ex-offenders are fortunate to go back to living with their families, who become their pillars of support in the difficult journey of integration.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But many also go from prison to less than ideal home environments or are disowned by their families who want nothing more to do with them.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: This was the case for a resident who came to me to appeal for a rental flat.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: He had been sleeping rough for a few weeks.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: He claimed that he had approached the Family Service Centre (FSC) for shelter but had been told the shelter was full.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: He came every week with the same appeal for four weeks in a row, looking worse each time.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Upon investigation, I learned that he was in the intensive care unit (ICU) after being attacked.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: After his discharge, he stayed with his niece for a short while and then stopped coming back home and was no longer contactable.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I could not help but wonder if he would have been better off if he had stayed in prison.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Another ex-offender wrote to me for help with an appeal to be eligible for the Enhanced Housing Grant.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: He has four children, the oldest in polytechnic and the youngest is one year old.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: While in prison, he resolved to turn his life around and provide a better living environment for his family.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But at the time of the appeal, a month before his scheduled key collection, he had worked very hard for 12 months to support his family to be ready to buy the house.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Cancelling the application would also cost him his $1,000 deposit, not a small sum for him.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Early intervention programmes on housing, even prior to release and more flexibility on eligibility requirements can go a long way to giving our ex-offenders a better shot at re-integrating and turning their lives around.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The third group of Singaporeans I wish to highlight are Singaporeans who are struggling with debt.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Sometimes it is a business loan or loans taken on to finance necessary expenditure like healthcare or education, but more often than not, the struggle is due to unsecured loans, credit card debt, renovation loans and yes, gambling debt, that have been allowed to balloon. "I made a mistake," they say.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And they find it very hard to dig themselves out of the hole.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It can quickly go down a downward spiral, breaking up relationships and families.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Perhaps more can be done in raising awareness of various debt management and repayment schemes, and provide more counselling and support to these individuals.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But I think the true answer lies in going upstream, investing further on financial capability building.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I stress financial capability, not just financial literacy.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It is not enough to increase knowledge of financial concepts.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Ultimately, Singaporeans must change their behaviours in positive ways.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: There are also initiatives such as the Financial Education Network and financial literacy programmes in schools, workplaces and the community.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: A lack of financial resilience also often leads to high risk-taking that one is ill prepared to manage and the proliferation of scams.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But beyond the "what", allow me to say a word about the "how" as we try to help Singaporeans build resilience.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Building resiliency does not mean removing adversity or pain altogether.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Adversity helps to develop new skills, capabilities you may not know you had.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But too much adversity can overstrain a person, such that it delays recovery and growth.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I echo Mr Sitoh's call for greater empathy.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But let us do it by setting goals for someone who is being assisted, that gets progressively higher and harder as he or she gains in capabilities and confidence.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And let us remove unproductive stress and frustration that is created through excessive complexity and bureaucracy.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: So, can we spend less time on a multitude of forms, CPF statements and bank statements, and more time on real conversations to push people to grow?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We said then that we were facing the crisis of our generation.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We drew on our reserves to keep Singapore and Singaporeans afloat throughout the pandemic while continuing efforts to keep our economy competitive.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Today, we have emerged from COVID-19, DORSCON Green and our economy is in relatively good shape.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Yet, new storm clouds have gathered and we are in a new era of increased complexity, uncertainty and competition, even while we tackle domestic challenges of ageing and slowing social mobility.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We need a Budget that can move us forward in a new era.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Our response in Budget 2023 is clear – to build resiliency.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Notwithstanding my suggestions to improve some existing schemes to help some segments of our population to bounce back, I support the Budget.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Some of these invisible forces are unique to Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: As a father of a young two-and-a-half-year-old son, all I am asking for is for us to pause and have a think.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Ask ourselves: how are our family units faring, in terms of being that nurturing fortress and safe space where love is unconditional, and where no topics are too taboo or too awkward to be talked about?

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: If we could give a score to how Singapore families are doing in this respect, what might our score be?

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: I loved Singapore Broadcasting Corporation (SBC) and subsequently, Television Corporation of Singapore (TCS)'s Channel 8 drama serials: 雾锁南洋 (The Awakening), 青春123 (Happy Trio) and 咖啡乌 (The Coffee Shop).

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: These drama serials served two important functions for me.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: One, I reinforced what I learnt during English classes by diligently reading onscreen subtitles.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Learning to sing and play the theme songs on my recorder were good supplementary music lessons.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Mum always told me quite plainly: study hard, be somebody useful someday.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: That year, I became a father for the first time.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: I was over the moon, but also afraid of heights.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: I fret incessantly over the little one's eating habits, sleeping patterns, developmental milestones.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Quite clearly, I am the worrywart between me and my better half.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Compared to my parents, my wife and I have a very different parenting approach.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: To me, one of education's key mission is to pique the young mind's curiosity for the world and to ignite the child's passion to uncover and learn about the many wonderful things around him.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: My wife and I often talk about future planning for the little one late in the evenings.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: One area we sometimes talk about – tuition and enrichment classes, outside of school curriculum. "Should we sign him up, simply because other parents will be doing so for their children?

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: What if we miss discovering some talents that he has but we miss it because we do not sign him up for the classes?

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: If other parents are doing it, and if we do not, will he lose out?" We often end such conversations thoroughly exhausting ourselves, agree on one fact, that is, the need to respect his choices too, and then heave a sigh of relief that we have a few years more to go before we come head-to-head with some of these decisions.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: As a worried and overwhelmed parent, I cannot help but feel at times that the feel-good vibe of "keeping up with the Joneses" that I experienced as a kid growing up in the 1980s and 1990s have today taken on a somewhat fiercely competitive tone.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: In my interactions with young people today, some anecdotes ring alarm bells.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: I remember being told not once but several times over, that competition in academic settings today is so rife.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Some students, as I was told, deliberately share wrong answers with other students just so they get to pull ahead of the pack.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: A fine line divides a relentless pursuit of excellence from an unscrupulous clamour to the top.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: There is absolutely nothing wrong with striving to be the best versions of ourselves, but at what cost?

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: What values do we really treasure in society today?

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Are we keeping up with the Joneses, chasing our white picket fence pipedream, or are we more intent on one-upping the Joneses, whatever it takes?

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: I also worry for my son because of how we perceive and define success today.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Many of them are talented, creative, and not to mention, lovely to hang out with.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: These students may not be as academically inclined as their peers and oftentimes, their strengths are glossed over simply because they carry the "ITE label".

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: When can we start seeing ITE students for who they really are?

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: If my son turns out to be not quite the "academic type", would this society still embrace him for his non-academic strengths and talents?

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Beyond school, would he still be able to realise his full potential in life, even if he is not equipped with a university degree?

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Would he be respected and appropriately remunerated if he so chooses to pursue a trade or profession and become a carpenter, mason or artisan?

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: We often hear complaints that our youth belong to a generation of lab-bred strawberries: pretty on the outside, soft on the inside and very easily bruised.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: To this view, I respectfully beg to differ.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Youth today are dealt an entirely different deck of cards and challenges.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: The recent retreat from globalisation aside, Singapore today is more connected to the world than ever before.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Our youth must deal with a barrage of adulting challenges us digital migrants could only begin to wrap our heads around.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Truncating attention span, information overload, the constant thirst for social validation, the fear of missing out (FOMO), the inevitable exposure to negative influences online like pornography, cyberbullying, online predators are unfortunately here to stay.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Just how well equipped are our families to serve as "social and emotional safe harbours" for our young ones?

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: For that matter, how well do we really know our young ones and the challenges they face?

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: And I look up to the viewing gallery of these Chamber right now.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Addictions to social networking sites, pornography, cyberbullying, fraud, radicalisation, hate speech, to name a few.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: How prepared am I as a father in helping my son navigate life as we now know it?

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Like many parents, perhaps in the Chamber, perhaps who are viewing this session today, I am frankly quite clueless.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Growing up, I did not have a social media account and what free time I had were either spent roaming the HDB void decks or faithfully tuning in to my next episode of 早安老师 (Good Morning, Sir!), not endlessly scrolling or doing up short form videos to share with the world how I am getting on in life.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Fellow parents, whether we know it, whether we like it or not, we need help.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Parents naturally want the best for their children but not all necessarily know how.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Just because we live in the same household does not mean we naturally know our young ones well.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: It also does not naturally follow that they will continue to look up to us as they did when they were little.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: An episode narrated to me recently was instructive.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: A psychologist at the Ministry of Social and Family Development (MSF) recounted to me her experience at an engagement session.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: When asked who their children would likely consult on matters concerning mental health, one mother replied confidently that her child would approach her.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: The child's reply caught this mother by surprise.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: The child said, "Well, I would try not to approach my mom because I am not sure if she would understand, and I also do not want to burden her." In that instant, the mother broke down in tears.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: As we shape a more family-friendly society through legislation and policy-making, let us all remember to make time for our loved ones.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Pause, take a deep breath and experience all the beautiful things in this world together.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Have more heart-to-heart talks with our family members and treasure each memory that the family creates together.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: (In English): Mdm Deputy Speaker, this Budget holds plenty of promise for Singapore families to prosper and flourish, but the horizon is not without dark clouds.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: As we shape a more family-friendly Singapore through legislation and policymaking, let us all remember to make time for our loved ones in our lives.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Pause, breathe, watch the world go by together.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Have heart-to-heart talks with those that matter, on things that matter.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Treasure every moment that the family creates together.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: As a people, whether we spend time trying our best to outdo one another or we thoughtfully and purposefully make sure that as many amongst us as possible, flourish and thrive in our own ways, dump needless labels, connect to one another, starting within each family, person-to-person, soul-to-soul, the choice is ours to make.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: And these are things that legislation and policy can do so little to fix, and these are choices that we must make, one family at a time.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Other potential crises will emerge, and we must try to be prepared.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The rising costs of living and economic slowdown are concerns that we devote resources to addressing.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: In addition, there may be other grey rhinos that may affect our future as a nation and I would like to highlight four of them.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: It is well-known that we are heavily dependent on foreign manpower.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: This may perhaps be a global problem but the labour shortage problem exists across many of our industries, including aviation, cleaning services, construction, F&B, retail businesses and, crucially, healthcare.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Our healthcare system and staff held up well throughout the pandemic.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: However, should another pandemic come around, we may not be as fortunate.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Finding workers to work in the cleaning services is a real challenge and it is getting harder to get help in the F&B and retail sectors.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Similarly, our construction will soon grind to a halt if we do not automate more.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We have discussed various approaches to reduce manpower reliance by increasing productivity via automation, work process redesign, upskill workers, raise salaries and provide better benefits to workers.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We hope to achieve this via the Progressive Wage Model (PWM) and Progressive Wage Credit Scheme (PWCS), National Productivity Fund (NPF), Enterprise Innovation Scheme (EIS) and SME Co-Investment Fund and Singapore Global Enterprises (SGEs) initiative.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Our local construction companies are aware that they need to leverage technology to automate, innovate and redesign their work processes.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: However, regardless of manpower savings downstream, automation can be an expensive investment and small companies will not be able to finance the upfront investment.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Perhaps, the Government can consider an interest-free loan scheme with a reasonable loan period under NPF to encourage our small- and medium-size enterprises (SMEs) to invest in automation in order to reduce reliance on foreign labour.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Automation may assist certain sectors but there will always be a requirement for people interaction in multi-tasking micro roles that entail wide variability or high touch.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: For cleaners and security guards, the PWM wage increase for cleaning started five years ago and the increases for security and landscaping wages have been active for almost three and two years respectively.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Currently, the proportion of local staff in these three essential services sectors seem to be still faced with the same challenges.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: And most importantly, we must find a way to attract Singaporeans to join the healthcare industry.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: This leads me into the next grey rhino, the Silver Tsunami.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We are trailing very closely behind Japan, at 83.7 years old, in terms of the countries with the longest average life expectancy.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: With medical science advancements, Singaporeans will likely be able to live longer but there will be questions on the quality of life and health when the Silver Tsunami hits our shores over the next decades.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: During the debate on Healthier SG last year, many Members in this House have spoken about the pressure on aged care facilities that is required.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: In my Adjournment Motion on dementia, I mentioned that family members may need to consider compromising their careers to care for their loved ones and medical spending for seniors will also be a major concern.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: During the pandemic, there was a shortage of hospital beds and staff.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Will our infrastructure be able to handle our greying Singaporeans when the Silver Tsunami hits us and do we have a clear plan to manage these challenges?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The third grey rhino is energy, a concern that may cause massive disruption.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Hence, to maintain energy security, we will need to diversify sources.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Natural gas is cleaner than coal but it is still responsible for 40% of Singapore's carbon emissions.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We will need to transit to cleaner fuel.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Unfortunately, Singapore does not have any alternative energy sources other than some solar energy.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Before hydrogen-powered electricity becomes a reality, we would have to import clean energy from regional power grids such as Malaysia, Indonesia and Laos.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The ongoing Russia-Ukraine war is severely affecting many European countries.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: This is a stark reminder for us because many of these European countries are dependent on Russian natural gas.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Do we have a fall-back plan, should our electricity supply be disrupted for a prolonged period?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: While we are coming up with steps to accelerate the next chapter of our green energy transition, do we have the scientists and engineers, like they do in Australia, Germany and Spain, where the expertise in this area exists?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: And should we not be investing more to attract experts to Singapore and to develop local talents, to focus on the solutions required in our energy sector?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: To add, it is uncertain when and if green hydrogen-powered electricity is economically viable and how do we ensure the import supply will be extended infinitely while the cost of imported electricity can be kept affordable.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The fourth grey rhino has reared its head during the pandemic, but it may charge at us more aggressively in the future.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Singapore is a tiny island with only 720 square kilometres of land and is one of the lowest-lying countries in the world, with about 30% of our land that is less than five metres above sea levels.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Extreme weather may cause sea levels to rise by as much as four to five metres, taking into account coastal surges, extreme high tides and land subsidence.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: If heavy rainfall coincides with high tide, there will be flash floods that are worse than what we are experiencing now.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: If we do not have effective mitigation solutions, many homes, beaches and public infrastructure, like Gardens by the Bay and Merlion Park, will be affected.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: In view of the latest global temperature rise estimates and reports by sea level scientists, I have four questions: one, will we be able to bring forward the construction of coastal protection infrastructure?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Two, can we accelerate our technology and construction research, and implement pilots more aggressively?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Three, how do we ensure 100% protection against sea levels rising beyond one metre?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: And four, how do we test the effectiveness of the solutions or steps taken?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: (In Mandarin):   During my recent Chinese New Year house visits, I met five seniors in their nineties, who are all still in the pink of health.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: One senior in her 80s is still working in McDonald's just to stay active, even though she does not need the income.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: I asked them about their secret of youth.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: All of them shared that they eat moderately, exercise regularly, stay engaged and do not fret over the small things.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: For the rest of us who are barely half their age, we still have a good chance to live both a long and happy life if we can follow their advice.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The Healthier SG programme will help us better monitor our health status, but really, the ball is in our own court.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Staying engaged is extremely important for one's physical, mental and emotional health.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Hence, to better prepare for the silver tsunami, our seniors should stay employed or be involved in volunteering work for as long as they can, even past the statutory retirement age.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: One of my colleagues in Singapore Table Tennis Association (STTA), affectionately known as Auntie Amy, is 76 but she looks like 56.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: She could have retired but chose to continue working to keep herself active and engaged with younger people around her.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: (In English): Mdm Deputy Speaker, I would like to say a few words now in Malay.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Employers and voluntary welfare organisations (VWOs) are key partners to help our seniors age better.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: I hope they will continue to allow seniors to contribute even if they are past 67 years old.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: (In English): I look forward to the Minister for Manpower sharing more details about the schemes at the Committee of Supply debates.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Hopefully, with the interventions through Healthier SG programmes and with more seniors staying employed, our next generation of seniors will age gracefully and healthily into the next decades ahead.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The COVID-19 pandemic has reminded us of the importance of planning ahead.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: If we are not prepared, then Singapore's future can be severely impaired.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: With a vibrant economy and a resilient and fair taxation system, we will be able to continue building our national reserves.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We must deploy both local and foreign top talents to create new solutions to tackle the difficult and complex problems.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: These solutions must be deliberate, long-term and must not be left to market forces.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: It was their strategy to develop capabilities in the public sector and it was their achievements for Singapore that developed the trust the Government required from Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: I have faith that our 4G team will continue to develop Singapore into a happier, more prosperous and progressive nation.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Notwithstanding my queries and suggestions, I am heartened that many low-income families and young families will benefit from Budget 2023 and I am happy to positively endorse the Budget.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: I hope with these incentives, coupled with the power of the zodiac dragon year next year in 2024, Singapore will see a record number of babies born next year.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Hot-button issues like inflation and public housing are also being addressed.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: This is a budget that recognises the impact of high inflation on our cost of living and how we should embrace ourselves to face challenges ahead as we restructure and seek to re-energise our economy beyond the COVID-19 pandemic era.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: This month marks the one-year anniversary of the Russia-Ukraine war.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: The war has resulted in severe disruption of gas and oil supply causing huge increases and fluctuations in the prices of energy and fuelled global inflation as well.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: It exposed our vulnerability due to our over-reliance on natural gas and oil for our energy needs.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: I suggest we need to urgently explore more ways to expand and ramp up our adoption of solar energy.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Every time I look out at our buildings – residential, commercial and industrial – from a high vantage point, I noticed there are many, many roof tops that we could have used to install solar panels and increase our national solar energy production.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: We should do more to expedite and increase our solar energy production.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: For example, we could offer grants to private home owners for the installation of solar panels or provide grants to companies to use the rooftops of their industrial and commercial buildings for solar power generation.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Additionally, I would like to boldly suggest that the Building Control Authority (BCA) can consider revising its building code to make the installation of solar panels mandatory as part of its Minimum Environmental Sustainability Standard for all new building projects.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Next, what about the use of nuclear energy for Singapore?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Monday, 5 December 2022, was an important day in science.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: The experimental result is a massive nuclear energy breakthrough in a century-long quest to unlock the power of the sun on Earth.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: With more research and financial investment, researchers now believe we are just a few decades away from producing 100% clean and limitless energy.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: The possibility of using nuclear energy in Singapore has been under discussion for many years.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: It is also time for us to make a bold decision, whether this is one of our best options to ensure our energy resilience.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Naturally, we should consider factors such as cost, technology and safety, particularly since we lack the significant open space.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: But we have never shied away from challenges due to Singapore's limited size constraints.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: We can explore building a nuclear power plant on an offshore island or on a man-made rig in the sea.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: We can also consider building it deep underground, or even on the seabed.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Currently, France is the forerunner in the development of underwater nuclear reactor technology with DCNS prototyping a 100-meters cylindrical small nuclear power reactor called the Flexblue.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: This is one of the possibilities we can explore.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: I understand the Ministry of Trade and Industry (MTI) has been closely monitoring developments in nuclear energy, studying building capabilities to better understand and assess their safety, security and environmental implications.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: It normally takes about 10 to 15 years to build a nuclear power plant.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Singapore should be prepared if nuclear energy becomes an inevitable option.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Therefore, I would like to ask is there a timeline in pursuing this option?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: It is crucial for us to set a clear target date as we evaluate the feasibility of using nuclear energy for Singapore.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: At present, we are planning to import renewable energy from our Southeast Asian neighbours, which is a positive development, but it does not enhance our energy resilience significantly as we are still very vulnerable as such supply can be interrupted by the export country anytime.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: What is the risk of our natural gas source being interrupted?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: What is the current capacity of our liquefied natural gas (LNG) terminal and how long can this storage sustain us in the unlikely event of a natural gas disruption?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: In addition, just as we prioritise food security, we must focus on supply diversification to reduce our reliance on piped natural gas.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: How are we progressing in making Singapore a key LNG hub by empowering private players to build, own and operate offshore LNG terminals?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: The COVID-19 pandemic has been a wake-up call for many businesses and company owners who have been operating under Singapore's very stable economic and political environment without worrying about the possibility of a black swan event.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: The Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome (SARS) outbreak in 2003 took only months to be reined in and for normalcy to return.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: However, the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic was unlike that of SARS.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: It was more prolonged, severe and had a greater transmission rate, with the virus easily spreading from human to human.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: It ravaged the global economy and forced countries to close their borders.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Factories were closed due to sick workers as well as quarantine measures.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Travel, both air, land and sea, came to a standstill as a result of lockdowns and supply chains disrupted, with goods and produce stacked up in warehouses, unable to move.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: If not for our Government's timely intervention, spending billions from our reserves to assist Singapore companies to tide through the difficult period, our economy could have suffered a deeper and more severe decline.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Companies were kept afloat by various forms of reliefs such as grants, cash flow assistance, business loan schemes, tax rebates, rental rebates and job-support schemes.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: The Government also rolled out innovative schemes to give Singaporeans vouchers to support our heartland retailers, hotels and local tourist attractions.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Despite all these efforts, there were still casualties.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Hence, we must not let this pandemic pass without learning its lessons.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: As we learn to live with the COVID-19 virus, international trade and travel are gradually re-opening.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: We are now beginning to breathe a little bit easier, but the business environment has also changed.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Just as our country undergoes a transformation in the post-COVID-19 era, companies need to go back to the drawing board as well.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: We need to identify the weaknesses of our local companies when confronting black swan events and help them better prepare them for the future.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: There has been a significant shift in the business environment.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Even for today, many are still struggling to get both feet on firm ground.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Economic resilience is key and critical to Singapore's future.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: If Singapore’s economic engine loses power, how long can we survive relying on our precious reserves?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: The last topic is on climate change – on environmental resilience.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Today, we are seeing more extreme weather events happening globally.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Europe experienced an unprecedented cold winter, while nearer to home, Australia was hit by severe flooding caused by heavy rainfall.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: New Zealand declared a national emergency after being battered by Cyclone Gabrielle.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: There has been widespread flooding, landslides and huge ocean swells that forced evacuations.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Last year, in the US, it was the third wildest year in terms of extreme weather events and it cost over US$1 billion in overall damages.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Here, we are not spared as we are seeing heavier downpours with water ponding occurring more frequently.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: It rained almost continuously in the last two weeks of January and into February, with a surge of strong winds and more days with temperatures falling to low 20°C.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Certainly, we need to pay more attention to the changing weather conditions and speed up our efforts to build infrastructure to protect our low-lying areas.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: What can we do to cope with the extremes in weather conditions?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: What can we do to become a climate-resilient society?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Are our people and our businesses prepared to cope with sudden severe weather conditions?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Do we need to review, tighten and enhance surveillance checks on our buildings to ensure that everything is stable?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Are claddings on high-rise office buildings and shopping malls checked for stability to withstand increased incessant rain and heavy wind surges?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Our underground gas pipes, power cables – are they able to withstand any undue soil movement underground?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Do we have the necessary resources on standby?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Prime Minister Lee said working on climate change defences should be done steadily over the years and will be over several generations.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: But do we have the luxury of time as the climate change clock is ticking away and seems faster?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Can we accelerate the construction of the ponder and help our local enterprise who are in this field to develop their capabilities in this new growth area?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Bring forward the timeline for climate change defences projects will also create new land for Singapore and other new developments to enhance our attractiveness as a city to attract talent?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: I have outlined in my speech three areas on resilience building, that is, energy, economic as well as environment.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The withering effects of COVID-19 continue to be felt.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In the budget debates we had the two years before, we were discussing public health issues, taking measures to minimise the loss of life and prevent people suffering the serious effects of COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The travel, tourism, retail and F&B industries were hard hit as people cut down on travel and going out.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The war in Ukraine has been another body blow to the world economy.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Ukraine was the largest wheat producer in the world and also a large producer of corn, barley and sunflower oil.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Russia was one of the largest producers of oil and gas.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Now that these supplies have been disrupted from the world market, energy prices have spiked, as have food prices because wheat and the other materials produced are not just food for us but also food for livestock.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This coupled with the supply chain disruptions caused by COVID-19 have caused inflation and rising costs on the global scale.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: To deal with inflation, central banks in many places have started raising interest rates.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There is not much that Singapore can do to change these global forces.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Against this backdrop, I support the Budget measures which provide much needed support and relief to individuals and businesses faced with cost crunch and disruptions.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There is a wide range of assistance to both individuals and businesses to deal with these challenges.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: For the housing issue, a comprehensive proposal has been put forward which I am sure will be elaborated on in Ministry of National Development (MND)'s Committee of Supply debates.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Now these are commendable and, I think, these are measures that we can take because we have the luxury of strong reserves as well as prudent financial planning and these measures will alleviate some of the immediate cost of living pressures for many people.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: However, high prices and high inflation is likely to be here to stay and the only real long-term solution would be to ensure that Singapore continues to grow and remain an attractive place to invest and do business and this in turn will create attractive jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This Budget provides significant support for multinational corporations (MNCs) that choose to locate here, people who do R&D, for local enterprises to build up as well as for local enterprises to go global.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Singapore is one of the few places where the Government provides such significant and wide-ranging support to the private business community to help them to grow and develop.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: One suggestion I have though is that when the Government gives out generous grants to businesses or tax breaks, the Government should also put into place requirements for them to share the benefits and profits from such investments – at the very least with employees at all levels, and at best, with the broader community.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I think it is fair to put conditions and expectations on private enterprises that benefit from the public purse.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This will also ensure a more equitable distribution of the profits if those ventures do well.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: (In Tamil):   The previous year has been a challenging one.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Although the COVID-19 restrictions have eased, the war in Ukraine has caused global commodity prices to spike and this in turn has caused inflation all the way down the value chain.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: To deal with this inflation, central banks have raised interest rates and this has added to cost of business for companies and cost of living for ordinary people.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This Budget has a wide range of measures to help alleviate the immediate cost of living issues we will face – GST Vouchers, CDC Vouchers, Cost of Living, U-Save Vouchers.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There is a special bonus for seniors, which is fair since many of them will no longer be able to continue working.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I support this Budget that provides important support to assist with the cost of living and which allows for people to face the upcoming year with optimism.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In it, I will also address some of the measures in Budget 2023 that deal with wage levelling, early intervention for children in poor families and raising productivity.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: While I do not necessarily agree with all the arguments Sandel makes in this book, I would heartily recommend it to all Members here.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In essence, Sandel says that meritocracy in the US today has become a tool to justify inequality and condescension towards those without university degrees.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It is also an unfair game because from the pursuit of these academic credentials that are often said to define merits, some have advantages of genetic endowments, social capital, parental guidance and resources that others lack.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: He calls for a re-focusing of attention on vocational and trades jobs which, in the past, would yield more stability and respect to balance up the advantages now conferred by a university degree.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: There is a strong case for raising floor levels of living standards and dignity for those who have skills that are less marketable but doing so in ways that are economically sustainable, like retraining and so on.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We should reject the notion of a natural aristocracy of merit – that the more successful behave like aristocrats did in feudal societies.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I received some interesting comments on my social media posts on meritocracy but let me quote an excerpt from one of those comments that I found gut-wrenching, and I am paraphrasing here a little bit and I quote, "I am not an academically driven person.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I used to study in ITE but I dropped out.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I don't wish to be discriminated against as a lowly-educated person, thus I pursued my diploma after NS.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The point here is that there is a perception that those who went through university at NTU, NUS, etc., these are the best people, not only at school but at work.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Going to job interviews, employers will outright tell me that my grades are bad, why should they consider my application?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The discrimination for those who didn't go through good schools with good grades is real, not to mention usually in workplaces, those with university degrees were often be pushed up the career ladder faster than those who don't have.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I seriously don't know why people have to shame those who are not well-educated like myself." I am sure we can all feel the pain of this person that comes not only from the sense of the economic game stacked against him but also the pain of feeling disrespected in society.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Anecdotally, in my conversations with younger Singaporeans, many expressed that the intense competitiveness in Singapore at work and academia coupled with a high cost of living and housing is taking a toll on their ability to live holistically meaningful and purposeful life with enough time for family, hobbies and passions.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Jobs should go to people with the best abilities.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Ours should not be a society where we punish those who can invent, lead, create, take responsible risks, inspire others even as we strive to uplift the least advantaged.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We need a high productivity, innovative economy to grow the pie.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: If we fail in this, the poor will be the hardest hit.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But to get that economy, do gaps in income and economic security need to be so large?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Some countries seem to generate entrepreneurism and economic dynamism with smaller gaps.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Sweden and Denmark come to mind as examples.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Taking this idea seriously is important and not only because we want to be fair to those who have been less successful in conventional academic economic terms, though that alone would be enough.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: No, but this is also important because as scholars like Richard Wilkinson have argued, high inequality weakens everyone in society.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: His work suggests that more unequal societies generally have poorer physical and mental health, trust levels, child well-being and so on.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: So, Madam, I return to the question I began with: what kind of meritocracy do we want?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I think our answer to that question has to be not an unbridled winner-take-all meritocracy.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The remainder of my speech, Madam, will provide specific suggestions on just how to do that.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I have spoken at length in this House on this subject in the past.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We need a concerted policy effort to improve wages, skills, productivity, working conditions, societal respect in trades jobs, for example, carpentry, plumbing, air-condition repair, forklift and crane operators and so on.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We need this so that the Singapore core can be attracted back to these jobs since, anecdotally, it would appear that there are a few younger Singaporeans entering such trades, a theme I will come back to later.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I would also add to this list skilled artisanal or craft jobs like jewellery designers and historical architecture conservationists.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Some of these jobs, such as delivery or transcribing, for example, will gradually become obsolete due to technologies like drones, autonomous vehicles and artificial intelligence (AI).

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We need to nudge Singaporeans in these jobs to consider a career switch to other jobs, including revamped trades jobs.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This would entail expanding the range or capacity for Career Conversion Programmes (CCPs) where capacities are now limited in terms of their share of the workforce.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: More importantly, this would need a change of mindsets and that in turn would need to be catalysed through education and communication efforts.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Interestingly, even now, some of these jobs like prime mover drivers, for example, which require much skill and experience, offer fairly decent pay, though that can be increased further, as I will explain.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But these blue-collar jobs seem to be attracting few young Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Pay could be part of the reason but other reasons may include negative perceptions, working hours or conditions.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I believe what is needed is to develop job redesign and career laddering plans for these trades jobs in conjunction with industry chambers and stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We should nudge or move towards more training and productivity for such jobs, which would enable better pay and conditions.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This would need to be accompanied by educational campaigns to change mindsets and remove the social stigma some associate with such jobs.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Such trades jobs are skilled and should command respect in society.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Lastly and most importantly of all, our national strategy towards these trades jobs should include two more elements.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Nothing nudges employers to take better care of workers than the prospect that that worker may leave and be hard to replace.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Next, I would suggest that our economic development agencies like the Economic Development Board (EDB) and Enterprise Singapore try to nudge foreign investors and local firms towards hiring some Singaporeans with lesser educational credentials so as to retrain them in skills that are adjacent to the skillsets that they have but are more future-proof and enable them to operate at a higher level of productivity that can command better pay.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Perhaps this can be one consideration – not the only one, of course – in the award of economic incentives.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Next, I would like to move to the subject of productivity.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Raising productivity is a necessary but not sufficient condition for improving the lot of those in trades jobs.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I tried searching for information on the NPF and the Productivity Fund Administration Board, and I found it difficult to identify its activities and investments every single year.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: All that was readily available from an admittedly basic online search were reports on activities from 2010 and 2017.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Most importantly, I would like to ask what would be the KPIs for how the funds are used?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Also, does the NPF funding give sufficient focus to non-tradeable domestic sectors where there are productivity problems, perhaps, are the worst, as I will explain later.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I ask this because it is important for such funding to be very results driven.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: A case in point – was there evidence that the old Productivity and Innovation Credit (PIC) Scheme actually had a causal effect in raising productivity – a question I have raised in this House previously.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: However, there are some sectors in Singapore that are fairly productive by global standards, for example, manufacturing and financial services.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The main problem seems to be non-tradeable domestic sectors such as F&B, retail, personal services, construction and so on – sectors which provide services that are not exported but consumed in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Has the Government studied if and why our productivity is lower than other developed countries in these sectors?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I would suggest that we work with trade associations and chambers (TACs) to benchmark more productive countries in these sectors and then use schemes such as NPF funding to nudge our small- and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in particular to implement more productive business processes and technologies.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In an extended analysis of Singapore's productivity performance in 2020, economists Manu Bhaskaran and Nigel Chiang provided data to show that our "TFP growth—is poor relative to our peer group as well as the OECD group of developed nations and has been worsening substantially over the years.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: After a surge in 2003 to 2004, TFP growth began to decelerate before declining outright after 2005." Could managerial skills play a role here?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: On this note, I filed a Parliamentary Question (PQ) on the latest findings of the World Management Survey, which suggests poor results for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Next, I will move to another topic relevant to our meritocracy – ensuring fair minimum floors for those who are less successful in life and doing more to bring about equality of opportunity for poor children.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I acknowledge the expansion of KidSTART and ComLink as referred to in Budget 2023.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: These are moves in the right direction but I have a few suggestions here.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The earlier we intervene to help children from disadvantaged backgrounds, the less of a disadvantage they will face when they enter primary school and the less likely they would be to drop out.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I set out the detailed arguments for this and why it is different from ad hoc smaller banded classes in an Adjournment Motion in this House in 2017.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: My colleague, Assoc Prof Jamus Lim, has also spoken about this.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The Workers' Party made this proposal in its 2020 manifesto, which is for SkillsFuture to disburse a zero-interest loan for adult CET.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This thrust could support the upgrading and future-proofing of trades and blue-collar jobs that I spoke about earlier.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Access to such loans could be made more readily available than the supply of special SkillsFuture grants, but weighted towards those with lower incomes and towards CET programmes that support retraining to a sunrise industry like high-tech farming, for example.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Fifth, would Government agencies work with industry bodies to nudge companies to offer more internships and attachments to students from less popular secondary schools?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Such students would benefit from understanding the culture and work norms in companies.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Right now, some companies do engage with the universities and polytechnics to secure interns but it is less easy or common for them to engage with secondary schools and junior colleges to the same end, particularly, the less popular ones.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Lastly, our social service agencies should provide more generous levels of aid to poor families but in such a way as to encourage positive behaviours that will help them improve economically and break the poverty cycle for their children – healthier eating and cooking habits, regular health screening, financial literacy training and so on.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I recently had the privilege of working with a few non-governmental organisations (NGOs) in one of the rental blocks in the Serangoon ward of Aljunied GRC.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: They held sessions at the block to help families take better care of their mental health and physical confidence and to support the children in terms of confidence building, decision-making and goal-setting skills.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I will speak more about this at the Ministry of Social and Family Development (MSF) Committee of Supply.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I come to the final part of my speech, Madam.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: How do we address the issue of prejudice against those lacking degrees, high levels of education and great career success?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: How do we make sure that Singapore does not become the "two Singapores" that the Leader of the Opposition alluded to, that we do not become a society where such people are looked down upon and face either quiet or overt condescension?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: How do we ensure, in Michael Sanders' words, "that credentialism does not become the last acceptable prejudice"?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: (In Malay):   There are different approaches the Government can take here.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But upon deep reflection, I think the onus here is not only or primarily on the Government but on all of us.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It is very difficult to successfully choreograph events and policy practices that set out to foster mingling and respect across socioeconomic lines unless culturally, Singaporeans bring to such engagements the right mindsets and values.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: So we should always guard against prejudice when deciding on awarding a contract or promotion or choosing a service provider between someone with credentials and someone with less; rather, we need to focus on their ability to do the job.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We should always guard against the lionisation of book-smarts and the undervaluing of street smarts.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We should be vigilant to not privilege conventional pathways to success at the expense of those who are successful in other fields that are more craft-intensive.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And to paraphrase Martin Luther King Jr, we should always, as the cornerstone of Singapore culture, judge and value each person not on their credentials and net financial worth, but on the content of their character.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: (In English): In conclusion, Madam, we should reject a meritocracy that creates a natural aristocracy.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The term "meritocracy" comes from the British author, Michael Young.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: He coined it in 1958 as a satire to parody the concept of an unbridled meritocracy as a dystopia.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In his satirical work, he envisioned a popular revolt against meritocracy in the year 2033.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: It gives me great trust and also gives me the liberty to set my sights further into the future.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: I ask this House for its indulgence to listen with an open heart, an open mind, an open will as well as an open imagination for what I would like to share in my speech today.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: I am very thankful and glad for the Budget provisions that Deputy Prime Minister Wong has made for Singaporeans, especially the measures to increase paternity and parental leave as well as the legislation to advance flexible work arrangements as a norm.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: All these go a long way to enhance the well-being of our people and it has been long due.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: I am very inspired by the theme of this year's Budget, "Moving Forward into a New Era".

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: It is time, I feel, for us to think boldly in order to meet the new realities we are facing as a nation as well as globally.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Abroad, quiet quitting, a phenomenon that emerged last year, is a silent protest within the workforce across the developed world against a state of work that is demanding too much of people.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: The cost of living is going up drastically.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Our core inflation was just 1% in 2019.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: It is no longer just the bottom 10% or 15% of Singaporeans who feel anxious about their ability to put food on the table.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Singaporeans are working harder than ever before and our standard of living has improved.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: In my parents’ younger days, for most families, a rare treat was going to the movies and buying a 10-cent kacang putih wrapped in newspaper.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Today, having a $4 cup of bubble tea or coconut shake might be an equivalent, and for certain more well-off segments of our population, it might be enjoyed too frequently to be considered an indulgence.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Many more of us can afford more things in life, many more non-essential things to adorn our lives but we do not seem to be happier.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Our sense of insecurity about meeting basic needs appears to be getting worse.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Of course, these anxieties are real and pressing, given that there is inflation and various global uncertainties presenting multiple pressures.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: At the same time, we are also one of the wealthiest countries in the world and we have emerged out of COVID-19 triumphant.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: So, what else might be perpetuating and driving this pervasive sense of insecurity?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Is it perhaps time to rethink and review our national narrative and model of progress that we are just a small red dot with no resources, constantly fighting for our survival?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: With this narrative, we have pushed our people harder and harder, through various iterations of workforce development initiatives and industry transformation maps, relentlessly chasing for ever higher productivity.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Is this survivalist narrative presenting a disconnect with the fact and reality of our progress?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Could it be entrenching more anxiety in our people than is really necessary?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: My hon colleague Mr Sitoh Yih Pin’s comment in his speech yesterday resonated with me.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Is it really true that our glass is always half empty and are our prospects as a nation only getting bleaker?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Is the best already behind us or is our best yet to be?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Other than within the geopolitical context, is it really still true that Singapore is vulnerable with no resources to rely on?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: From our humble beginnings in the 1960s to 2023, we have become a nation that is abundant in many aspects.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: We have a world class education system, we have built robust financial system and governance structures with a stellar reputation for trade and business, we have greatly admired urban planning blueprints and methodologies that many countries are keen to learn from.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: We continuously innovate and we have a population of people who are honest, hardworking and seen as a reliable and trustworthy pool of talent internationally.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Since our Independence, our main priority has been economic growth because it had to be thus far.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Economic progress was the way to survival for a nation scarce in natural resources.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: It helped us Singaporeans make great leaps in our quality of life that many countries today are envious of.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Hence, it is only natural that economic growth seems to be the only way we understand quality of life.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: It has served us so well that it may seem mad to anyone to talk about deliberately slowing down economic growth.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: But is it not equally mad to continue this drive for ever higher economic growth when our only resource – human resource – is coming under great threat?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: How will this impact our workforce and the quality of our talent pool, and how may our current way of life be contributing to this phenomenon?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: If the premise for our nation’s progress is that human resources are our biggest national resource, then protecting it and allowing it to thrive should be the key agenda.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: After all, what is growth for, if not for our people’s well-being?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: As hon Member Mr Seah Kian Peng also reminded us during his speech, that our founding father Mr Lee Kuan Yew made it his business to ensure our people’s happiness.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: How can a people be happy, if we are constantly anxious or under stress?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: In the background of many anxieties lies the real existential threat and crisis of the global fossil fuel and climate change crisis.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: By the world, it means the human race.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: As Ms Poh Li San and Mr Lim Wee Kiak has reminded us, our electricity is 95% reliant on natural gas.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: What happens when we are out of natural gas by 2060?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: When that happens, I will be hopefully still alive at 87 years old, my nieces and many of my young residents will be in their 50s or 60s.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: The children born today will be only 47 years old.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: I am not alone in feeling anxious about climate change.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
