text: Climate anxiety is a logical reaction to an existential threat.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: This is the single most important threat we face as Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: It is a huge obstacle that stands in the way of our progress as a nation.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Economic growth has resulted in increased energy consumption, which then leads to greater greenhouse gas emissions.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide – all these emissions trap heat in the atmosphere, leading to global warming, climate change and extreme weather conditions.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Our current economic model does not account for our people and our planet's well-being as a measure of growth.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: We need a more sustainable, tenable model of progress that does not leave our planet and our people's well-being out of the equation, but instead sees progress and wellness as one and the same that respects the Earth’s limits.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: I want to make sure that what we do today ensures that we pass on a thriving Earth, not a depleting one to our next generation.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Governments around the world are investing in green technology and alternative energy research in a bid to slow down this global energy depletion and mitigate this threat.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: While such efforts are absolutely necessary, it is not enough.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Solar, hydro and nuclear, while they present good options as alternative energy sources, are still highly complex and highly extractive in nature.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: It means they still require vast amounts of steel, metal and materials to build the necessary infrastructure and equipment to harness secondary sources of energy.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: What happens when we run out of the materials to run these plants that power our lights, our transport and our computers?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Our primary source of energy, fossil fuels, which took millions of years to form, is now running out.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: The only way to avoid the crisis is to consume and produce in ways that are transformatively different from before.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: If we do not start regenerating our Earth, we are consuming it to death and putting humanity on the trajectory to an era of war and destructive competition, which is already beginning to set in.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Once we understand these key truths of the 21st century, as political leaders, we must have the gumption to lead our people to a different future.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: One of the world’s most important living economists, Kate Raworth, designed a new economic model to guide countries’ transition from having an extractive relationship with the Earth to a more harmonious one.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: It provides a map for how to establish a better relationship between the economy, the planet and people.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: It illustrates an outer ring which is the limit that Earth can support and an inner ring which is the base that we need to build to allow humans to thrive.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Our actions and our policies will have to reside between those two rings.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Go beyond the outer ring or fall within the inner ring, and we will be in trouble.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: This model values well-being and a solid social foundation that helps people to rely on one another and nature harmoniously to meet our needs.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: In order for us and our world to survive, we must slow down the rate of economic growth or our future generations will suffer its consequences.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: This requires us to reshape our national narrative and understanding of progress.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Ms Nadia Samdin asked a really important and worthy question – can there be a different version of the Singaporean dream?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Progress in the next era of growth for Singapore must be measured less in terms of economic numbers and account for our human limits and planet limits.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: I offer a motto that not only gives us hope, but also gives practical steps in guiding us towards a future beyond fossil fuels.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: I propose two key imperatives we must start doing.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: One, cultivate sharing communities by redesigning work and housing to optimise resources and extend the "reduce" pillar to the ways we live and work.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Making work-from-home the norm for professions that allow it can drastically reduce daily transport fuel consumption, reduce vehicles on the roads and reduce the need to keep building more roads or expressways.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: The Government can set an example by making work-from-home the norm across the civil service and associated statutory boards.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: On the housing front, creating more community living formats such as the ones we are piloting in Queenstown to aid in eldercare.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Community Care Apartments (CCAs) can be built also for single parent families, families with special needs members and co-living precincts for young adults and singles can be designed and built in neighbouring precincts to these CCAs, so that they can conveniently volunteer for these families who need more help.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: For all we know, co-living communities for singles could help us to improve our marriage and birth rates!

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: I will elaborate more on these in my Commitee of Supply cuts.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: In our daily lives, we currently have an increasing norm of online shopping where we can buy something for as cheap as $1 or $3 and have it shipped to your door in layers of boxing and packaging.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Such rates of consumption as a norm for a society creates tremendous waste of energy and resources.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Instead, we can make swapping and sharing the default way of life to reduce wasteful consumption.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: I hope that every neighbourhood can have a sharing movement to make this the new norm for Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Two, invest in permaculture and other regenerative nature-based solutions and research.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Localised permaculture reduces the carbon footprint of growing and transporting food.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: It helps to capture carbon from the environment.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: It will also help us reduce our dependence on foreign industrial agricultural techniques that have worsened the climate crisis.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: I will elaborate more on this during the Committee of Supply cuts on how permaculture holds multiple benefits, including increasing our food security.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: In the 1930s, in the midst of the Great Depression, Americian President Roosevelt implemented a “New Deal”, which greatly invested in environmental conservation.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: It was a huge risk at the time and went against conventional wisdom.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: I believe it was Winston Churchill who said towards the end of World War Two, “Never let a good crisis go to waste”.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: In fact, many of our own Ministers have said similar things in Parliament, especially in the last two years of the pandemic – that we can turn crisis into opportunity.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Getting a miracle out of a crisis is not new to Singapore.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: We created a miracle when we became independent in 1965 and became a first-world nation by the 1990s.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Similarly, I believe we have what it takes to turn the global energy crisis into another miracle with our unique Singaporean way.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Investing in and rebuilding our relationship with the planet has the potential to open up new industries for Singapore to be leaders in and improve the economic opportunities for our people.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: I am very glad that the Green Economy initiative under the SG Green Plan has already started to invest in nature-based technologies and research.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Again, I will elaborate more in my Ministry of Education (MOE) Committee of Supply cut.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong mentioned during his Budget speech that we need to increase Singapore’s resilience in response to climate realities.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: He mentioned efforts in coastal protection and so on, to prepare us for rising sea levels.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: But we need to go beyond and take an even more proactive approach to pioneer a new way of life that the world can look to.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: We have the opportunity to be a global change-maker by engineering and actualising a new model of progress.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: If we put our hearts and minds together, we can achieve this, referencing the Doughnut Economic Model, applied to our specific Singaporean context.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Given how small we are as a country, we may not significantly impact the actual amount of energy saved globally.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: But we still can make a really substantial impact by showing and leading the way to a different progress model.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: In doing so, we can inspire other urban cities and countries to chart their own path to a more regenerative economy that meets the needs of all.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Our strong social fabric, highly collaborative, cooperative population and high trust between Singaporeans and our Government are the assets that we have to rely on to do this well.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: What I look forward to, as do many Singaporeans of my generation and younger, is a regenerative city state and a system that ensures the well-being of our People and Planet.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: We must start to intentionally REdesign our way of life, work and play.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: To do this, Ministries including National Development —

speaker: Mdm Deputy Speaker
text: Ms Tan, you have a minute to round up.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: A truly progressive nation is one in which its people are well.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: I was very moved by Senior Parliamentary Secretary Eric Chua's speech earlier.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Perhaps it is time for us to collectively take a pause, a slowdown, to smell the roses and perhaps that is what it truly takes for our nation to be able to be truly wealthy in our minds, bodies and spirit.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: He also presented the outlook for 2023, including the uncertainties and downside risks linked to the global economy, as well as new opportunities to add vibrancy to our own economy and create more jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: In other words, Budget 2023 recognises and addresses many of the bread-and-butter issues that Singaporeans are understandably concerned about.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Another issue of concern this Budget also touches on is climate change.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Given the tight fiscal position that Singapore is in and the socioeconomic challenges we face, why should we continue to invest in climate resilience and sustainability?

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Some of us may think that we are saving the planet.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: But the planet has been around for billions of years before us and will continue to be around for billions of years after us.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: It had recovered from at least five mass extinction events over the last 500 million years.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: By comparison, we modern humans have been around for only the last 200,000 years or so.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: The reason why we need to cut emissions, stop deforestation, protect biodiversity, reduce pollution and reverse ocean acidification is because we need to live within the finite and safe operating space of our planet for which humans can survive and continue to thrive.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: In other words, we need to take climate change and sustainability seriously, not to save the planet but to save ourselves, to ensure a liveable Singapore for this and future generations to come.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: This may require us to constantly reflect on our assumptions, our priorities and our way of life.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Our way of life in Singapore reflects our social compact, which is underpinned by our shared purpose and values.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: I believe we want to be a fairer and more inclusive society, a kinder and more gracious community.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: And as we refresh and strengthen our social compact, we must also take seriously the desire of fellow Singaporeans, especially the youths, for stronger climate actions and a just transition to a sustainable future.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: We must ensure that climate change and sustainability are always among the bread-and-butter issues we focus on.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: And as we address the impacts of climate change, we must ensure that the most vulnerable among us are well supported and the able are doing their part by contributing appropriately.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time, our climate and sustainability efforts must be considered in light of other societal priorities and their trade-offs, particularly when different priorities require common and limited resources, such as our land.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: We have to consider the value of our land not only for its climate and biodiversity benefits, but also for its contribution to meeting our housing, education, healthcare, transportation, economic, defence and other societal needs.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: In other words, we must recognise that no single interest should be considered absent of the others.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, the greatest challenge we face as a small island state arguably is the reconciliation of all our priorities.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: As I had mentioned in this House before, this tension between priorities can be painful.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: But it can also be helpful to remind us that as we transition to a climate resilient, more sustainable and more equitable society, no one succeeds until everyone succeeds.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore's climate mitigation measures include progressively raising the carbon tax, improving our energy efficiency, greening our buildings, electrifying our transportation as well as transitioning to solar and other cleaner sources energy.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Our adaptation measures include increasing our vegetation cover, building a polder at Pulau Tekong and establishing a Coastal and Flood Protection Fund, to support the construction of coastal and drainage infrastructure.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: We can create positive climate impacts beyond our shores by supporting regional and global efforts as a strategic partner in R&D, capacity building, green growth and policymaking.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: This measure can help grow a new carbon services industry in Singapore as well as support impactful climate actions internationally, including nature-based solutions such as forest conservation and restoration projects.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Unsurprisingly, there is a wide disparity in the quality of carbon projects and products in the market today.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: There is also a disparity in the credibility of carbon accounting standards.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Indeed, these underlying issues of quality and credibility have created confusion and anxiety, leading to recent controversies around the use of forest carbon credits.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: The fact is, nature-based solutions are integral to every mitigation pathway to achieve the goal of the Paris Climate Agreement, as recognised by the Inter-governmental Panel on Climate Change.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: In other words, meeting the Paris goal requires us to implement nature-based solutions in addition to our decarbonisation efforts.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: There is no perfect methodology and we should never let perfect be the enemy of the good.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Here is where Singapore has another important role to play.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: We can help to improve the credibility of carbon accounting standards and our ability to discern the quality of carbon credits.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: I declare that I am the principal investigator of this programme.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: In his speech to the UN Climate Ambition Summit in December 2020, Prime Minister Lee emphasised that climate change is an existential threat for the global community and especially for a small island state like Singapore.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: By thinking and acting beyond our geographic constraints as a small island state, Singapore has the opportunity to create climate impacts beyond our borders.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Our businesses can support climate actions beyond their value chains.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: We can become a world-embracing global city for sustainability.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Ultimately, the highest quality carbon credit is the one we will never need.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Sometimes, I like to imagine how Singapore would look like in 2050.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: In 2050, every building in Singapore would be solar-panelled.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: These electric vehicles would be silently plying our streets.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Our streets would be lined by a few million more trees, creating a dense network of Nature Ways.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: These Nature Ways would be home to a rich diversity of native birds, mammals and other animals – a testament to the foresight of NPark's Rewilding Plan.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Our waterways and coastlines would be a showcase of technology-based and nature-based solutions, offering optimal protection against storm surges and sea level rise, while also providing recreational and other benefits to society.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore would be an international hub of climate and sustainability solutions, providing services and products to the rest of the world.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Our investments in Research, Innovation and Enterprise through the decades, would have ensured not only our climate resilience but also our long-term prosperity in a green economy.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Our new economy would be supported by a robust green talent pipeline, creating a workforce with sustainability competencies as well as opportunities for a lifetime of upskilling and meaningful contributions.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: I hope to be still alive then, in 2050, as a 74-year-old grey-haired professor, perhaps sipping tea from the balcony of my Community Care Apartment with a pair of binoculars, peering out into the forest canopy below, taking comfort in having been a part of this journey.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: I believe for this to be more than my personal daydream, we will require a whole-of-society paradigm shift now.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Everyone must recognise that climate change and sustainability are not fringe issues.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: They are bread-and-butter issues, top-of-mind planning issues, quality-of-life issues, existential issues.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: As we move forward together in a new era, climate resilience and sustainability must be the zeitgeist of our times.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Everyone from every sector has important contributions to make.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: We need local Singaporeans, overseas Singaporeans, returning Singaporeans, foreign talents, from Government, businesses, civil society and Institutions of Higher Learning (IHLs) to be able to visualise, articulate and work towards the common climate resilient and sustainable future that we all want for ourselves and our future generations.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: We must intuitively know that while we address the very real and immediate challenges of the day, we cannot afford to ease up on our efforts to achieve climate resilience, meet our sustainability goals and become a low carbon society, a City in Nature.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: I am glad to share that many residents affirm the measures, especially those that support young families in making housing more accessible for them.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Budget 2023 also address enhanced employment support for the seniors, the lower-income, persons with disabilities and ex-offenders, which many of us welcome.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: In line with that, may I respond to the Budget statement by highlighting a need for a specific group of people that we should not miss: employment support for caregivers of people with severe disabilities.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: In my brief time serving in the Purple Parade, a movement that supports inclusion and celebrates the abilities of persons with disabilities (PwDs), I have had the joy to meet some of the most inspiring PwDs and their caregivers.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: One of these outstanding groups are the people at the Rare Disorders Society (Singapore), also known as RDSS.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: These members are not large, in light of the many competing needs in Singapore, and yet, for the same reason, it is easy for their real and valid needs to be overlooked.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Many caregivers of people of severe disabilities want to seek employment due to the high and ongoing expenses from their children's or ward's treatment, especially if they stem from rare disorders.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The severity of disability means that their wards are not work-capable and need to be cared for consistently.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Due to the rarity of their illness, the cost of treatment can be extremely high.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: In the United States, the average annual cost of treatment per patient in 2019 was $42,000, with treatments ranging from $8,000 to $670,000 per year.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: While there are various Government schemes and charities that provide generous grants and subsidies that may alleviate some of these costs, the financial burden remains great on the caregivers, especially if one parent has to stop work to become the main caregiver to their child.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: For these group of Singaporeans, finding work and work presents itself with great challenges.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Respite care for people with severe disabilities is hard to come by due to the unique medical conditions they have.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: While there are various daycare centres for PwDs, very few are for people with severe multiple disabilities, such as those of the members of the rare disorders' community.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: As such, short of having an available grandparent or a helper to care for their child, it will not be possible for both parents to stay at work.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: I take heart that the Ministry for Social and Family Development's (MSF) Enabling Masterplan 2030 includes the establishment of Enabling Services Hub, to provide respite care and engage PwDs in the community.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Some of these caregivers may require daily visits to hospital for treatments for their ward, while others need to be responsive to sudden accidents and emergencies.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: As such, jobs with flexible work arrangements (FWAs) are the only viable options for them.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: These refer to jobs that allow for work-from-home (WFH), provide flexible timing or shift work that allows caregivers to work at night.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: At the same time, because of their need for FWAs, caregivers tend to be streamlined to certain job roles that are generally more administrative and many times, as a consequence, jobs that pay less per hour.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: While many of the caregivers are educated and competent individuals with a range of skills to offer, in order to supplement the family's finances, they accept jobs that under-employ them and pay them significantly less because of the flexibility the jobs afford them.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Even with these lowered job expectations, it is still hard to find work because of the bias that some employees may have of them as being less productive.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Amongst the caregivers in RDSS, those who found work that afforded them flexibility needed, opportunities often come through personal networks, rather than the traditional routes of finding employment, even after undergoing skills upgrading.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: We cannot assume that every caregiver will have access to such personal networks, given the amount of time consumed by caregiving.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: For caregiving parents who are in the workforce, childcare leave halts when a child is above 12 years old, because it is assumed that the child should be sufficiently independent by then.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This is not true for the parents of children with severe disabilities.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The level of care needed does not reduce with age and may, in fact, increase depending on the progression of the disease.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: In fact, some caregivers have had to approach employers to ask if they can use their personal medical certificates (MCs), in lieu of childcare leave, for their child who is above 12 years old, given their commitment to stay healthy to care for their children.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Each day is a physical, mental and emotional balancing act of spending as much time as they can with their child, not knowing which day would be their child's last.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This, while trying to address the increasing cost of long-term medical care, on top of finding ways to secure retirement adequacy for themselves and their wards.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: These caregivers are simply looking for a fair opportunity to participate in the workforce, bring value with their competencies to earn a sustainable living and at the same time, show love to their parents while they can.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: I have no doubt that employers that hire these Singaporeans will find for themselves some of the most diligent and resilient individuals, with valuable perspectives because of their unique life journeys.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The question remains: how might we be more intentional and progressive in finding ways to support and integrate caregivers who are fully capable, highly motivated and willing to be employed?

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: With this, Mr Deputy Speaker, I am thankful and I am in full support for Budget 2023.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I think we can all agree that motherhood is one of the noblest vocations.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We often speak of it in glowing terms: nurturing, caring and sacrificing.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In reality, it is much more complex and complicated.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Ask any mother and words sometimes like mess, stress, distress and tiredness will come up, but it does not take away the intangible joys and rewards of parenthood.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But neither can we gloss over the pressures that the role brings.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Motherhood, therefore, to my mind, is the greatest and, yet, most neglected roles in society.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We expect mothering to come naturally with motherhood.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Unfortunately, it does not; no manual prepares you for it.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Even having more than one child is not a trial run.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Jocelyn and I have four children, we know it does not prepare you for the next child when it comes along.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: However, there is an impression, unintended perhaps, that even as we support parenthood and motherhood in our society, that there are different categories of mothers.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Some people have mentioned that there seems to be an emphasis on the economic value of mothers.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But it says much in the title: Working Mother's Child Relief, the operative word being "Working".

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore (IRAS) website explicitly states the intent of this particular measure to encourage women in Singapore to remain in the workforce after childbirth.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Under Early Childhood and Development Agency (ECDA) guidelines for additional childcare subsidy, the emphasis is also on working applicants, even for those seeking special approval, the first priority is those that are looking for a job.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Consider them for the role, an important role that they play in society today, especially a country where our total fertility rate (TFR) is so low.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We are doing a lot already, but we should continue to do more because mothers are mothers, and not because of the economic potential, as I have mentioned.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: With our low TFR, I would, therefore, like us to consider the merits of adopting the following.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: These are existing examples that other countries have introduced.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Norway has generous subsidies for childcare and daycare.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And also, the French have a universal preschool system.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Of course, all these are not without challenges, as each example in each country would throw up different varieties of issues.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But, there is more that we can do.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And if the Minister for Finance would indulge me as well, even if we do adopt all of these, we should continue with Singapore's very generous Baby Bonus system.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The second issue I would like to raise today has to do with death and taxes.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Two Finance Ministers ago, I characterised the Budget 2015, which was announced by then-Senior Minister Tharman at the time, with Beyoncé's lyrics, "to the left, to the left".

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: A number of good things have been said about it by residents and friends that I have met since its delivery on 14 February 2023, but there are murmurings of disquiet in some areas, two of which I would raise today.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The one announcement that raises the most heckles in our "kopi tiams" is the increased tobacco tax.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Based on latest available statistics, smoking prevalence is now around 10%, down from a higher 16% earlier this decade.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: While increase may help encourage some already intent on quitting to accelerate the move, the impact may be muted.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Many of those who are affected by this increase are older, blue-collar workers.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The 2018 price hike, based on surveys, saw no discernable drop in sales.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: People eventually get used to the price increase.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Thus, the increase may drive more towards: one, illicit products such as vaping, less "healthier" choice, I am using inverted commas, like unfiltered rolled cigarettes.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And these will have the opposite health outcomes of what we are trying to achieve.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Please do not get me wrong, I would prefer to eradicate tobacco.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: While the current increase will still raise much needed, not-that-high revenue, I do not believe that the current tax increase will change smoker behaviour.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The second issue has to do with property tax increase.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: While not part of this year's announcement, the impact is being felt this year.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Retirees in owner-occupied properties are experiencing increases, with rising house values and increasing rentals prices, many properties purchased decades ago are now seeing much higher Annual Value (AV).

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Those we broadly refer to as "asset rich, cash poor" are affected.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Some have said they feel it unfair, they worked hard to buy their own home decades ago but have to pick up a higher tab because of economic progress.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Last of all, Mr Deputy Speaker, I would like to turn to the singular focus of why we do what we do in this august Chamber.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We have had a remarkable journey for close to six decades, one that we hope will continue onwards and upwards.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As one people, we have traversed through challenges and much difficulties.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Difficulties that could have easily overwhelmed us in our nascent days.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: From nothingness, our unexpected nation has made tremendous progress from third world to first.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Because we have walked as one people, one Singapore, COVID-19, our most recent challenge, has seen us at our best.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: People coming together to help each other through a crisis like no other.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Our common struggle and heart for each other proves that this is a nation worth fighting for.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: How we perform will depend on whether we act as one nation, or as a people divided unto ourselves.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We have succeeded and will continue to succeed because we act as one – people and Government together, people and people together.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: There is no binary Singapore – one versus another.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Regardless of our backgrounds or stations in life, the Singaporean way has been one where we all play our part in co-creating a home that we call our own.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This is not a tale of two cities.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The indomitable spirit of Singaporeans has stood the test of time.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: That same spirit of endeavour, hard work, unity and common aspiration will carry us onwards.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I would not be able to respond to all of them in this round-up speech.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Some specific issues, for example, on education, energy, healthcare and workplace safety, will be discussed later in the Committee of Supply debates.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But I assure you that we have heard every feedback and will study your suggestions carefully.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We want to get back to a more sustainable fiscal position.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But we cannot taper down support too quickly because the economic outlook remains uncertain.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We want to help Singaporeans tackle cost-of-living pressures.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But we must be careful not to inadvertently generate more demand and worsen inflation.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It is less expansionary than last year's Budget because we are coming off from the high levels of spending and that explains the negative fiscal impulse which he cited.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But the Budget does provide some support for what is likely to be a weaker economy this year, although we are careful not to overdo the spending in order to avoid fuelling inflation; which is something Ms Foo Mee Har also cautioned.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: At the same time, it is not possible for the Budget Statement to cover everything.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In the end, we have to be clear about our priorities.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And in this Budget Statement, we have focused on securing economic competitiveness, supporting families and vulnerable groups and strengthening our resilience.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The questions raised by Members during the debate broadly revolve around three buckets of issues.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: First, are we taking too much and giving back too little?

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Second, are we doing enough to stay competitive and help our businesses and workers?

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Third, are we doing enough to help Singaporeans and households in need?

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I will address each in turn and explain how we are updating our strategies for this changed world.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: First, is the Government taking too much and giving back too little?

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Mr Leong Mun Wai claimed that we have "excess fiscal resources".

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, he inferred that we had $32 billion of spare resources lying around.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: During the pandemic, our society and economy were in an entirely different state.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Projects were deferred and many planned and budgeted activities could not be carried out.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, the Government re-allocated these resources towards the more urgent task of fighting COVID-19.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Now that we are in DORSCON Green, these funds have to be channelled back to what they were originally meant for.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Mr Leong also claimed that the $24 billion injected into Funds in FY2022 and FY2023 were "excess resources", as the actual expenditure from these Funds would only occur in the future.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: All spending in the Budget, be it direct expenses or top-ups to Funds, are resources we set aside to meet real needs – be it to strengthen safety nets, improve productivity, or build critical infrastructure.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We set up Funds to meet specific funding commitments that are needed today and are stretched out over multiple years.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For example, the GST Voucher Fund and Progressive Wage Credit Scheme Fund require top-ups when we enhance the parameters of the underlying schemes, as we have done last year and in this Budget.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The monies in these Funds are already being drawn down today and not just in the future.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: There are a few Funds where the disbursements are lumpy and not so predictable.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For example, the outlays from the Changi Airport Development Fund for the development of Terminal 5 and other aviation facilities will be made in accordance with the progress of the infrastructure projects.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For such large and lumpy expenditure items, the responsible thing to do is to set aside some resources whenever we have the means, so that we smoothen out the spending and we do not end up in a crunch when the monies are needed.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: From time to time, we do get some revenue upsides.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is what happened in FY2021 and FY2022.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Our fiscal position turned out better than initially projected only because we were able to get through the pandemic in much better shape than we had earlier feared.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We have put these additional resources to good use, channelling them to support Singaporean households and businesses.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is why, as Ms Foo Mee Har has noted, our expenditure in FY2022, including special transfers, was revised upwards.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: More importantly, as Mr Liang Eng Hwa highlighted, the right way to assess our fiscal position is to consider, not the year-to-year changes, but the broader medium-term trend.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We have always been upfront and transparent about these fiscal projections and continually review and enhance the information we put out.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: As part of these efforts, MOF released an Occasional Paper earlier this month, and I am glad many Members referred to it and found it useful.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In fact, even prior to the publication to the Occasional Paper, I had already highlighted this information.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But surely he must understand that nominal spending will increase with inflation and with a growing economy.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: On the revenue side, without the GST increase and other tax moves we have made in last year's and this year's Budgets, the projections clearly indicate that we would not have sufficient revenues to cover the increases in spending.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And so, you can see the gap in this chart.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The revenue situation improves with the GST increase and the other tax changes made in last year's Budget.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We have also updated the chart, from what was in the Occasional Paper, to take into consideration the tax changes in this year's Budget.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Combined, the revenue moves will help to close the funding gap.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But this assumes that we are able to keep our spending at 20% of GDP by the end of this decade.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In fact, over the past decade, Government spending had risen by about three percentage points of GDP, and you can see it clearly from the chart – from around 15% to 18% today.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, to keep it at 20% of GDP by the end of this decade would already demand some moderation in spending increase, compared to past trends, which we all know is not easy to do.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Furthermore, these projections have not yet taken into account additional spending that may arise from new policy initiatives.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: There may well be very good reasons for more Government intervention, some of which we are contemplating under the Forward Singapore exercise.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And many Members in this House have also suggested good ideas, but all of that means additional spending and the additional spending will then need to be anchored by a fiscal plan that is sound, sustainable and fair.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: MOF will continue to monitor these revenue and expenditure trends closely.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And even as we increase the GST rates, we are also implementing and updating the GSTV, GST vouchers and Assurance package to cushion the impact of the increase.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Incidentally, Assoc Prof Lim said that the increase in the GSTV restores the Government's original promise to offset the GST increase.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Because it suggests that somehow, the promise had been broken in the first place, which is factually incorrect.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We have been very clear in the Government – consistently saying some Budgets ago when we talked about the GST increase, that the GST comes with the GSTV and the AP.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The GSTV is a permanent scheme and is targeted at lower-income households and the elderly and it is meant to keep our overall system of taxes and transfers fair and progressive.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: All that was stated publicly and I have also consistently said that we will update the parameters of both schemes to make sure that they remain relevant as economic conditions change.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is about delivering on a promise that the Government had made.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And this is what the PAP Government has consistently done and will continue to do.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We had discussed this extensively in this House.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But let me, again, address the various suggestions raised, both in the run-up to the Budget and in the debate.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: As many Members noted, we already tax wealth in Singapore through property tax, stamp duty and motor vehicle-related taxes.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And the taxes were raised in this and the last Budget.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The net wealth tax, which the Workers' Party had previously suggested, is a specific form of wealth tax that taxes the net wealth of individuals.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: On paper, it sounds attractive, but in practice, it is very hard to implement effectively.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Many jurisdictions have tried, but no one has done it well.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is why many countries have done away with net wealth taxes over the years.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Even in Switzerland, which is often cited as a model, the reality is that the net wealth tax does not only target the very wealthy, who are able to avoid the tax through tax planning.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And in the end, it is the middle-income and upper-middle-income groups who end up paying the net wealth tax.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The Swiss collect about 2% of GDP in revenues through wealth taxes.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is comparable to what we collect in wealth taxes from property tax and stamp duties.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Second, corporate income tax, which several Members spoke about, including the impact of BEPS.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Pillar One of BEPS re-allocates profits from where economic activities are conducted to where consumers are located.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, given our small market size, Singapore will lose revenue under Pillar One of BEPS.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Pillar Two effectively sets a global minimum effective tax rate.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The intent of Pillar Two is for large MNEs to pay more taxes wherever they operate.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, when Pillar Two comes into play and Singapore implements the Domestic Top-Up Tax (DTT), we will get additional revenue, assuming the affected MNEs here do not leave.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Because the reality is, despite the professed intent of BEPS to tax MNEs more, countries are now rolling out vast subsidies to strengthen their competitive advantage over other countries and to re-shore and onshore activities.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The US passed the CHIPS and Science Act and the Inflation Reduction Act last year and the EU is now responding with its own scheme – the Green Deal Industrial Plan.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, competition for global investments will only get tougher.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We may not be able to outbid the major powers in spending, but we certainly cannot afford to stand still.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Contrary to what Mr Louis Chua thinks, the MNEs based here are not stuck with us permanently.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: They are mobile and they have options, and they will certainly have more options when they decide where to locate their next investment project.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Within the region, there are many other places where land and electricity are cheaper and wages are lower.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The MNEs are already making clear to us in our consultation sessions with them.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Because of BEPS, they will no longer enjoy the same tax advantages in Singapore.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Meanwhile, other countries in the region are cheaper while their home countries are offering very generous incentive packages.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, they ask us: what else can Singapore offer to stay competitive?

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, when Mr Louis Chua and Ms Hazel Poa talk about raising taxes for MNEs, my response is: please be very careful; we cannot afford to price ourselves out of the competition, or else Singapore and Singaporeans will end up the biggest loser.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In fact, as we move to align ourselves with the BEPS rules, we will have to review and update our broader suite of economic development schemes to stay competitive as I mentioned in the Budget Statement.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: That will require more funding resources, and that is why MOF’s assessment is that the net fiscal impact of BEPS is unlikely to be favourable.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This was discussed last year; and Ms Hazel Poa highlighted it again in her speech.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: She suggested then and now that we spend from land sales proceeds by treating it as revenue divided over the period of the lease.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, basically under the proposal, the land sales revenues or proceeds will be spread out over the duration of the lease.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In other words, if you have a 99-year parcel of land, you will get about 1% of the proceeds each year.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In fact, this alternative is not likely to generate more revenue than what we are already getting today from land sales over a period of time.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Currently, when the state sells land, the financial proceeds go into Past Reserves, and they are invested to generate a stream of income into our Budget through the NIRC.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The effect is that we will be able to spend more than 1% of the proceeds each year, because the reserves are being prudently invested and they generate long-term returns, half of which we get to spend as revenue.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We believe this is a more sustainable way of deriving value from the land we own, through the NIRC that benefits us now and in the future.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I have gone through three alternative revenue options but the fact remains that it is very hard for any of them to replace the GST.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And given our growing needs, it is not a matter of choosing between GST and any of these alternatives.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Contrary to what the Workers’ Party believes, we will need all of them and a mix of taxes – on income, consumption and assets – to provide sound and stable public finances in Singapore.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is considerably lower than most other advanced economies, as the chart illustrates.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In other words, compared to citizens elsewhere, Singaporeans pay much less in taxes and yet are able to enjoy high-quality public services.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: At the same time, this low tax burden rewards hard work and enterprise, and allows our people and businesses to keep most of what they earn.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Aside from a low tax burden, some may ask: is the distribution fair and progressive?

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And here, our philosophy is that everyone has a part to play in building our nation.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Everyone contributes, but those who are better off contribute more.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Everyone benefits from Government spending, but those with greater needs benefit more.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We believe this is what makes for a fair and inclusive social compact.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The outcomes are evident when you look at the benefits and taxes across different income groups.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The top 20% bear the heaviest burden in taxes and receive the least in benefits.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Conversely, the bottom 20% paid the least in taxes, and received the most in benefits.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Several Members including the Leader of the Opposition Mr Pritam Singh, Mr Xie Yao Quan, Ms Nadia Samdin and many others shared concerns of this group.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And I assure you that the Government remains very focused on advancing the well-being of the broad middle of society.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: First, by ensuring that they continue to enjoy real income growth.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In fact, among the advanced economies, we are one of the few where people in the middle have enjoyed significant increases in real incomes in the last 20 years.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It is higher than what the middle-income in the US and most other European societies experienced and well above other Asian societies like Japan and Hong Kong.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will continue to do everything we can to help our broad middle raise their standards of living and support them in meeting their aspirations.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Second, by keeping the tax burden low for this group.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: How does this compare to other advanced economies?

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: My team did some estimates for the US, UK and Finland based on publicly available data.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In his speech, Mr Leong said that the middle-income in Singapore are, I quote, “already over-taxed relative to their income”.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I think the facts and figures speak for themselves.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Several Members, including Ms Jessica Tan, Mr Louis Chua, Mr Dennis Tan and Ms Hany Soh were concerned about the impact of the changes to the Working Mother’s Child Relief (WMCR) on the middle-income groups.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: When the WMCR was introduced, it was intended to encourage married women, and especially higher-income married women, to have children and continue working.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: At that time, higher-income married women had fewer children on average.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And that is why the incentive was weighted toward this income bracket.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But from our experience over the years, young couples in this income group typically base their decisions to have children on other factors and not so much on the WMCR incentive.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Fertility has been declining across all income segments and we need to encourage couples in all income groups to have more children.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And that is why we decided to change the basis of the WMCR.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And with the fixed dollar relief, we focus instead on providing support for children regardless of the mother’s income.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And effectively, we are tilting the help towards those with greater needs.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Importantly, the WMCR changes should not be seen in isolation because they are part of a package of moves to support marriage and parenthood in this and previous Budgets.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And that includes enhancements to the Baby Bonus Scheme, the increase in parental leave provisions, all of which will benefit young couples, including higher-income couples, as they embark on their parenthood journey.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This brings me to the third point about what we do for the middle-income, because we really should not just look at individual schemes and changes to individual schemes, but we should focus on the overall taxes and benefits for the middle-income group.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Here, again, it is clear that the middle-income on the whole receive more in benefits than the taxes they pay.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This compares favourably with other jurisdictions, like the UK and Finland where the middle quintile received around $1.25 of benefits for every dollar of tax they paid – 1.25:1 – whereas our ratio is 2:1.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is for the middle quintile but some say, well, the middle-income group is very broad, but you can look at the slides.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Even the upper middle-income groups, those in the 61st to 80th percentile, received about the same or slightly more in benefits compared to what they paid in taxes.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: They may not get as much in direct cash benefits compared to the lower-income groups, but they enjoy access to affordable housing, healthcare and world-class education.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Of course, in every Budget debate, comparisons will be made about made about why some groups got something and others appear to be left out.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For example, over the last two days, we have heard Members like Ms He Ting Ru and Ms Shahira Abdullah asking about benefits for singles and single parents.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I understand their concerns but we should not look at the Budget Statement in isolation.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In fact, the entire Budget itself provides for all groups.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: There are many existing schemes not highlighted in the statement per se but are in fact part of the Budget which everyone benefits from.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And as the charts I have shown demonstrate, our system is fair, inclusive and progressive.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: At the same time, we review all our schemes from time to time to ensure they remain relevant.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, we enhanced our parenthood and family-related schemes in this Budget.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Next time, we will look at other schemes so everyone will get a chance.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It reflects our values and our sense of solidarity as a people.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We encourage and support everyone to excel and be the best that they can be.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But we recognise that outcomes in life will not be equal.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, for those who are fortunate enough to do well and be in the top 20%, we hope they will feel that sense of commitment and responsibility to contribute their fair share and help uplift their fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This compact goes beyond monetary support because everyone in Singapore, everyone including the higher-income, benefit from something very precious here in our society.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We are a high trust society, stable and harmonious with strong governance and rule of law.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This gives all Singaporeans the safety and security to raise our families, build our lives and pursue our dreams.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This sense of solidarity and trust is what makes Singapore exceptional.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And that is why through the Forward Singapore exercise, we are refreshing our social compact so that it remains strong and relevant amidst a rapidly changing world.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Many Members spoke on this theme, including Mr Liang Eng Hwa, Mr Sitoh Yih Pin, Ms Foo Mee Har, Mr Sharael Taha and Mr Vikram Nair.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Mr Edward Chia and Mr Derrick Goh also highlighted sentiments from the business community where some have wondered, has the Government changed, has the People's Action Party (PAP) Government changed?

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Only then will we have the resources we need to redistribute, strengthen our social compact, and progress as one people.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Pursuing growth will not be easy amidst a more challenging external environment – I mentioned that just now.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Competition and geopolitical tensions will continue to rise as the major powers race for the commanding heights of the global economy.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Singapore has to adapt to this new era.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And the good news is that we are moving forward from a position of strength.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We are seeing healthy flows of investments, capital and talent into Singapore.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And we are seizing these opportunities to build capabilities, strengthen our value proposition, and ultimately, create more jobs and opportunities for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We must build on our strong foundations and leverage our competitive advantages fully, while managing our inherent and permanent constraints, especially in the areas of manpower, land and energy.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will always be a "little red dot".

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Manpower resources will always be insufficient, land will always be limited, and we will always be energy constrained.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And so, we cannot compete on the basis of cost alone.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Instead, we must focus on differentiating ourselves in terms of quality and value.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For example, we are not the lowest-cost seaport in the region, or the world.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Yet, shipping companies prefer for their goods to transit and transship through Singapore, because of our good connectivity, robust port infrastructure and comprehensive range of maritime services.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Our port is highly efficient, containers do not get lost, shipments are cleared promptly and reliably without shippers having to make any special or informal arrangements.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is just one example of how we differentiate ourselves.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But clearly, given the more challenging external environment, we must redouble our efforts to raise our game.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And we certainly cannot score own goals, do moves that will price ourselves out.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Because having more high-quality investments here will help to grow our economy and create more jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And this will also benefit our local ecosystem, especially through the transfer of technological know-how and expertise to our SMEs.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We have built this up over the years, anchored by MNEs like Waters Corporation, Illumina and ResMed.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: These companies have brought cutting-edge capabilities to Singapore through their investments.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Over the years, they have sunk roots here and contributed to the growth of our medtech ecosystem.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: They have developed strong partnerships with local companies like Richport, Nanofilm and Sunningdale, enabling our local enterprises to improve their capabilities and scale up their businesses to reach out to more customers.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: At the same time, we are continuing to put in significant resources to nurture and grow our local enterprises, especially our SMEs.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The number of Singapore enterprises that we supported to build new capabilities, innovate and expand overseas increased by about 60% over this period.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The additional schemes introduced in this Budget demonstrate our continued commitment to supporting our SMEs.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Several Members, like Mr Seah Kian Peng and Ms Janet Ang, highlighted the challenges that SMEs face amidst rising business costs.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But the main thrust of our support for SMEs is focused on helping those who are prepared to take steps themselves to restructure their businesses, raise their productivity and venture into new markets and products.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Because, as Prof Hoon Hian Teck said, this is the only way for enterprises to survive and thrive on a sustained basis.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We take a sectoral approach through the Industry Transformation Maps to help our economy restructure and transform, because the circumstances, needs and starting points of each industry are very different.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And several Members like Mr Pritam Singh and Miss Cheryl Chan spoke about this.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Overall, we have made good progress in this transformation journey.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In particular, outward-oriented sectors like manufacturing and financial services have achieved strong productivity growth and job creation.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But as Ms Poh Li San and Mr Leon Perera highlighted, the domestically-oriented sectors like construction, retail and F&B face more challenges.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is not unique to Singapore at all.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: All countries face similar challenges. in these sectors, they will need to adopt structural solutions to increase productivity and grow sustainably.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In the construction sector, for example, more firms are moving towards Design for Manufacturing and Assembly, which includes using prefab modules and units.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In the F&B sector, we have seen more companies with multiple outlets adopt central kitchens to automate and streamline their operations and take advantage of economies of scale.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: These and other strategies will help such sectors raise their productivity and reduce their reliance on manpower.
