speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It was meant to be a set of fiscal rules that we live by, not to change at the time when we need money, which is what the Workers’ Party is proposing.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, yes, at the time when we put in place this set of fiscal rules, this framework for us to use the reserves as an endowment fund in a disciplined, responsible manner, I think the Workers' Party agreed to the framework.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But what we are highlighting is, so soon after this framework was finalised, at the first sign of needing money, why the attitude of then going back to change the rules?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Should we not live by the rules that we have set for ourselves and agree and put in place?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And maybe down the road, years later, after the benefit of lots of experience, yes, we can come together to review this again because I have said that nothing is cast in stone.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We should review but not so soon after we have finalised a framework and at the first sign of needing money.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We do not think that is sound nor does that reflect the values that we want to uphold in our fiscal system and in our society.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, I would like to ask the Finance Minister will he make this Occasional Paper less occasional going forward?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I want to hear from the Finance Minister the rationale for doing that.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Would we not want to keep more contingency funds in this environment where it is more disruptive and uncertain?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I mean these medium-term projections do not change so quickly because we are not tracking year-to-year.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We are tracking over a long period of time.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And I do not think you will have very sudden changes in the projections.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But over a period of time, as there is new information, maybe new revenue items, maybe new expenditure items, then obviously there may be some changes to the longer-term outlook.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And yes, if that were to happen, we will either put out more information on the website, in the form of an Occasional Paper, or we will even update it in the speech.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Because in fact, if you look at the Occasional Paper, a lot of the facts there, are not entirely new because we have put it out previously in various Budget Statements before.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: You needed to be able to tap on funding quickly and you did not know where the needs might emerge from and there was therefore a need to do so.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But now that that emergency period has passed, so to speak, we are in DORSCON Green, we felt that there was a need to go back to fundamentals and go back to that discipline that we have in budgeting and planning our resources, setting aside Ministry by Ministry, how much we have to spend.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: You will still need a contingency, but that contingency does not have to be so large.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I just wanted to ask the Deputy Prime Minister.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We all know that  the NIRC contributes towards half of our Budget — Yes, the point I want to make is that what is very clear is that returns from investments are uncertain and yet our needs will always increase – be it for healthcare, education, defence.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Given this too, in a scenario where the returns are coming down, could Finance Minister Deputy Prime Minister share with us how can we ensure that our spending and the programmes that we have are kept on an even keel?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Because there are headwinds to our investment returns and you can never be sure that you can continue to get the kind of returns we had in the past, given such an uncertain environment.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But all the more we say, stick to the framework that we have.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The ups and downs in the market cycles, we take care of, because we have smoothening formulas for that.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And we apply an expected return, remember, in our NIRC, not actual return.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, we take care of the ups and downs in the markets with some smoothening formulas, but the broader point that this may come under pressure is a real one.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That is why we have consistently said to the debate or to the question that Mr Perera asked earlier as well, let us stick to the framework, let us abide by it.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And then, over time, we will see what our needs are.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And we will have to think very hard if our needs were to continue to grow, how best to raise finances to cover these growing needs.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I wish to respond to what the Deputy Prime Minister said earlier about my proposal for land sales proceeds to be taken as revenue divided over the period of the lease.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: He said that under the current arrangement, where the land sale proceeds go into reserves and we get NIRC, it generates higher returns or we get more revenue from that because we can get more than 1%.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I wish to refute that by pointing out two facts.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One, if 1% of the land sale proceeds goes into revenue, the other 99% still goes into reserves and continue to earn investment returns.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, the drop in NIRC is only with respect to the 1% that did not go into reserves.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, again, you will not have higher revenue under the current arrangement.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, that misunderstanding having been cleared up, will the Deputy Prime Minister reconsider?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I think she is right, if you work out mathematically, if you use her method.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In the initial years, maybe you can get more.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But we are not looking at just a "sugar rush" from an immediate injection of funds.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We are looking in the longer term – what is the sustainable and what is the best approach.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: When we look over a longer period of time, frankly from our assessments, the revenue generated is not very different.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And we believe what we are doing is a better, more sustainable method, because the proceeds are kept in the reserves, we generate returns from the reserves and the returns benefit both today and on an ongoing basis.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I would just like to seek further clarification in terms of the consultations with employers.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To what extent is it not just about what Government can do for employers, but also about what the employers can also share in the social compact renewal, especially for all the Forward SG conversations and our SMEs consulted in depth in their role in this renewed social compact?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, we are continuing our engagements and our conversations with them.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Given the current pressures that many SMEs face, unfortunately, when you talk about their responsibilities as part of a new social compact, they sometimes look at these as additional obligations and burdens, which may therefore explain why they see a shift in Government thinking.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And we have to continually explain to them, that this is not about a shift from pro-growth, to pro-redistribution.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This is about how all stakeholders in society – employers, unions, workers, Government – all of us have a part to play and we do think that there are many things that employers can do.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: For example, in terms of HR – which many Members did speak about and I think the Member himself, did highlight – better HR, skills, training, fair progression, career progression, fair hiring, many roles that employers can play as part of our renewed compact.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The first is around the Working Mother's Child Relief, which several Members of Parliament have spoken about.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: My question is, what percentage of mothers will benefit from this change?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As Deputy Prime Minister said in the opening speech as well as the round-up speech, it is supposed to benefit lower- to middle- income mothers.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But based on my calculations on just one child alone, it seems that the lower-income mothers will not benefit and a very narrow base of working mothers will.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And if you have more children, I am just not sure what is the number of mothers who would actually benefit from this change.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Second, is in relation to the CPF annual salary ceiling.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I do recognise that the higher monthly salary ceiling will be raised over the next four years, but I think in this House you have spoken a lot about giving businesses visibility, certainty.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And so, in that regard, what is stopping the Government from giving that visibility as to the in tandem moves with the annual salary ceiling?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Third, I spoke about the reintroduction of the NAV tax on higher-end and secondary properties, which I think during the Global Financial Crisis, Senior Minister Tharman, then as Finance Minister, abolished.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: What are the concerns by the Government on this, since I did not quite hear about that in the round-up speech?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: There was a reason why at that time when this scheme started – we wanted to address concerns and encourage higher-income married women to have more children at that time.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The experience has shown that they do not really base their decisions on the incentive alone; there are many other factors.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Since then, as I said, fertility has come down across all income groups.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, it is not just about who benefits, calculating that marginal difference, but it is really a change of philosophy.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That we want to make sure that the support is directed at the children, regardless of the mothers' incomes.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I think it is the right thing to do, given the current circumstances and we have explained the rationale for the change.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, there is no need to talk about what might happen or to give any advance notification to employers on this regard.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: On the annual value tax that Mr Chua highlighted, this was indeed removed back then.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But Mr Chua may not have picked this up – when we removed this at the time of removal, we had a not so progressive property tax schedule.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I have one clarification for Deputy Prime Minister.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Whilst we cheer the Government Budget this round, with the generous support to household.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: And I think we all support and cheer.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I did mention in my Budget speech that some economists have cautioned that the Government handouts, such as the GST vouchers and cost of living support may actually stoke inflation pressures, as we have seen in other countries.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I think Deputy Prime Minister has acknowledged that in his speech.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I think there are a lot of economists wanting to hear your view about whether our inflation pressure is under control.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: So, if you could just share, in planning the support, that we will still have inflation under control.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That is why we have to manage and calibrate this carefully.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And that is why in rolling out or designing the package, we have not made it a broad-based support scheme.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The first is the reason why economists actually use a simple difference between revenue and expenditure to evaluate the fiscal stance is simply because every dollar received by the Government is one less dollar in private sector.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Hence, I accept the Government has different justification for its accounting standards.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And this was indeed the basis of my claim.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: So, I wonder if I may ask the Minister, if this has changed, if MOF can confirm that our gross operating surplus or net lending is indeed negative for FY2022.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I will, of course, happily retract, my original claim of a contractionary fiscal policy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: My second clarification has to do with a redundancy insurance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I take the Minister's point that there are concerns about staying longer in unemployment than necessary and his suggestion that support will be tied to retraining.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I do not find this objectionable per se, but only stress that of course, bills and financial commitments do not take a breather when one is made redundant.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And yet, it does take time for an individual to be matched to retraining and reskilling.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: So, if I may seek the Minister's assurance that should a retraining contingent unemployment support scheme be implemented that payouts would not be unduly delayed at the point of redundancy?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I am sure Assoc Prof Lim is well familiar with the difference between the fiscal impulse and the fiscal multiplier.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We think it is appropriate, given the weakness of the economy, but we cannot overdo the support because it will then lead to additional inflation.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The fiscal impulse is really an accounting measure.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It gives you a rough proxy but it is not a full assessment of the impact that a budget or fiscal measure has on the economy which we work through our economic models.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And we will take into consideration what Assoc Prof Lim has suggested.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I thought that I just wanted to seek clarifications on two points or should I say two suggestions.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: But at the same time also, we noticed a gap, as several of us have highlighted on career advisory and coaching and support services, particularly strong at the early career guidance level when they are still in school, particularly strong when they are unemployed, retrenched and laid off but a big gap where new entrants into the workforce as well as those who are in between or in employment.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I thought this part we will make some rallying calls.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We hope for Deputy Prime Minister and team to support the Labour Movement as we want to endeavour into this space.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We do want to see how we can empower individuals to take charge of their own careers.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, the Ministry of Manpower has some ideas in this regard and I am sure they will be happy to share more, maybe in their Committee of Supply, or certainly in due course when they are ready.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Deputy Prime Minister said that I have said an outright falsehood.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I categorically reject that and I will ask him a few questions to demonstrate that he has been trying to pull wool over our eyes.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If the land cost is not considered a tax, but the subsidies given to BTO is considered a benefit, it is no wonder that the benefit tax ratio turns out to be very favourable for middle-class Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But that does not reflect the true picture.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The second question I want to ask: The Deputy Prime Minister has always said that the Net Investment Returns Contribution (NIRC) is money that we can spend as revenue.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: After having gotten us agree to not touching the reserves and ploughing back 50% of the net investment return to the reserves.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Then if the NIRC now is not spent when most of it is being tucked away in endowment and trust fund each year, how can you say that that money is being spent because it will only be spent very slowly into the future?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is even more insidious when the Government, on one hand, tucked away all these revenues and then tell Singaporeans that we have not enough fiscal resources as a result "I need to raise GST and other taxes".

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Third question, the Deputy Prime Minister said that the total revenue – the total expenditure in 2023 cannot come down, it has to stay at $100 billion because, and that is despite the end of the pandemic, because of the effect of nominal GDP growth which I think that is what his chart shows.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Has our nominal GDP growth by that amount over the last three years?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And also, if what the Deputy Prime Minister said is correct, then I would expect the $25 billion increase in expenditure to be spread uniformly across the Ministries, but you look at the $25 billion difference, between 2019 and 2023 actually the increases were lumped up in mainly three ministries – Ministry of Health, Ministry of National Development and Ministry of Defence.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Lastly, last question: In his obsession with the reserves, this Government has actually lost its bearing.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can I ask the Deputy Prime Minister how can the affordable home scheme as proposed by Progress Singapore Party (PSP) which guarantees every Singaporean of each generation an affordable HDB flat because he only paid the construction cost, how can that be less equitable to the current BTO system, where future generations of Singaporeans will have to worry about how high the BTO prices will go?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Given that we have not exhausted debating about the two schemes – BTO scheme and the affordable home scheme – in the sake of time, I will not go too much into that, but I hope the Government will consider our proposals carefully because they are overwhelming advantages in the affordable home scheme versus the BTO scheme.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I did not rely on tax and benefits per se.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I highlighted if you look at the tax on the middle-income household, 10% of income, total taxes that they paid.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And then if you say well, 10% is more, then let us look at other countries and I showed the chart.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I do not want to elaborate further or get into a to-ing and fro-ing with Mr Leong.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The facts and figures, as I said, in my speech, speak amply for themselves.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: On the Net Investment Returns Contribution (NIRC) and whether there is excess NIRC, never mind the argument that we have made before that it is not about NIRC, it is about revenues all coming together in a Consolidated Fund.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But Mr Leong insists on not taking – recognising this, so he specifically says that there is excess NIRC because of Fund top-ups.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I, actually, had a whole treatment on that in my remarks.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, again, I should not belabour the point because I have already said in my remarks that Fund top-ups are not all spent in the future, considerable number of them are drawdown Funds, Funds for which the monies are needed today and on an ongoing basis.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: On Government's expenditure rising and in nominal terms, how far it has gone again, the facts are straightforward.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: You can look at where we are today as a share of GDP.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: By all means, go to Department of Statistics (DOS)'s website, check where the nominal GDP figures are, match expenditures today and expenditures in 2019.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Expenditures have risen but as a share of GDP, they have not.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is not just because of a growing GDP, it is inflation.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, that is quite obvious, is it not?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: If you were to keep spending constant in real terms, how do you pay more for salaries, how do you pay more for projects, all of which cost more money.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But what is important is to track spending as a share of GDP and, as I mentioned, it has maintained at the same ratio over 2019 and today.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: On public housing, I really do not want to get into a debate on that because we have gone through that extensively before.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: As I mentioned in the exchanges just now, the Government welcomes all ideas.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We studied Mr Leong's and the PSP's proposal on affordable housing.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It will not be good for Singapore and Singaporeans and that is our conclusion.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In the end, Singaporeans can judge for themselves.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: First, I want to thank the Deputy Prime Minister for a budget that would help workers navigate through very challenging times.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It is very reassuring that Deputy Prime Minister said that those who work consistently will be able to meet their basic retirement needs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Would the Government also look at those who are nearing retirement and have a limited runway left to build up their retirement savings?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: And how about those self-employed persons which are actually growing in size?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: What is Government's direction towards helping such groups of people?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Second, how can we help the NITEC and Higher NITEC Diploma holders to make career switches, perhaps earlier in life so as to be more resilient in their whole career journey and also to close the gap with degree holders?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I note that in this debate Mr Pritam Singh and a few others have talked about, for example, the proportion between OA and SA contributions.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, we are reviewing all that with a view that younger workers can work, contribute to CPF consistently and through that meet their basic retirement needs.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, that is something that we are studying.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It could be through the Silver Support Scheme.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It could be through other schemes but we are looking at that as a separate group to support.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, we have taken care of that group of younger workers, but we will have to study more broadly what we could do for self-employed persons, recognising that not all of them want to be on the CPF system.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Some of them may choose the flexibility not to, and how do we respect their wishes, give them the flexibility that they desire but, at the same time, find ways to make sure that they are able to save adequately for their future retirement.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, these are things that we are, indeed, studying.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: ITE students and how we might help them after they graduate?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is something that is on our minds, because we must ensure that ITE students not only graduate with skills that will get them a good job.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, it is certainly something on our minds.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: I will take another two to three more clarifications because we breached over an hour of clarifications.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: I saw two more hands and I will call both.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I think Leader of the Opposition has a clarification as well.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But I just wanted to make one point in response to the Deputy Prime Minister again on our 2019 housing paper.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: He read out this sentence, "Would the HDB have a vacancy rate problem compounded by a still steady stream of 16,000 to 17,000 BTO units in the last few years which will continue to increase supply up to 2022." If you look at the sentence, what the sentence is saying is not that there is an imminent risk of vacancies, not that there is going to be vacancies in 2022.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It is saying that there will be, there is a risk of vacancies if you continue to build following this kind of pattern.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: So, there is no time frame attached to that and I would remind the Deputy Prime Minister again that the whole context of our argument or focus on this paper is longer term housing dynamic trends.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: More importantly, I would remind the Deputy Prime Minister again, that this first paragraph does not amount to a call to action, to a proposal, to a suggestion.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We go on to say "BTO projects should continue".

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: If we had meant to say "BTO projects should be cut back", we would have said that.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: So, I really hope the Peoples' Action Party will stop propagating this falsehood that our 2019 paper called for a cutback to BTO supply in 2019.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And if it does not do that, I would really question if the PAP has become a party that propagates falsehoods to gain political mileage.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The second clarification, on the exchange with the hon Member Ms Hazel Poa, I think initially the Deputy Prime Minister mentioned that based on his economic modelling, Ms Poa's proposal would not yield more revenue.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But later on, when questioned by Ms Poa, he, to my mind, unless I misheard him, the argument changed to one of a "sugar rush".

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: So, I just wanted to ask if, based on the Deputy Prime Minister's original response that the economic modelling shows that her proposal would not generate any revenue, could that model be shared so that economists and the public can scrutinise it?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We might as well publish exactly verbatim whatever the Workers' Party has said in the Working Paper in 2019 and in the end, Singaporeans will be the judge of the matter.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I think we have said enough on this point.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The reality, as I have described it from my perspective at that time, was a very different reality.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And do not talk about cutting; no one at that time even thought about building more flats.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Everyone was asking cut back, cut back, cut back; no one said build more flats.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: With the benefit of hindsight now, it is so easy to say build more.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But I just want to have some perspective here, that during that time, when resale prices were coming down, it was a very different context, it was a very different circumstance.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And we can just put out what the Workers' Party said and everyone can be the judge of it.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: You do not need to be a rocket scientist to work out the assumptions.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Just put it in a spreadsheet, do your sums and anyone can figure out that; actually, it is not very different from what we have today.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Last two clarifications – Ms Carrie Tan and then we will close off with Mr Pritam Singh.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Could I invite both Members to please keep their clarifications concise and short?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I think what I have just experienced in this House reinforces the point I would like to make, which is to clarify that — Thank you, first of all, Deputy Prime Minister, for addressing the point that I and Ms Nadia Samdin made about slowing down.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I think many in this House and also many of our Singaporeans can attest that when we are all overworked, spending too many hours in too many meetings, what happens is our brains – and science supports this – our brains go into what we call 钻牛角尖 mode. 分明讲的清清楚楚听起来糊里糊涂.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: In the end, we end up in very unproductive, unconstructive meetings – like this very, very protracted housing debate, for example.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: So, I would like to ask the Deputy Prime Minister to consider and invite him in his already very stretched bandwidth, whether in this tripartism that we have, that is such a beautiful and unique way of managing Singapore, whether we can approach productivity in a slightly different way with a commitment and a focus on our people's wellness.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I think if we just slow down a little bit, we may be able to harness more clarity, more creativity in our people when we are less stressed.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: So, that is only thing I am asking.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Can we consider the possibility that taking a slowdown can actually help us to boost the creative potential that we have as a people?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I thought you were going to take two questions at a time.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And if indeed there are segments in our society who are feeling stressed out, burnt out, then that is not something we want to see either.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, we should look at it holistically and certainly we welcome suggestions from Ms Carrie Tan and we will continue to work with her and Members in this House and other stakeholders, and also with our tripartite partners, to continually advance the well-being of all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: First one, again, I also do not want to belabour the issue of the point about the WP's housing proposal.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The Deputy Prime Minister was saying we will have it published.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: It is already publicly available for people to read.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And the key point in there is the context that Minister speaks of in terms of his experience in MND is actually a subset of the larger context that WP was talking about, which was the announcement of VERS.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The Finance Minister said there is no embarrassment in just changing your position and view – I agree with him.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: In fact, in 2018, it was Minister Lawrence Wong himself who identified a particular infographic, I believe, that the Workers' Party had put out on the capital reserves in PUB.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And indeed, we took a look at it and our representation was incorrect; and so we corrected it.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: So, I do not think there is any difficulty that the WP faces in trying to correct something which is inaccurate.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But I do not think the PAP has dealt with the housing paper in an even-handed way.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: No genuflection and we certainly do not intend to keel over when we feel that a relevant point has to be made.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: It does not require a response from the Finance Minister.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The second issue was the fifth clarification I put to the Finance Minister pertaining to the reserves.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But the other thing that the Finance Minister did not say was including Temasek in the NIR framework, will provide the Government with additional fiscal resources in the years to come.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: So, that is the point that I pegged my response to, and I think I have made the representation in this House before, that the position in 2015 resulted in more fiscal resources, more reserves being employed by the Government.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: That is the point that the Minister did not state in his response to clarification number five.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And just to set it out here, three reasons why these additional revenues were required: one, healthcare; two, human capability training, SkillsFuture, all this would be required, strengthening education; three, transport infrastructure, Changi Airport Terminal 5, Tuas Sea Port.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: These were the reasons why the tap was opened.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: There would be additional fiscal resources and because there is a need.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The need for the hour calls for it.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And that is the perspective that the WP are bringing when we speak of looking at the reserves differently.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: On the second point, on the inclusion of Temasek in the NIR.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is largely in the private equity space and therefore we had to take some time to work out how Temasek could be part of this framework.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We always knew that there was going to be additional resources.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I mean, that is to be expected, right?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Once you put Temasek into the framework, obviously there would be additional resources.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, the intent was made clear from the outset.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The reasons why we had to take time was because of complexity more than anything else.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Maybe many, many years down the road, we will have a rethink, a review, we will have new information, circumstances will change, and we will all have another discussion with maybe a different Finance Minister.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And if the Workers' Party agrees with that, then, hopefully, we can channel all our energies productively in thinking about how best to manage our rising expenditure needs without having to come back to the same old points about using more reserves.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I am not asking new questions but the Deputy Prime Minister did not answer any of my four questions.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Can I just request that he answer two questions?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I will take care of the other two, at the Committee of Supply.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Mr Leong, I listened to your clarifications quite carefully.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: I think they amounted to four or five.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: We have ended with the Leader of the Opposition and we have gone for more than an hour of clarifications.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: It is the decision of the chair that the question will be put to the House.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 3.20 pm.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 2.58 pm until 3.20 pm.﻿
